title: The Loneliness Club
oneLiner: In a small house in Grassy Park, pensioners gather each day not just for care - but for companionship in a world growing lonelier by the year.
summary:
The Loneliness Club: Every morning, cars begin arriving outside this modest house in Cape Town’s Grassy Park. Drop-off starts around 7:15am. People are helped carefully out of passenger seats. Bags are unpacked. Jerseys are folded over chairs. There’s tea already brewing in the kitchen. Inside, the day begins with music. There are games and laughter and little exercise classes. Painting, singalongs, dancing. And then after lunch, the mood changes completely. The lights dim. Blankets come out. The room goes quiet. It’s nap time. One by one, everybody settles down for an afternoon sleep while they wait to be fetched at three o’clock. And honestly, if you watched it from a distance, it would look almost exactly like a daycare centre. Except the people sleeping under those blankets are in their sixties, seventies and eighties. And that’s what makes this story so emotionally powerful. Because inside this ordinary home in Grassy Park, 53-year-old Estherline Meyer has quietly created something extraordinary: an elderly daycare centre called Leap of Faith for families who can no longer safely leave ageing parents alone during the day while they work. It operates Monday to Friday, from 8am to 3pm, with cognitive exercises, games, music, gentle physical activity, meals, companionship, and structure. But emotionally, what’s really happening here is much deeper. This is a story about loneliness. Quiet loneliness. The kind that settles slowly into old age after spouses die, children emigrate, bodies slow down, memories fade, and entire days pass without meaningful conversation. Some of the pensioners who come here are widowed. Some spend most of the week alone. Some are beginning to struggle cognitively. Others simply don’t want to sit in silence all day waiting for somebody to come home. And what makes the story nuanced is that their families aren’t failing them. They’re exhausted. Adult children are trying to survive modern life while carrying ageing parents at the same time - balancing work, finances, caregiving, school runs, and enormous guilt about leaving loved ones alone all day. So this house becomes something far bigger than daycare. It becomes an emotional safety net. A place where somebody notices if your mother hasn’t eaten lunch. Or taken her medication. Or laughed that day. And globally, the story taps into this fascinating and deeply unsettling conversation around human connection. Researchers are increasingly linking chronic loneliness to depression, dementia, cardiovascular disease, cognitive decline, and premature death. Around the world, people are beginning to create entire economies around companionship: renting friends in Japan, paying for cuddling services in South Africa, searching for ways to fill emotional absences modern life keeps creating. But inside this little house in Grassy Park, the antidote is incredibly simple: music, routine, conversation, touch, tea, community… and nap time. Visually, it’s rich with warmth and texture: morning drop-offs that feel like a school run in reverse, pensioners dancing in slippers, old friends teasing each other over a fame of dominoes, blankets lined up across the lounge, someone standing quietly at the gate waiting to be fetched. It’s funny, heartbreaking, tender, and deeply human. And underneath all of it is this really haunting question: What happens when people are living longer than ever before… but feeling increasingly alone?

In Cape Town, a modest home is becoming an emotional lifeline for elderly people navigating the quiet epidemic of loneliness. It's a daycare - for the elderly.
caseStudies: Estherline Meyer

title: My Big Fat Madlanga Commission
oneLiner: The Dummies Guide to the Madlanga Commission of Inquiry into Criminality, Political Interference, and Corruption in the Criminal Justice System
summary:
109 days of evidence have been heard by the Madlanga Commission which has been televised since 17 September 2025. It is a vast, sprawling investigation which has thrown up its fair share of drama, intrigue, tension, comedy and tragedy. The entire top leadership of our police force has been suspended or arrested, leaving a vacuum vulnerable to more organised crime. This will be a concise story of who the players are, the key witnesses, what they told us, and why it matters. It's a highlights package of high drama and high crimes.

Presenter in a studio with a black/grey backdrop and a giant Jenga set representing the ideal criminal justice system: three solid, secure, impenetrable pillars of justice - the police, the courts and the prisons. As the story of the Madlanga Commission unfolds, the presenter removes a series of blocks from top to bottom, placing them on top. These represent the Big Five crime cartels that have infiltrated the system, the Minister of Police and all the SAPS members who have been suspended or arrested. This visual device will carry us through the months of evidence presented to the Commission, leading to the downfall of SAPS top brass. It’s not just a game that our viewers know well, it also creates tension and suspense as everyone anticipates the collapse. Through a combination of links and cutaways 32 blocks are displaced; the holes in the system are glaring; the tower grows tall and unstable, teetering on shaky foundations until eventually the entire structure collapses in chaos.

title: UPDATE: PHILIPPI VILLAGE STILL STANDING
oneLiner: A decade after Carte Blanche first reported on the pressures facing Philippi, and nearly three years after the Cape Town taxi strike devastated Philippi Village, we return to ask whether this communit
summary:
UPDATE: We will return to Philippi Village to find out what has changed since our September 2023 insert "Taxi Strike: Counting Costs," using the 2016 "Philippi Horticultural Area Under Siege" insert as broader context for the pressures Philippi has always faced. The update will use archive from both inserts as the "then," with new interviews and current footage providing the "now." Then and now points: Then: In 2016, Philippi was already a community under pressure from crime, urban development and the fight to protect community resources. Now: those pressures have never gone away, and Philippi Village represents one attempt to build something lasting in that environment. Then: Philippi Village was targeted during the 2023 taxi strike, with five containers vandalised and small businesses looted. Now: has the Village physically and operationally recovered, and what security and community structures changed as a result? Then: Bushra Razack was CEO, managing the crisis in real time through community networks. Now: she has transitioned to a Non-Executive Board and mentorship role, with Simphiwe Nkani appointed as the new CEO. What does this mean for leadership succession and long-term sustainability? Then: entrepreneur Nomafu Mdlambuzi was counting her losses after her sewing business was looted. Now: has her business recovered, and are entrepreneurs at the Village better supported and protected than they were? She declined the interview Then: Philippi Village was described as a sanctuary for work and play that became suddenly vulnerable. Now: is it still functioning as a safe community space despite ongoing violence across the Cape Flats? Then: the story was about surviving a specific crisis. Now: the bigger question is longevity. Community initiatives often begin with promise but struggle to last. Why has this one endured? Interviews: We will interview Bushra Razack as the human thread of the update. She was central to the 2023 insert and her transition from CEO to Non-Executive Board Member is one of the key new developments. We will interview Simphiwe Nkani, the new CEO and former General Manager of Philippi Village, to establish who is now running the initiative day to day, what he inherited, and what the Village looks like under new leadership. Interview confirmed

When Carte Blanche first visited Philippi in 2016, we found a community already under siege. Farmers were fighting rampant crime, urban developers were eyeing agricultural land, and residents were struggling to protect what they had built. As one farmer put it at the time: "I will have to be an activist in order that I can farm." That fight never stopped. When Carte Blanche returned in September 2023, it had taken a new form. Philippi Village, a community hub and business incubator operating from a renovated concrete factory, was caught in the violence of the Cape Town taxi strike. A mob with a bulldozer moved on sixty small businesses housed in shipping containers. Five were vandalised. A seamstress lost her machines, her finished orders and her income. Security manager Vuyokazi Tinise had not slept in days. CEO Bushra Razack was working her community networks to hold the Village together in real time. Nearly three years later, Philippi Village is still standing. It has survived not only the taxi strike but subsequent fires, floods, extortion challenges, attempted land occupations and ongoing safety threats on the Cape Flats. Bushra Razack has now transitioned into a Non-Executive Board and mentorship role, with former General Manager Simphiwe Nkani stepping up as the new CEO. The update is not a profile of Bushra or Simphiwe. It is a public-interest question about longevity. Community initiatives spring up across the Cape Flats all the time, but very few last. This one apparently has. Why? What has changed? What still threatens it? And with Cape Flats violence back in the headlines, what does Philippi Village's survival tell us about whether community-led development can succeed where policing and state support alone have not?
caseStudies: Bushra Razack Simphiwe Nikani

title: Artisanal pots made from scrap metal - are they poison bombs?
oneLiner: Tonight on Carte Blanche South Africa’s traditional cooking pot, the potjie, used across all cultures. But cheap knock offs, sold across the country are a poison bomb.
summary:
We need to clarify the difference between a cast iron potjie made by for example, Best Duty, who are based in CT , and an artisanal pots, which incidentally have been molded to look like these original brands. Its all in the production and that’s very visual The first case study would be an artisanal pot makers, document the collecting of scrap metal, car and bike parts, aluminium, car batteries. Film the smelting down and pouring the cast. The cast has replicated the original Falkirk pots. It’s extremely hard work . The final touch is to spray it with silver paint. We can explore the issue that they are ignorant of the legal requirements Contrast this to the production of a cast iron Falkirk pot and most importantly the final coating which is extremely expensive but makes the one safe and the other not. The 2nd Case study is Dr Angie Mathee from MRC. She has spent the last 20 years doing this work. She spotted these pots on the side of the road for sale Avalon Court area by street vendors. Having read studies in other countries about the impact of artisanal pots on people health, she started to study them. She did blood work and swabs on the potmakers and the community but her most recent study on the food cooked in these pots is the most recent and explosive evidence We show Pap and chakalaka cooked in both pots and then measured the iron content the pap has the highest levels and shows the silver paint on the food.. –She explains Siting the findings from international studies and the outcomes on people health – she points out how funding cuts have prevented the kind of study CB wanted. And unpack the impact the implications for children in poor communities. Small doses at school every day, then at home and then in the community and what this accumulation does. Pointing out foetal health which is the greatest impact. We will show how widely available these artisanal pots and chat to traders about whats sells the most. They are light , cheaper and use less fuel so they widely used. Comparing the cast iron Falkirk pots and artisanal pots on local markets, and now also sold in stores. . Weddings, family gatherings, funerals. Show them used in school feeding scheme and see kids being fed out of these pots daily.

The informally made Silver potie pots ( which look exactly like the black cast iron poties) are widely available in both rural and urban environments. They are made from scrap metal, e-waste and car and motorbike parts, including car batteries. This artisanal cookware can potentially be a multi-metal source. The Medical Research Council has been studying them over several years but the most recent study, of testing the food cooked in these pots revealed the pap contained over 100 times higher lead levels than the EU maximum permissible. They have also done blood tests on the potmakers and the community to detect the lead levels. These pots are being increasingly sold in urban markets and used in feeding schemes, they are even available online. Although there are SAB approved standards for cookware these pots go below the radar and the people making them are unaware of their danger.
caseStudies: Angela Mathee

title: Wrath of the Breede: Ruin and Renewal in Robertson
oneLiner: When the Breede River breached its banks in mid-May, it unleashed an unprecedented deluge that brought the historic Robertson Wine Valley to its knees. We track the sheer, terrifying drama of the floo
summary:
When the weather warnings came, the Breede river quickly became a violent surge that obliterated the 100-year flood line in hours. Defensive dykes, raised walls, and levees were simply swallowed. We set the scene of the sheer force of nature—a destructive energy that echoed through the valley, trapping workers, submerging roads, and cutting off power and communication. 200mm–300mm of torrential rain funnelled directly into the Robertson valley, swelling the river to a terrifying 1,655 cubic metres per second. As the water's rose in the middle of the night, a frantic NSRI and disaster management scrambled to evacuate trapped farm workers

Fantastic footage, current footage of rebuilding and wine bottles being cleaned, interviews with those who faced the raging torrents head on and reflecting the amazing spirit of South Africans who have come together to help rebuild
caseStudies: Springfield wine estate Robertson Van Loveren Wine Estate Robertson

title: Road to Nowhere
oneLiner: We expose alleged corruption at the Road Traffic Management Corporation (RTMC)
summary:
Story focusses on how the CEO - Adv. Makhosini Msibi - knowingly entered into a contract with an outside supplier while he is a director of one of their own sub-contractors. In addition, the story highlights several issues around the RTMC - basically bankrupt, entering into contracts for the supply of vehicles to provinces who don't want them, employing traffic police who are not gainfully employed (i.e., sitting around doing nothing while on the payroll), irregular increasing of license disc fees (in contravention of PFMA rules for Treasury approval) etc. all of this while the actual work of the RTMC - road safety - is woefully being neglected and underfunded.

Exposing corruption within South Africa's lead agency for road safety

title: UPDATE: Nelson Mandela Bay
summary: Two months ago, we visited Gqeberha to report on a questionable tender at the municipal pound - and found a city in crisis. After the SPCA’s contract to manage the Kariega pound expired in December, an emergency tender was awarded to a little-known company and the SPCA was given hours to leave. Concerns surfaced around animal welfare, and money allocated to the pound. The municipality denied money was missing, but admitted that the pound wasn’t functioning fully. The dispute has now reached court, where a settlement was reached last month: while the pound remains in the hands of the municipality and its chosen company, a court order has laid out measures to safeguard animal welfare. Meanwhile, the municipality has threatened to go to court to evict the SPCA. But the state of the pound is just a microcosm of the city’s infrastructure and leadership crisis, which is only widening…

title: Slow Crime (Tortoises)
oneLiner: An underground wildlife trade hiding in plain sight — where protected tortoises are stolen from the wild, sold openly online, and tracked by a detective determined to expose the networks behind them
summary:
This story follows Leon Rossouw — a long-serving detective, once described as South Africa’s Sherlock — who is now focused on wildlife crime. It opens on a real bust. Leon is on site with law enforcement, searching for an animal they know is there but can’t find. They’re about to call it when he steps onto the floorboards and realises there’s space underneath. He kneels down, looks closer… and a small head appears through a gap. A tortoise, hidden beneath the floor, alive. It’s a moment that’s stayed with him — because it takes a lot for a tortoise to come out of its shell. This isn’t a one-off. Leon now works across the country, following leads — often starting online. He uses undercover Facebook profiles, engages sellers, sets up stings. And one of the things that keeps coming up, over and over again, is tortoises. Most of it comes down to the pet trade — people buying them as garden pets. There’s also some muthi use, and a smaller international demand. But what’s clear is that this isn’t isolated behaviour — it’s something happening consistently. In terms of how we access the story, there are a few clear ways in. The strongest — and the one we’d lead with — is the roadside trade. Along routes like the R556 and R510 towards Sun City, tortoises are being sold openly, every day. The approach isn’t to focus on the roadside seller, but to go in undercover, do a controlled buy, and then follow that chain back to the supplier. In some cases, those suppliers are already known, which opens the door to a more meaningful enforcement operation. This would be done alongside law enforcement — including Stock Theft, the Endangered Species Unit, local SAPS — and, where needed, the SPCA. There are other entry points too. In Lenasia, there’s a pet shop linked to Turf Pets where tortoises are being advertised and sold through WhatsApp groups — something that is accessible to us. Then there’s the online side. Leon is already running undercover profiles. On their own, these buys are small, but they often lead to clusters — multiple people in one area keeping tortoises illegally. When those cases are acted on, it’s not just one animal being removed, but ten or twenty at a time. So we’re not waiting for a story — we already have ways into it. Once animals are confiscated, the story shifts. Tortoises can’t just be released. They’re far more complicated than people realise. They need medical care, and they need to be returned to their exact home range. Many of them end up at the Johannesburg Wildlife Veterinary Hospital. This is where Wendy and her team come in. She describes it simply — show her a tortoise, and she can tell you its life story from the shell. They’ve taken in around 250 tortoises this year alone, with only a small number coming from legal surrenders. They’re also involved in around 20 court cases across five provinces. So this isn’t abstract — it’s something they’re dealing with every day. In KZN, where I’m based, centres like FreeMe are seeing the same pattern. Of around 50 tortoises in their care, only one actually originated from the province. The rest have been moved in from elsewhere. So these animals aren’t just being taken — they’re being moved. In terms of scale, South Africa is globally significant. We have 13 species of tortoise — more than anywhere else in the world. In the Western Cape, conservation teams are working to protect species like the critically endangered geometric tortoise, even using trained dogs — Delta and Dash — to find them in the wild. It’s a huge amount of effort just to keep these animals safe, while at the same time others are being taken out of the wild and sold. And then — when they are rescued and rehabilitated — they have to go back. Carefully. Scientifically. Their blood is tested to pinpoint where they come from, so they can be returned to the right environment. In some cases, they’re moved across provinces to get them home. Both FreeMe and the Johannesburg Wildlife Veterinary Hospital have releases coming up, which means we can follow that full journey — from the bust, through rehabilitation, to release. We can travel with them, even fly with them, as they’re moved back to where they belong. It gives us a complete story — and, for some of these animals, a rare second chance.

The unique selling point is the contrast. Nobody expects tortoises to lead you into organised wildlife crime. At first glance it feels almost ridiculous — slow-moving garden animals being sold online — but the deeper Leon digs, the darker and bigger the world becomes. Also, unlike a lot of conservation stories, this isn’t passive. We’re inside active investigations. Real listings. Real confiscations. Real court cases. Potentially real stings unfolding in real time. And visually it doesn’t feel like a traditional wildlife insert. It plays more like a detective thriller hiding inside a tortoise story.

title: Ensure Security
oneLiner: Beaten and Missing: The Ensure Security Assault That Raises Questions No One Is Answering
summary:
Ensure Security was granted the contract to provide security to the Durban CBD by eThekwini Municipality in September las year. But a few months into that contract, a disturbing picture begins to emerge. In December last year, complaints had already been raised by the Navi Pillay Research Group, warning the city of systemic assaults on homeless people. Reports of men being beaten with sjamboks, some requiring medical treatment, were already in the public domain. Then, near midnight on the 18th of December, a video captures what appears to be that warning becoming a reality. On one of the main streets in Durban, five Ensure security officers surround a homeless man lying on the pavement. What follows is a sustained assault. The man is beaten and kicked as he cowers on the ground. He is struck repeatedly with a sjambok, at least forty lashes. Other officers stand by and watch, as though this is something that happens all of the time. And officer approaches the victim on the floor with a bottle of water, but the water is to wash the pavement clean. At the end of the video, the man is roughly lifted up, placed into an Ensure vehicle, and driven away. He has not been seen since. The Denis Hurley Centre, which works closely with Durban’s homeless community, says this is not an isolated incident. They report multiple cases of men arriving at their clinic with injuries consistent with beatings, some severe enough to require medical attention. Director Raymond Perrier says he raised these concerns repeatedly. When no action was taken, the Centre released the video publicly. Ensure Security’s response came only after the video was made public, and it was not limited to condemning the conduct of its officers. Through its lawyers, the company sent a formal letter to the Denis Hurley Centre objecting to the release of the footage and the accompanying commentary, suggesting the publication was unlawful and damaging to its reputation. In response, the Centre, represented by ENSafrica, stood firm, arguing that the video was authentic and that its publication was justified in the public interest, particularly given that the incident involved a publicly contracted security company operating in a public space. But despite clear video evidence of what appears to be assault with intent to do grievous bodily harm, there is no indication that the officers have been criminally charged. Ensure claims the man was taken to a police station. But there is no record of that. The Municipality acknowledges that Ensure is contracted to operate in the CBD and confirms it accepted the company’s internal disciplinary process. It has taken no visible action beyond that. Meanwhile, attempts to open a police case were initially rejected. Officers reportedly told complainants that only the victim could lay charges, despite the existence of video evidence showing a violent assault. A case was eventually opened. But weeks later, there has been no apparent progress. Police have not requested the video, nor contacted key witnesses. Four months on, the victim in the video has still not been found. And the question remains: In a city that calls itself “the most caring in Africa,” how does a man get beaten in the street, driven away in a marked security vehicle and simply disappear?

A brutal assault caught on camera shows private security officers beating a homelessman in Durban’s CBD before driving him away. The company admits its officers were involved — but despite clear video evidence of what appears to be assault with intent to do grievous bodily harm, no criminal charges have been laid. The victim has not been found.

title: UPDATE: Kimberley Sewage Crisis
oneLiner: A year after Carte Blanche exposed Kimberley’s sewage crisis, the SA Human Rights Commission has now recommended that Sol Plaatje’s sanitation collapse be declared a provincial disaster. But for r
summary:
In May 2024, Carte Blanche investigated broken promises across the Northern Cape, including failed infrastructure, unfinished public projects, sewage problems and communities who said they had been abandoned by government. The insert included Kimberley’s collapsing water and sewage infrastructure, with sewage running through streets and concerns over public money spent without visible improvement. In November 2025, Carte Blanche returned to Kimberley for the 1 Billion Rand Housing update. The insert revisited Nellie Frans in Roodepan, who had been waiting decades for a proper home after government promised a R1 billion housing project, a school and a hospital. The same insert also moved into the wider Sol Plaatje sewage crisis, including Platfontein, the Goga pump station, and the sewage lake affecting the Khwe community. Carte Blanche found that Platfontein did not have a sewage network, yet sewage from elsewhere was flowing into or near the community’s land. The previous insert also showed the Goga pump station being switched on while the crew was filming, only to be switched off again shortly afterwards, with sewage continuing to overflow into the environment. The new development is the release of the SAHRC inquiry report into service delivery failures in the Northern Cape. The report recommends that Premier Zamani Saul declare a provincial disaster in relation to sewage spillages and associated sanitation failures in Sol Plaatje Municipality. The update will ask what practical intervention should follow, who is responsible for implementation, and what residents can expect within the next six months.

Carte Blanche first showed the broken promises and sewage failures in Kimberley and the wider Northern Cape. Now, the SAHRC has formally found that Sol Plaatje Municipality’s sewage and sanitation crisis is severe, prolonged and widespread enough to warrant a provincial disaster declaration. This update asks what happens next, and whether the people living with the consequences will finally see action.
caseStudies: Uzair Adams Johan Smit Delmain Christiaans

title: Extraction – Venezuela: A Nation Reawakens
oneLiner: Months after Trumps presidential abduction in Venezuela we head to Caracas to find a society emerging from decades of repression - with a South African telling the story through their eyes. And amidst
summary:
Content Overview For the first time since the capture of President Nicolás Maduro, a South African television crew enters Caracas. The story is anchored through Ansophie Niemand, a South African teacher living in the city, who has endured Venezuela’s economic collapse and is now witnessing the first fragile signs of recovery. Through her, we experience a society cautiously reawakening — young entrepreneurs rebuilding, public spaces filling again, and a sense of possibility returning. Running parallel is a second, more powerful narrative: A rapid influx of foreign capital and political repositioning as global players move to access Venezuela’s vast oil reserves. This dual narrative — human recovery vs economic extraction — forms the backbone of the story. Research Findings ● Venezuela holds the largest proven oil reserves in the world, making it a key strategic asset in global energy markets. ● Years of underinvestment and sanctions severely reduced production capacity, but infrastructure is now being reactivated. ● Early signs of Western and American commercial re-entry into Venezuela’s oil sector. ● South Africa’s longstanding diplomatic alignment with Venezuela may not translate into economic advantage in this new order. ● A visible disconnect between citizen recovery and elite deal-making is emerging.

For the first time since the capture of President Nicolás Maduro, a South African television crew enters Caracas. We experience this moment through South African eyes. Ansophie Niemand, a teacher living in Caracas, has lived through Venezuela’s collapse — and is now witnessing something unfamiliar: the first fragile signs of hope. But as ordinary Venezuelans begin to breathe again, a different story is unfolding — faster, quieter, and far more powerful. A new Venezuela is being built. The question is: for whom?
caseStudies: Lindiwe Maseko Astrid Bedell Ansopie Niemand Nicolás Ernesto Maduro Guerra Rodrigo Naranjo

title: Middelpos: Town for Sale
oneLiner: Long before Middelpos made headlines as a town for sale, it was built on survival — and we meet the people who made it what it is.
summary:
At the turn of the 20th century, a Lithuanian refugee named Joel Sher arrived in South Africa, part of a wave of Jewish migrants fleeing hardship in Eastern Europe. Like many of his contemporaries, he made a living through “smousing” — travelling across the remote stretches of the Northern Cape, trading goods with isolated farming communities around Calvinia. It was through this work that he came to a place then known as Stinkkuil — a modest outpost in the Karoo, already home to a small trading post owned by an Englishman, believed to be Tomlinson. But the tensions of the time — particularly between English settlers and Boer communities — forced the owner to sell. Sher, together with his brother-in-law Weinrich, saw an opportunity. They purchased the farm and established a new trading business under the name Weinrich & Sher — laying the foundation for what would become Middelpos. From the outset, the town’s identity was shaped by its location. Sitting between farming districts, it became a vital stop for surrounding communities. As the business grew, so did the need for services: a police station and post office were established by the government, recognising the area’s importance to farmers scattered across the Karoo. Joel Sher raised four children — three sons and a daughter — and in time, the sons joined and eventually inherited the family business. While one moved to Cape Town to run an export operation dealing in raw hides and skins, two remained behind, continuing to build the enterprise at Middelpos. What emerged was more than just a trading post — it was a self-contained rural hub. The Sher family expanded their operations to include: The sale of agricultural supplies The buying of wheat, wool, hides and skins A hotel, which became the social heart of the town A service station for passing farmers A hall that hosted dances, meetings, and community events Middelpos became a place where life happened — not just commerce. There were tennis courts, a shooting range, and even a library service. The trading store stood at the centre of it all, anchoring both the economy and the social life of the area. The family also played a role in shaping the social and educational landscape of the town. Arthur Sher, one of the brothers, was instrumental in supporting a local school for white children, including the establishment of a boarding house for farm children who lived too far to travel daily. At the same time, a separate primary school for Coloured children existed on the farm — reflecting both the realities and divisions of the time, while also fostering a small, settled community. The Sher family earned a reputation as fair and respected traders, known across the region not only for their business, but for their role in community life. They provided their hall free of charge for church fundraisers, dances, and local gatherings — embedding themselves deeply into the rhythms of the district. But like many small rural towns, Middelpos was built on conditions that would not last. As the years passed, the family began to change. The next generation needed education, and that meant moving to the city. Living and working in such close quarters also brought its own pressures. In 1965, Arthur Sher relocated to Cape Town, while his brother Nicky and his wife remained behind to keep the business running. At the same time, broader economic forces began to erode the town’s viability. Improved roads and transport meant that farmers no longer needed to rely on small, local trading posts — they could travel to larger towns for better prices and more variety. The devastating droughts of the 1960s further strained the agricultural economy, forcing many farmers to leave the area altogether. Slowly, the district began to empty, and Middelpos — once a vital centre — started to fade. Eventually, ill health and economic pressure made the decision unavoidable. The business and property were sold, bringing an end to the Sher family’s chapter in Middelpos — a place they had not only owned, but built into a functioning community. Today, as Middelpos once again finds itself on the market, its story is not just about land or buildings, but about a particular moment in South African history — when towns were created out of necessity, sustained by people, and ultimately reshaped by forces far beyond their control.

Middelpos may be making headlines as a town for sale, but at its heart lies a deeply personal story. Through the eyes of Vivian Gottlieb — the last grandchild of the Sher family to grow up in the Middelpos hotel — we trace a childhood shaped by passing strangers, family legacy, and life in a remote Karoo outpost. As she and her brother return to the town, they reflect on its history, its people, and the moment their family let it go. Alongside voices from the current owner, auctioneers, and surrounding community members, the story explores the tension between memory and modern reality — asking what it means when a place filled with history is put on the market, and whether a town can ever truly be sold.
caseStudies: Vivian Gottlieb Anthony Sher Koos van der Huisaman

title: Small Worlds
oneLiner: In Gqeberha, a 90-year-old woman creates tiny, enchanting worlds by hand
summary:
Behind an unassuming door in Gqeberha lies a world of quiet wonder. Here, 90-year-old Anne Whitefield spends her days building miniature homes - each one filled with hand-cut wallpaper, delicately placed furniture, and the kind of detail that makes you lean in closer, just to be sure your eyes aren’t playing tricks on you. At first glance, it’s charming. Sweet, even. But the deeper you look, the more these tiny rooms begin to feel like something else entirely - little pockets of calm, carefully made and lovingly kept. Anne doesn’t rush. She doesn’t use kits. Some of her creations take years - even decades - to complete. And yet, she returns to them with the same gentle patience, shaping worlds small enough to fit in your hands, but rich enough to hold your attention completely. She’s not alone. Anne is part of The Little Steps, a group of 26 women in Summerstrand who meet every two weeks to share their work, swap miniature treasures, and indulge in a shared delight for the tiniest of details. There’s laughter, a touch of competition, and a quiet pride in getting things just right. Together, they remind us that creativity doesn’t have to be loud or grand to be meaningful. Sometimes, it lives in the smallest gestures - a perfectly placed curtain, a carefully made chair, a room that exists simply because someone loved making it. This is a story about joy, patience, and the gentle magic of making something - no matter how small - beautifully.

Anne Whitefield is 90 years old, and still obsessed with the magic and nostalgia of dollhouses.
caseStudies: Anne Whitefield Lorraine Allem

title: Update: Bubble boy
oneLiner: He was born without an immune system and given almost no chance of survival. Today he’s thriving, but what about the children who come after him?
summary:
When Carte Blanche first told the story of Ayaan Ahmed Sheik in 2018, he was a critically ill toddler born without an immune system, living in strict isolation and battling life-threatening infections. At the time, his only chance of survival was an experimental gene therapy trial at St Jude Children’s Research Hospital in the United States. After a long and uncertain journey, the treatment was declared a success, and Ayaan returned home to South Africa. Now, eight years later, Ayaan is living a full and active life. He is in primary school, no longer dependent on chronic medication or a feeding tube, and has developed a natural talent for music, playing the piano by ear. His progress offers rare insight into the long-term success of gene therapy for SCID. But this update is not only about survival. While Ayaan’s outcome represents a medical breakthrough, access to similar treatment remains extremely limited for South African patients. Gene therapy is now becoming more widely available internationally, yet it is still not accessible locally. At the same time, the issue of newborn screening, first raised in the original story, remains largely unresolved. A simple test at birth could have identified Ayaan’s condition early and prevented years of trauma and medical intervention. This update revisits Ayaan’s journey through the eyes of his mother, Shamaa, while asking a broader question: if a child were born with SCID in South Africa today, would their outcome be any different?

A rare long-term follow-up on a South African first. Nearly a decade after receiving groundbreaking gene therapy for Severe Combined Immunodeficiency, Ayaan Ahmed Sheik is thriving. His story offers a powerful human outcome to a once-experimental treatment. But while the science has progressed globally, access in South Africa remains limited. This update combines an emotional revisit with a critical look at whether meaningful change has followed.
caseStudies: Shamaa Sheik Shamaa Sheik Ayaan's mother
experts: Hedi van der Watt Dr. Ewelina Mamcarz Ail Suliman

title: Reforesting the Cedarberg
oneLiner: The iconic cedar tree is under threat and local volunteers and residents of the Cedarberg are stepping up to reverse this trend
summary:
In 2015 they counted 15 000 cedars, now after the fires they down to 7000. And the older the Cedars, the less seeds they produce. There are also not enough baboons in the area to spread the seeds like they did in the past. But a local environmental organization, Sustainable Cedar is combining community-based replanting solutions and drone technology to replant the wilderness, at scale. Using drones and hardened germinated seeds, Sustainable Ceder are attempting to reverse the demise of this iconic tree, by literally dropping trees from the sky. Sustainable Ceder won the forest category of the European Outdoor Conservation Association award last year. So far, they have planted 10 000 cedars. Working with local residents to harvest the seeds they propagate them in a nursery at Drie Hoek farm. When the saplings are ready, the old men fill old Teabags with aqua gel and coconut Coia to transfer the saplings to give them the best possible chance of survival. Hardening the saplings back in the area where the seeds come from, they will be planted in the winter, when the sun is less extreme and there is more rain for the roots to establish themselves. Young people from Cedarberg have been trained and they work with local teams from the area where they are planting. They will hike for two to 3 hours high into the mountain finding locations that will survive fires, like crevasses in the rocky peaks. They carry specially designed back packs to transport the saplings A drone will fly up to them with seedling trays to restock them, or literally drop sapling from the sky into remote locations. Because the saplings have the teabag plug and they are young and flexible even if they land on their sides, they will right themselves and grow. Then there are the volunteer trail runners who carry specially designed moonbags to carry the saplings high up on the remote trails. Weekend planting sessions with a larger network of people who are passionate about preserving and restoring the Cedarberg which like all wilderness locations is being exposed to abuse. “Keeping it wild” organises work weekends where volunteers come and clean wild campsites, clearing litter and alien vegetation. They also work alongside Cedarberg residents helping restore roads to community campsites.

The Cedarberg is a spectacular 250sq km Wilderness area outside Cape Town. And the iconic Clanwilliam Ceder tree is endemic to this rocky region growing to over 300 years old. 100 years ago, with advent of the telephone, the population was decimated to make phone pylons. Now it is critically endangered. The population has declined 94% in one generation due to a combination of human interference and climate change factors, like fire and reduced rainfall. A massive fire late last year , burning 53 000 hectares of the Cedarberg, once again decimated the protected Cederberg wilderness area, home to the Clanwilliam Ceder tree.
caseStudies: James Joubert Dawie Burger

title: Passion in Action
oneLiner: Traditional leaders and conservationists in Kwazulu-Natal have been channeling energy and Passion into social upliftment and conservation.
summary:
Fifteen years ago Lawrence saved 7 elephants from being culled and relocated them to Thula Thula. Unfortunately the matriarch died and a young male had to be put down but the rest thrived and soon the herd grew. After 28 years since the creation of Thula Thula, Françoise Malby-Anthony sums up her journey with one word: “Passion.” It is a life dedicated to the greater good, for animals and humans alike - because, as she says, the two cannot be separated. Her recently released book, Dining with Elephants, explores the lessons learned from elephants’ social behaviour: life should be about caring, giving, helping, and sharing. Françoise’s commitment to wildlife conservation intensified in 2012. Just two weeks after her husband Lawrence passed away, one of her rhinos was attacked by poachers. The incident crystallised the reality she had long known: her life would be devoted to protecting vulnerable creatures. Since then, she has reshaped anti-poaching strategies and strengthened the protection of wildlife on the reserve. Even during COVID-19, her anti-poaching unit remained vigilant 24/7, underscoring her dedication. But the elephant population grew rapidly and the 5000 hectares wasn’t enough to sustain the herd. That’s when the Inkosi and local Ubiso approached Francoise and offered over a thousand hectares to be incorporated into the reserve. Thula Thula would lease the land from the community. This has enabled Thula Thula to introduce more species like rhino

We know that land reform and the ownership of land is a highly emotional and contentious issue but not here in the area called Zululand about 2 hours from Durban and an hour from Empangeni. Thula Thula game reserve is situated here and this is where the community came together in a project to enhance not only conservation but also to improve the living standards of local communities.
caseStudies: Francoise Malby-Lawrence Thomas Cebekhulu Mzikayise Sikakane

title: Last Right
oneLiner: Two lives, one question: when suffering becomes unbearable, who gets to decide how it ends?
summary:
South Africa’s debate over medically assisted dying has unfolded over decades, shaped by a patchwork of legal precedent, constitutional principles, and unresolved moral questions. Under common law, assisted dying remains prohibited, reinforced by earlier rulings such as Hartman (1975) and Davison (2018). The South African Law Commission considered the issue in 1998, acknowledging its ethical complexity but the law was left unchanged. The debate sharpened with the landmark Stransham-Ford v Minister of Justice and Correctional Services in 2015, where the High Court initially found that a terminally ill man should have the right to assisted dying, grounded in dignity and autonomy. That ruling was later overturned by the Supreme Court of Appeal on procedural grounds, leaving the constitutional question unresolved....and setting the stage for the current legal challenge. Now, a fresh case seeks to directly test whether South Africa’s blanket ban is compatible with the Constitution of South Africa, particularly the rights to dignity, bodily integrity, and freedom from inhuman or degrading treatment. It is a case that could force the courts, and ultimately Parliament, to confront whether the right to life includes the right to choose one’s death. At the heart of this legal battle are deeply personal stories that reflect the opposing sides of the argument. Dieter Harck, living with motor neurone disease, represents those who argue for autonomy. He is facing a progressive loss of control of his bodily functions and speech, and wants the legal right to decide how and when his life should end. In contrast, Petra Burger, who survived a catastrophic car accident and now works in palliative care, embodies the opposing view. Petra has been paralysed since age 24, confined to a wheelchair. Once desperate to die, she now sees meaning in what happened to her and describes it as a "gift" and "divine intervention". She fears that legalising assisted dying in an unequal healthcare system could expose vulnerable patients to harm. Together, their stories bring human urgency to a legal question that has lingered for decades: whether dignity is best protected by preserving life at all costs, or by allowing individuals the freedom to choose when enough is enough.

This story goes beyond the courtroom to reveal the deeply human stakes of assisted dying, through two people whose lived experiences led them to opposite conclusions. As a landmark legal battle unfolds, it captures a country at a moral crossroads - where dignity, choice and the value of life itself are fiercely contested.
caseStudies: Lynne Grubb Petra Burger

title: The Archivist
oneLiner: One man has been documenting the stories of the people of Garankuwa for two decades
summary:
The Archivist - Andrew Sefolo (60 year old photographer,) In the 80s and 90s it was common in many townships and villages to have a photographer. The photographer would take photos of people, especially on Sunday because that is when they wore their best clothes, on Christmas day and New Year's Day, that's when children wore new clothes. The first documentors/ archivists of township live....self trained photographers who captured weddings, birthday parties, street life printed and delivered to your home, for keep or framing. With time, especially with the introduction of cellphones, things have changed. People were documenting their own moments and we lost the local photo guy. BUT in Ga-Rankuwa and Mmakau (Pta North), Bra Andrew is still holding it down for 20+ years. He is booked and busy for celebrations and just ordinary life when someone feels like they are dressed their best. Without a car, he mostly walks to his clients. Bra Andrew isn’t just a photographer, he’s a living archivist of township life and of the lives of families having captured their celebrations, victories and pain.

At the age of 60, Bra Andrew is still Garankuwa's favourite photographer. From film to digital.

title: Hot Soup
oneLiner: When billions are budgeted to feed the hungry… why are children still starving?
summary:
KwaZulu-Natal frequently records the highest number of child deaths due to malnutrition in the country.Recent Mortality Rates: Between April 2017 and April 2025, 555 children under the age of five died from moderate acute malnutrition in KZN public health facilities. In the province, government is spending hundreds of millions to feed the poor. But on the ground, the food being served is raising serious questions. At the centre of our investigation is eThekwini’s soup kitchen programme — a system meant to feed thousands daily. Officially, the municipality says it’s spending around R141 million. But internal documents point to a R240 million figure

A government feeding scheme where it's unclear exactly where the food is and...who is really being fed.

title: THROWFORWARD: House of Pain
summary: A look at an upcoming insert on the subculture of amateur wrestling.

title: UPDATE: Ukraine Cricket
summary: Three years ago, we shared a story of survival and an extraordinary journey. When Russia declared war on Ukraine, South African cricketer Kobus Olivier was living in Kyiv with his four small dogs. He’d settled there to teach – with the goal of establishing cricket formally in Ukraine. But war brought his plans to a grinding halt – and at the urging of his friends, Kobus joined the crowds of refugees fleeing Ukraine. What followed was a gruelling journey to Zagreb, Croatia, followed by friends all over the world. His story eventually became a documentary. But the relief didn’t last. Two years ago, Kobus returned to an intensifying war in Kyiv – where his passion for cricket continues to give him purpose.

title: GO NOW OR STOP SOON - an e-scooter entrepreneur fights for a share of the road in Stellenbosch
oneLiner: Tonight we get stuck in a traffic jam in Stellenbosch - as traditional traffic bosses seek to close down an e-scooter entrepreneur
summary:
GoNOW or StopSOON? How a pioneering electric scooter start-up is being pushed off the streets of Stellenbosch For the past five years, a homegrown electric scooter start-up, GoNOW, has quietly transformed how thousands of students and residents move through Stellenbosch — offering cheap, safe, app-based transport in a town choking on traffic. Now, just as fuel prices threaten to skyrocket amid global tensions (Iran war) and Stellenbosch hits daily gridlock across three peak rush hours, the municipality is moving to shut the service down — citing vague, unnamed complaints. This is the story of innovation colliding with bureaucracy. It begins with 19-year-old Capetonian Jacob Levitan, who imported the idea of app-based electric scooters from Europe and launched in Stellenbosch with municipal support. At the time, officials were actively encouraging non-motorised transport as the town expanded rapidly — with new developments, rising tourism, and a swelling student population of around 30,000, many now bringing cars of their own each term. Levitan started with 100 scooters. The town adapted. Demand grew. Two years later: 200 scooters. Today: 500. They now clock between 40,000 and 50,000 trips a month — criss-crossing Stellenbosch day and night. For students, they’re more than a convenience: they’re freedom. A lift to class when you’ve overslept. A safer ride home after a night out. A way to beat congestion entirely. The system is simple: download the app, unlock a scooter, ride within a geo-fenced area, and leave it at your destination. Each night, teams collect and redistribute them. The model is efficient, scalable — and, until recently, embraced. Schools like Rhenish Girls’ High have even approached GoNOW to install dedicated scooter parking, citing improved safety for learners traveling to extra murals. Levitan has years’ worth of unsolicited thank-you messages from users who say the scooters have changed their daily lives. But in late February, everything shifted. Levitan received an email from the municipality referencing complaints — with no detail. When he asked to meet, there was silence. Then, suddenly, an ultimatum: present yourself within two hours or face mass impoundment of all scooters. At the eventual meeting — attended by Traffic Chief Gavin Solomons and, curiously, the Head of Procurement — Levitan was told the scooters could be impounded due to complaints and a lack of legislation governing electric vehicles of this kind. While the legal gap is real, officials refused to disclose the complaints: how many, from whom, or what the issues were. After four years of operation, the business now faces an existential threat — with no clear explanation. Behind the scenes, Levitan has been told the push may be coming from the mayor’s office. He suspects the programme could be repositioned as a municipal tender — raising questions about whether innovation is being sidelined for control or profit. ( I am not sure whether he will say that on camera – but it’s a question we can ask) At the heart of the story is a bigger issue: South Africa has no clear regulatory framework for emerging electric mobility. GoNOW has effectively been operating as a real-world pilot — a transport guinea pig — in a country increasingly desperate for affordable, local alternatives as fuel costs rise. What happens in Stellenbosch could set a precedent nationwide. Tone & treatment: Energetic, visual, and slightly irreverent. The presenter experiences the entire story on a scooter — moving through the town, linking from key locations, and immersing viewers in the very transport solution now under threat. In many ways it’s a story about whether South Africa really has an appetite for electric mobility — and despite all the lip-service to non-motorised transport, whether innovation is being enabled or quietly shut down.

We will show Stellenbosch stuck at a crossroads - between embracing electric mobility or sticking to traditional ways to manage traffic congestion - either by building new roads or forcing residents to wait in long traffic jams at their intersections. We have unique access to the founder of the e-scooter company, Jacob Levitan, and the date he has collected. His scooters are wildly popular with students, and takes mobility in the town on trend globally. But they leave the local traffic officials scratching their heads, and digging in their heels, while older residents fume at what they perceive to be feral unlicensed modes of transport.
caseStudies: Wikus van Niekerk Jacob Levitan Richard Gordge Noah Chego
experts: Richard Gordge Inge Van der Westhuizen Tracey Megom

title: Who shot the Sheriff?
oneLiner: Sheriffs are the enforcement arm of the courts. Without them the justice system would cease to operate. But what if this vital arm of the justice system has been captured, by the very people who are s
summary:
Sheriffs are the enforcement arm of the courts. Without them the justice system would cease to operate. But what if this vital arm of the justice system has been captured, by the very people who are supposed to ensure its smooth functioning. What if a shadow syndicate, allegedly run by its own "Mr. Clean" Chairperson, has captured the board, turning a vital arm of the justice system into a cash-for-jobs franchise. We reveal a story that is chilling as a board member is gunned down, the driver reveals all, but later retracts and is promoted to a deputy sheriff by the very board member he has made allegations against, and Sheriffs who have served the public faithfully over many years are pushed out.

Case studies willing to go on camera, damning emails, an affidavit from a driver revealing bank account details and amounts of payments for positions, and a former deputy minister prepared
caseStudies: Taka Seboka Iqubal Mohammed Yvonne Thomson

title: Dignity Denied
oneLiner: The City of Ekurhuleni fails the most vulnerable of our society
summary:
Last year, the City of Ekurhuleni was among the municipalities that received a tongue lashing from President Cyril Ramaphosa for failing to utilise the yearly budget allocated to them by National Treasury. The City returned R9,5 million that had been budgeted for infrastructure maintenance and repairs for city-run buildings. The irony however, is that at least five city-run retirement villages could have benefitted from the money that was returned. Presidentia, Rusoord, Markville, Tweedy Park and Silver Krone are all retirement villages that fall under the City of Ekurhuleni. Another thing they all have in common is that they are falling apart and have been so as far back as 2021. Residents are drowning in sewerage as burst pipes are not being attended to by the city. People who are in their 80s and 90s take cold showers because the geysers are not working. Sinks and toilets are broken, roofs are leaking, it’s just a nightmare and the elderly can do nothing about it without city intervention. Worse still, despite there being a budget allocated for security at these facilities, the city has decided not to deploy any security. That has resulted in robbers targeting the place and strangling residents nearly to death in the process of robbing them of their belongings. The poor grannies and grandpas live in constant fear and have to take shifts falling asleep because they are worried that if they all sleep at the same time, they will be robbed again. This is a story about government failing the most vulnerable of our society and both the Department of Human Settlements and the City of Ekurhuleni will be held accountable. The residents have also previously reported their concerns to the Human Rights Commission, so they will also add a voice to the piece. An organization called Serenity Senior Services has also been trying to get both the City and the Department to act. They will also add a voice to the piece.

Accountability interview
caseStudies: Margaret Botha Ann Supra Dorothy Oberholzer

title: Moonshot
oneLiner: One woman. One idea. One shot at the Moon.
summary:
But getting there has always been the challenge: Lunar missions cost hundreds of millions of dollars — far beyond the reach of most research teams. Until now. In 2023, China issued a global call for scientific experiments to join its future lunar programme. Countries around the world applied — including South Africa. After two years of evaluation, Carla’s Africa2Moon project was selected to fly on China’s Chang’e-8 mission, scheduled for 2029. The prize: a free ride to the Moon. For the first time, South Africa will be able to send scientific instruments into space at no launch cost — turning Carla’s decade-long vision into a real mission. But the opportunity comes with pressure. At SARAO in Observatory, Cape Town, Carla and her team are now racing to assemble and test the first Moon Ball prototypes. Budgets are tight, timelines are critical, and much of the work relies on collaboration, donated components, and determination. Carte Blanche has secured access to this project at a pivotal moment — as Carla’s idea moves from theory to reality. We would have a front row seat to the assembly and go with a presenter to meet the team. Carla says we can go to the top of the telescope and do an interview with the presenter looking at the moon, while discussing her dream. “People imagine huge telescopes,” Carla explains. “But our instruments are small. The Moon Balls are about thirty centimetres across — simple spherical antennas that can work no matter how they land.” For this initial mission, only three of the spherical antennas will be sent — a proof of concept. If successful, it could pave the way for a much larger array on future missions. With visuals from SARAO and the SKA telescope array (which Carte Blanche has reported on before), alongside NASA’s lunar archive and international launch footage, the story offers both scale and intimacy: a global race to the Moon… driven by one woman’s persistence. Because if this mission succeeds, Carla Mitchell’s small metal spheres — built in a lab in Cape Town — could help humanity listen back to the very first moments of the universe. “The first words spoken by God in the Bible are ‘Let there be light.’ In a way, that’s what we’re looking for — the first light in the universe, the first stars being born. One of the most exciting discoveries in radio astronomy is about trying to detect what we call ‘first light.’” And after more than a decade chasing the idea, she still looks up at the Moon with the same thought. “Sometimes I look up at the Moon and think — my balls are going to be there one day. I’ve been praying for this on my knees for years.” And in doing so, mark Africa’s first step onto another world.

Moonshot – Race to the Moon There’s a new global space race underway — between the United States, China, Russia… and unexpectedly, South Africa. But this time, the race isn’t about planting flags or sending astronauts. It’s about turning the Moon into a giant listening device using Radio Astronomy Telescopes — capable of detecting signals from the very beginning of the universe. Scientists believe the Moon could hold the key to answering some of the biggest unanswered questions in physics: How did the universe begin? What is dark matter? And are we alone? The reason everyone is trying to do this? Lies in a simple problem: Earth is noisy. Our atmosphere blocks certain radio signals travelling through space, and billions of electronic devices generate constant interference. In other words, scientists are trying to hear a whisper… in the middle of a stadium. But just 384,000 kilometres away, the Moon offers something unique: silence. With no atmosphere and minimal interference, it provides a rare opportunity to detect faint signals that have travelled billions of years — clues to what astronomers call “first light,” the moment the first stars formed after the Big Bang. At the centre of this mission is Carla Mitchell, an unlikely space pioneer based in Cape Town. Not an astrophysicist, but an economist working at the South African Radio Astronomy Observatory, Carla has spent more than a decade chasing an idea many believed was impossible: placing radio astronomy instruments on the Moon. Her solution is deceptively simple. Instead of one massive telescope, Carla has designed small, spherical antennas — each about 30 centimetres wide — that can survive the unpredictable conditions of lunar landing. She calls them “Moon B.A.L.L.S.” — Bounced African Low Lunar Spheres. The design solves one of space exploration’s biggest challenges: landing. Traditional instruments can fail if they tip or land incorrectly. A sphere works no matter how it touches down. Her long-term vision is bold: to place dozens of these spheres across the Moon’s surface, allowing them to work together as a single, powerful telescope array — potentially the first of its kind on another world. And the ideal location? The far side of the Moon. Because the Moon is tidally locked, one side always faces Earth. The far side never does — making it naturally shielded from our planet’s radio noise, and one of the quietest places in the solar system.
experts: Ms. Adriana Marais Space tourist Carla Mitchell Thomas Kusel keitumetse molamu

title: Update: SAHPRA/Adcock
oneLiner: SAHPRA recalls CITRO-SODA!
summary: After the broadcast of our insert on the alleged infringements at the Adcock Ingram Clayville manufacturing plant, SAHPRA has investigated and are recalling some batches of CITRO-SODA.

title: Glenharvie Down
oneLiner: As the gold mines closed, and the zama zamas moved in, the picturesque West Rand town of Glenharvie sank into chaos. But one paramedic refuses to give up.
summary:
Glenharvie is a forgotten West Rand town with a population of just over a few thousand people. Much of the town’s current problems are blamed on two rival gangs of zama zamas operating in the area one from the Welkom area and one group from Stilfontein. Those problems started when two events coincided. One was the police crackdown in Stilfontein in late 2024 and early 2025, which forced many zamas operating in the area to seek greener pastures. The other was the closure of several gold shafts operated by Sibanye-Stillwater, all within a ten-minute drive of the town. Locals say the place is now run by the zamas, and with a police station manned by only two officials which closes at 4pm everyday, they’ve been left defenceless. Signs of vandalism and theft can be seen everywhere – hundreds of meters of copper cable dug up and stolen next to busy streets in the centre of town, the local rugby stadium’s pavilion roof is missing all of its corrugated iron roof, and even the police station’s security fence has been stolen. But dig deeper and the problems are much darker and much more violent. A local paramedic, André Boshoff has seen the violence first hand. His first encounter with zamas was the day they arrived at his neighbour’s home, a local security guard who’d been giving information on the zama zamas to the police and mines. Armed zamas ambushed the guard in his driveway, and opened fire. He was shot and injured. When his wife and daughter came running out of the house, they were both shot and died. Then the zamas walked over to the still living security guard and executed him. André has decided to fight back. He’s mobilised community patrols and is actively engaging with the mines, municipality and police. But he says the community are fighting a losing battle. On the 18th of December last year, the war between the two opposing zama factions reached critical mass. They had a massive shootout on the streets of Glenharvie. At least a 100 zamas were involved, some of the shooting was captured on CCTV cameras from local shops. They show armed zamas carrying an assortment of machine guns like AK 47’s. One zama was executed within a few meters of a nursery school. Adriaan Vos, a local farmer, whose house sits right in the middle of land the zamas use to cross between shafts, was ambushed in the early hours of the morning. When he heard his dogs barking, he went to investigate. A group of men, dressed in the balaclavas and traditional blankets of Basotho zamas, opened fire. André was hit in the knee and the lung. While he lay bleeding, some of the men entered his house and det it on fire. André, the paramedic, responded to the scene. When he got their Adriaan’s whole house was engulfed in flames. André tried to save Adriaan’s beloved dog, who was trapped on the second-floor balcony. He also had several prized parrots in the house. But a gas bottle exploded, and all the animals were engulfed in the flames. Adriaan survived the shooting. He was in hospital for more than a week. Not a single police officer arrived to take a statement. The motif for the attack is unclear. The zamas didn’t steal several vehicles on site. But the night after the fire, they returned and started stripping the farmhouse of copper and steel. Another farmer was murdered in his farmhouse. This house has since become the base of operations for one of the two groups of zamas. The second group operate from a bush camp behind a hill just outside of town. We won’t be able to approach them without serious risk, but we can fly a drone over the areas. We do have some footage of the shootings etc. We can accompany André and the other volunteers on a patrol. We can use André and his attempt at reclaiming the town as the central narrative of a story about a once thriving community being devastated by violent gangs and turf wars. All this after earlier this year, just a few kilometers away in the town of Randfontein, at least 300 people said they were forced out of their homes by zama zamas and took refuge in a local town hall. Meanwhile, in his SONA last month, Pres Cyril Ramaphosa announced deploying the SANDF to Gauteng to combat illegal mining. If they do plan to help out in Glenharvie, they haven’t shown up yet.

The picturesque mining town Glenharvie, situated on the West Rand, was once a thriving community. But as many of Sibanye Stillwater's shafts in the area shut down, crime took hold. Residents blame much of it on large groups of zamas waging a turf war for control of the unprotected assets. We have exclusive cctv and cellphone footage showing large groups of armed men running the streets of the town, videos showing shooting incidents where hundreds of rounds are fired, and residents who are at their wits end.
caseStudies: André Boshoff Adriaan Vos

title: House of pain
oneLiner: South Africa has an unknown wrestling scene — and for thirty years, these ordinary nine-to-fivers have been secretly building it, one body slam at a time.
summary: Inside South Africa’s Secret Wrestling World By day they are electricians, sales consultants, graphic designers and security technicians. By night, they become villains, heroes and champions inside a wrestling ring in Parow. Carte Blanche steps inside the bizarre, bruising and little-known world of the Africa Wrestling Alliance and the ordinary South Africans risking their bodies for a dream few take seriously. The Hook In a modest civic centre in Cape Town’s northern suburbs, grown men and women in face paint, leather and championship belts battle it out in front of a roaring crowd. It looks like theatre. It feels like sport. It’s violent. It’s dramatic. It’s deeply personal. And almost nobody outside this subculture knows it exists. Is professional wrestling in South Africa just a bizarre pastime or is it a serious athletic pursuit fighting for legitimacy? The Premise The Africa Wrestling Alliance (AWA), founded in 1994, claims to be South Africa’s premier professional wrestling federation. With over 30 years of history, it operates out of the Parow Civic Centre , dubbed the “House of Pain.” But what makes this story compelling isn’t just the spectacle. It’s the people. These wrestlers aren’t full-time entertainers earning global contracts. They are: A quality auditor A jewellery sales consultant An electric fencing technician A senior graphic designer A travel associate A business owner By day, completely ordinary. By night, they transform into characters like: Romeo “The Chosen One” Valentino -the cocky heel Mike “The Magnificent” Xander - the arrogant champion Johnny “The Italian Stallion” Palazzio - the veteran people’s champ Ed Electric -the Cape Minstrels-inspired brawler Nicky Vex -the new-generation female heel They train through injuries. They work full-time jobs. They perform for modest crowds. And they are chasing a dream most South Africans don’t even know is possible.

title: Thanda Choir
oneLiner: A global success story or a sophisticated scam? We go behind the scenes of the world-famous Thanda Choir to find out why South Africa’s 'internet darlings' are performing for the world while starvi
summary:
The Thanda Choir is South Africa’s latest global export, a soaring beacon of hope rising from the under-resourced streets of Khayelitsha to the shortlists of the Oscars. With a social media following in the millions, they have transitioned from a local community group into a star-studded sensation, sharing stages with the Dave Matthews Band and Melody Gardot, while performing for elite global entities like META, Prudential, and international football star Memphis Depay. To the world, they are the "darlings of the internet" and a vivid symbol of South African transformation—but as the choir’s global profile skyrockets, a discordant pattern of professional and financial abuse is emerging behind the scenes. While the choir's management markets a story of empowerment, the singers themselves are trapped in a cycle of poverty that stands in chilling contrast to their fame. On average, these world-class performers earn a staggering pittance of just R400 a month, supplemented by a food hamper valued at R250. When members dare to question this meagre stipend, management reportedly weaponises the choir’s namesake, "Thanda," telling the singers they should perform for "love" rather than money. Those who persist in seeking transparency are met with retaliatory expulsion. The numbers simply do not add up. While the performers struggle to survive, nearly R400,000 in donations intended for the choir’s upliftment remains unaccounted for, alongside at least R600,000 in performance fees generated since November alone—and that is a conservative estimate based only the figures that have come to light. The choir now fears their funds are being siphoned by their management: two 21-year-old, private-school-educated men from affluent backgrounds who allegedly funnel payments into private accounts to "avoid tax." Despite being registered as an NPO, there are claims that no income is being declared to SARS, leaving the choir’s legal and financial standing in jeopardy. Now, trapped between their lifelong passion for music and the crushing weight of exploitation, the members of Thanda Choir are finally breaking their silence, in an exclusive. They are a "family" terrified of losing their purpose, yet they can no longer ignore the R400 barrier that stands between their global success and their personal dignity.

Exclusive Access: This is the first time the choir has broken their collective silence. Carte Blanche has the sole opportunity to document the "unmasking" of a global sensation, providing a narrative that contrasts their public "love" persona with a private reality of systemic exploitation. High-Impact Media Synergy: The story offers a prime opportunity for multi-platform collaboration. Given the choir's digital-first fame, the investigation is primed for viral reach across social media, radio, and international print, ensuring it remains a headline-dominating topic across all demographics. Unprecedented Public Interest: With a collective reach of millions of followers, the Thanda Choir is one of South Africa’s most visible cultural exports of the decade. Any disruption to their narrative is guaranteed to spark massive local and international engagement, tapping into a global audience that feels personally invested in their success. International Celebrity Involvement: The narrative extends beyond South African borders, featuring high-profile international elements. This includes the potential for exclusive commentary and interview requests from global icons like The Dave Matthews Band, Melody Gardot, and Memphis Depay, all of whom have been unwittingly drawn into the choir’s orbit. A Landmark Social Justice Case: At its core, this is a story of Transformation vs. Exploitation. It tackles the intersection of race, class, and the "gig economy," highlighting the vulnerability of township artists against affluent, private-school-educated management. It is a powerful pursuit of justice for a "national treasure" being held hostage by its own success.
caseStudies: Julio & Luke Teixeira & Bernhardi Lisakhanya “Prince” Maqhajana Asandisa Siswana Zizipho Mathontsi Mathontsi

title: Muti Murders
oneLiner: British tourist Lorna McSorley’s mysterious disappearance in northern KwaZulu-Natal revives fears of muti murders and exposes alleged police inaction.
summary:
In the remote reaches of KwaZulu-Natal, where quiet roads wind through bushveld and small communities live far from the reach of urban life, a series of chilling cases has reignited fears about so-called muti murders. These crimes, widely believed to be rare, are often spoken about in hushed tones, yet for some families, the horror feels all too real. In September last year, British tourist Lorna McSorley vanished without a trace near the town of Mkuze. She had been on holiday with her partner and was out on a walk when he turned back, leaving her to continue alone. Not long after, she asked a nearby farmer for directions back to her accommodation. He offered her a lift, but she declined, choosing instead to walk. It was the last confirmed sighting of her. Despite extensive searches involving police, volunteers, and even aircraft, almost nothing was found - only the map she had been carrying. For the farmer, Koos Prinsloo, the memory of that brief encounter still lingers. Lorna appeared calm and untroubled, he recalls. There was no sign that anything was wrong. Days later, his daughter would discover the discarded map, the only clue left behind. For those who searched the area, the lack of evidence was deeply unsettling. It was as if she had simply disappeared. Lorna's brother Geoff McSorley is still reeling from the horror of what may have happened to her. With just an eleven month age gap, Geoff is Lorna's older brother and feels not enough has been done to solve his sister's disappearance. Lorna's partner, 81 year old Leon Probert, returned to England a few days after her disappearance. The couple had been together for about thirty years, and Leon raised the alarm after Lorna failed to return to the hotel after their walk. Behind the scenes, there were leads...leads that some believe were never properly pursued. Former police investigator Francois Nel began analysing cellphone activity in the area during the exact window of Lorna’s disappearance. Within a 100-metre radius, four cellphone numbers were detected. None of them were registered under South Africa’s RICA system. Nel passed this information on to police, urging further investigation, including an application that could have granted access to the phones’ records. According to him, that never happened. As speculation grows, so too does the shadow of a darker theory...that Lorna may have been targeted for her body parts. It’s a claim that remains unproven, but one that echoes in other cases in the local community. Traditional healer organisations have strongly condemned the use of human body parts for muthi, insisting they have no place in legitimate cultural practices. According to leaders within the community, the use of human body parts is not only illegal but goes against the core values of traditional healing. Still, they acknowledge that there are individuals operating outside these boundaries, feeding a shadowy and secretive trade that is difficult to police. Authorities, meanwhile, urge caution. Colonel Robert Netshiunda says investigations Lorna's case are ongoing and warns against unverified speculation. Fear is, however, spreading in the local communities. In response to a string of around eleven suspected muti murders in recent years, residents held a church service to pray for protection and justice. The local traditional leader also attended, showing the depth of concern and the desire for communal healing. But in communities where fear lingers and answers remain scarce, the questions are growing louder. Are these isolated tragedies...or signs of something far more organised and hidden? For now, in the quiet landscape where Lorna McSorley was last seen, there is only silence. No trace of what happened. No resolution. Just the unsettling possibility that, in some places, the line between belief and brutality is far thinner than we would like to think.

In the remote reaches of KwaZulu-Natal, where quiet roads wind through bushveld and small communities live far from the reach of urban life, a series of chilling cases has reignited fears about so-called muti murders.
