Despite extensive searches involving police, volunteers, and even aircraft, almost nothing was found - only the map she had been carrying.

title: Rivers for sale
oneLiner: A thirsty city. A hidden trade. And water worth more than gold.
summary:
In Gqeberha, a seemingly lucrative trade is brazenly thriving in the shadows. Tanker trucks move through suburbs and industrial areas, pumping and delivering thousands of litres of water every day to a city desperate for supply. But where this water comes from remains largely unseen. Our investigation reveals a brazen underground industry of opportunists drilling illegal boreholes, siphoning municipal water from fire hydrants and pumping from rivers and private properties before selling it across the metro. The trade has existed for years, but over the past year it has surged, fuelled by weak enforcement and few real consequences. Guided by an insider who knows the network but fears being identified, we follow the tankers to expose the hidden supply chain behind the city’s thirst.

We follow the trucks no one is supposed to notice. From hidden pumps to city streets, we trace the underground journey of Gqeberha’s water.
caseStudies: Peter Hart

title: Chippa Football Academy
oneLiner: We take a deep dive into the newly named Africa School of Excellence, and find out why former staff and parents are blowing the whistle on Chippa Mpengesi.
summary:
Transnet School of Excellence was founded in 1994 as a joint venture between Transnet and SAFA, run by a Board of Trustees. The Trustees included Transnet, SAFA, SAFCOC, Department of Basic Education, a representative of the Community and a representative of the Private Sector. In 2020 the Trust was dissolved and the school was taken over by the Transnet Foundation as part of its CSI responsibilities. Transnet donated R20 m annually to run the school. Last year they decided they could not continue and put out a call for new sponsors. Some sponsors stepped forward and requested Financial Records for the school. NO FINANCIALS AVAILABLE. In August 2025 they published a tender as Request for Proposals, asking for a donor to take over the SOE. They had five bids, including Pitso Mosimane who runs a very successful academy partnering with Curro schools; Thulani Majola a controversial businessman who was previously in liquidation, and Chippa Training Academy (Pty) Ltd, a company belonging to Chippa Mpengesi. One of the criteria was a proven track record educating high school pupils. But, the Chippa Training Academy is a company that trains security guards. What due diligence did Transnet do? The only evidence of a school is social media calls for enrolment at the Chippa Academy in East London in July 2025. The school never opened. Instead, those pupils from the Eastern Cape have been bused to the Germiston campus.

The Transnet Football School of Excellence in Kempton Park has been handed over to controversial businessman and Chippa FC owner, Chippa Mpengesi. In just two months, the once proud legacy of this birthplace of champions has been decimated. Staff and coaches have been fired, salaries have not paid, and the boys were left sleeping on the floor, eating 2-minute noodles.
caseStudies: Lindsay Jooste Gertina van der Merwe Gilbert Molala
experts: Michelle Phillips Chippa Mpengesi Maboreng Maharaswa
camera: Wimpie Ackermann Ruan Visser Kobus Zietsman Greg Govan Aristo Mukeba

title: Update: Women's Rugby
oneLiner: The increased popularity of women's rugby.
summary: On 5 March 2026 the SA Rugby Awards were held, honouring the best-of-the best. We take a brief look at the rise of women's rugby after the Springbok Women reached the quarter finals of the RWC last year for the first time.

title: sixteen down the river
summary: It’s one of the toughest endurance canoeing races in the world, 3 days of gruelling paddling, carrying, and focusing. Andy Birkett is the only human to have ever won the race 16 times. “Nothing is given in the Dusi; you have to earn your way down the river every day” This is the story beyond the river. It has taken the boy who first paddled the Dusi solo at 13, to become the man who finished first 16 times. If you ask anyone to describe Andy, the first word is always humble. But humility doesn’t make you a world champion athlete, or does it? In 2022, he thought his career was over. Asthma, poor performance results and younger guns taking more titles. But then he pushed harder, and with every burst of doubt, he pushed harder and took the world games championships He is an elite athlete, father and husband, which comes first? How do they come together, and can the river teach us all something about life?
caseStudies: andy birkett

title: ESKOM GHOST VILLAGE
summary:
More than a decade after it was conceived as a solution for worker accommodation at Eskom’s Kusile Power Station, the Wilge Residential Village remains exactly what it has quietly become: a taxpayer-funded ghost town. Built to house hundreds of construction staff during Kusile’s build, the 336-unit complex has never meaningfully housed anyone. Instead, it has swallowed close to R1-billion, ballooning from an original budget of around R160 million. That works out to roughly R2.5 million per empty apartment. Investigations dating back to the News24 Eskom Files in 2021 exposed how procurement inside the project spiralled into excess, including inflated furniture tenders and alleged collusion between officials and contractors. Items like desks, couches and even leisure equipment were reportedly marked up far beyond market value. The spending kept flowing. Occupants never came. Fast forward to 2025 and now early 2026, and nothing fundamental has changed: • The buildings stand unfinished and unoccupied • The site shows visible decay and vandalism • Attempts to sell or transfer the property have not materialised • Parliament and opposition MPs continue to label it fruitless and wasteful expenditure • The Special Investigating Unit has kept Wilge within broader Eskom corruption probes, but no public recovery of funds or prosecutions linked specifically to the village have been announced. All the while, Eskom has paid for alternative accommodation and transport for workers the village was meant to house, effectively paying twice. The optics are stark. N almost-billion-plus housing estate sitting empty in a province battling housing backlogs and unemployment, while the utility asks consumers for tariff hikes. But Wilge is not just an abandoned development. It is a physical monument to state capture era procurement, weak oversight and consequence-free spending. A concrete reminder that billions were lost not only in coal contracts and power station delays, but also in the small, supposedly practical things. Housing. Beds. Roofs. As of 2026, Wilge is still empty. Still decaying. Still paid for. And there’s still no accountability.

A story of how Eskom has wasted hundreds of millions of rand on a "ghost" development, while at the same time seeking to raise power prices for South Africans.
caseStudies: Rob Stand

title: Poverty For Profit
oneLiner: When poverty is repackaged for profit
summary:
The Money Across South Africa, over R7 billion has been allocated this year alone to upgrade informal settlements. Jumpas Informal Settlement, in Denver, east of Johannesburg, is one of the beneficiaries. R75 million was allocated for electrification. On paper, it’s a development story - an informal settlement upgrade. On the ground, only 64 concrete poles and a mini-substation stood — while thousands of residents remained without electricity. Until Cllr Neuren Petersen began highlighting the issue in 2025. The question emerges: Where is the money going? The Letter At the centre of the story is a letter written by the project’s Community Liaison Officer, Masande Madikane — written while he was still free. In it, he names contractors and officials. He describes an alleged secret meeting at Mike’s Kitchen in Parktown where beneficiaries were reportedly pre-selected. He details intimidation and alleged bribery attempts. The letter becomes our roadmap. We follow the names. We test the claims. We trace the money. But as the allegations surface, tension escalates inside the settlement. The Violence Jumpas has seen three murders in the past year — including the killing of Masande’s mother, a community activist who opposed shack farming. Masande reported threats. Masked men in a blue car allegedly targeted him. After his mother’s murder, allegations emerged that he had been seen disguised as a zama-zama — allegedly to avenge her. He was later arrested and charged with murder. But the letter alleging corruption came first. So the central question remains: Is Jumpas a crime story? Or is it a corruption story wrapped in crime?

This is a story about how billions of Rands are spent to "upgrade" poverty
caseStudies: Gogo Muriel

title: BJK Stink
oneLiner: A Rendering plant in prime agricultural land is polluting the air with the most gut rendering stench and causing major health issues and the community appeal to the authorities falls on deaf ears
summary:
The Green scorpions acknowledge that BJK has been a problem for many years. BJK need to install a biological scrubber which is an industry standard for the volatile Organic compounds for Ammonia and sulphur dioxide and chlorine emissions, but BJK say it’s too expensive. Instead it seems they extended their chimneys, so they release these gasses higher into the atmosphere- all that’s done is spread the stench further. The main shareholder is an exceptionally rich Brit called Danny Sawirj of the Leo Group who owns a similar plant in Penrith England. BJK Industries is Leo Group’s South African subsidiary. Ironically the UK plant is lauded as being a major contributor to renewable energy and is punted as an environmental green solution. Its highly profitable enterprise but faces similar issues. Residents in Halifax and Bradford have complained about the noise and smells emanating from the company's factories. Apart from the stench the trucks transporting the chicken waste drip and spill and leaving trails of blood and guts on the roads. The waste is not transported in refrigerated trucks and decomposes enroute. Many of the roads these trucks use are dirt and BJK takes their time before they clean it up. The goo spilling from the trucks stinks and causes fly infestation. In Britian they have been prosecuted for similar violations- here nothing happens. Its not only the people that are suffering it’s the livestock as well. Trucks trundle the dirt roads all through the night and production never ceases. The stench can be smelt 20kms away depending on which way the wind is blowing. And over the years it got worse. Two years ago, the plant shut down for three weeks when two workers died in the plant from asphyxiation. The owners of the plant refuse to release the report to the community. But the shut down in production was a massive relief from the stench. Anecdotally, residents say when they leave the area for holidays elsewhere their health improves The water on the neighbouring farms was tested by water department, but they refuse to release the results to the farmers. Independent tests show high levels of ecoli and ammonia – but why won’t the water department release the results? Residents approached the CSIR and various Universities to monitor the air quality and analyses the emissions, but were told it cost R100 000 residents can’t raise that kind of money.

Grootvlei and Greylingstad once known for its clean air and idyllic farmland has become a living hell for its residents. Having a braai in their gardens, a country wedding, or an outride on a horse they are buying from the stud farm is a gamble. If the wind is from the East they hide indoors and even then, they can’t escape the stench. The smell is described as worse than a decomposing rat, it’s more like a decomposing human said one resident. Others describe it as the smell of cat pee, and apart from the gut-wrenching smell it’s impacting their health severely and their businesses. Migraines, increased sinus infections, Asthma, shortness of breath, constantly coughing, blood clots on the lungs plague the residents and no number of appeals to the authorities seem to make an impact. The source of the stench is BJK – a rendering plant that trucks in chicken feathers, blood, fat and offal and converts it into animal proteins, oils and minerals and frozen products which they sell to the pet food industry. It’s a lucrative industry but the surrounding community are paying the price
caseStudies: Carel Pienaar John Coetzee Suzelle Stein Andre Meyer Thokozni Mbhele

title: Whale Song
oneLiner: JOURNEYMAN FOREIGN SPECIAL
summary: "The Whale Song" delves into the enchanting world of humpback whales and their remarkable ability to communicate through song. While it is widely known that these majestic creatures sing to communicate with each other and our documentary unveils their vocal powers. Humpback whales pick up each other's best tunes and ingeniously remix them to create globally renowned hits. Our film draws a fascinating parallel between the musical talents of world-famous DJ Sam Feldt and the melodious humpback whale, narrated by the renowned marine biologist Nan Hauser. We witness DJ Sam Feldt's incredible transformation of whale songs into a human chart-topper, demonstrating the astonishing synergy between nature and art. Additionally, Nan Hauser's personal story of being rescued by a benevolent whale serves as a poignant reminder of the deep connection that can exist between humans and marine life. "The Whale Song" is not just a documentary; it's a sensory and emotional journey that will captivate audiences of all ages. Its visually stunning cinematography, compelling storytelling, and the fusion of music and nature make it a standout piece in the world of short documentaries.

title: Kruger Floods + INT: Bonné de Bod
oneLiner: The aftermath of devastating floods in January 2026
summary: Severe flooding in Limpopo, Mpumalanga and northern Kruger causes havoc in January. We recap on Deluge in Limpopo and speak to Bonné de Bod about what she found on the ground in Kruger during a recent visit to the park.

title: UPDATE: Bulungula
oneLiner: A year and a half after we reported on a crime wave engulfing a picturesque Eastern Cape village, residents lay positive news at our door.
summary: In September 2024 we visited Dave Martin and his wife Rejane Woodroffe at their tourist lodge on the Wild Coast, Bulungula. For twenty years they had built a life and a community there... but in recent months, violent crime overshadowed their lives and threatened the tourist economy they all depended on. Homeowners were left seriously injured and one killed by armed robbers; the whole community was shaken and fearful. The mayor promised arrests and a new police station. But in March 2025, we returned to more bad news. Crime had continued unabated. Despite promises of increased police visibility in the area, there had been no assistance for communities living in fear. One couple had been violently attacked again, shot and beaten. Tourism had taken a massive knock. Now, Dave has been in touch to share a positive development at last. One suspect has been arrested with guns and goods that were stolen from victims. He is currently in jail and awaiting a bail hearing on 25 February. One well-known criminal and major suspect died in a SAPS shootout two weeks ago. And best of all, the last attack in the region was more than one year ago. We catch up with Dave to hear how he and the community are recovering.
caseStudies: Dave Martin Rejane Woodroffe

title: RECAP: Adcock Ingram
oneLiner: Allegations from a whistleblower
summary: We recap "A Trusted Source" That went out on 22 FEB 2026, ahead of an interview with CEO of SAHPRA. The story highlights alleged safety concerns at the Adcock Ingram Clayville Manufacturing Plant. RECAP is followed by a live interview with SAHPRA CEO -- Dr. Boitumelo Semete-Makokotlela

title: UPDATE: Kuruman
oneLiner: Residents demand our return to a remote town where we witnessed municipal decay - and had a brush with crime.
summary:
Three years ago, we took a trip to a tiny, remote town in the Northern Cape. Once a tourist attraction, for years Kuruman has suffered a slow decline. Nowhere was the damage more devastating than here: the Eye of Kuruman, the southern hemisphere’s largest natural spring. Residents shared harrowing stories of crime. And our crew had its own touch-and-go experience. Municipal Manager Martin Tsatsimpe admitted that the situation was challenging. Promises were made: a new reservoir, restoration of the Eye, and crackdowns on illegal business. So, what’s happened in the years since our visit? Ward councillor Braam van der Westhuizen, who we interviewed last time, says service delivery has literally become a battle. Complaints have flooded our inbox: power outages – burst pipes – raw sewage flowing into the Eye. It’s a picture of a town in collapse. Finally, last week, desperate residents united in protest. The petition demanded the resignation of the Municipal Manager. Martin Tsatsimpe still holds the position. Back in 2022, he agreed to an interview, but this time, he seems reluctant to answer questions. Our phone calls are ignored and our emails go unanswered. Amidst official silence and rumours of infighting, the community is left with dwindling hope.

We’ve visited our share of small towns – and usually, it’s to bring you stories of the quirky, the unique, and the inspiring. But when our crew took a road trip to the far-flung stretches of the Northern Cape in 2022, it was to tell a very different story. Kuruman was once a firm favourite with tourists, home to the Moffat Mission, where the Bible was first translated into Setswana, and for its spectacular natural spring, the famous Kuruman Oog. But by the time we arrived, its reputation had been soiled. This year, Kuruman was brought back to our attention as residents flooded our inbox. So, we asked what – if anything – had changed in the more than three years since our visit.
caseStudies: Braam van der Westhuizen

title: ZUMA RECRUITS RETURN FROM THE FRONTLINE - A TALE OF TWO MOTHERS
oneLiner: We interrogate the return of the Zuma recruits to South Africa - and the consequences for the Zuma and other families
summary:
Seventeen recruits return home from seven months on the frontline of Europe's bitter war between Russia and Ukraine, into the arms of their relieved but very stressed families. They return with horrific war stories which are the stuff of nightmares, such is the horror that they have endured as the meat in the meat-grinder of the Russian Army, witnessing the depravity of war and its slaughter. Their families believe they were conned into war by three individuals, the most noteworthy being former President Jacob Zuma's daughter, Duduzile, and his current lover, Siphokazi Xuma. Now that the men are returning, the focus shifts to the recruiters who must face the family members they sent to a possible death. This event has divided the extended Zuma family, with cousin accusing cousin of betrayal. And it has also thrust into the spotlight, the mothers of the men who were sent to Russia, to skill up to become MK security. Another mother, however, who is feeling no joy, is also a family friend of Duduzilem through the child's father. She alleges that Dudu persuaded her to send her boys to Russia for personal training. They had not been heard of since August, presumed dead. And she is very angry.

We have been tracking through WhatsApp conversations two of the 19 Zuma recruits who are returning now from the frontline, after desperate pleas by their families, in particular a woman known as Sis Pumla Zuma, sister-in-law of Jacob Zuma who fought hard to get her family members back from Russia, after seven to eight months of unbearable struggle. The two we have engaged with are Thapelo from Rustenberg who appears to have been caught up in the recruiting while looking for a job; the other is Prince Mzobe, a family member of former President Jacob Zuma.
caseStudies: Thulani Mahlangu Kitso Molatlhegi-Boiteto Zolani Zuma Phumla Zuma

title: Gun Shop Hijack
oneLiner: A career conman is now hijacking gun shops. What could go wrong?
summary:
It began with a submission into Carte Blanche. A firearms dealer, Cobie Englebrecht, wrote in with a warning: two men tried to take over his firearm shop called Gunsafe in Sasolburg – the fronter is a man called Hendrik van Zyl. They arrived as would-be buyers, talking about partnerships and expansion. But Cobie says once they were inside his business, the deal turned dark. They tried to change his CIPC documents to make one of them the director. And the money he was promised? It never arrived. He is being threatened, but luckily he believes he caught on just in time. Others, he says, did not. One of those dealers, Adri Nel of Marksman Arms, has gone on record in a sworn affidavit. She describes how Van Zyl and his associate wanted to buy their business in Pretoria. Payments for the purchase of the shop never arrived. Next they were told the CIPC directorship changed, and before any more was paid over (R50,000 over 2 years for a R1million) Hendrik was named as director. They also sold a whole bunch of firearms that had already been sold – people often buy while they’re waiting for their licenses to be approved… many disappeared during this time from the safe… When access to the premises was later demanded by Hendrik, SAPS were called to intervene. Her statement paints a picture of a firearms dealership being quietly hijacked while the court and police struggled to catch up. Then a second, more familiar name emerges in the background. In contracts, he is described as an “adviser”. But multiple sources allege he is deeply involved in driving these deals: Johnathan Clive Stephenson — a man previously featured on Carte Blanche in a 2021 investigation into alleged solar scams. Remember him? He essentially apologized in the story, and said he will fix the issues, but never did. Of course that’s not he how he remembers it… He’s told everyone he wronged him, and he was innocent etc. So I went into the Marksmans Arms undercover, and guess who was on the phone with the manager? Stephenson! I obviously took over the phone conversation and he boasted on the phone about he’s importing firearms “from all over the world – 19 different countries” and opening a gun shop now in Texas too. Turns out there are other gun stores that say they have had the same problem… Still tracking down those… But I spoke to the police, and they confirmed the investigation and are happy to meet with me and hand over information because… turns out you need a license to be able to sell firearms and that is hard to get! So Stephenson went to court to get that, and told a judge the police were preventing him from operating this store – he and his lawyer neglected to tell the court that there’s a dispute of ownership – but the police said its clear this store was stolen at CIPC.

We have undercover footage of him telling us he's expanding his gun business and importing. We have a police source. We have amazing informaiton on the conman Jonathan Stephenson from a previous case study. We did a previous story on Stephenson (Graham did a story on a solar scam in 2021) We have potential to catch him at a hijacked gun shop.
caseStudies: Alberto da Silva Cobie Englebrecht Adri Nel Jonathan Stephenson

title: Manna from an invasive tree
oneLiner: How a pest choking South Africa's drylands is being transformed into jobs, hope - and a roasted caffeine free drink.
summary:
In March every year the quiet Karoo town of Calvinia comes alive as hundreds of residents harvest seedpods from one of South Africa’s most destructive invasive alien trees: the Mesquite. Introduced over a century ago as a drought solution, the Mesquite has since spread uncontrollably, draining groundwater and infesting more than eight million hectares of land in the Northern Cape. While government eradication programmes struggle to contain it, one entrepreneur believes the tree might offer an alternative solution. We follow the unlikely journey of Mesquite seedpods — from township streets where pensioners and unemployed residents collect them for cash, to a Somerset West factory where they are roasted and ground into the world’s only Mesquite coffee, now exported internationally. At the centre of the story is Brandt Coetzee, whose decades-long relationship with the tree has evolved from furniture-making to nutraceuticals, and finally to coffee. His operation employs nearly 700 seasonal harvesters in Calvinia alone, providing a critical income stream for people living on government pensions. The story also revisits the tree’s complicated past through farmers who once relied on it as livestock feed — and now live with the unintended consequences of its spread. It examines whether commercialising an invasive species can realistically curb its expansion, or whether it risks entrenching the problem further. Story Overview In March, harvest season begins. Residents — many surviving on government pensions — scour the town and surrounding veld for Mesquite seedpods. For some, it means food on the table. For others, it means dignity, purpose, and community. Community leader Donavan du Plooy calls it “Christmas in March,” earning up to R8,000 for a ton of pods while sharing profits with helpers. Yet the Mesquite’s legacy is complex. Farmers like Hennie Visagie, now in his seventies, remember when the tree was deliberately planted — watered by hand — and celebrated as “mother’s milk” for livestock during droughts. That same tree now infests more than 8 million hectares in the Northern Cape alone. Government eradication programmes like Working for Water have struggled to keep pace. Coetzee’s approach is different: instead of cutting it down, harvest the seedpods before they spread — and pay people to do it. Key Themes Environmental unintended consequences Innovation born from scarcity Job creation in rural South Africa Sustainability versus eradication Why It Matters Manna from an Invasive Tree is a uniquely South African story with global relevance — blending science, environment, economics, and human resilience. It challenges conventional conservation thinking while asking hard questions about long-term ecological responsibility. The story combines strong characters, striking visuals, and ethical complexity. It reveals how forgotten communities adapt to environmental crises, and whether hope can be found in the most unlikely places.

It's one of South Africa's most destructive invasive trees....chocking the land, draining precious water, and costing millions to eradicate. But in the Karoo town of Calvinia, it's become something else entirely. Once a year, hundreds of residents harvest its seedpods - turning a pest into income, dignity, and survival. Now one man is taking it even further - transforming an environmental disaster into a globally exported coffee.

title: A Sugarcoated Collapse
oneLiner: Along the north coast of KwaZulu-Natal, sugar built an empire over the past 130 years but now, its future no longer looks so sweet.
summary:
This is one of South Africa’s most important and underreported historical and economic stories, one that many younger generations may barely know. It began in 1860, when ships carrying indentured Indian labourers arrived on the shores of Durban to build what would become one of the country’s most influential agricultural industries. Over the decades, the sugar industry grew into a vast economic empire, shaping communities, sustaining generations of families, and controlling some of the most valuable land in South Africa. Entire towns were built around its mills, and its influence defined the development of KwaZulu-Natal’s north coast. Now, more than a century later, that empire faces an uncertain future, as corporate collapse, global competition, and a government widely criticised for failing to protect local industry, threaten to dismantle one of the country’s oldest economic foundations.

This story captures the human cost of industrial collapse, following families whose lives span generations of sugar production, from indentured labour to modern land reform beneficiaries, now facing an uncertain future.

title: The Foreign Fighter File
oneLiner: Carte Blanche brings you an exclusive interview with a South African that fled the war in Ukraine - providing firsthand proof South Africans have been sent to the frontlines by Kyiv
summary:
As South Africans who fought alongside Russian forces prepare to return home following diplomatic engagement between Pretoria and Moscow, a critical legal question surfaces: What happens to South Africans who fought on the side of a foreign power in direct violation of the country’s laws governing military service? Carte Blanche has secured exclusive access to a South African who enlisted in Ukraine at 19 and is now living in legal limbo as an illegal immigrant in Europe. We call them Lerato Venter. In the early days of the war, Lerato presented at the Ukrainian Embassy in Pretoria and was instructed to travel to Europe to join Ukraine’s military effort. As part of the effort she was sent to the Polish embassy for Schengen VISA - she jumped the queues and A travel delay — the absence of a required transit visa — postponed departure. Days later, the training facility they were initially assigned to was bombed. Lerato ultimately reached Kyiv, where they underwent basic military training, including weapons handling. After two months, concerns grew. Repeated requests to surrender their passport and unease about the symbolic role of foreign volunteers and the potential to be used as a tragic piece of propaganda led Lerato to flee. Now residing in Spain and seeking to regularise their immigration status as part of a recently announced , Lerato fears potential prosecution under South Africa’s Regulation of Foreign Military Assistance Act (1998). Proposed scenes Scene 1 – The context (Opening) We run through the ongoing plight of South Africans serving in the Russian military after being duped. And how they will now supposedly return home in coming weeks after a deal was struck between Putin and Ramaphosa. But… They weren’t the only South Africans directly involved in this 4 year old conflict. Scene 2 – The Confession (Opening) Concealed interview. Lerato recounts leaving South Africa at 19, the embassy visit, the delayed arrival, and the bombing of the original training camp. Scene 3 – Inside the War Supplied footage from Kyiv: training drills, weapons handling, barracks life. Lerato describes growing doubts and the pressure to relinquish their passport. Scene 4 – Flight and Fear Lerato explains the decision to abscond and current life in Spain under legal uncertainty. Scene 5 – The Law Graphic explainer of the FMAA. Military legal expert Rian Bode: participation or intent constitutes contravention. Professor Michelle Nel: prosecution is legally viable but politically complex. Scene 5 – Dirco Dirco officials at the embassy in Madrid explain their inability to help Lerato when she presented herself. Possible doorstop of embassy staff. Scene 6 – Diplomatic shock Ukrainian and Polish embassy to answer allegations they sent South Africans to the frontlines. Scene 7 – The local context South Africans have fought for Russia, Ukraine and the Israeli Defence Forces. With Russian-aligned contractors reportedly returning home, will the state enforce the law consistently? Scene 7 – Another South African illegal immigrant After almost 4 years living in the shadows, Lerato will now take advantage of a fresh amnesty for immigrants illegally in Spain that will be granted a path to citizenship. We show visuals of hundreds of illegals queuing to take part in this amnesty and speak to one or two. Scene 9 – Return to Lerato (Closing) Back to Lerato: reflection on idealism, consequence and uncertainty. Final question: If neutrality is policy, how is it enforced? Why now South Africa maintains official neutrality in the Ukraine conflict, yet its citizens have participated in multiple foreign wars. With returnees expected and geopolitical tensions ongoing, enforcement of the FMAA becomes unavoidable. This story reframes South Africa’s involvement in this international conflict, poses questions about a domestic legal reckoning and exposes how widespread this issue could be. Carte Blanche will be the only media organisation to show a South African involved in the war on the other side of the fence. Visual & Access ● Concealed on-camera interview ● Exclusive training footage and stills from Kyiv ● Legal graphics explaining the FMAA ● Dirco and Ukrainian embassy and Polish embassy comment requests An exclusive, timely investigation anchored in one young South African’s decision — and the unanswered legal consequences that may follow.

Exclusive proof of South Africans fighting for Kyiv in the Ukraine Russia war

title: The Bay of Broken Promises
oneLiner: Nelson Mandela Bay, despite interventions, ignores treasury, the SIU and the Auditor General warnings and its collapsing under its own rot
summary:
THE FLASH POUND TENDER When animals at their most vulnerable are used to make a quick buck, without any consideration of their welfare, the people behind it, grab our attention. This time it’s a dodgy tender given in an emergency over Christmas to manage the pound, to a company with no experience, and a man that appears to be connected to Acting director Analisa Dyakala, the director of the Health Department, who has a history of handing out emergency contracts. The SPCA have been warning for months that the contract had expired. For 50 years they have managed the pound on behalf of the municipality, then in January after a company called Busy Bee, with no experience was awarded the emergency contract for 6 months, Busy Bee evicted them from their offices. The SPCA was given 24 hours to vacate. They are currently in containers on the property still trying to help the animals that do come in, but that too will come to an end at the end of this week. They are frantically trying to raise money for a new property, but funds are well short of what they need, threatening the existence of the SPCA itself. Why would the municipality do that? Well it seems money and spite may be two drivers of their actions. The metro didn’t like the SPCA asking for its bills to be paid on time, and the ACTING HEALTH DIRECTOR Analise Dyakala may have seen a gap to make a quick buck. What she didn’t count on was the fury of the public at what is unfolding – which is already an animal welfare crisis. Meanwhile two million rand allocated to build a new pound has disappeared and Dyakala told councilors in November she has no idea where the money went. But co-incidentally in August, Dyakala bought a new property for R2.5 million rand. Even more suspicious is that a pitbull that was flagged by Darren Mann, the broadcaster who visited the pound, was taken to a small holding in Crockart’s hope, owned by Analisa Dyakala. Shots rang out and the pit bull has disappeared and the new owner of the pound Stanley Adam, apparently spent the night at this property. Critics are questioning whether a romantic relationship exists between these two people. But when questions are asked, about the competency, the impending animal welfare crisis and the deeply suspicious money trail, all that the municipality will say is that everything is above board and its confidential. These responses have infuriated the public who are simply not buying it. The complete absence of transparency, the obvious question unanswered around what looks like a suspicious transaction is symptomatic of such a deep malaise of rot that hangs over this Metro. With just over a million residents the R30 billion rand in unauthorized, irregular, wasteful expenditure is the largest in the country. It will be impossible for this money to be recovered.

An unfolding drama that could lead to animal abuse, a money trail and corrupt officials
caseStudies: Babalwa Lobishe

Years of legal wrangling later, one man, now in his 80s, is still resisting extradition. But in the wake of our story, pressure has grown – and yet more victims have come forward.

title: Book Hotel: A hotel where stories sleep on the shelves
oneLiner: What if you could check into a hotel and wake up inside a story? Well you can inside the Royal Hotel in Bethulie Free State. One of South Africa's hidden gem's a hotel in the form of a massive book co
summary:
The hotel is significant for its history with the Anglo-Boer War. The hotel itself once served as a refuge and gathering place during turbulent times, it was used as a headquarters for the British Soldiers. As the years progressed it became a social spot with its famous bar and stage for Afrikaans singers to perform. In the 2000s it was acquired by Anthony Hocking who began his collection. Literally books on every part of the place, kitchen, bathroom, living room and furniture resembling books. Also in Bethulie is one of the worst run concentration camps where Afrikaans women and children were kept. Because of this almost 2000 died from disease and mulnutrition. There is a wall of rememberance erected there today.

In the quiet Free State town of Bethulie stands the Royal Hotel better known as The House of Stories where 120,000 books line the walls, vinyl records hum softly in the background, and history lingers in the creak of wooden floors. The Royal Hotel is one of only five “book hotels” in the world.

title: Crayfish Crackdown / Poachers vs Patrols
oneLiner: On KwaZulu-Natal’s coastline, a community task force patrols the shore, trying to protect a fragile balance between conservation, crime and survival.
summary:
Driving along the N2 on the KZN coast, it is not unusual to find roadside vendors selling everything from avocados and golf balls to crayfish — despite the species being strictly protected and currently in closed season. This story follows the Coastal Marine Task Force (CMTF), a relatively new multi-agency enforcement group working alongside SAPS and the Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment, as they conduct anti-poaching operations during a period when it is illegal to possess any crayfish. Many of the members previously operated as informal community vigilantes, responding to growing frustration around coastal crime and marine poaching before formal partnerships with authorities were established. The story explores how that transition from community enforcement to recognised operational support has shaped both the task force and the communities they operate within. Through embedded access, the insert focuses on the people within the task force — who they are, what motivates them, and the risks they face as they attempt to protect marine resources while navigating tensions with coastal communities dependent on ocean harvesting for survival. Crayfish poaching serves as the narrative thread, allowing the story to move between enforcement operations, harvesting communities, roadside trade and the legal small-scale fishing sector.

Embedded Access to the Coastal Marine Task Force Rare, frontline access to a fast-growing, community-driven enforcement unit working alongside SAPS and DFFE during active anti-poaching operations. Powerful Character-Driven Storytelling Compelling personal journeys within the task force, including members with direct past links to poaching and coastal crime, creating authentic and emotionally layered storytelling. Time-Critical Filming Window Filmed during the final days of the closed crayfish season and the February new moon spring tide — a peak period for illegal harvesting and enforcement activity that is difficult to capture at any other time. Crayfish as More Than a Commodity The story reframes crayfish as a vital reef species, using underwater footage and ecological context to raise environmental stakes beyond the seafood trade. High-Impact Visual Storytelling Night patrols, spring tide rock pools, roadside trade, enforcement busts and underwater reef environments create a visually dynamic and cinematic narrative.

title: Viv the Violin
summary: FINDING VIV On her tenth birthday, Diana Neille is given a violin by her father, a gift that carries weight long before its meaning is fully understood, because to raise a violinist is to endure years of unmelodious sound, the scrape of bow on string that can feel like chalk dragged across a school board, demanding patience before it offers anything like beauty in return. Diana practises, she plays in eisteddfods, and slowly, through the accumulation of hours and repetition, the violin settles into her body, becoming part of her muscle memory, something held instinctively between chin and shoulder, a physical extension through which her musical voice reaches the world. She names the violin Viv. Then, twelve years ago, Viv disappears, stolen during a house robbery at a moment when Diana’s life is already unsettled. At the police station, the charge office is full of people reporting hijackings, assaults and murders, and it feels almost impossible to explain that what has been taken is a violin, an object that is deeply personal but difficult to place alongside the violence surrounding it. Instead of persisting there, Diana turns elsewhere, appealing to a different kind of authority, the diffuse reach of the internet. She creates a Facebook page and writes that she has lost what feels like a limb, a violin she calls Viv, carefully listing every identifying detail she can remember. One detail matters more than the rest: the bridge was hand carved by her violin teacher and mentor, Bernard Wozny, a respected luthier who signs his bridges and stamps his name into the wood. And then she waits. Days turn into months, months into years, and eventually more than a decade passes with no response. Diana buys another violin, one that does the job but never quite feels right, its sound unfamiliar, its weight slightly off, and playing becomes effort rather than instinct. Over time, the sharpness of the loss fades, and Diana moves away from music making and into film making, carrying the memory of Viv quietly rather than actively. Recently, at supper, Diana’s niece tells her that she has started learning the violin, and Diana says she wishes she could have passed Viv down to her. If this were a piece of music, this would be the long pause, a rest held in the score. Not long after that pause, Diana receives a message from a stranger called Kyle, who says he thinks he may have her violin. At this point the story shifts, becoming a kind of whodunnit told in reverse. How did the violin survive? Where has it been all this time? Who handled it, and how did it make its way back? Kyle explains that while cataloguing his collection of instruments and music memorabilia, he noticed a name carved into a violin bridge. Curious, he searched it, and the old Facebook page appeared. He tells Diana that he bought a large collection of instruments from a friend who emigrated overseas, and that among them was this violin, which his friend had bought years earlier from a Cash Converters in Johannesburg, shortly after the original robbery. Kyle is an unlikely detective. Formerly a data analyst, now a devoted collector of musical objects, his tastes are eclectic rather than classical, his house filled with instruments and memorabilia gathered for love rather than profit. He meets Diana at a Woolworths, and when he walks in, he is carrying the case. Inside it is Viv. When the violin is found, Diana contacts her former teacher, Bernard Wozny, the man who carved and signed the bridge that ultimately solved the mystery. Bernard is now in his eighties, recently weakened by a stroke that has forced him to give up his workshop and pass his tools on to a younger luthier, Albertus Bakkes. There is another unresolved thread here too: Bernard’s own home was robbed not long ago, and several violins he had restored were stolen and never recovered. Viv is taken to see him. Bernard recognises the instrument immediately, not by its sound, but by the bridge. The question that remains is simple and unanswered: how many more stories like this are still sitting quietly in cases, waiting for the right detail to be noticed.
caseStudies: Diana Neille Kyle Fenton Albertus Bekker Bernard Wozny

title: Pedigree Lies
oneLiner: Families paid for pedigree puppies. What they got instead was heartbreak. When the puppy never arrives… where does the money go?
summary:
Pedigree Lies - She promised pedigree puppies. What followed were excuses, heartbreak, and court battles. It’s a consumer-fraud story with court action happening this week, backed by financial records, showing how someone kept taking money while unable to deliver — and why the system didn’t stop it sooner. This investigation centres on Nolene Pretorius, currently a Gold Retriever breeder operating from Middelburg. She operated under various names including Burenwag Golden Retrievers, Jubilee Golden Retrievers, and Nolene Golden Puppies. (Also Dreamland, which is owned by someone else.) While her operation appeared legitimate on the surface — complete with contracts, photos, videos of puppies, and claims of KUSA registration — Carte Blanche has identified at least 15–20 confirmed case studies (70 complaints on Facebook group) across multiple provinces alleging the same pattern: upfront payments demanded; puppies promised and delayed; shifting explanations involving “nature”, “parvo”, or “dead litters”; refunds refused, delayed, or only partially paid For the few buyers who did receive a puppy, the consequences were often devastating… But this isn’t just another puppy scam. Beneath the lies, court records and financial evidence reveal the true state of the operation.________________________________________ A Pattern Across Provinces Victims from the Western Cape, Gauteng and Mpumalanga describe near-identical experiences: upfront payments, shifting timelines, claims of dead or sick litters, hostility when questioned, and at best partial refunds. Jason’s court case has allowed these buyers to find one another, revealing a pattern that extends far beyond a single dispute. The Confrontation The investigation culminates in Middelburg, where Carte Blanche would seek to accompany the sheriff executing a court order, documenting any attachment of assets and confronting Nolene Pretorius with the ruling, the allegations, and the growing list of victims. This is both a consumer fraud story and an animal welfare story. At its core, it’s about trust exploited — and one individual’s determination to force accountability when the system appeared slow to respond. For dozens of families — and dogs like Charlie and Bali — this investigation may be the first real chance at justice. For years, buyers chased puppies that never arrived. Now, accountability may finally be catching up. https://www.instagram.com/nolenepretorius11/ https://homeofjubilee.co.za/cgi-sys/suspendedpage.cgi (accoung suspended) https://www.gumtree.co.za/u-seller-listings/nolene-van-buuren/v1u104274424p1 EMOTIVE VISUALS and good visuals from social media and broll will be good with cute puppies… Drama Why – once and for all Papertrail to show that she’s a scammer Confront Addition for socials

Jason Baretta – The Legal Backbone: At the heart of the investigation is Jason Baretta, whose attempt to buy a family pet became a two-year legal battle. When Jason first dealt with Nolene Pretorius, she was based in Knysna. She appeared credible and professional. Jason paid R12,000 for a Golden Retriever puppy. After repeated delays, communication deteriorated. Jason received aggressive voice notes, followed by claims that puppies had died — including allegations of parvovirus, accompanied by graphic images. Shortly thereafter, Nolene cut off contact. Jason then tracked her to Middelburg and pursued the matter through Small Claims Court. Over two years, he has won every stage of the process. But it was the court process itself that revealed the most disturbing findings. Through court-ordered scrutiny of Nolene Pretorius’s bank statements, a troubling picture emerged: • In just a three-month period, she took money from at least 14 new buyers • This was despite having a significant backlog of customers who had already paid and were still waiting for puppies • The financials showed no realistic capacity to deliver puppies to either old or new buyers • Despite this, money continued to be accepted Jason says the evidence revealed that she was continuing to take money while knowing she could not deliver puppies — a key indicator of intent, not misfortune. The financial records also reflected spending on non-essential and luxury items, suggesting buyer funds were not being ring-fenced for animal care or breeding costs. Jason’s case is now due in Middelburg court this Friday (23 January), where he expects to receive the final authorisation allowing the sheriff to attach assets at Nolene Pretorius’s property. We can accompany the sheriff when they go into the property. ________________________________________ Natasha & Charlie – When the Puppy Did Arrive Not all buyers walked away empty-handed. Natasha, based in Cape Town, did receive a puppy — Charlie. But by just five months old, Charlie was diagnosed with: severe bilateral elbow dysplasia; cryptorchidism; fractures and joint incongruency consistent with genetic and irresponsible breeding Veterinary experts say these conditions are commonly linked to: breeding dogs with poor elbow scores, lack of genetic screening, unethical breeding practices Charlie has already undergone multiple surgeries and treatments costing well over R50,000, with lifelong pain management expected. ________________________________________ When Puppies Were Delivered — They Were Often Sick Another buyer, Cayla van den Heever, eventually received her puppy, Bali, after months of delays and contradictory explanations. Within 24–48 hours, Bali was diagnosed with a severe congenital heart defect (tricuspid valve dysplasia). Vets advised euthanasia. Bali was put to sleep shortly after. Buyers allege that the breeder either knew or should have known the puppy was not healthy. OTHER LEGS: The Parvo Narrative Across multiple cases, buyers report being told — often only after full payment — that puppies had died of parvovirus. Vet documentation was disputed or inconsistent, refunds were delayed or refused, and breeding or advertising allegedly continued soon after. Veterinary experts say active parvo outbreaks should halt breeding entirely. The KUSA Question Nolene Pretorius repeatedly claimed her dogs were KUSA registered — a key reason buyers paid premium prices. In these cases, valid KUSA papers were not supplied, some documentation appears misleading, and KUSA says there is no list of "registered breeders," you can only register puppies, which raises serious concerns about misrepresentation.
caseStudies: Jason Baretta Natasha Murray Samandtha van den Heever Nolene Pretorius

title: Rents Due
summary:
This story says: People are homeless not because the state lacks resources — but because those resources are redirected. In July 2024, newly appointed Public Works and Infrastructure Minister Dean Macpherson vowed to drastically reduce government’s reliance on leasing private buildings. Yet last year, four new leases worth R290 million were approved — despite the department sitting with a R30 billion maintenance backlog and owning hundreds of underutilised properties. Public Works says more than 800 lease requests were denied, raising a critical question: Why does leasing still appear to be the default — even when the state already owns buildings that could be refurbished and occupied? Nowhere is this contradiction more stark than in Gauteng. In April 2025, public outrage erupted over the Gauteng Provincial Government’s R34 million monthly rental bill for 11 privately owned buildings — amounting to R408 million a year. Premier Panyaza Lesufi publicly expressed shock, saying he was unaware of the expenditure, and announced an independent probe, promising a report within two months.

This story: Exposes false scarcity Challenges the idea that government failure is accidental
caseStudies: Sabelo Chalufu Zelda Rasilingwane

title: UPDATE: SANDF in the dock
oneLiner: Ongoing developments in the trails of alleged
summary: Three years ago, we began to investigate allegations of a shadowy faction conducting illicit operations from inside our military. Investigations linked a car photographed at the secretive docking of a sanctioned Russian cargo ship in Simon's Town to the abduction of two men in Gauteng. Then, the man investigating the abduction was assassinated. Finally, in June last year, twelve SANDF members were arrested on charges including kidnapping, conspiracy and murder. It looked like a positive development. Instead all twelve were granted bail. What's followed is a protracted legal battle. Last month, a high court judge revoked bail for six of the men, saying they are a danger to society, the state has made a strong case that it has evidence of criminality, and allowing the accused to go free risks threatening the ongoing prosecution and investigation, the safety of witnesses that are involved and potentially whistleblowers. BUT they failed to turn themselves in, instead appealing the order. That appeal was dismissed. In a twist, the SANDF announced early this year that one of the accused, Brigadier Solly Lechoenyo has been promoted to head of Special Forces: the very unit under which the so-called “dirty dozen” operated. Lechoenyo steps into a position once held by his co-accused, Brigadier Herbert Mashego. This promotion comes even as the SANDF faces censure for apparently ignoring a Presidential order to remove Iranian warships from multinational naval exercises last month. As the wheels of justice slowly turn, the question remains: are the forces entrusted with our country’s safety operating as a law unto themselves?

title: The Science of Laughter
oneLiner: In South Africa’s most overstretched hospitals, a small band of entertainers is proving that laughter isn’t just comic relief — it may be a quiet, evidence-backed form of medicine.
summary: They arrive with red noses, music, jokes and oversized energy ,but what the Laughter Heroes do is far more than entertainment. At Lombano Hospice, Chris Hani Baragwanath Academic Hospital, and Helen Joseph Hospital, a small group of trained performers regularly enter some of the most emotionally and physically demanding spaces in South African healthcare. Their job is simple: make sick children laugh. The impact, however, may be far more complex — and scientifically significant. For decades, laughter has been associated with improved wellbeing. From reduced stress hormones and lowered blood pressure, to improved immune response and pain tolerance, international research increasingly suggests that humour and play can be powerful therapeutic tools — particularly for children undergoing long, invasive, and frightening medical treatments. This is not the romanticised version popularised by Patch Adams; this is structured, intentional intervention in clinical environments. We speak to paediatric oncologists Dr Thandeka Ngcana from Bara and Wits Lecturer and , palliative care specialists and psychologists who work alongside Laughter Heroes and have observed tangible changes in their patients: reduced anxiety before procedures, improved cooperation with treatment, better mood regulation, and in some cases, faster recovery times. Dr Ngcana will speak anecdotally but critically ,drawing on real case studies and years of frontline experience, while referencing peer-reviewed research that supports these observations. At Lombano Hospice, laughter becomes a tool for dignity and relief at end-of-life care. At Bara and Helen Joseph, it helps children reclaim moments of childhood in sterile, intimidating hospital wards. For parents and staff, the presence of Laughter Heroes often shifts the emotional temperature of entire wards ,easing burnout and restoring humanity in spaces dominated by illness. We follow the Laughter Heroes themselves The Marvelous Stewart Mcnab(A…lets just say a quite boisterous clown and the rather awkward clown Themba Mathabela) ,trained practitioners who understand boundaries, trauma, and timing. Their work requires emotional intelligence, resilience, and an ability to read medical environments in real time. This is not performance for applause, but precision interaction designed to support healing. Through observational filming, expert interviews, and case studies, this story looks at whether laughter can be measured, studied, and respected as part of modern medicine and why South Africa’s most overstretched hospitals may need it now more than ever.
caseStudies: Stewart Kaan Thandeka Ngcana Themba Mathabela Fransiska Van Niekerk

title: PLETT CULT
oneLiner: A small town murder, linked to a spiritual cult.
summary:
Plettenberg Bay is widely seen as a low-crime, holiday town - not a place associated with violent death. But on Sunday, 18 January 2026, that perception was shattered when Nicky van Heerden, a 54-year-old former police detective, was found dead near the Keurbooms River after reports of a woman screaming. The man charged with her murder is Bevan van Druten, a Garden Route driftwood sculptor whose work has appeared widely both locally and internationally. He denies the charge; the State is opposing bail. What makes this a Carte Blanche story is what existed before that night. Long before Nicky met him, at least six women had already sought protection orders against Van Druten, alleging intimidation and threatening behaviour. Each case was treated in isolation, no escalation followed. Since Van Druten’s arrest, residents - including pensioners - have told media they were terrified of him for years, claims police say are not part of the murder case but which raise serious questions about what was known and ignored. Then there’s the voice note. Ten minutes and 29 seconds long, recorded shortly before Nicky’s death and sent to WhatsApp contacts. According to reporting, it reflects fear and distress and is now with investigators as they reconstruct her final hours. Nicky was not naïve, she was a detective. So how does someone trained to assess danger end up dead when warning signs were already on record? This story is about how systems fail when risk is documented but never connected.

One man wreaked havoc across the Garden Route for over two decades. But it would take the murder of a former police detective for him to face the law.
caseStudies: Rocco Viljoen Samantha Cartwright Hein Bruwer

Three years later, they have surpassed all expectations and walked away as overall winners of the Cape 2 Rio Yacht Race.

title: HOT WATER, DIRTY BUSINESS
oneLiner: Cheap refurbished geysers cut costs, but also corners when it comes to safety and compliance – we go undercover to expose a so-called manufacturer putting South African Homes at risk.
summary:
South Africans are under pressure and saving money matters. But when it comes to geysers, South Africa has strict rules on what can be manufactured, refurbished and sold to the public - because when these systems fail, the damage can be catastrophic. In a market driven by quick profits and desperate buyers, those regulations are being ignored.

title: Oscar's Final Fight
oneLiner: Canoeing legend Oscar Chalupsky has survived the toughest oceans in the world. Now he's fighting terminal cancer, and a medical aid system he says would rather fund lawyers than life-saving treatment.
summary:
Oscar Chalupsky is a 62-year-old canoeing legend now fighting for his life. The renowned South African paddler captained the national team at the 1992 Barcelona Olympics and is a 12-time World Surfski Champion. In 2019, he was diagnosed with multiple myeloma, a blood cancer that affects plasma cells. While once considered a death sentence, major medical advances in recent years have transformed how the disease can be treated. Chalupsky began treatment in 2020. In 2023, after his maintenance therapy failed, his oncologist prescribed Daratumumab or Darzalex, a targeted cancer drug now widely used internationally. Despite multiple myeloma being classified as a prescribed minimum benefit under the Medical Schemes Act, which legally requires medical aids to fund treatment regardless of plan type, Discovery Health Medical Scheme agreed to cover only 50 percent of the cost. As a result, Chalupsky was left to pay about R275,000 out of pocket. He lodged a formal complaint with the Council for Medical Schemes, where his legal team argued the treatment was clinically justified and should have been funded in full. Discovery, however, argued the medication fell outside its approved sequencing for this cancer. The Council ruled in Chalupsky’s favour. Discovery refused to pay and has since appealed the decision twice. Discovery's appeal was due to be heard in March, but in an about turn the medical scheme withdrew the appeal just days before our scheduled interview with the CEO. The last ruling was delivered in April 2025, yet the appeal was withdrawn eight months later. Why the delay? Oscar went public with his fight with Discovery in December, and the response was overwhelming. Chalupsky has chosen to make his battle public, saying he is fighting not only for himself but for hundreds of patients facing similar denials. He told me a priest has read him his last rites twice in the past two years, yet he refuses to give up. Discovery has spent an estimated six million rand on legal costs, instead of reimbursing the R275,000. Chalupsky says the scheme, which reports billions in annual profit and has millions of members, is prioritising shareholders over patients. He has received free legal representation and says he has been overwhelmed by public support. A post detailing his struggle on social media drew more than 500,000 engagements. Chalupsky also established a personal fund called No Retreat, No Surrender, which enabled him to seek treatment in China. Within two weeks, he raised two million rand. That treatment ended due to unforeseen circumstances, and he is now preparing to participate in a clinical trial in the United States. Lauren Pretorius from Campaigning for Cancer says South Africa’s medical funding models urgently need reform. She has spent years advocating for cancer patients and says treatments that were unavailable a decade ago are now standard elsewhere, yet often inaccessible locally. Doctors, she says, are forced to rely on outdated therapies because medical aids refuse to fund innovation. She believes patients deserve transparency about what their monthly contributions truly cover. Meanwhile, Chalupsky continues to train three times a day, even while on chemotherapy and steroids. He says he feels a responsibility to fight for those who do not have the same support. “Most people lose the will to fight,” he says. “I won’t.”

Oscar Chalupsky’s fight against cancer has exposed a high-stakes legal battle over whether medical aids must pay for modern, life-saving treatments.
caseStudies: Oscar Chalupsky Clare Chalupsky

title: Goodbye Sandton
oneLiner: We expose a syndicate behind the decay of Sandton.
summary:
We are constantly told property is the best investment because the value appreciates over the years. But what happens to the value of property when squatters move into the neighborhood? Or worse, what happens when a property syndicate hijacks your home? This is what is happening in Bryanston and many other neighborhoods across Sandton. According to the City of Joburg, in Bryanston alone, 17 houses have been hijacked while at least 21 houses have been hijacked in Buccleuch. The syndicate targets homes of owners who live abroad or mostly travel for work. We will focus on exposing the property syndicate because it is important to inform South Africans as well as prevent them from taking over more homes. The city is owed millions in debt for electricity, yet all of these properties seem to have electricity that has been connected illegally. So that means not only are they stealing from the homeowner but they are also stealing from the city and the taxpayers. Some of the houses also have free access to water, while the rest of South Africans have to pay for water.

We will have two confrontations.
caseStudies: Clint Brink Maggie Nkomo X X

title: Livestock lockdown
oneLiner: Foot-and-mouth disease didn’t defeat South Africa’s livestock industry, delay did, in a system where permission mattered more than prevention
summary:
Foot-and-mouth disease in South Africa has crossed a critical threshold. What began as a series of outbreaks has evolved into an endemic crisis affecting multiple provinces, collapsing livestock markets, and threatening food security. Experts warn the country may not yet have reached the peak of the outbreak. South Africa currently has SAT-1, SAT-2 and SAT-3 strains circulating, with sheep and pigs now also affected, widening the crisis beyond cattle. South Africa has an estimated 14 million cattle, of which approximately 5 million are communal cattle. For millions of households, especially in rural areas, livestock functions as a bank. Cattle are sold to buy food, pay school fees, and cover medical bills. Quarantine restrictions, which can last up to a year, prevent farmers from selling animals while costs continue to rise. Livestock must still be fed and maintained, but without income. Auctions have been postponed for months, leaving farmers with no route to market. Many describe the situation as a COVID-style lockdown for cattle farmers, except this time there is no relief fund, no safety net, and no timeline. South Africa requires an estimated 100 million vaccine doses immediately, followed by another 100 million within three months, to suppress transmission. Yet the state-owned manufacturer, Onderstepoort Biological Products (OBP), is unable to meet this demand. Between 1984 and 2006, OBP successfully produced foot-and-mouth vaccines, but these were based on virus strains circulating at the time. Since then, the virus has mutated. New strains emerged, but updated genetic material was not submitted timeously to the international reference laboratory in the United Kingdom, where strain confirmation and vaccine matching are conducted. As a member of the World Organisation for Animal Health, South Africa is expected to submit this material, but industry stakeholders allege this was delayed to retain intellectual property control. The department disputes aspects of this timeline, stating samples are being prepared, but infections continue to spread. An Argentinian manufacturer with decades of experience in foot-and-mouth disease control has licensed a South African private company to distribute vaccines compatible with earlier strains. These vaccines could be imported under Section 21 of South Africa’s medicines legislation. However, even if regulatory approval is granted, import permits require authorisation by the Director of Animal Health. That authority currently rests with a single office, and industry stakeholders allege that approvals have stalled during the most critical phase of the crisis. In the absence of decisive leadership, pressure has mounted to route all vaccine supply through OBP, despite its inability to produce at scale. The human cost is escalating. Large commercial dairy farms have become sites of mass animal burials. A volunteer-run crisis hotline has been established to deal with suicide threats from farmers facing financial ruin. Critics argue the state has normalised the outbreak rather than stopped it, leaving farmers powerless, animals suffering, and livelihoods destroyed.

This investigation exposes how South Africa’s worst animal-health disaster is unfolding as the cure is trapped by bureaucracy and the greed embedded in a system that controls it.
caseStudies: Corne Nel
experts: Danie Odendaal Rodolfo Bellinzoni Theo De Jageer John Steenhuizen Mooketsi Ramoketsi

title: Studio interview: Ricardo Teixeira
oneLiner: A defence analyst joins us in studio to discuss disturbing allegations that the national defence forces has defied presidential orders.
summary:
This week, in Simons Town in the Western Cape, our navy took part in sea drills with counterparts from the so-called BRICS Plus countries. Led by China, the exercise included ships from Russia and, more notably, Iran. Described as an exercise in strengthening ties, the gathering has been controversial from the start. But, in the past few days it’s emerged that the SANDF may have defied an order from its Commander-in-Chief, President Ramaphosa, for Iran to be excluded. Joining us in studio to discuss what happened is defence analyst at the Institute for Race Relations, Ricardo Teixeira.

It was an unusual sight for locals this week, as Simon's Town harbour is filled with warships. But did the SANDF defy a direct order in sending an Iranian ship to sea?

title: N2 Hell Run
oneLiner: The N2 approaching CT International airport is a crime hot spot - how do you stop this scourge? Will a R180 million rand wall make a difference?
summary:
There are 285 CCTV camera monitored 24/7. Concrete fences constructed which have been systematically torn down. The pedestrian bridges covered with wire” cages”. 37 new officers deployed in October 2025, increased number of patrol officers and vehicles and a ghost squad in place. Now they are talking about constructing R180 million rand wall. SANRAL has already begun constructing a wall on the R300 as “a Pilot" – but this is one of the most elusive problems to police as perpetrators pop up and disappear within minutes, any time of the day or night.

The N2 approaching Cape Town International airport and the R300 have long been described as “The Hell Run” as far back as 2005 and the City of Cape Town and Sanral have attempted to deal with the problem. But it remains one of the most dangerous stretches of road that even law enforcement is fearful to hang around. 2025 was a bumper holiday season for Cape Town- and everybody cashed in- and so did the gangs of kids attacking passing motorist and motorcyclists.

title: War in the DA. John Steenhuizen and Willie Aucamp versus Dion George.
oneLiner: Brutus. Clandestine. Captured. Conflicted. John Steenhuizen, leader of the DA has deliberately abused his power to advance his own political interests, and he is aiding and abetting singular commercia
summary:
Brutus. Clandestine. Captured. Conflicted. John Steenhuizen, leader of the DA has deliberately abused his power to advance his own political interests, and he is aiding and abetting singular commercial interests that violate South Africa’s own animal welfare legislation. So says Dion George who was replaced as minister of the Environment, Forestry and Fisheries late in 2025 by Willie Aucamp, a man that George accuses of not declaring his commercial interests, and with links to the captive lion industry- the very industry George was trying to shut down. For his part, Aucamp has also put in a complaint to the public protector against Dion George for possible abuse of state resources. George claims this is a smear campaign with no evidence. In his latest complaint to the public protector, Dion George has released his inner Fire Horse onto the DA leader. He accuses him of cadre deployment amongst a raft of other allegations. George’s accusations are serious and not good for the DA in an election year. George accounts how, as he sought to build on the legacy of Barbara Creecy, who was in the process of dismantling the captive breeding industry of lions, an industry with links to international crime syndicates, Aucamp and Steenhuizen, he claims are fraternizing with members of this industry and he provides proof of these allegations. In effect his complaint implies that both Steenhuizen and Aucamp are captured by this industry and are determined to undo all the work done by the high-level panel whose recommendations to phase out this cruel practice with no conservation value, is being turned around. George questions why. He has requested the public protector to gather the full record of communications between Steenhuizen and the president on this matter and any communications between Willie Aucamp and PHASA, Wildlife Ranching and SucoSA – all vociferous members of the captive breeding industry.

A story of conflict, accusations at the heart of the DA, and a former minister of the Environment spiling the tea on the leader of the opposition in an election year.
caseStudies: Dion George John Steenhuizen

title: GOING TO WAR - Uber drivers tempted to the Russian frontline
oneLiner: We investigate the underground recruitment drive of Zimbabwean Uber drivers to fight on the Russian frontline for pay
summary:
Russia is losing thousands of soldiers on the frontline in the war against Ukraine, in a combat which resembles World War 1 trench warfare in the scale of death and destruction. To bolster its war effort, Russia is recruiting vulnerable communities in developing nations, luring young men under false pretences to fight with little training and no understanding of the war for financial gain against the Ukrainian army and drones. Already there is a high-profile criminal investigation underway in South Africa against the daughter of the ex-President Jacob Zuma, Duduzile Sambudla-Zuma, as well as a Safm broadcaster, Patricia Mantula, and others for attempting and succeeding to lure young South Africans into a situation which could easily cost them their lives and which is illegal. Now we have access to a Zimbabwean community which is being duped in the same way, through a closed WhatsApp group available to uber drivers in Jozi.

We have exclusive access to WhatsApp networks which reveal how the recruitment of Zim uber drivers works, and what impact it is having in this vulnerable community in Gauteng, when individuals are lured with the promise of money, jobs and citizenship to the frontline of the Ukraine/Russian war where there chances of survival are slim.
caseStudies: Darren Olivier Bornwell Siya Nkiwane Mawie Malinga Naadira Munshi Olexander Scherba

title: Gautrain 2.0 – Full Steam Ahead, or Financial Dead-End?
oneLiner: Tonight on Carte Blanche we ask if the proposed Gautrain expansion will transform the province’s transport, or be a fast-track to spending billions on a single project
summary:
Hailed as an answer to Gauteng’s congestion problems – specifically on the N1 between Tshwane and Johannesburg - the Gautrain has failed to reach pre-launch ridership numbers or reduce congestion. While it is world class, clean, on time, and safe, the Gautrain is also expensive and out of reach of poorer commuters, it is aimed at people who are already mobile, and it is running at a massive loss, costing taxpayers billions of Rands through the PG annually. Gautrain expenditure is also diverting funds from other transport solutions in poorer communities, raising the question of where the GPG’s priorities lie in providing mobility solutions for all in the province. In this context, is an extension of the service (which will cost additional billions to construct and maintain) viable and necessary, and why does the Gauteng Premier, his government, and the GMA believe it is? Critically, the piece will also ask the question of why there is so much secrecy around the project, and why the GPG and the GMA have been more forthcoming with the public.

A comprehensive, easy-to-understand explanation of the current Gautrain costs, the proposed expansion plans, and what the people who are most affected have to say about it. Unlike other reports which have already been written on the proposed extensions, this story will unpack the contentious issue of the justification of the expansions, especially in the context of the current system which has already cost Gauteng taxpayers close to R23bn because of low ridership numbers.
caseStudies: Edwin Mmutlane JC Wouters Nicolette Joubert

title: DEATH IN THE INNER CITY
oneLiner: DJ Warras wanted to fix crime in Joburg’s inner city. Instead, he ended up a victim of it.
summary:
On 16 December 2025, DJ Warras (Warrick Stock) was shot dead in broad daylight outside Zambezi House in Johannesburg’s CBD. There is no publicly released CCTV footage of the shooting. What is known comes from police statements, court records, and eyewitness accounts. DJ Warras was not performing or socialising, he was working - involved in security-related operations linked to hijacked buildings - spaces widely recognised as operating under organised criminal control. This investigation examines what was known before the killing, including documented threats and multiple protection orders, what protection existed in practice, and how the case is now unfolding as it enters court. It situates DJ Warras’ death within two overlapping realities: the largely hidden violence surrounding hijacked buildings, and the reality of organised crime in Joburg’s inner city. With new on-record information emerging about a hijacked-buildings intervention blueprint under development at the time of his death, and the case returning to court on 06 January, 2026, the story interrogates risk, protection and accountability while the record is still being written.

New information has emerged over the murder and targeted attacks.
