title: Pride, pollution and prejudice
oneLiner: South Africa's ghastly history of forced removals is being repeated by Sasol in the United States south
summary:
A small Louisiana community of Mossville — a settlement founded in the late 1700s by the descendants of freed slaves is about to be wiped out by Sasol. Once home to over 8,000 people, it now stands half-empty, sick, and fading. And at the centre of this slow erasure is Sasol — a proudly South African petrochemical giant that champions transformation and empowerment at home, but whose operations in the United States have left a historic Black community fighting for survival. In 2013, Sasol announced an $8.1-billion expansion of its Lake Charles industrial footprint — the largest single foreign manufacturing investment in America at the time. It came with a “voluntary” buyout programme for residents of neighbouring Mossville. But families say the choice was false: accept a payout far below the real cost of uprooting your life, or remain in a community being choked by pollution, deteriorating health, and the disappearance of public services. Today, Mossville is on the verge of vanishing entirely. This is the story of the people still holding on — and the South African multinational they say helped push them to the brink. The heart of the film is the fate of Stacey Ryan, once the last man standing in Uptown Mossville, now displaced and in declining health. Around him: families like Monique Harden, Erica Jackson, and community organiser Destinee Jones, who are trying to save what remains of a once-proud Black homeland. This is not a story told through emissions charts or policy jargon — it is a story of land, loss, and legacy. A South African company’s decisions, and the American community paying the price. Protagonists ● Stacey Ryan – The final holdout of Uptown Mossville, forced out as his health faltered. ● Monique Harden – Long-time advocate chronicling Mossville’s environmental trauma. ● Erica Jackson – One of the last homeowners refusing to walk away, but running out of room to fight. ● Destinee Jones – Organiser working to preserve what’s left of a 200-year-old Black community. ● Maryum Jordan (EarthRights) – Lawyer representing affected families in ongoing legal battles. ● Sasol North America executives – The company at the centre of the controversy (requested on-camera). Key Themes 1. A Community Being Erased Mossville once represented Black self-determination — a rare place where freed slaves built land, homes, and generational security. Now: ● Empty houses ● Vanishing streets ● Elderly residents stranded ● Ancestral land being swallowed by industry The story is not about history — it’s about witnessing a community disappear in real time. 2. The Sasol Expansion ● 2000: Sasol purchases land in the area. ● 2013: Announces an $8.1bn expansion — the largest manufacturing FDI in US history at the time. ● Introduces voluntary buyouts, soon criticised as coercive. ● Many residents claim they were pressured: either sell, or remain in an increasingly hostile environment. ● Those who stayed saw their properties rezoned to “heavy industrial” and services cut. For many, the payout didn’t buy freedom — it bought medical debt. 3. Pollution, Health and the EPA Exemption Sasol received a Trump-era EPA exemption, despite being named the second-worst air polluter in the United States by the EPA’s own toxic release inventory. Resulting impacts: ● asthma ● rare cancers ● chronic respiratory illness ● premature deaths ● escalating medical bills Residents link their declining health directly to a lifetime of industrial exposure. 4. Forced Choices, Shrinking Futures With buyouts halted due to “market conditions”, the remaining families face impossible decisions. ● Erica Jackson: tired, cornered, but still refusing to leave. ● Monique Harden: documenting the human cost with decades of archives. ● Destinee Jones: offering a generational voice on the collapse of Black landownership. For them, leaving is not just relocation — it’s erasure. 5. Accountability Across Borders Sasol is a company deeply entwined with South Africa’s identity: job creator, empowerment story, global flagship. But Mossville raises a question South Africans have never seen asked: What does responsibility look like when the harm is exported? This film brings that accountability home. Visual Approach Bookends in Mossville Opening shot: Driving through Uptown Mossville — foundations where homes once stood, chimneys with no houses attached, petrochemical stacks rising in the background. Bauer standing in the middle of a silent street once filled with children. Closing shot: Outside Sasol’s Lake Charles facility. If they refuse an interview, a confrontation at the gates underscores the silence. Community Texture ● Archive photos of families, churches, school events ● Slow walk-throughs of abandoned blocks ● Tracking shots of chemical flares lighting the night sky ● Close-ups of inhalers, medical records, rezoning notices ● Homes with air purifiers running 24/7 ● Residents showing physical scars, bottled tap water, damaged property Character-Driven Moments ● Stacey Ryan revisiting the plot where his house once stood ● Erica Jackson holding onto her home despite constant pressure ● Destinee Jones organising meetings in a nearly empty neighbourhood ● Lawyers walking us through EPA documents and legal filings Atmosphere as Narrative Not statistics — stakes. Not corporate statements — community testimony. Sound design built from: ● plant machinery ● the low roar of chemical stacks ● the quiet of a town nearly gone

No other South African media house has covered this story in person in Mossville, Louisiana

title: UPDATE: Fracking
oneLiner: The debate about fracking is back on radars as government publishes new amended regulations for public comment.
summary: A decade ago, it was the source of a raging debate over the future of the Karoo. Fracking, or hydraulic fracturing, is a controversial mining method. Water, sand and chemicals are pumped into the ground at high pressure to open up cracks deep underground and release oil and gas. It’s illegal in several countries, including South Africa. But now that’s about to change. In 2012, government lifted a year-old moratorium, allowing companies to apply for exploration licences. There was immediate backlash from civil and environmental groups across the country. In 2019, a long court battle came to an end when the Supreme Court of Appeal declared the initial fracking regulations unlawful, ordering that responsibility for the environmental regulation lies with the Department of Environmental Affairs – not the Department of Mineral Resources. But now the fight is back on. The amended regulations have incorporated recommendations by TKAG and others, but Deal says there are still significant concerns, like the fact that companies aren’t required to assess the health of surrounding communities before exploration begins. When a well closes, toxic chemicals can leach into the ground and water – but if information about the chemicals used is no longer available, there is no way to assess or reduce the damage. And strangest of all: a clause that allows automatic approval of licences. The public has until the 7th of December to comment on the amended regulations. If they pass, it's estimated that full-scale fracking will begin in the Karoo – and perhaps elsewhere - within the next two to three years.

title: Zachary's Law
oneLiner: -In the fight between money and medicine, a little boy’s life is the line they’re willing to cross.
summary:
Zachary’s Law -In the fight between money and medicine, a little boy’s life is the line they’re willing to cross.________________________________________ Opening Act [OPENING – VISUAL SEQUENCE] Raining, water dripping, and it dissolves into a drip bag filling – an infusion. The drip line is prepared for infusion by Zach’s parents… See Zachary getting the infusion. Govan watches. (Govan VO) This tiny vial carries a price tag of R3 million a year, and it’s the treatment that keeps Zach alive. And although he’s able to get it today… it’s because it’s being donated, not because his medical aid is paying. (Govan link) Imagine hearing your child needs life-saving treatment — and then your medical aid turns you away. What would you do? For Jacques and Michaney de Wet, the answer was simple: you fight. (Govan VO) Zachary is five years old. He has a rare genetic condition called Hunter Syndrome — or MPS II — that slowly attacks the body and brain. There’s only one treatment that can slow the disease down: Elaprase. Each vial costs thousands of rand, and he needs it every week. (Govan Link) To understand this case, we need to talk about something called a Prescribed Minimum Benefit — or a PMB. It’s the law that protects every medical-aid member in South Africa. And for families like Zachary’s, it can be the difference between life and death. (Govan VO) PMBs are the treatments that medical aids must pay for — in full — no matter which plan you’re on, or how much the treatment costs. The law says the standard of care is what the state provides. So if a government hospital offers a particular treatment for a PMB condition, every medical aid has to match it. Link: In Zachary’s case, the state treats Hunter Syndrome with a drug called Elaprase. That means Elaprase is the legal minimum standard of care. But despite this Medihelp – the families’ medical aid - still refuses to pay. ACT 1 ends… RECAP OF previous story: VO: In 2022, we first met Jacques and Michaney de Wet, and their toddler Zachary. Michaney: “When he learns something new, you’re almost… holding your breath. Because you don’t know how long he’ll be able to keep it.” VO: He’s just been newly diagnosed, and they were already facing Medihelp’s refusal to pay. Jacques: “If his heart deteriorates… if he loses his ability to walk or talk… there’s nothing we can do. That’s why we can’t afford to wait.” VO: And that’s why our story ended with them going to court. LINK outside court: Today, that same family stands at the centre of a showdown with three court orders, a contempt ruling, and the possibility of a medical-aid executive going to jail — all because a five-year-old boy needs treatment the law says he must receive. Fade to black… Visuals: Footage of Zachary laughing at home, playing with toy cars, his parents preparing his medication day. Visuals: Cut to Michaney and Jacques interview – intimate home setting. (Michaney/Jacques) When Medihelp refused to pay, we had no choice. His doctors said without Elaprase, he wouldn’t survive. So we took them to court. TIMELINE DEVICE: [Govan VO) [COURT VISUALS / DOCUMENT GRAPHICS] In 2022, Judge Anthony Millar ruled in the family’s favour — finding that Hunter Syndrome is a Prescribed Minimum Benefit, or PMB, and that Elaprase is standard treatment, because it’s provided in public hospitals. Megan Harrington-Johnson and her firm’s team took the case on pro bono, Medihelp was ordered to pay within 30 days. (MEGAN HJ) That judgment was clear — the law says medical aids must fund PMB conditions in full. But Medihelp chose to fight instead of pay. But also Millar noted, that the Medihelp conceded it was a PMB. Read it with Megan… GOVAN VO: Medihelp’s argument? The family hadn’t filled out the right paperwork. The billing codes were wrong — basically, ‘computer says no.’ You’d think the battle ended there right? But instead, Medihelp would just stall and appeal for the next three years – and refuse to comply with the order the pay. GOVAN (VO): But what about Zachary in the meantime? His treatment continued thanks to donations and the pharmaceutical company supplying Elaprase while the legal battle drags on. MICHANEY (to camera): “It’s donated. Every vial. That’s the only reason he’s still alive.” [TRANSITION – CHILD PLAYING / MUSIC SWELL] Fade to black. Title card: “ACT 2 – The Bigger Battle” WHO ARE MEDIHELP? VO: Medihelp is one of South Africa’s big six open medical schemes — more than 200,000 members, over 120 years old, and entirely non-profit. In 2023 alone, it held more than R2.3 billion in assets and paid out over R3.3 billion in claims. At its helm is Principal Officer Varsha Vala, the person legally responsible for ensuring Medihelp complies with the Medical Schemes Act and with court orders. LINK: So this isn’t an anonymous bureaucracy. It’s one of the country’s major medical aids — and a leader who could personally face the consequences if the scheme continues to defy the law. ________________________________________ ACT 2 – THE PRECEDENT THAT COULD CHANGE EVERYTHING VO: Timeline: After the 2022 case, Medihelp appealed, and went to the Council for Medical Schemes, while initially they ruled in favour of Medihelp that decision was overturned – and importantly Elaprase was again deemed a PMB. Megan: Medihelp wants to adhere to the first decision, and is trying to ignore all the other decisions that are not in their favour – which is everything. VO: But this decision was again appealed by both sides. Megan: They said that despite it being a PMB, Medihelp didn’t have to pay because weren’t solvent. GOVAN LINK : This is Medihelp’s strongest defence, they say they legally cannot pay. The scheme told the medical regulator that its solvency ratio has dropped below the required 25 percent — and that funding Elaprase would breach solvency laws and threaten the financial stability of the entire scheme. But the courts have been clear on this: solvency is not an excuse to refuse a Prescribed Minimum Benefit. Judges have rejected this argument every time it’s been raised, saying solvency rules exist to protect members, not to deny them life-saving treatment. While that appeal process is underway, Megan’s team again took Medihelp to court, which only happened in November last year (THIS WILL AIR IN JAN). Megan: This was to make them comply with a court order to pay. VO: In short the court agreed, Medihelp must pay pending the CMS appeal process. However, Judge Swanepoel was scathing. [COURT GRAPHIC – PULL QUOTES] “I have no doubt the applicant is in contempt of the order of Millar J.” – Judge Swanepoel, 2025 VO: But went further calling them cynical and their behaviour bad-faith conduct. “I have no doubt that the applicant has taken the view that it will not fund treatment… and that its conduct is mala fide.” “In my view the applicant’s conduct is deserving of punishment.” “The applicant’s explanation for not paying… does not hold water… it is untenable and should be rejected.” “The applicant has deliberately chosen not to abide by the order…” SEE GOVAN READING link: If Medihelp does not purge its contempt, the court may issue a writ directing the commanding officer of Brooklyn Police Station to immediately arrest the Principal Officer of Medihelp and commit him/her to prison until the contempt is purged. That’s a legal first! Principal Officer Varsha Vala could go to jail if they don’t comply. [VO – GRAPHICS + INTERVIEW] ACT 3: VO: For families fighting rare diseases, there is one person they turn to when the system shuts its doors. Kelly du Plessis has walked this road herself as we’ve shown in our previous story— as a mother and as an advocate — she knows better than anyone what happens when medical aids refuse to pay. KELLY DU PLESSIS (Rare Diseases South Africa): “Medihelp isn’t just fighting one family — it’s defending an entire industry model. Because if this judgment stands, every medical scheme in South Africa will have to match the state’s standard of care.” GOVAN LINK: “If you read between the lines of Medihelp’s filings — and listen to what’s said quietly — a clearer picture emerges. This fight isn’t really about one child, or one drug. It’s about precedent. If Medihelp pays for Elaprase as Prescribed Minimum Benefit treatment, then every medical aid in South Africa may have to fund these rare-disease therapies in full — therapies that can cost millions a year. And that’s the line the industry doesn’t want to cross. Judge Swanepoel makes the point bluntly in his ruling: Medihelp isn’t fighting the law — they’re fighting the consequences of following it. In other words, they’re fighting precedent… not the child who needs the treatment.” VO: She says this judgement is so important to hold medical aids accountable. KELLY DU PLESSIS: Medical aids are now delaying or denying enzyme replacement therapies, even where there’s overwhelming proof they must pay. This is the first time a medical aid’s been held in contempt for refusing care — and it confirms PMB conditions must be judged by availability in the state sector, not whether the state pays.” GOVAN VO: Some viewers may wonder why Zachary simply go to a government hospital? [Govan Link: But as his parents explain, that door simply isn’t open. At Charlotte Maxeke, the entire annual budget for paediatric rare-disease treatment is about six million rand — and Zachary’s therapy alone costs half of that. The public system works on a first-come-first-served basis, and once a child starts lifelong therapy, that slot is gone for years. And legally, the state cannot fund treatment for a child already on medical aid. That’s exactly why PMB laws exist — to stop medical aids from pushing complex, expensive patients onto an already overstretched public system. So for Zachary, there is no state alternative. His medical aid is the one legally required to pay, and that’s why this fight matters.] Jacques: Budget for paediatric rare diseases at Charlotte Maxeke = ±R6 million a year. Zach’s treatment alone costs R3 million. Only one or two patients can be treated at a time. The PMB law exists to prevent private medical aids from dumping patients onto the state. GOVAN LINK In short, the state can’t take him. The law says his medical aid must. VO: But Medihelp has made it clear — it will appeal all the way to the Constitutional Court, even if that takes years. Kelly believes it may be cheaper to keep fighting than to pay. [TRANSITION – COURT GRAPHICS / DOCUMENT SCAN] Paragraph 42: “Financial hardship cannot justify defying a court order.” GOVAN LINK (outside Medihelp in Pretoria): “Medihelp has been around since 1905 — one of South Africa’s oldest medical aids, serving more than 200,000 members. We asked them for an interview. They declined. In a written response, Medihelp said it respects the legal process and intends to pursue all available appeals.” (GOVAN VO) Medihelp denies that it has acted unlawfully. The scheme says it believed the 2022 court order no longer applied after the medical regulator initially ruled that Elaprase was not part of the prescribed minimum benefits. Medihelp maintains it acted in good faith. GOVAN LINK 3: Medihelp has long argued that Elaprase can’t be considered Prescribed Minimum Benefit treatment because the state doesn’t fund it — even though it’s provided in several government hospitals through donor and compassionate-access programmes. Their position has been simple: if the state doesn’t pay for it, neither should they. But that argument has now been rejected at every level — by the CMS Appeal Committee and by both High Court judges. The law looks at whether the treatment is available in the public sector, not who pays for it. And in Zachary’s case, the state does use Elaprase. Which means medically and legally, it is PMB care. HAPPIER ENDING – THE MEDS ARE WORKING! YAY! GOVAN VO: Behind the legal arguments and billion-rand precedents is a little boy whose treatment is working. Doctors say Zachary met every entry criterion and has responded exceptionally well — his disease has stabilised. MICHANEY (tearful): “It’s easy to forget there’s a child in all of this. Every court date, every delay — that’s time he doesn’t have.” Cut to Megan HJ: “This isn’t about one case. It’s about whether medical aids think they can outspend the law. And it’s about whether we, as a country, will let them.” [CLOSING SCENE] Soft visuals: Zachary plays with his dad; laughter echoes. GOVAN LINK (closing): “In the end, it’s easy to talk about billions, percentages, and legal precedent — but it all comes down to one small life. And sometimes, the majority doesn’t outweigh the one.” Fade out. Teasers: One: One family. One child. And a medical aid that would rather fight in court than pay to save a life.” “It’s easy to forget the numbers — until you remember they belong to a five-year-old boy.” “In the battle over policy, codes, and court orders, it’s easy to lose sight of the truth: a child is running out of time.” “This isn’t a claims dispute — it’s a fight for a child’s life.”

Zachary’s Law: STORY PITCH A David vs Goliath story of when a Medical Aid Defies the Law ONE LINE SUMMARY: A mother won in court. Twice. But her medical aid still refuses to pay for her child’s rare disease. Now, a judge has said: obey — or go to jail to the medical aid. It started as one mother’s desperate fight to save her son. Now, it could change how medical aids treat every South African patient. A 5-year-old boy, Zachary De Wet, has Hunter Syndrome (MPS II) — a rare genetic condition that slowly attacks the body and the brain. There’s only one treatment that can slow it down: Elaprase, an enzyme-replacement drug. Yet, his family’s medical aid — Medihelp — refused to pay. Initially, Medihelp argued in court that Elaprase was not a Prescribed Minimum Benefit (PMB). But in 2022, a judge rejected that argument — ruling that not only is the condition a PMB, but that the standard for determining treatment is simple: “What does the state do?” And in this case, the state provides Elaprase. They then argued that while the state gives the drug, it’s only done through a “compassionate programme” — so they weren’t obliged to fund it. That single interpretation has now exploded into one of the biggest legal fights in South African healthcare. THE STORY: Zachary’s mother, Michaney De Wet, turned to attorney Megan Harrington-Johnson — a name Carte Blanche audiences will recognise. We previously told Megan’s own story, when she fought for her daughter’s future after a childhood cancer diagnosis — using cutting-edge science to preserve her little girl’s chance of having children one day. Now, she’s on the other side of the table — fighting for another family, against a medical aid giant. Her firm took the case pro bono in 2021, arguing that because the state provides Elaprase, it must also be covered by private medical aids under the law governing PMBs. Different layers: The First Win (2022) Judge Millar rules in favour of the De Wets: • Hunter Syndrome (MPS II) is a PMB condition. • Elaprase is the standard public-sector treatment — so Medihelp must pay for it. • The ruling sets a powerful precedent for rare-disease coverage. Despite this, Medihelp refused to pay, and backed by an army of advocates representing other medical schemes, they appealed. According to Kelly du Plessis of Rare Diseases South Africa, this fight went far beyond a single family’s struggle. “This wasn’t just one fund defending itself — it was the entire medical-aid industry protecting its profit model.” Layer 2: The Showdown (2025) Last week, Judge Swanepoel handed down a scathing judgment. He upheld the earlier decision and went further — finding Medihelp in contempt of court for ignoring Judge Millar’s order. He wrote that Medihelp’s conduct was “cynical, aggressive, and mala fide” — and warned that if they don’t pay, the Principal Officer could be imprisoned. It’s one of the most blistering rebukes of a medical aid ever seen in South Africa. Megan HJ: Two judges. Two rulings. One medical aid defying them both. CHARACTERS: • Zachary (5) — bright, funny, and brave. He still receives his life-saving treatment through donations, but his future depends on this ruling being enforced. • Michaney De Wet — a mother who’s spent years fighting bureaucracy while trying to keep her son alive. • Megan Harrington-Johnson — lawyer, mother, and rare-disease advocate. Her personal story gives this case an extraordinary emotional echo. • Rare Diseases South Africa (Kelly du Plessis) — the NGO that’s stepped in where medical aids have failed, supporting families like Zachary’s across the country. EXTRA INFORMATION: Carte Blanche first explored this issue in 2022 — exposing how families with rare diseases were being denied essential, life-sustaining treatments. This case takes that story a decisive step further. At its core, it asks a fundamental question of South African healthcare law: must medical aids meet the same standard of care provided by the state? Since that earlier report, medical aids have continued to delay or deny enzyme replacement therapies (ERTs) — even when medical and legal evidence shows these treatments must be fully funded. Now, for the first time, a medical aid has been found in contempt of court for refusing to provide care-related treatment. The ruling sets a powerful new precedent: PMB conditions can’t be defined by whether the state pays for treatment, but by whether that treatment is available within the state system — even if supplied through a compassionate or donor programme. We’ll, of course, request an interview with Medihelp — though it’s unlikely they’ll agree. In that case, we can head to their head offices in Brooklyn, Pretoria, and give viewers some context about who they are. Medihelp has been operating since 1905 and today serves more than 200,000 members. In 2023, the scheme reported R2.39 billion in assets and paid out R3.3 billion in claims. As Principal Officer, Varsha Vala is the public face of Medihelp’s leadership — and in this story, she’s the person whose accountability will come under scrutiny if the scheme continues to defy two court orders. I believe this story will hold strong until January, as Medihelp is expected to seek leave to appeal to the Constitutional Court. That means the legal battle — and public interest — will remain active. Even if the court process takes time, the core issue of accountability won’t date: a major medical aid defying two High Court orders and facing possible contempt proceedings is a story that will stay relevant and develop further in the months ahead. title: Behind the rogue EMPD Unit
oneLiner: A group of hopefuls, dedicating their lives to fulfilling civic duties by doing the work of police reservists lands them in a job under the banner of Ekurhuleni Metro Police– the catch they end up.
summary:
A group of volunteers of the EMPD finds itself at the centre of attention after the Madlanga Commission into police interference reveals that they were operating illegally. This is no news to them who had been trying to get incorporated into the system but were ignored, and after all the work they did they were simply let go off. We will tell the story of how they would write in the OB book and were given pocket books, used state vehicles, were given weapons and made several arrests (They have case numbers to confirm this allegation). They also allege they were appointed as escorts in some council meetings, where they were used as VIP protection. Another complaint is that they were allegedly promised employment post-covid yet the EMPD did not deliver this promise after making them work for years with state resources, for free. I will tell that story through the images they have of these. I will also incorporate visuals of different crime scenes and arrests. We visit them in their homes, after the effect, seeing how life has turned out. Lastly we need to get an- on camera interview with City of Ekurhuleni officials to answer to the allegations.

The heads of the Ekurhuleni Metro Police Department including Isaac Mapiyeye and later Julius Mkhwanazi illegally operated up a unit of volunteers who were promised employment later on. They were hired to do the same job that official EMPD members do, yet without the proper training nor a formal contract. They did more than that, they effected arrests and worked as VIP security in council.

title: Mowbray Maternity Angels
oneLiner: Tonight on Carte Blanche… no big budgets, no fuss — just heart, grit, and the miracle of life at Mowbray Maternity.
summary:
Mowbray Maternity Hospital sits quietly between Groote Schuur and Red Cross Children’s Hospital. It doesn’t have the big budgets or shiny equipment. What it does have is heart. Nearly 10 000 babies are born here every year. Many arrive too soon. Many start life with a fight. Led by the softly spoken but fiercely committed Ms Janine Joemat, this team of mostly female nurses and doctors keeps going no matter the odds. A 110-year-old building leaks and cracks. Budgets shrink. Yet inside these wards, hope is protected with everything they have. They make plans. They brighten corridors. They comfort scared mothers. They care for babies as small as a packet of sugar. They even designed evacuation aprons so each nurse can carry four newborns to safety if disaster strikes. This is a rare good-news story in the public health system. A small hospital with a giant spirit — where South Africa’s future is held gently in the palms of women who refuse to give up.

A rare good-news story in the public health sector — showing the remarkable women who keep South Africa’s future alive against all odds.

title: Hooked: How South Africa's towing industry preys on consumers
oneLiner: How the First Help towing company is preying on consumers ...
summary:
Under-regulated, opportunistic, and often predatory, the towing industry thrives in a grey zone. And with more than eight million uninsured vehicles on the road, many motorists only learn the true cost of being in a crash after the dust has settled. Tow trucks are a familiar sight, skipping lights and ramping curbs to be first on the scene of an accident – but what happens after your vehicle is towed can come as a nasty shock. Exorbitant fees, vanishing vehicles, and costly repairs all add up to skyrocketing anxiety and expense for owners. Carte Blanche exposes the darker side of an industry few understand, and most encounter only in moments of crisis.

First Help is the biggest towing operator in South Africa but among it's fleet of towing operators there appear to be rogue elements who continually scam and take advantage of consumers, especially in a time of need after an accident. This story is made more topical because of the time of year and presents insight into how the towing industry preys on motorists.

title: KANNALAND RAPIST MAYOR
summary:
In December 2022, Carte Blanche exposed Kannaland’s scandal-plagued mayor Jeffrey Donson - a convicted child rapist who, despite national outrage, continued to hold public office. Three years later, he’s still there. Convicted in 2008 of statutory rape and indecent assault of a 15-year-old girl while serving as Oudtshoorn’s mayor, Donson has worn the mayoral chain three separate times - before his conviction, again in 2021, and once more in October 2022, just months before our exposé aired. Public pressure forced his temporary removal in January 2022, but coalition politics between ICOSA and the ANCbrought him back. In October 2023, ICOSA suspended him for “gross misconduct and bringing the party into disrepute.” But within weeks, Donson reasserted control - and remains Executive Mayor of Kannaland in 2025. Now, Action Society is pushing for a constitutional amendment to bar convicted sexual offenders from public office - what activists call “the Donson Clause.” October 2025: IDonson remains mayor despite his 2008 conviction and failed suspension. Action Society campaign: Renewed national call to change eligibility laws. Upcoming elections: With local government polls looming in 2026, Donson’s case epitomises the collapse of accountability in local politics. Political stakes: Parties that once backed him - or stayed silent - will now have to answer to voters. National relevance: In a country that preaches “zero tolerance” for GBV, a convicted rapist’s survival in politics exposes the emptiness of that promise. This story isn’t about one small-town scandal - it’s about a democracy without moral guardrails. If a convicted child rapist can outlast exposure, suspension, and scandal - and still run a municipality - what does that say about the system itself? Taxpayers pay his salary. Survivors see justice mocked. Voters are asked to choose between ethics and apathy. As South Africa heads toward another local election, this story shows what’s truly at stake: not just ballots, but belief in the power of accountability.

title: Forgotten Special Schools
oneLiner: A collapse of special needs schools across KwaZulu-Natal is brewing — threatening to leave thousands of children with disabilities without classrooms, care, or support.
summary:
The situation is being described by education activists as a humanitarian emergency. What was once seen as administrative inefficiency has now spiralled into a systemic failure driven by years of underfunding, mismanagement, and indifference. If urgent intervention does not come soon, KwaZulu-Natal could face the complete collapse of its special needs education system, effectively abandoning the very children the Constitution promises to protect. Special schools, which cater for learners living with disabilities, are collapsing under the weight of systemic neglect. Many have been unable to pay staff, run school transport, or cover basic operational costs like electricity and insurance. In Chatsworth, the Truro Prevocational School has officially shut its doors after becoming insolvent. In Dundee, Pro Nobis School for Learners with Special Needs — home to more than 300 children — is on the brink of closure. These are not isolated incidents. They are symptoms of a provincial crisis that has been unfolding for months. While the KwaZulu-Natal Department of Education admits to “delays in the payment process,” its reassurances have done little to restore trust. Parents, teachers and governing bodies — led by the South African Association for Special Education (SANASE) — insist that the crisis extends beyond late subsidies. They demand systemic change: reliable transport for every school, sufficient support staff, new hostels for displaced learners, and urgent appointments of psychologists, nurses, and occupational therapists.

Seventy-six special schools, both public and private, all dependent on state subsidies, have either shut their doors or are on the brink of closure due to months of delayed payments and ongoing neglect by the provincial Department of Education. The crisis cuts across every district in KZN. Truro Prevocational School in Chatsworth has already closed its gates. Ningizimu Special School in Durban is struggling to meet even its most basic needs. In uMhlathuze, Isikhwezi Special School has been forced to suspend operations amid a worsening financial meltdown, with teachers going unpaid and critical services collapsing. Behind these names are real children — some of the province’s most vulnerable learners — now left without food, therapy, transport, or education. Many cannot access public transport safely, and for some, school meals are their only guaranteed source of nutrition.

title: James Ketchell - round the world
oneLiner: British adventurer James Ketchell sails into Cape Town after months at sea — but this time, it’s not just about breaking records. He’s helping the South African Weather Service drop high-tech se
summary:
British adventurer James Ketchell arrives in Cape Town after months at sea on his solo circumnavigation. As part of his mission, he’s partnering with the South African Weather Service to deploy Argo floats — ocean sensors that collect vital climate and marine data. It’s a story that brings together human endurance, ocean science, and South Africa’s role in global research.

An adventurer’s journey meets local science — James Ketchell’s Cape Town landing links exploration with the South African Weather Service’s work to better understand our oceans. Overview: British adventurer James Ketchell set sail from Gosport, England, on a nine-month, 30 000-nautical-mile journey around the world. His goal is to become the first person in history to circle the globe by air, land, and sea. Along the way, he connects with classrooms across the world — sharing lessons from the ocean and stories of endurance and discovery. Why Cape Town & South Africa Matter: Cape Town is one of the key stops on James’s global route. After months alone at sea, he’ll finally reunite with his family for a few days before continuing his voyage. While here, he’ll also work with the South African Weather Service to drop Argo floats — ocean sensors that gather important information about sea temperatures and currents. This data helps improve weather forecasts and climate research. What We’ll Cover: • The journey: James’s world challenge and what drives him to keep going. • The South African link: Cape Town as a crucial stop where science meets adventure. • The Argo floats: How they work and how they help local weather scientists. • The human story: Life alone on the ocean, and the emotional moment of seeing his family again. • The presenter’s experience: Our presenter will join James on the boat to get a real sense of what it takes to sail one of these yachts — from handling the ropes to facing the wind and waves. • Visuals: The Cape Town coastline, James’s arrival, his family reunion, the Argo floats, and sailing scenes with the presenter.

title: Justice Insulted: The Murray family's search for closure
oneLiner: While the Murray family wait for cops to investigate the assassination of Thomas and Cloete Murray, it seems the generals in charge of their investigation were lining their pockets with bribes from cr
summary:
It’s been two years and eight months since Cloete Murray and his son Thomas were assassinated on the NI highway near Midrand on a Saturday afternoon. Thomas and his father had been working on a multimillion-rand case for Investec and they had left Melrose Arch and were travelling home. What they did not realize is that they were followed and gunned down by three men in a bakkie near the New Road offramp. The family have been shattered, but they are healing as best they can. The police have been appalling despite promises from two of the nation’s top cops, General Shadrack Sibiya and Richard Shiburi. These two generals promised the family justice after the first law enforcement team failed them. But they have failed them too and now perhaps we know why. In the last few weeks, startling revelations from the Madlanga commission suggest that these men were busy lining their pockets from a man accused of looting Thembisa hospital and attempting to murder his girlfriend. While the allegations remain untested and come from a man accused of serious crimes, the level of detail that were given to three law enforcement officers by Cat Matlala is startling.

We have two family members and Witness A B and C at the commission which puts a different spin on the story

title: A Living Legacy: Carte Blanche Making a Difference Trust
oneLiner: As the Trust heads into its 18th year, we celebrate its work and recognise the contributions of donors and partners in its coming of age.
summary:
The Carte Blanche Making a Difference Trust was founded in 2008 for the show’s twentieth birthday. It builds and equips dedicated paediatric facilities in state hospitals, filling gaps in care such as burns treatment, emergency and trauma units, operating theatres, and so on. Behind everything the Trust does is its Patron, Karolina Andropoulos. Her daughter Georgina died aged seven of cancer in 2008, after many years of treatment both in South Africa and in Australia. After her death, Karolina became driven to help create support for South African children in state hospitals similar to what had been available in Australia. Karolina approached George and asked him to tour Charlotte Maxeke’s paediatric unit with her to see what was needed, and so the Trust was born. The initial idea was to raise funds to contribute towards equipment for a local hospital. What it turned into was multiple projects in hospitals all over South Africa - not only equipment donations, but building and equipping operating theatres, centres of excellence and so on. Carte Blanche periodically features the Trust’s work in stories - usually at the handover of a new project - partly because the Trust’s ongoing success and ability to raise funds is dependent on its association with the Carte Blanche brand, and partly to recognise the incredible contributions of donors and partners. Several companies have donated many millions of rands over the past two decades, many of them more than once, and numerous professionals and their companies have donated time, skills and materials.

The Trust turns 18 next year, in 2026. Its latest project (a neonatal unit at George Provincial Hospital) will be completed to coincide with the birthday. We reflect on the lives touched, communities served and stories told. We celebrate the leap of faith that donors and partners make with us, and the idea that all of us are a brick in the wall, contributing towards projects that are always more than the sum of their parts.

title: Cagey Cajees
oneLiner: We bring you the real story of the Africrypt rug-pull, and what happened to the brazen brothers who pulled off South Africa's biggest Bitcoin heist.
summary:
It was the cyber heist of the century. R3 billion in Bitcoin disappeared overnight in April 2021. The Africrypt whizz kids Raees & Ameer Cajee claimed they were hacked, but by then they were living comfortably in Dubai with Vanuatu passports. It later emerged that amount stolen was closer to $10 million. Desperate investors hired lawyers and liquidators tp pursue criminal charges. Then an angel investor appeared on the scene - Pennython Project Management from Dubai offered to refund the investors 70 cents in the Rand, on condition that all criminal charges were dropped. 95% of the investors took the deal. But in the interim the Cajee brothers profited hugely on Bitcoin that had increased dramatically in value. In a dramatic Dubai kidnapping, Bilal Cajee, father of Raees and Ameer was snatched while visiting the Dubai court. When the brothers finally went to the police they pinged his phone. Bilal was found in the Millennium Hotel near the Dubai airport, tied to a chair in a hotel room. The brothers were tight-lipped, but it is believed a disgruntled South African investor had held him captive until the Cajees repaid what they'd stolen. In late 2021 Ameer Cajee was arrested in Zurich when he tried to stash a Trezor stick, containing the stolen Bitcoin, in a Swiss bank vault. Accused of money laundering he spent 6 months in a Swiss detention centre. Once Pennython had paid out the South African clients, they agreed to release him on CHF 300 000 bail. He spent another year under house arrest in the Five Hotel, in the luxurious $1000 a night penthouse. In the interim his brother organised a second Vanuatu passport for him. When the Swiss authorities released him, they flew back to South Africa on Turkish airlines, via Istanbul.

Interviews with two associates who met Raees and Ameer Cajee in Dubai after their escape from South Africa, helped them relocate and set up residence and introduced them to new clients. We find out how they skipped the country in a hurry, where they lived, where they partied, where they holidayed, what they spent their investors' money on. And ultimately, how they stole another $10 million in a second rug pull before relocating back to South Africa .
caseStudies: Ryan Pile John Hanafin Gerhard Botha Shaheed Dollie

title: Oom Bennie
oneLiner: Where the clippers hum and the past still cheers — Oom Bennie’s shop is where rugby, memory, and community meet.
summary:
[OPENING SEQUENCE – ATMOSPHERE] Soft morning light spills over Newlands. A key turns in a lock. Clippers buzz to life. Rugby crowd sounds faintly echo as the walls come into view. (Govan VO) Tucked away in Newlands, near the old Sophiatown Police Station — in a part of Johannesburg most of us barely know — is a small corner where history still breathes. Visuals: The sound of a razor glides. Don’t see Bennie yet, just his hands and extreme closeups… (Govan link) From the street, it looks more like a corner deli than a barber shop — a faded sign, the hum of clippers mixing with the smell of frying chips from next door. But inside, it’s a tiny shrine to something unexpected: rugby. Visuals: Wide shot of the shop front — “Oom Bennie’s Haarkapper.” Two chairs. Tight space. Inside, walls exploding with green and gold. We were going to get closeups of razors, scissors, put the barber black bib over the camera… slowmo. UPSOUND (Bennie chuckling): “Ja, dis ‘n leë muur daar agter — miskien moet ek nog iets daar sit!” (underneath visuals – don’t see Bennie yet) See Govan walk into the store…Govan takes it in, awe on his face. UPSOUND (Bennie chuckling, in Afrikaans): “Ja, dis ‘n leë muur daar agter — miskien moet ek nog iets daar sit!” First time we see Oom Bennie - hero shot – “Oom Bennie on the screen” – with “barber shop graphic look” Hear rugby sounds under the visuals Pan across jerseys, caps, match programmes, mud-stained boots. Every wall bursting with colour and memory. Close-up of faded signatures and Ellis Park mud stains. (Govan link) Step inside Oom Bennie’s Haarkapper, and it’s like walking into a time capsule wrapped in green and gold. Every inch of wall space — even the ceiling — tells a story. TRANSITIONS: Barbershop sounds (scissors, clippers) serve as transitions — razor wipes to next scene. ACT 1: [Govan and Bennie speaking, Govan will sit down with him, he’ll talk to him while getting a cut, but he’ll also talk to him while he has customers. On the background is Danie, whom he plans to leave the shop to] Visuals: Govan sits in the chair. Danie sweeps in the background. Clippers hum. GOVAN (Afrikaans): “Bennie, jy het hier begin sny toe rugby nog net op radio was — hoekom het jy nooit opgehou nie?” BENNIE: “Dis nie net oor hare sny nie, dis oor mense. Dis oor onthou.” Bennie can introduce - Danie – and Danie can say something about how long he’s been there… (Govan VO) For more than three decades, Bennie’s stood behind the same chair — scissors in hand — trimming the hair of legends from Francois Pienaar to the late Piet Malan, once South Africa’s oldest living Bok at 96. Pause…Their faces still watch over the walls. Pause – hear the sounds of rugby from the walls Bennie’s not just a barber — he’s the keeper of half a century of stories, and I’ve come to hear some. Govan and Bennie Chat about ONE story on the walls… TRANSITIONS: Barbershop sounds (scissors, clippers) serve as transitions — razor wipes to next scene. (Govan VO) Just as Bennie finishes his story, the bell rings — and guess who walks in? Another Springbok. Seems the stories here have a way of showing up in person. Visuals: Door opens — in walk Jaco Kriel and [second player], smiling. (Govan VO) Jaco Kriel — the dynamic flanker best known for captaining the Lions, celebrated for his fearless runs and big heart. Visuals: Close-up: Govan standing, Bennie trimming shaving Jaco beard. The camera catches their reflection in the mirror. Govan, Jaco and Bennie chat JACO (laughing): “Bennie, jy’t seker al elke Lions game gesien van die begin af, né?” BENNIE (grinning): “Ek het nog nooit ’n seisoen gemis nie! Elke jaar koop ek my kaartjies — dis my kerk, daai stadion!” JACO: “Dis ongelooflik, Bennie. Jy’s meer getrou as sommige van ons wat daar gespeel het!” VO (Govan): Bennie’s been a Lions supporter longer than most players have been alive — never missing a season, still buying his own tickets, still shouting from the stands. Upsound: They talk about something on the walls – item two (Govan VO) These days, Kriel’s passing on his experience to young players in Gauteng — but today, it’s his turn to get a little advice from Oom Bennie. Upsound: Oom Bennie advice to Jaco… …then Kriel leaves through the door… (Govan VO) Another happy customer. ACT 2: [OUTDOOR WALKABOUT – THE COMMUNITY] Visuals: Bennie and Govan walk through the streets of Newlands. Bennie waves at neighbours, stops at a small soup kitchen. Slow-motion: him ladling soup, greeting locals. Upsound: Bennie: I’ve been in this neighbourhood for 61 years! Govan: Wow that’s a long time… Bennie: I turn 80 next week. Govan Link: In a neighbourhood that’s slowly changing, Oom Bennie’s barbershop feels like one of the last constants. For many here, it’s more than a place for a haircut — it’s where you’re known, heard, and remembered. And when Bennie finally hangs up his scissors, it’s hard to imagine what will fill that space. (Govan VO) But there’s more to this story than rugby. Every lunch break, Bennie walks down the road to a small soup kitchen — one he helps keep running, just as he’s kept this community fed with kindness for decades. Speaks to Govan while they are walking, shots of them walking Upsounds of Bennie and kids at soup kitchen – we are gaining permission for this Transition back to the shop: see them walk back in… VO Transition line to come after soup kitchen. (Govan Link) These walls aren’t just decoration — they’re donations. Most of these pieces were given to Bennie over the years… some by players themselves, others by families after loved ones passed on. Every jersey, every photo, carries a memory someone wanted to keep alive — and Bennie’s shop became the place to do it. Upsounds (Govan VO) He’s seen South Africa lift four Rugby World Cups — and his walls tell every chapter. Just in time to meet some of the objects on the walls is another former Springbok Willem Alberts. Willem: Hi Oom! (Govan VO) The powerhouse they nickname ‘The Bone Collector’ for his bone-crunching tackles. The loose forward is now focused on family and guiding the next generation. We’ll pick a story from Bennie and talk about Third Item with Alberts and Govan Govan, Willem and Bennie chat Bennie: “Julle sien, ek sê altyd — die beste hare kom van die sterkste koppe!” (Govan VO) And of course, no visit’s complete without a bit of Oom Bennie wisdom… Bennie Gives Willem Advice…building to a conclusion with this… ACT 3: (Govan VO) In a world where everything changes so fast, his shop stands still — steady as his hand. Do we break the third wall and have the camera man put down their camera and then come tell the story? Visuals: Kobus sets down the camera and sits in the second chair. (KOBUS) I’ve been coming here for years — it’s not just a cut, it’s a catch-up. You walk out smelling like Brylcreem and nostalgia. (Govan VO) Even our cameraman, Kobus Zietsman, drives from Northcliff just for this. Because Bennie doesn’t just cut hair — he keeps history alive. Kobus gets his advice Visuals: Back in the shop. The day fades. Clippers quiet. Sunlight hits the framed jerseys. Bennie sweeps up hair from the floor — slow motion. BENNIE (final line, Afrikaans): “Jy sien, elke hare het ‘n storie. Jy moet net luister.” (Govan VO) It was time for me to leave with more than just a fresh cut. I need some trademark advice… Govan gets his advice (Govan Link) Here in this little barbershop in Newlands, the stories don’t just get told — they stay. Maybe that’s the magic of a barber: they listen, they remember, and somehow, they keep a community stitched together. Visuals: Bennie sweeps up hair from the floor. Govan watches quietly. BENNIE (Afrikaans, soft): “Ek gaan dit eendag vir Danie los. Hy werk nou al lank saam met my… Ek het nie meer ’n seun nie.” Danie: upsound Govan: For me, it started as a story about a barber — but it became a lesson about legacy. (Govan VO) Change comes for every community, and one day these clippers will fall silent. But what Bennie built — the kindness, the connection — will echo long after the last haircut. That’s why he’s passing it on to Danie — to keep the chair, and the stories, alive. Bennie and Danie: Closes up the shop and leaves

Set in Newlands, on the edge of Sophiatown, Oom Bennie’s tiny two-chair barbershop is a living museum of South African rugby. Every wall — even the ceiling — is covered in Springbok memorabilia collected over decades. It’s a space where nostalgia, sport, and neighbourhood life meet.
caseStudies: Bennie Van Zyl Jaco Kriel Willem Alberts Kobus Zeitsman

title: Medals Before Children
summary:
Gymnastics SA: Medals Before Children Last year, we exposed how Gymnastics South Africa (GSA) was covering up abuse within the sport, allegations the organisation vehemently denied. At the time, Hayley Walker, then head of safeguarding, defended GSA’s systems, insisting the organisation had learnt its lesson and that children were finally safe. Less than a year later, Hayley has resigned, and now she’s ready to speak out. She reveals a culture of systemic abuse and intimidation. At the centre of this latest scandal is Louis Fourie, one of South Africa’s top Olympic coaches, who runs his high-performance gym at Tuks. More than ten gymnasts have come forward accusing him of physical and emotional abuse. Instead of investigating the claims, GSA allegedly moved to suppress them, protecting the coach rather than the athletes. This is a hair-raising exposé of how a national sports body continues to put glory before children, ignoring its own safeguarding policies while young athletes suffer in silence.

Extract from Investigation 1 - words of the victim Do you believe that the system will ultimately fail other girls as well? Absolutely. If the same people stay. If the same people are on the panel, if the same people are participating in the Free State, if the very same people are in GSA, why would anything change now? Fast forward to 2025. I get a call from Hayley Walker, the former safeguarding officer at Gymnastics South Africa. The same woman who once defended the organisation during our investigation — now ready to talk about a systemic cover-up inside the sport.
caseStudies: Hayley walker Tyde Gymnast Adele Heine Patience PRO

title: A Trusted Source
oneLiner: What's in your syrup?
summary:
Adcock Ingram is a Proudly South African company, and a leading South African pharmaceutical manufacturer. Founded over 130 years ago in 1891, the Company is listed on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange and its extensive portfolio of products includes well-known household brands like Panado, Allergex, Epi-max, Citro-Soda and Myprodol. Adcock’s annual turnover as at June 2025 was 9.8 billion. In October a whistleblower approached Carte Blanche with numerous concerns regarding the efficacy of Adcock’s manufacturing processes. He didn’t come empty-handed; he had receipts including videos, pictures, emails and documents that if proven true - could be explosive allegations against Adcock. He’s a qualified pharmacist and his role on the manufacturing floor was to ensure that the processes followed were aligned with Adcock’s standard operating procedures. In short, he says - they didn’t. Despite numerous complaints to the site manager - who he says is a non-professional with a logistics background - the whistleblower says, there was repeatedly pushback with a view to maximizing output over compliance. Last month, fatigued with his incessant insistence on compliance which slowed down production, the whistleblower says he was dismissed for being a workplace bully and unofficially, a whistleblower who allegedly once declared - “Ive closed down factories before”. An allegation he dismisses as absolute drivel.

One of South Africa's largest pharmaceutical companies is accused of failing to comply with good manufacturing processes.

title: The Hotel on the Hill
oneLiner: A luxury hotel we reported on three years ago makes an appearance in the Madlanga Commission.
summary:
In 2022, it was the site of a bitter dispute between John Assor, his fiancée Phia, and the man who bought their Northcliff guesthouse. The buyer, businessman Thami Ndlala, signed two agreements totalling R10 million rand. Once he settled the first R8 million, he wanted to move in - in violation of the agreements. Thami Ndlala rented the property next door and had started cutting down an interleading palisade fence. John Assor confronted him and their showdown was captured on this video. John denies he was armed. Later Thami cut the gate locks, and stationed security guards with semi-automatic weapons around the property - he also cut the electricity. After this altercation, police arrived at Assor’s house and imprisoned him on charges of intimidation, assault and pointing a firearm. Assor spent a night in police cells. We received no response to our questions from police. Ndlala promised to show us a video that would prove his allegations – but never did. According to Witness A, the party invitation came from a man known to the police since 2022 as someone who could assist with investigations, a man called Vusi Ndlala. It wasn't long before social media users tried to connect the dots - linking Thami Ndlala to the hotel and questioning whether he had any knowledge of shadowy police get-togethers. Ndlala came out swinging, sending a legal letter to online commentator Mighti Jamie in which he distanced himself from the entire saga. The hotel released a statement emphasising that a “so-called Vusi Ndlala” is neither the owner nor involved in any capacity. It also denied that any event was held on the day alleged by Witness A, and said it “is not, and does not condone being used as, a meeting-hub for criminality.” Meanwhile, General Shibiri has declined to comment, saying he will give his own evidence in front of the Commission.

Last week, Witness A, a member of Gauteng Organised Crime, testified at the Madlanga Commission about alleged political interference in criminal investigations. He alleges that top cops attempted to cover up the 2024 murder of Vereeniging engineer, Armand Swart, whose company flagged tender irregularities at Transnet. Following Swart’s murder, three suspects were arrested. According to Witness A, National Head of Organised Crime, General Richard Shibiri, tried to protect them. Investigators were allegedly promised bribes… and invited to a party at 12 on Hillel Villa and Spa, a boutique hotel in Northcliff, Johannesburg. But this isn't the first time the venue has crossed our radar.

title: The Lighthouse Keeper
oneLiner: On a rugged stretch of the West Coast, one man keeps the lantern burning. We follow the story of one of South Africa's final lighthouse keepers - as he keeps watch over the sea that has shaped his lif
summary:
OVERVIEW Amid crashing waves and coastal winds, Cape Columbine Lighthouse stands as a steadfast beacon. At 52, Wayne Brown has spent most of his life fulfilling that duty. Born in Paternoster and raised within sight of the tower, Wayne’s bond with the ocean runs deep. His grandfather captained a crayfish vessel; his parents worked on the lighthouse reserve. Mentored by veteran keeper Japie Greeff, Wayne inherited both the tools and the calling to keep the light burning, no matter the weather. Cape Columbine, built in 1936 and named after a ship wrecked nearby in 1829, remains one of the last manned lighthouses on South Africa’s 3,000-kilometre coastline. Most others have been automated — visited only occasionally by technicians. Yet Wayne remains, faithfully tending the beam that still cuts through fog and darkness to guide sailors safely home. “Every time a ship passes,” he says, “I know I’ve helped it find safe passage.” STORY OUTLINE ACT 1 — INTRODUCTION We open on a windswept coastline at dawn. Waves crash against the rocks as the revolving light fades into morning. A single figure walks the narrow path to the tower — Wayne Brown. Through reflective narration and natural sound, we meet the man behind the beam: a custodian of history, solitude, and purpose. ACT 2 — A LIFE BY THE SEA Through interviews and observational sequences, we trace Wayne’s life story — his childhood in the reserve, the mentorship of Japie Greeff, and the rhythm of his days at Cape Columbine. The film captures his maintenance routines, logbook entries, and quiet rituals that keep the lighthouse alive. ACT 3 — KEEPING THE LIGHT ALIVE As automation spreads, Wayne reflects on being among the last of his kind. The tone becomes more introspective: what does it mean to dedicate your life to a duty few now understand? Wayne’s voice anchors the narrative, culminating in his poetic reflection: “Die vuurtoring is ‘n lig vir die mense wat op die see is... Jy moet liefde hê vir die werk. Jy moet alles kan insit.” (The lighthouse is a light for those at sea — to show them where the safe path lies. You must have love for the work. You must give it your all.) The story closes at dusk — the light once again sweeping over the waves, a quiet testament to endurance. THEMES Tradition vs. Technology – A human craft fading in the digital age. Solitude and Purpose – Finding meaning in isolation and service. Legacy and Heritage – Preserving South Africa’s maritime past. Faith and Devotion – The lighthouse as both a beacon and a metaphor for steadfastness. TONE & VISUAL STYLE The tone is contemplative, poetic, and authentic — rooted in natural sound, minimal narration, and strong visual storytelling. Visual Style: Cinematic, slow-paced camera movement with emphasis on texture and light. A restrained colour palette of muted blues, whites, and greys, reflecting the Atlantic coast’s timeless quality. Wide aerials juxtaposed with intimate close-ups of Wayne’s hands, the turning lens, and salt-worn metal. Use of archival photographs and soundscapes (waves, gulls, foghorn) to evoke continuity and nostalgia. Key Visual Sequences: The revolving lantern at dusk and dawn. Wayne performing routine maintenance. The foghorn echoing across the sea. Archival stills of lighthouses on the South African coastline. Expansive views of the Cape Columbine Nature Reserve. WHY THIS STORY MATTERS The Lighthouse Keeper is a tribute to the quiet guardians who have watched over South Africa’s shores for generations. As automation replaces human presence, Wayne’s story preserves a piece of national heritage — reminding us that some lights still need a human touch. This is not just a story about a lighthouse. It is about duty, legacy, and devotion — a deeply human story told through the lens of one man’s enduring relationship with the sea. DELIVERABLES Broadcast-ready short documentary insert (8–10 minutes) Supporting stills of some of the lighthouses on the South African coastline ______________________________________________________________________________________________

Lighthouses stand as timeless symbols of hope, safety, and endurance - their beams cutting through the fog and darkness to guide sailors home. But behind every shining light once stood a keeper: a quiet guardian who ensured the flame never went out.
caseStudies: Wayne Brown

title: Transport Angels
summary: (Open on a vast, star-filled night sky, then pan down to the dimly lit, labyrinthine streets of a Cape Town township. The air is cold, the shadows deep.) The Call in the Dark The official vehicles won't go here. The police and ambulance services draw a line on the map, a boundary dictated by fear and danger. But beyond that line, in the deepest, most underserved corners of the Western Cape, are children fighting battles no child should face—battling life-limiting illnesses. Every morning, before the city truly wakes, two men receive their dispatch. They are Sonwabo and Humbert, and they are the drivers of a different kind of train: the Super Sam Hero Transport. This is not just a drive; it's a commitment to the impossible. For over 382,510 km, they have taken on the mantle of essential lifelines, safely moving 13,491 young patients to the care they desperately need. (Cut to a shot of a clean, vehicle navigating a deeply potholed, dark road. The contrast is stark.) The Super Sam Express Inspired by the sheer, unwavering hope of the "Polar Express," our story begins and ends with the journey. Imagine the quiet ritual: Sonwabo or Humbert, a beacon in the pre-dawn dark, carefully pulling up to a shack or a small, isolated house. The streets are menacing; the threat of crime is constant. Yet, they step out, calm and utterly focused. They don't just open a door; they usher a child into a sanctuary. In the back of the Paedspal vehicle the world of illness and danger momentarily fades. For these young VIPs, this vehicle is a bubble of warmth, dignity, and unwavering safety. The drivers' warm smiles and gentle hands lift children in wheelchairs, secure prams, and transform a terrifying necessity into a journey of respect. (Cut to a close-up of a driver's hand on a child's shoulder, offering a word of encouragement. The child looks fragile but offers a small smile.) The Unseen Route We need a ride-along not just to document the logistics, but to witness the courage. This is the heart of the "Carte Blanche" treatment: putting the viewer in the passenger seat as Sonwabo or Humbert deliberately cross the lines others won't. The Danger: We will visually contrast the polished hospitals of Cape Town with the brutal reality of the routes—the tension in the air, the need for hyper-vigilance. The Mission: Every trip is an act of resistance against despair. More than a driver, they are a counsellor, a friend, a steady anchor for overwhelmed parents and frightened children seeking vital medical appointments, therapy sessions, and psychosocial support. The Resilience: Through candid interviews in the quiet moments between pickups, we’ll uncover the deeply human side of these drivers. What compels them to face down the danger, day after day? The answer lies in the hope they deliver. Where it all started : We speak to the founder Melissa- This is an important interview for context and to highlight the wonderful work done. (Close with a shot of the sun rising over shacks . The Super Sam Hero Transport is seen driving toward the light, carrying its precious cargo.) This is not a story about statistics; it is a profound testament to what is possible when pure, courageous empathy refuses to acknowledge boundaries—a journey of dignity forged on the most dangerous roads.

title: Becoming Duma
oneLiner: the Transformation of a circus and Zoo elephant into a wild African Elephant and the story of those left behind
summary:
The narrative of a circus animal that became a Zoo elephant at the National Zoo in Pretoria for decades living in half a hectare to his freedom in a 200 hectare wildlife reserve in Limpopo and the court case to free the 3 remaining JHB zoo elephants who barely get enough food on a daily basis.

Beautiful footage and undercover footage and a triumph over adversity narrative
caseStudies: Duma The elephant
experts: Lammie the elephant Megan Carr Lesai Seema Elizabeth Oriel

title: Death In China
oneLiner: What happens when a South African citizen dies while working abroad.
summary:
In August last year, 26-year-old Jarred Anthony Clegg left South Africa for China, where he would be teaching. It was an exciting time for both he and his family as teaching was his passion. Jarred had gotten hold of the opportunity through an agent that had previously sent many South African teachers to China. All was well until June this year. Four months ago, Noeleen Venter, Jarred's mom, received a call from someone who identified themselves as Jarred's friend and colleague who was also based in China. The caller told Noeleen that Jarred had died and the family needed to make arrangements to bring his body back to SA. Noeleen then contacted the agency Jarred was employed by and they confirmed his death, stating that he had died naturally in his apartment. However soon after, Noeleen received a document stating that Jarred had died in an accident and had been convicted of manslaughter. While she was processing this information, she received a document stating that Jarred had died under suspicious circumstances and the matter was now handed to the police for a criminal investigation. Lastly, she was told that her son was a victim of an accident where a vehicle had crashed into him and he died. Sitting with four official documents stating different causes of death, she reached out to a lawyer. Months later, she is desperate to get her son's ashes back but is now receicving a cold shoulder from Dirco, the Chinese Embassy as well as the agent that Jarred was employed by. All Noeleen wants is to know what happened to her son and just where are his ashes. In an effort to get more information, researchg has led us to Nadia who is a South African teacher based in China. She explained that many families find themselves in the same position as Noeleen. She says on many occassions, she has had to carry ashes of deceased South Africans in her luggage during her visits back to South Africa. She says they do this in order to cut costs of transporting the back to SA. We've also gotten hold of an agency that is based in Pretoria, they help place teachers in China and help them get their paperwork processed. The agency says they constantly have issues with DIRCO and the SA consulate in China not playing ball in cases where there are issues or even deaths of SA citizens in China.

We speak to someone who has been tasked with bringing back bodies of South African teachers who die abroad, her methods, unconventional to say the least.
caseStudies: Noeleen Venter Nolubabalo Mqokozo Nadia Meintjies

title: HOT COPPER
oneLiner: South Africa is being unplugged. We expose a shadow industry of large-scale copper heists where syndicates, smugglers and silent buyers strip the nation for profit.
summary:
LOGLINE Copper is the lifeblood of South Africa’s infrastructure and criminals are ripping it out. This we know, this we’ve covered. But the crime trend has morphed, from live power cables and rail lines to a next level large scale criminal operations targeting cargo trucks, foundries and warehouses.

title: Pollytics
oneLiner: A missing African grey sparks a legal tug-of-war in Mbombela, raising big questions about ownership, animal welfare, and the blurred line between pet and family.
summary:
BRIEF OVERVIEW: In Mbombela, a missing parrot story takes flight — and lands in court. After searching for her beloved African grey for over a year, Crystle Pachos finally finds her bird, Zazu. But her relief is short-lived: another family insists the same African grey, named Zippy, belongs to them. What begins as a touching reunion soon unravels into a full-blown custody case — and a national debate about ownership, attachment, and what it means when an animal is considered “property” under the law. Pollytics examines this extraordinary story with wit, warmth, and curiosity. Through one parrot’s tale, we explore the intelligence, emotional capacity, and vulnerability of African greys — a species capable of speech, memory, and affection, yet too often misunderstood and mishandled. With interviews from both families, welfare advocates at Cheeky Beaks, and legal experts, this insert goes beyond the custody fight to examine the broader plight of African greys — one of the world’s most trafficked and misunderstood birds. It’s a courtroom drama with wings, a love story with feathers, and a reminder that sometimes the loudest truths don’t come from people at all. LONGER OVERVIEW: In Mbombela, an unusual custody battle has taken flight — over an African grey parrot. Crystle Pachos’s parrot, Zazu, disappeared in May 2021. For over a year she searched and waited, convinced he was out there somewhere. On 10 May 2021, she got a tip that a grey had been found. Two days later she went to see the bird and believed immediately that it was Zazu. On 13 May, she had him microchipped, certain her family was whole again. But at the very same time, another family was living through the same heartbreak. Obert Ntuli, a lawyer, says his parrot Zippy also went missing in May 2021. So when this single African grey surfaced, both households claimed him. For a while, Zazu stayed with Crystle. Then, in July 2023, Ntuli filed legal papers. After months of arguments and evidence, a magistrate ruled in 2024 that the bird should be returned to Ntuli. Crystle was forced to hand over Zazu — the parrot she had searched for, reunited with, and lived with again for three years. There is even footage of her final hour with him before the handover. But the story isn’t finished. Crystle has appealed, and a cross-appeal is set for October 2025. It’s not politics — it’s Polly-tics: two families parroting their case, feathers ruffled, one perch to stand on. For both Crystle and Obert, this is not just a pet — it’s family. The case has also sparked bigger questions. African greys are among the most intelligent and long-lived birds on earth. They mimic human voices, form strong emotional bonds, and live for decades. Earlier this year in England, five African greys at Lincolnshire Wildlife Park had to be separated for swearing at visitors — a headline that shows how sharp and expressive they are. Experts here disagree on what proper care looks like: some warn about stress, self-plucking and even the danger of a single lick from a dog; the SPCA stresses freedom and enrichment. South Africa is also at the centre of the global African grey trade. Tens of thousands are bred and exported every year, even as the species is listed as endangered in the wild. Mortality during transport, smuggling risks, and weak oversight all form part of the wider story. So this begins with a missing “boy,” a miracle reunion, and a courtroom handover that broke a heart — but it grows into a story about welfare, ownership, and responsibility. It’s a human drama that will resonate with Carte Blanche viewers who see their own animals as family. Polly doesn’t want a cracker — Polly wants a parent. Whose perch is it really — and what does this fight say about people and their parrot pets?

Human story with a twist: A heartfelt custody battle where the “child” is an African grey parrot – an emotional, relatable story wrapped in an unexpected premise. Timely legal angle: One of South Africa’s first animal custody disputes to reach the High Court, testing how ownership, possession, and animal welfare intersect in law. Emotional and visual impact: Genuine footage of Crystle’s final moments with her parrot, strong characters on both sides, and a visually rich contrast between courtroom formality and vibrant bird life. Broader relevance: Opens discussion on the welfare and intelligence of African greys, a species both endangered and traded, exploring how we define family and responsibility toward sentient animals. Carte Blanche fit: Balances wit, heart, and investigation – a distinctive story that is topical, emotional, and uniquely South African.

title: Illegal Sand Mining
oneLiner: Illegal sand mining in Limpopo is drying rivers, destroying farmland, and leaving communities and wildlife struggling to survive.
summary:
In Limpopo, illegal sand mining is wreaking havoc on the environment and the livelihoods of local communities. Once-thriving rivers, like the Kubjanama in the Moping district, have dried up, leaving residents without water and wildlife struggling to survive. Farmers, such as those running Tshipise Safaris, face repeated incursions by unregulated miners, resulting in devastated land, lost crops, and costly legal battles. Despite repeated complaints to the police and the Department of Mineral Resources and Energy, enforcement remains weak, allowing illegal operations to continue. Through the eyes of Edward Malatjie, who once relied on the river for fishing, and legal expert Christo Reeders, who documents the mining activities with drone footage, the story highlights the human and environmental cost of this booming but largely unregulated industry. The narrative also explores the broader national context, showing how the demand for sand in construction fuels the ongoing crisis and questioning whether South Africa’s regulatory frameworks are sufficient to protect communities and natural resources.

From dried-up rivers to ruined farms, illegal sand mining is taking a devastating toll on Limpopo residents.
caseStudies: Christo Reeders Juaq Turner Tshepiso Morena

title: UNIONDALE GHOST TOWN
oneLiner: Uniondale straddles the fragile line between myth and memory, and how communities reinvent themselves to stay alive.
summary:
Tucked deep in the Little Karoo along the legendary Route 62, Uniondale looks like any other sleepy farming town - stone churches, dirt roads, and the smell of fynbos in the air. But beneath its postcard charm lies a tale that refuses to die. In 1968, a young woman named Maria Charlotte Roux was killed in a car crash just outside town on the Barandas road. Since then, travellers swear she still appears - a polite hitchhiker in white who vanishes mid-ride. The Uniondale Ghost has become one of South Africa’s longest-running urban legends, blending tragedy, tourism, and a touch of the supernatural. But there’s more to this “ghost story” than just bumps in the night. Uniondale’s spooky claim to fame has become the town’s most reliable breadwinner. Cafés, padstals, and guesthouses lean into the legend - from “The Hungry Ghost Café” to souvenir T-shirts that proudly proclaim “I Got Ghosted on Route 62.” This Carte Blanche feature explores how one tragic accident became the cornerstone of an unlikely local economy. We revisit the ghost’s origin story - the crash, the sightings, and the people who claim to have met her - but also the living townsfolk who’ve turned folklore into survival.

The Uniondale Ghost has become one of South Africa’s longest-running urban legends, blending tragedy, tourism, and a touch of the supernatural.
caseStudies: Zelma Oosthuyse Dirkie Coetzee Jimmy Zondagh Anthea Du Toit

title: THROWFORWARD GOMA
oneLiner: BATTLE FOR GOMA
summary:
Summary: South African bases at Sake and Goma were overrun by M23 rebels earlier this year during the SANDF's SAMIDRC (South African Development Community Mission in the Democratic Republic of Congo.) 14 SANDF soldiers lost their lives, and a reported 174 were injured - some of them suffering life changing injuries. Some of the soldiers who've returned are willing to speak to us on condition of anonymity. They site failures in planning, intelligence, logistics and leadership as the core issues behind South Africa's lack lustre performance against advancing M23 rebels. A base commander was absent during the heat of the battle, soldiers were hung out to dry after they were caught outside the base when fighting started, and general mayhem ensued when the fighting reached fever pitch. Even after the fighting, when the SANDF had reportedly surrendered, the bases were a scene of chaos. On their return from the DRC after an equally disorganised withdrawal, the SANDF called their deployment in the DRC a success, but angry soldiers say they' ve had enough of the subterfuge and want to tell their stories. This after claims that SADC allocated R108 000 per month per soldier over the period of deployment, while the troops only received R32 000 per month.
