title: Knysna Revisited - Update
oneLiner: Our recent update on the failed attempt to place Knysna under administration generated a significant response, notably from residents who opposed the move.
summary:
On September 12, the Western Cape DA provincial government tabled a notice of dissolution of the Knysna Local Municipality, and planned to appoint an administrator in a bid to restore service delivery. Western Cape MEC for local government Anton Bredell said the decision was due to protracted and ongoing systemic governance and service delivery failures. But, the decision was ultimately blocked by the NCOP on September the 26th. Knysna is governed by an ANC-led coalition with the PA, PBI and EFF. In Knysna, the Democratic Alliance supported the plan to place the town under administration, but all other parties represented on the municipal council, including the Knysna Independent Movement (KIM), opposed it. The town has been plagued by political infighting and service delivery failures for years. The ANC led coalition has been in power since August 2022. Former ANC Mayor, Aubrey Tsengwa, has been blamed for many of the problems, and some residents say the town finally has stability under new ANC Mayor Thando Matika. He took office at the end of February. Knysna Infrastructure Group, an apolitical organisation trying to assist the Municipality to restore service delivery, believes Matika needs to be given a chance to turn things around. KIG's Eugene Vermaak believes placing the town under administration would have been disruptive and would have triggered further political instability. Carte Blanche visited Knysna in February 2024 when the town was showing visible signs of collapse. A decomposing body had been found in one of the reservoirs just weeks before our visit, in December 2023. Sewage spills were common, and refuse collection was non-existent resulting in a rat infestation in the centre of town. When we returned to do another story in June 2025, we found a town still struggling with service delivery failures. But, many were opposed to the town being placed under administration, arguing Knysna was being used as a pawn in a political game, and that the new Mayor needed time to resolve the issues.

Our recent update on the failed attempt to place Knysna under administration generated a significant response, notably from residents who opposed the move. They felt our update didn't provide a full picture, so we returned to Knysna to get their views. Last month, the National Council of Provinces blocked the Western Cape provincial government's move to dissolve Knysna's council and appoint an administrator.

title: Where's the Money
oneLiner: Delving into theDelving into the murky world of business rescue, and the brazen killing of an insolvency lawyer leaves many questions unanswered
summary:
Our story starts with the brazen killing of insolvency lawyer Bouwer van Niekerk. His murder comes almost three years after the assassination of liquidators Cloete Murray and his son Thomas. After van Niekerk's hit all eyes turned to the latest business rescue he was working on with BRP Kurt Knoop. NTC Global Trade , an Crypto trade company turned out Ponzi scheme. We tell the story of the investors and how they were scammed and the BR process put in place by v Niekerk and Knoop. We also take a close look at the another business rescue involving V Niekerk and Knoop - Optimum Coal Mine one of the biggest scandals of the state capture era.

In in-depth investigation into the world of Business Rescue and Liquidations . We uncover an industry where disputes are often solved with a bullet and creditors are left penniless.

title: UPDATE: 1 BILLION RAND HOUSING NORTHERN CAPE
oneLiner: A year after the Premier’s billion-rand promise, the people of the Northern Cape are still waiting no houses, no hope, just politics built on empty ground.
summary:
In April 2024, Carte Blanche visited the Northern Cape to investigate broken infrastructure and undelivered promises in towns across the province. Among the voices that defined that story was Nellie Frans, a 55-year resident of a shanty settlement outside Kimberley, who told us she had been waiting her entire life for a proper home. During that interview, we confronted Premier Zamani Saul about the stalled R1 billion housing project announced only months earlier. Standing on a sewage-drenched street, he assured Carte Blanche that “by the end of the month, a contractor will be putting up site there.” Eighteen months later, nothing has happened. The community says no contractor ever arrived, no foundations have been dug, and no houses are planned for the site where the Premier made his pledge. Residents claim that the few housing allocations that have gone ahead in Leratoville have been politically selective — allegedly limited to ANC-aligned individuals — and that the newly built houses there are structurally unsound, with cracks, collapsing walls, and poor finishes. For people like Nellie Frans, who once believed that promise might finally bring change, the disillusionment has deepened.

Before the elections, the ANC promised change again but in the Northern Cape, not a single brick has been laid, and the only thing still standing are the lies.
caseStudies: Nellie Frans

title: The Final Shift: Beeshoek
oneLiner: A town built on iron now stands on hope alone
summary:
On the edge of the Kalahari lies Beeshoek, a mining town built on red earth and iron ore and on the life that grew around its heartbeat, the mine club. For decades, the Ammosal Club was where miners celebrated paydays, children learned to swim, and families gathered under the floodlights after long shifts underground. It was the soul of a community sustained by the mine’s rhythm. Now, that rhythm is faltering. As South Africa’s steel industry declines and ArcelorMittal slows production, Beeshoek’s future and the life built around it hangs in the balance. The ore that once forged the nation’s pride now sails east to feed foreign furnaces, returning as imported steel at a price South Africans can no longer afford.

As South Africa’s industrial heart falls silent, one small mining community on the edge of the Kalahari faces a reckoning: what happens to a town when the mine that built it begins to fade?
caseStudies: Leonie Horn Michale Mabolo Wilna Venter

title: Death of a Diplomat: Unanswered Questions in Paris
oneLiner: South Africa’s ambassador dies in Paris, leaving more questions than answers - Did Nathi Mthethwa fall — or was he pushed? In the City of Light, a diplomat’s death casts a long shadow
summary:
Main Hook On the night of 28 September, South Africa’s ambassador to France, Nathi Mthethwa, fell to his death from a room at Paris’s Hyatt Regency. Was it a tragic accident, suicide, or something more sinister? French prosecutors remain silent, fuelling speculation. The timing is striking: just days earlier, Mthethwa’s name resurfaced in South Africa at the Madlanga Commission into corruption at the South African Police Service. He was accused of political interference during his tenure as police commissioner — a reminder of the controversies that followed him into his diplomatic career. Carte Blanche travels to the French capital to piece together the ambassador’s final days — from his joyous interactions at a memorial in Longheuval, to the window from which he plunged, to the unanswered calls for clarity from grieving families and colleagues. This is not only the story of one man’s untimely death, but also of how France’s justice system handles sensitive investigations in the glare of international scrutiny.

Carte Blanche will be the only South African media house with local expertise on the ground
caseStudies: Rafael Miro David Labranche

When an insider becomes the accused.

title: Kempton Park's Haunted Hospital
oneLiner: Dubbed South Africa's ghost hospital, the Kempton Park hospital closed in 1996. Since then it's become a destination for thrill seekers, but its draining millions from the public purse.
summary:
The hospital has become the stuff of legend. Ghostly sightings and a disgraced doctor have become folklore and paranormal “hunters” allegedly bribe guards to gain access. On the social media platform TikTok, dozens of videos showing the inside of the hospital have been posted. Comments on the posts indicate security guards were bribed between R50 and R150 to gain access. The Gauteng Department of Health spends over five million rand a year on security (revealed in a provincial legislature reply), yet the site has been stripped bare. Patients at Tembisa Hospital just 22 minutes away sleep on chairs and floors. Those living in Kempton Park are referred to Tembisa hospital, where conditions are dire. Yet, the Heatlh Department’s promises to refurbish the Kempton Park hospital have come to nothing. Ideas of refurbishing, demolishing or rebuilding, have gone nowhere. Costs ranged from 1,7 billion to 3,6 billion. Costs for security have ballooned to R35 million since its closure in 1996. The Democratic Alliance's Michael Waters, who inspected the site recently, said the building is an empty shell, with broken windows, ripped-out electrical outlets, smashed furniture and graffiti on the walls. He said it's clear the building has been illegally invaded, and something needs to be done urgently. Mother nature has taken over the site, and its clear that money is not being spent on the grounds. This is visible outside the hospital, where the land has become completely overgrown. Ghost tour operators have been doing tours of the hospital - a content creation company called Space did a series of videos of haunted places in Joburg, and visited Kempton Park hospital with a ghost tour operator. The videos show clear evidence of ash from recently burnt fires. It's seems access, if you are willing to bribe the security guards, is not an issue. On Halloween, it apparently gets very busy as hunters of the paranormal seek their thrills at the abandoned hospital.

Kempton Park Hospital, a vast, decaying landmark closed suddenly in 1996 and was left to rot for nearly three decades. Once a state-of-the-art facility, it is now dubbed South Africa’s “ghost hospital,” known as much for its haunted reputation and thrill-seeking trespassers as for the millions it still drains from the public purse.

title: Gwala Ka Jan - A Pollsmoor Production
oneLiner: We see how creative writing and acting can set convicted prisoners free
summary:
Gwala Ka Jan – A Pollsmoor Production When a convict enters a new prison in South Africa he is asked Gwala Ka Jan? Which is the lingo for: Who are you? His or her answer will determine where he sleeps, who he associates with and where he sits in the prison hierarchy. Gwala Ka Jan is the name of a play developed by Pollsmoor offenders with the help of a creative writing teacher, Suzette Leal, who volunteered earlier this year at the prison, not quite knowing how drawn into the lives of individual convicts she would become. Nor did she know that the “narrative therapy” she was using would become not only a lifeline, but the foundation for a play, written by prisoners, starring prisoners and engaging an audience from outside of the prison walls. It’s not been done before in South Africa. To capture both the interaction between a relatively wealthy woman and three prisoners, as well as to explore the success of narrative therapy, we have been given permission to go inside Pollsmoor, under the watchful eye of Correctional Services. We have asked to interview three prisoners who are part of the play. Characters: • Curt Vincer, artist, recovering addict in prison for murdering his grandmother • Fareed Pelton, senior general of 27 gang, convicted murderer, serving time for breaking parole, trying to retire from the Number • Mdu, professional opera singer who is serving time for housebreaking (itv not quite guaranteed yet) They will talk about their backgrounds, what got them into prison, the impact of Narrative Therapy, and how the play has taken shape. They will talk of how they want the play to impact the audience, and the wider public. We will touch on the themes of identity, rehabilitation versus punishment and the tension between physical incarceration and imaginative freedom. We will ask them what it is like to be in prison, about their routines, and the world it creates around them. We will have to be sensitive of how much they want to tell us about the crimes they committed – I have been told that Curt is very sensitive and unsure whether he wants to reveal the whole story. We will also see them doing the things that make them special. We will film Curt drawing, and being the librarian at Medium B. I attach some of his pictures. We film Fareed writing in class with Suzette Leal who has engaged them in her class since March this year. We film Mdu singing. (Shades of the Shawshank Redemption) We will also film them all in dress rehearsal with Natasha Dryden, a former Sewende Laan actress who is helping them get the play ready. We will interview Natasha in the recreational hall once the dress rehearsal is done, so that she can reflect on what she is able to teach them and what she has experienced directing this play. We are obliged to interview a Correctional Services representative. They can’t decide who but will tell us in time as the person “needs to be prepared”. Correctional Services is in the process of trying to rebrand themselves as a more loving, caring rehabilitative institution. The week before the play, 300 warders and offenders are travelling to George (where John is) for a literary festival which will include a Spelling Bee in all the official languages, including Nama. I have asked for some visuals of this, to flesh out the theme of rehabilitation as opposed to punishment, as well as to strategically signal to DCS that we are on their side. Suzette tells me that most of the prisoners seem to while away their time sleeping, so the literary festival is in stark contrast to the default slumber. Then we will leave the prison to go “outside” to Camps Bay where Suzette lives. We will interview her there, and maybe get B-roll of her on the beach. I would want to capture visuals of “freedom” – beach, sea, palm trees in the wind etc as a contrast to the prison interior. Then we will return to Medium B on the night of one of the performances. I have asked for the camera to be back stage, to catch the nerves of the actors – those who can murder and housebreak but are nervous about standing up and saying their lines in front of an audience. We will capture them asking the audience the question: Gwala Ka Jan? and then also the applause at the end. This will make the shoot longer but seeing it is in the same week as our interviews, I think it is worth getting it. It should count as another half day. All of this has been signed off in principle by Correctional Services.

We have unique access to a writing and theatre project inside Pollsmoor prison, thanks to the intervention of creative writing teacher Dr Suzette Leal who has been teaching prisoners creative writing, to the extent that they have developed a semi-autobiographical play which is to be performed for friends and family from outside the prison.
caseStudies: Curt Vincer Fareed Pelton Mduduzi Semanu
experts: Suzette Leal Natasha Dryden Brandon Verrooi

title: MURDER BY MARKETPLACE
oneLiner: When marketplace turns to murder.
summary:
He invited them to a wedding. They came to a funeral. 29-year-old Mogamat Yusuf Daniels should have been a groom. Instead, days before the ceremony, he was executed in a Facebook Marketplace ambush in Ottery. Two young women lured him under the guise of buying his iPhone. His fiancée had been with him just half an hour earlier. Yusuf took his cousin and the cousin’s child along for safety. But safety was a lie. When they arrived, the gunman stepped from the shadows, shoved his weapon against the boy’s head, and demanded everything. Yusuf drew his licensed firearm to protect the child. Shots cracked through the night. Moments later, he lay dead on the ground - a groom-to-be bleeding out in front of a terrified child. This isn’t random. It’s part of a new criminal economy built on Facebook Marketplace: In Winterveldt, a man was hijacked and locked in the boot of his own car. In Midrand, a fake sale ended in a police gun battle - five suspects shot, others fled. In Pretoria, five more were arrested in another syndicate sting, young women again used as bait. The blueprint is the same: lure, misdirect, test the goods, then ambush. A digital platform has become South Africa’s deadliest street corner. The investigation: Carte Blanche exposes the anatomy of these traps - how syndicates use women to bait, children to break victims’ resolve, and trust itself as the weapon. We’ll confront SAPS on why they only arrive after the body bags, and demand answers from Meta, whose platform has been weaponised into a marketplace of death.

In South Africa today, a man trying to sell his phone to pay for his wedding can end up in a coffin, and a child can stare down the barrel of a gun.
caseStudies: Anna Collard Abdurugman Jacobs Andre Traut

title: The Battle of Goma
oneLiner: With 14 dead and more than a hundred injured - the SANDF's withdrawal from the DRC was anything but covered in glory - now insiders paint a grim picture of a deployment gone horribly wrong.
summary:
South African bases at Sake and Goma were overrun by M23 rebels earlier this year during the SANDF's SAMIDRC (South African Development Community Mission in the Democratic Republic of Congo.) 14 SANDF soldiers lost their lives, and a reported 174 were injured - some of them suffering life changing injuries. Some of the soldiers who've returned are willing to speak to us on condition of anonymity. They site failures in planning, intelligence, logistics and leadership as the core issues behind South Africa's lack lustre performance against advancing M23 rebels. A base commander was absent during the heat of the battle, soldiers were hung out to dry after they were caught outside the base when fighting started, and general mayhem ensued when the fighting reached fever pitch. Even after the fighting, when the SANDF had reportedly surrendered, the bases were a scene of chaos. Rations were in short supply, and some soldiers were forced to eat food from fridges that were storing the bodies of the dead. Basic medical kits were nowhere to be found. On their return from the DRC after an equally disorganised withdrawal, the SANDF called their deployment in the DRC a success, but angry soldiers say they've had enough of the subterfuge and want to tell their stories. Defense Union SANDU is claiming each member deployed be paid R8000 per day as well as a compensation amount of $1428 per soldier. This after claims that SADC allocated R108 000 per month per soldier over the period of deployment, while the troops only received R32 000 per month. Where the additional funds went remains a mystery.

SANDF soldiers who were caught up in the attack by M23 rebels earlier this year on South African bases in Sake and Goma want to speak out. They paint a grim picture of a deployment doomed to fail from the get go - inadequate operational plans, ill equipped bases and a failure of leadership during the battle are just some of their complaints. Serious questions raised around what happened to monies meant for the soldiers while on deployment have just added fuel to the fire. Now soldiers are willing to risk their careers to tell their stories.

title: High on Ink
oneLiner: A “paperless” Joburg is hoarding over R100 million in ink, R40 million of which can’t be used —exposing chaotic procurement, mountains of dead stock, and a supplier address that leads to a bou
summary:
ROUGH SCRIPT:OPENING ACT – A city that’s high on ink Presenter VO: It was a slow Wednesday morning… one of our Carte Blanche producers drew the short straw: the July City of Johannesburg Council meeting. As expected —SOUNDUP: “Item 43” drier than a Joburg winter lawn. UPSOUND – Neuren: video of him at council “For a first-class African city, we should be doing better…” Presenter VO: And then, during one of Councillor Neuren Pietersen’s trademark report-backs from an oversight visit to the City’s storerooms… something actually piqued her interest. Cut to Council Audio (UPSOUND): Neuren Pietersen: “To date, the City is not privy to the detail of any contracts, which we are expected to note here today. We still don’t know how much we pay for a bottle of water, a pen, a ream of paper — or why we have R100 million worth of ink cartridges in stock that the City no longer uses!” Presenter VO: That’s the kind of line that makes journalists bolt upright—faster than dodging a Joburg pothole. This was a story, with the councillor providing the punchlines. Neuren in council: “To date, this councillor—yours truly—has never received an ink cartridge for my own HP DeskJet… something that’s meant to be included as part of a councillor’s tools of trade. I hope the Auditor-General is listening…” Presenter VO: Well, she’s not the Auditor-General—but she does WhatsApp the councillor. He sends photos from his oversight visit: floor-to-ceiling cartridges. INTV: Neuren: Turns out, at Smit Street Stores—one of the City’s storerooms—there are millions of rands’ worth of “dead stock”: expired cartridges, or cartridges for printers the City no longer uses. Presenter link: The city says it wants to go paperless, council has already gone that route, so how can they justify spending that amount on printer cartridges? This is like squid games, only instead of dead people, its dead stock. VO: At a time when the City is scratching around for money to fix potholes, keep the lights on, and even contemplating selling off public assets like our public parks— why are we spending a fortune on ink cartridges? ACT 1: Why Ink? Presenter VO: Neuren is a character — hard to miss in that Panama hat. His turf is Ward 118, from Linksfield to Cleveland — basically Joburg’s welcome mat as you roll in from the airport. Montage (cutaways): Uncut grass. Buckled pavements. A broken sever system. UPSOUND – Neuren: “This has been waiting nine months to be fixed because Joburg didn’t have money for material.” Cutaway: Substation has no security UPSOUND – Neuren: “The substation has lots of theft and vandalism because there’s no security.” Presenter VO: All of that is easy to see. But when he joined the finance committee, he spotted something you can’t see from the roadside. Of the City’s four consumables warehouses: Three were sitting at a few million each…but one then one was clocking over R100 million. Presenter link [outside the warehouse]: That warehouse is here on Smit Street: Turns out it isn’t hoarding gold; but stationery—mostly ink cartridges. A one-hundred million rand ink-vestment? Neuren: We spend R10 million on stationery per quarter—my guesstimate: R3 million on paper, R6 million on ink, minimum. It’s stockpiled in that warehouse. VO: It’s hard to be accurate when the city is not transparent – for the last decade no tenders have been posted online for the public, no number breakdowns are given to council – it seems it’s a state secret… Neuren: For example: we spent R10 million on paper products like toilet paper… but there’s no breakdown and we don’t know where the papers going, and we don’t know how much is used or left over… and council has gone paperless, but the numbers for ink and paper – weirdly haven’t gone down? VO: Exact figures? Hard to come by when the City treats numbers like a state secret—no tenders posted online for years, no line-item breakdowns to Council. Transparency is one item in the City perpetually out of stock. UPSOUND – Neuren: “For example: we spent R10 million on paper products—like toilet paper—but there’s no breakdown. We don’t know where it’s going, how much is used, or what’s left over. And Council has gone ‘paperless’, yet the ink and paper numbers haven’t dropped?” VO: Also—much of the City’s paperwork is outsourced. In our July story on Joburg parks, officials said most documents like tenders are prepared externally — and often printed off-site. SOUNDUP from previous story: (date it) Mac: Who writes these tender documents?” Tshabalala: “We compile a list of what needs to be done and we appoint service providers.” VO: And many departments don’t buy printers at all—they lease them: meaning toner is vendor-supplied. Neuren: I’ve checked departments—Revenue, Health, Road Traffic Management Centre—trying to find City-owned printers that actually need cartridges… I’m still looking. On my oversight visit I was told the majority of cartridges go to the JMPD. VO: But Whatsapps from a city insider says most of the JMPDs printers are leased. SHOW WHATSAPPS: [The printers] are all on a rental lease… when the ink is closer to being finished, the lease company is contacted. VO: So… if much of the printing is outsourced, and the leased printers come with their own toner… where is all this ink going? ACT 2: The undercover VO: Time to see for ourselves. We head to Smit Street Stores — undercover — with councillors Neuren Pietersen and David Foley, a ward councillor from Fourways, to illustrate the problem. We’re walked through by an employee reporting back to the councillors — unaware we’re filming. Downstairs, first stop: a room stacked wall-to-wall with thousands of expired printer cartridges. [41. 25 all expired stock] 41.31 all of these are expired S: so those lexmarks are expired? Yes. These ones are expired. over 10 years old S: 10 years? and you say it's over 2 million stock in here? Employee: yes 2.7 million worth of expired stock. VO: Ink economics aren’t sexy—until you’re staring at millions of rands of it - R2.7 million parked just in that corner. [Video pan of expired stock 41.51] VO: Roughly twenty million rands worth of stock is expired. So why is it sitting there instead of written off and auctioned? Neuren: The City did write off a fraction—about 0.3%. Clipboards and notepads. The cartridges? They could go on auction, but there hasn’t been one this year. And no one wants to take responsibility. VO: The employee gives us a clue why the cartridges haven’t been written off. Undercover video: 1:00:50 Councillor: I don't understand why they why they're not bringing that up to the fore, why are they so resistant to say okay we've made a mistake, write it off, move on. Employee: when you know that you have blundered, you will not stand up! VO: In other words, it’s the usual story… no one wants to raise a hand and own the mistake. [pause] Here’s the irony: councillors are entitled to one printer cartridge per quarter. And Neuren’s model is sitting right there.. But he still can’t even get one…as this city employee tells him… CALL WITH NEUREN and PRESENTER: Karabo… VO: But a bigger problem reveals itself as we wind through the two-storey warehouse. Shelves of “dead” stock: ink for printers the City no longer uses. Undercover video: Visual: 59.28 – 59.50 [WALKING ALONG SHELVES SEEING DEAD STOCK] Employee: all these cartridges are dead Sasha: Canon, HP, Brother… OKI, Lexmark. VO: Much of it is perfectly usable— Here’s a fact you didn’t ask for: what does R1 million in printer cartridges look like? Undercover video: Visual: 46:00 WE SEE BOXES OF CARTRIDGES IN CORNER JUST SITTING THERE, NO LONGER BEING USED. Upsound: 46.20 Sasha: and so wait so this is about a million rand here, but then I just wanna understand now, the amount of um…, that might not move again, so then what do you do with it? Employee: it might not move again, take a picture and save it, it might not move again, a million rand stuck, standing there. VO: And another million rand here — A monument to the City’s “procure first, plan later” mindset. Undercover video: [47.20 /53.08 see the boxes without him] 47.20 Eployee: This was the old cartridge that JMPD was using, another million. Ccouncillor: and how long has it been standing here? Employee: it's almost a year now okay Neuren intv: Presenter: How does that happen? Neuren: 1. The IT department just changes printers. 2. No one checks what stock they have OR speaks with the stores manager. 3. They have an expensive SAP system implemented that’s cost us billions that has the stock numbers in it, but apparently no one checks it… Show: 59.28 – 59.50 [WALKING ALONG SHELVES SEEING DEAD STOCK] VOICE OF ACTOR: 18:05 Employee: that thing hurts me, I alluded to that last time you were here, I have a problem where, you say to me, your department uses Lexmark 500, (shows hands giving) lexmark 500, how many do you want for a department? you say I want 1000 cartridges 18.23 a thousand uh cartridges I buy a thousand cartridges three months down the line, somebody decides from wherever I sitting to say I'm no longer using Lexmark now I'm using HP, now I've got your stock in storage which is no longer moving, and not just minimum stock, 18.39 I order in bulk, but that things are made on contract so if I order 500 cartridges and you take only 300, 200 gets wasted. Visual: 52.38 [walk down isle of stock that they no longer can use cos there’s no printers for them] VO: Row after row of useless stock. [pause] Sometimes IT seemingly changes printer models, other times they change suppliers. Undercover footage: 42.10 OKI (PRINTER COMPANY), we no longer order OKI, [he opens doors showing all the stock that we no longer order – just wasted left over stock] Sasha: so do we no longer have OKI as a supplier? C: have those printers just expire? Employee: we don't have those printers so nobody's collecting them VO: It all builds to a grim little punchline. Councillor: You probably carry more stock than an actual supplier haha VO: On paper: R104 million in stock. In reality: roughly R40 million can’t be used—either expired or there’s no compatible printer. Sasha: its 104 million? Employee: yes on this store alone. they've got four stores, but on this one is hundred million 53.55 and after 100 million maybe 40 million does not work anymore Sasha: maybe 40 million sho! Neuren: INtv:80 million? VO: The Bottom line? Millions converted into cartridges, gathering dust—because the City’s asset control is weak, it’s procurement isn’t standardised, and this mess invites exploitation. Undercover: Employee: 35:10 A cartridge, see will see, this one can easily cost R1,200, but here it's R2,800. Councillor: Double. and that's with profit probably. Councillor: 1,200 has already got a profit. 30% maybe. Employee: so others are making 60%, 200% Councillor: get rich quick? Employee: on cartridges 35.19 Councillor: that's a big money item CYAKHULA SECTION: VO: We finally got our hands on a partial invoice: R2.5 million paid last year to Cyakhula Business Solutions. On paper, they’re only one of the City’s ink suppliers. VO: On stationery, Pietersen says the City appointed 36 companies on an “as-and-when” panel—worth up to R45 million. The catch? Low-value items (think a R2 pen) aren’t worth the delivery run. Result: shelves stay empty, even with suppliers on paper. Neuren intv: Presenter: Who’s responsible for overseeing the stores? Neuren: Aubrey Mochela, head of IT. Neuren: “They do—but they don’t want you to know what’s going on.” Presenter: So what do we think is happening? Neuren: “If we can’t find where the ink is going, what are we left to suspect? Is the ink actually getting to a printer in the City of Johannesburg?” Presenter: And if it isn’t—what does that mean? Are we just… rotating stock? Neuren: “We don’t know. But as a public representative doing oversight, how can I tell residents we’re getting value for money—legally—if we can’t track it? VO: If the dead stock isn’t liquidated or auctioned, we’re watching up to millions go down the drain—the kind of money that could build a substation or 200 RDP houses. A City that says it’s broke—while this sits on a shelf.

We went undercover to the smit street stores to see the chaos. We have really great footage, and have a compelling story that will illustrate what a mess the asset management system is. In short: it says Joburg talks “modern, paperless city,” but runs on procure-first, plan-later. Transparency gap: basic spend and contracts aren’t clearly published or explained. Control failure: stock counts, write-offs, and auctions aren’t working; SAP/asset data isn’t driving decisions. No standardisation: departments/IT change printers without checking stores → waste by design. Misaligned incentives: outsourced printing + leased printers (toner included) while buying separate cartridges anyway. Service impact: money that should fix pipes, power and roads is frozen on shelves. Accountability vacuum: everyone’s “aware,” nobody owns it. Bottom line: not just wastage—a governance problem that bleeds budgets and trust.

title: Seeds of Survival: Svalbard’s Vault of Life Amid Arctic Tensions
oneLiner: A hidden “Doomsday Vault” in the Arctic safeguards the world’s crop diversity even as rising geopolitical tensions threaten this rare beacon of global cooperation against climate catastrophe.
summary:
Buried deep inside a frozen mountain, just 1,300 kilometres from the North Pole, lies the Svalbard Global Seed Vault — humanity’s ultimate insurance policy against ecological and agricultural catastrophe. Between 20 and 22 October, a new consignment of seeds will be deposited in this so-called “Doomsday Vault,”reinforcing a unique global pact: countries that often clash politically all entrust their genetic treasures to this single, icy outpost. But the Arctic’s political climate is shifting. Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and NATO’s expansion to Sweden and Finland, Svalbard’s strategic location has become a focal point for intelligence agencies and military planners. Norway’s first national security strategy now bluntly warns that “national control in Svalbard is to be strengthened.” Carte Blanche travels to this Arctic frontier to witness the next seed deposit and explore how rising geopolitical tension could threaten one of the world’s greatest experiments in international cooperation — a project designed to protect life itself from climate disaster. Protagonists Åsmund Asdal – Coordinator of Operation and Management, Svalbard Global Seed Vault. Explains the vault’s mission, security protocols and the significance of the October seed deposit. Dr Morven Muilwijk – NPI physical oceanographer studying sea ice decline and heat transport in the Arctic Ocean. Provides scientific context for how a warming Arctic underscores the vault’s urgency. Dr Ingeborg Hallanger – NPI research scientist specialising in microplastics and environmental pollutants in ice-filled waters. Highlights the Arctic’s vulnerability to global pollution and climate change. Leif Terje Aunevik – Mayor of Longyearbyen. Discusses how the world’s northernmost town balances scientific research, tourism and the growing presence of global powers. Ildar Neverov – Director of Arktikugol, the Russian state-owned company that operates the Barentsburg settlement. Offers insight (if possible) into the Russian perspective on Svalbard’s changing geopolitical significance. Key Themes Insurance for Humanity: How the Svalbard Global Seed Vault safeguards the genetic diversity of crops against climate change, conflict and catastrophe. Cooperation vs. Confrontation: The vault as a rare symbol of international trust — and whether rising geopolitical tension can fracture that trust. Arctic Frontline: Svalbard’s new strategic importance in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, NATO’s expansion, and debates over control of the High North. Fragile Ecosystem: Scientific evidence of how rapidly the Arctic is changing — from melting sea ice to microplastic contamination. Human Stories at the Edge: Life in Longyearbyen and the Russian mining settlement of Barentsburg as communities navigate the collision of science, climate and geopolitics. Visual Approach Opening Montage: Aerial shots of Svalbard’s stark, glacial landscape. Slow-motion images of seed crates being lowered into the frost-covered vault. Juxtapose with satellite images and archival footage of Arctic military manoeuvres and political summits. Inside the Vault: Accompanied by Åsmund Asdal during the October seed deposit; close-ups of vacuum-packed seeds, frost-encrusted steel doors, and the dramatic, ice-lit tunnels. Scientific Context: On-ice interviews with Dr Morven Muilwijk and Dr Ingeborg Hallanger, illustrating the rapid decline of Arctic sea ice and the growing presence of microplastics. Longyearbyen & Barentsburg: Walk-and-talk with Mayor Leif Terje Aunevik through Longyearbyen’s snow-covered streets, discussing the pressures of increased geopolitical attention. Journey by boat or snowmobile to Barentsburg: coal mines, Soviet-era architecture, and (if granted access) an interview or doorstop with Ildar Neverov on Russia’s role and intentions. Data & Graphics: Global seed diversity charts; maps of NATO expansion and Arctic territorial claims; Norwegian national security strategy highlights. Closing Sequence: The vault’s massive doors sealing shut after the October deposit, fading to a sweeping Arctic night sky — a stark reminder of both the resilience and fragility of international cooperation. Production Challenges & Approach Extreme Conditions: Harsh Arctic temperatures and limited daylight; specialist cold-weather gear required. Restricted Access: Travel to Barentsburg necessitates boat or snowmobile; Russian officials may decline interviews, requiring contingency filming. Geopolitical Sensitivity: Heightened tensions between NATO members and Russia demand careful editorial balance and legal vetting.

- Humanity’s Insurance Policy: An exclusive look inside the world’s ultimate backup plan for global food security—the Svalbard Global Seed Vault during a live seed deposit. - Rare International Cooperation: A project where nations in conflict still entrust their most vital genetic resources, making it a symbol of fragile but enduring global trust. - Geopolitics Meets Climate Crisis: The vault’s mission collides with a rapidly militarising Arctic as NATO expands and Russia asserts its presence. - First-hand Arctic Science: On-site interviews with polar researchers revealing the accelerating impacts of climate change and pollution in one of the planet’s most sensitive regions. - Dramatic Visual Storytelling: From the frozen vault tunnels to Russian mining settlements and stark glacial landscapes, a visually striking narrative of resilience and tension.

title: Hiding in plain sight
summary:
In early July, the KZN deputy police commissioner Nhlanhla Mkhwanazi shook the very foundations of the state during a press conference that looked more like a coup than a Sunday afternoon press conference. He arrived in camo gear flanked by bodyguards with semi-automatic machine guns slung across their chests. His message to the South African public was that the criminal justice system was corrupt and something needed to be done urgently. It’s not that the public didn’t know this, but coming from a high ranking general in the SAPS it carried an enormous amount of weight. And the police are notorious for saying nothing, so this press conference was explosive. Mkhwanazi named names, showed pieces of evidence, and overnight he became the heroic whistleblower, propelled almost to mythical status for a public worn down by crime and corruption. During the long briefing he made allegations against the police minister, municipal cops, top cops, the judiciary and a host of others. In response the President called for a commission of inquiry, put the police minister Senzo Mchunu on special leave and General Shadrack Sibiya who has been in line for the top job of the Hawks was suspended, his name tainted by the allegations. Sibiya’s legal papers challenging his suspension run to almost 2000 pages, and tell a completely different story, but he lost on urgency and will have to wait for his time at the commission to reveal his secrets- secrets which are just as eye popping as Mkhwanazi’s revelations.

Unique high ranking sources - one prepared to go on camera - with a view that challenges the prevailing narrative

title: From Okiep to the World
oneLiner: It’s a beautiful story, inspiring and quintessential South African stories in one of the most far-flung unlikely places.
summary:
But in the words of the founder Alfred Henkell these shows are just to raise money- their real audiences are in Springbok, Okiep, Nabaeep - that is who they care about. They have grown these audiences through screening their films and performing their craft to over 500 paying residences. They are telling their story and growing their passion in these far flung towns and they are a riot of pride and recognition. That’s who they are doing it for. Alfred Henkel and John Linden legends in the contemporary dance world retired to their hometown Okiep. They had spent decades developing contemporary dance in Cape Town, establishing the Jazzart Dance Theatre into South Africa’s premier performing arts training and performance institution since 1986. Alfred also establish dance as a subject in schools across the Cape Flats and its one of his prodigies Byron Klaasens that is the now the Artistic Director of the Garage Dance Ensemble – ironically he was also born in Okiep although he started dancing in Cape Town in one of the Flats schools But retirement was boring and Alfred and John once again they found themselves on the dance floor – or rather in the garage and re-egnited a group they had establish in the 80’s - Die Namakwalandse Dans Geselskap – based in the small towns of Nababeep and Okiep in the Northern Cape. Brandon grew up with his grandmother who taught him reel dance, Stoff dance, sakkie and Langarm- all deeply rooted in these communities. So, tapping into this deep well of dance they have woven it into their contemporary dance using a local actress to narrate their stories.

Okeip, Nababeep and Springbok- when one hears those names one thinks of small, stark, and desperately poor towns far up the West Coast. Okiep-a dusty mining town best known for the deserted copper mine who’s toxic dust still blows across the houses - is a tumble weeds roll away from Springbok. But today its being put back on the map by the Garage Contemporary Dance Ensemble. They have just returned from Germany after performing at Ruhrtriennale 2025 Premiere- this is on the back of many other successful European performances.
caseStudies: Alfred Henkell Brandon Klaasens

title: The Yeoville Dinner Club
oneLiner: we dine with the world, from right here in Johannesburg
summary:
When people think of Yeoville, they think dilapidated buildings, hustle and bustle, sometimes crime, just chaos. It's hard to imagine the the area was once the hub of South Africa's arts and music; also known for being vibrant and culturally diverse. Now, tt's an utter mess with neglected infrastructure and dirty streets In the middle of all that chaos is a dinner club that has hosted people from the world over. Guests, mostly tourists, sit along long tables and share a meal with strangers from different parts of the world while Chef Sandile Sanza serves dishes and drinks from countries on the continent. Each dish has a story and Sanza shares his wealth of knowledge not only of South Africa, but of the continent. It's about people coming together to experience Africa through food, music and art. Sanza Sandile founded the Dinner Club because he once lived there and wanted to revive or contribute to what it was once known for. He's cooked for some well known celebrities both locally and internationally. He has just returned from a US tour of sharing African cuisines.

A dinner club of strangers at the heart of Joburg

title: Patricia — South Africa’s Oldest Working Steam Locomotive
summary:
In 1897, Dübs & Company in Glasgow built a Class 6A engine for the Cape Government Railways. It was first numbered 194 under CGR, and in 1912 renumbered SAR 473 when the Union of South Africa was formed. Today it is privately owned by Clive Holliday. He bought the locomotive in 2016 and began restoring it at Germiston Steam Depot. Every part has been repaired or replaced. After years of work, it is now back in working condition. Our main character is Clive Holliday Clive is a private collector and rail-heritage enthusiast. He believes in preserving South Africa’s steam history. He didn’t buy this train for money or fame. He bought it because it matters — for history, for the people who remember, for those who will see it move. He committed a seven-figure sum. He committed years of work. He pushed through when parts were hard to find. He dealt with logistics, old metal, old drawings, restoration teams. Challenges • Restoration was expensive and complex. • He had to work with Transnet Engineering to use the Germiston Steam Depot. • Now there is a dispute: he is being charged high monthly site fees. The space needed is large. Some of it is unused by him, yet he pays for all. • If the fees stay high, or if he is forced off the site, the future of Patricia could be in danger. Relaunch Event Patricia will be relaunched on Saturday, 20 September 2025 at 10:00 AM at Old Germiston Steam Depot. It will be a public event to mark the completion of the full nut-and-bolt restoration. This is a story about history, a man’s resolve, and a locomotive that has been given a second life. But what now? It is finished and what happens next?

A man, his train and their story! This is not just another heritage item on display — Patricia is the oldest working steam locomotive on the African continent (built 1897, 128 years old). Its survival is thanks to one man, Clive Holliday, who personally invested a seven-figure sum and eight years of work to bring it back to life. The relaunch is both a celebration of South Africa’s rail history and a rare chance to see a Victorian-era locomotive run again — but its future is under threat because of high site fees and tension with Transnet.
caseStudies: Shaun Ackerman Clive holliday

title: Inanda Land Grab revisited
oneLiner: We revisit the Tea Estate near Durban where a fierce battle has been raging for almost ten years about ownership of farmland.
summary:
In 2018 we covered a story about land invasion in Tea Estate Inanda north of Durban. The Chief in the area claims the land belongs to the Qadi clan and he has the right over the land. Since our story aired the land invasions continued and the farmers obtained a court order against ha AmaQadi clan to stop them from selling and allocating land the farmers say belong to them. Large homes – including a three star hotel- have been built on the land. Roads, water and electricity have been provided to some of the dwellings by the municipality. The farmers association questioned why amenities are provided to unregistered properties but have not had any response. . In 2019 the High Courts ruled in favour of the farmers , ordering a halt to the sale or allocation of land by the chief, Inkose Mqoqi Ngcono. The farmersI provided title deeds , proving that the land belongs to them. They farmed mostly sugar cane. The order included the demolition of structures. No structures have been demolished to date. Farmers fear that there will be unrest if they take action. The disputed land comprises farms that have been carved up, sold, cleared and built on. . The farmers sought a final interdict to prevent Chief Ngcobo or his Nduna from inciting people to “invade, carve, fence, erect structures” such as houses on the land. In court papers, they contend that people occupying the land had said they paid between R20,000 and R50,000 to Nduna of Ngcobo. Ngcobo claims the disputed land, along with land in Ndwedwe, Ballito and Umhlanga, has been part of the AmaQadi clan land for centuries. He disputes the Tea Estate farmers’ contention that their title deeds are proof that their families bought the land more than 100 years ago. The farmers say they have been paying rates and fees for other municipal services. When we were there just more than 4 farms were impacted , seven years later 700 hectares have been invaded and luxury houses built. Protesting farmers have been intimidated with one farmer kidnapped, seriously beaten and his house petrol bombed( Video available) Other farmers had their tractors and sheds burnt to the ground and their lives threatened. Our source said that this will be his last year of farming as he won’t have enough land left and will have to let go of his 250 workers. Not any of the farmers have been compensated for their land. The farmer’s attorney has approached the provincial police and government departments without any success. There have been numerous consultations and meetings with police including Mkwanazi and Masemola but the 160 dockets have not been investigated. Verulam And Inanda police have not offered any assistance.

We revisit Tea estate Inanda near Durban where illegal farm invasions and illegal sale of farmland has been ongoing since 2016 . Landgrabs have escalated and racial tension is building daily.

title: Grand Undertaking
oneLiner: Taboo or not taboo? Everything you've been dying to know about the serious business of funerals
summary:
We visit 3 distinctly different undertaking businesses: 1. Centurion Funeral Directors Small family funeral parlour business in Centurion got into this by accident because they had a limo. They themselves suffered three deaths in the family in a short space of time and had to deal with very unsympathetic undertakers. In 2007 they decided to provide a service that would support community families in their hour of need. Their motto is “Compassion & Diversity Personified”. Now it’s a thriving enterprise with 8 hearses/limos servicing only the Pretoria/Laudium area, specialising in Hindu & Muslim funerals. Natasha now loves it, loves doing the makeup on the body; finds it meditative and calming, different to the drama of organising catering etc. within 24 hours. We can also go with them to the Rebecca Street Crematorium. 2. AVBOB Major corporate enterprise with massive HQ in Centurion. It began in Bloemfontein in 1918 in the aftermath of the First World War and the Spanish Flu pandemic. The South African landscape was littered with the makeshift mass graves of those devastated by disease and poverty. In the midst of this devastation, a partially-blind schoolmaster, HH van Rooijen, took it upon himself to create a burial society – a stokvel, if you will. The idea was simple: each human being is entitled to a dignified funeral, at an affordable price. 127 years later, AVBOB still operates as mutual assurance society with members who benefit from the profits. In January they paid out over R13 billion in profits. They now have branches nationwide with 8000 staff members. They offer funeral plans, investment and savings plans that have free funeral benefits. Also, life insurance & legal insurance etc. 3. Kings & Queens They cater for Zimbabweans, Malawians, Mozambicans etc; anyone who needs to be buried across the border. They handle everything. Many foreign nationals/migrant workers take out funeral policies with them, paying for family here and at home. It began in Orange Grove in 2004, moved to Doornfontein where they have a mortuary. They bought the Alhambra Theatre in 2020 and now have 3 chapels there. Congolese don’t repatriate deceased because of the war; they bury their loved ones here. Usually hold service in the main theatre: extremely noisy; hire DJ’s because they celebrate the life; also hire professional mourners to cry.

We accompany the undertakers from the moment they are called to collect a body from a home or a hospital, on their journey to the mortuary, to the preparation of the body for the funeral, the preparation of the gravesite and the final burial. We also go on a guided tour of the historic Alhambra Theatre, which is now the unique home of Kings & Queens Real Funerals. The three theatres are now three chapels, the backstage area is a coffin showroom and the offices are extremely busy arranging the cross-border repatriation of bodies.
caseStudies: Prudence Ncgongo Obey Ndebele Natasha Pillay

title: Inner City Hope
oneLiner: In the shadow of Johannesburg’s decaying Ellis Park precinct, one man’s love for tennis is reviving forgotten courts and giving new life to a fading sport.
summary: At the crumbling tennis courts near Ellis Park, Johannesburg, one man is fighting a lonely but determined battle to save a sport he loves. Alec Galanakis — a passionate tennis historian, teacher, and lifelong player — has devoted his life to reviving tennis in the inner city and protecting courts that once stood as proud monuments of South Africa’s sporting culture. In a landscape marked by decay and neglect, Alec’s mission is twofold: to keep the heritage of Johannesburg’s iconic courts alive and to pass the beauty and discipline of tennis on to a new generation. His initiative has transformed forgotten spaces into sanctuaries where children discover not only a sport, but dignity, purpose, and hope.
caseStudies: Alec Galanakis

title: THROW-FORWARD: Failure to Prosecute
oneLiner: A battle for justice that has haunted us for three years: as disabled children suffer and die without funds, a disbarred attorney walks free.
summary: It’s a story that’s haunted us for more than three years. In 2023, we exposed an Eastern Cape attorney claiming medical negligence damages on behalf of children born with cerebral palsy - then leaving them penniless. Children suffering without the funds they desperately need. Families lured by promises of help – and betrayed. We travelled from village to village, breaking the devastating news to one mother after another. At the centre of it all: one man. A disbarred attorney, with an arrest warrant in his name, who remains at large. In our latest investigation, we ask how he has been allowed to walk free, while children still wait for the promised funds, the NPA insists it is still pursuing him, and those meant to protect the most vulnerable drag their feet.

title: A REFINERY SOLD FOR A RAND - WITH A LEGACY THAT WILL COST BILLIONS.
oneLiner: We ask why two global oil companies - BP and Shell - have been able to away from a broken, non-functioning refinery, abandoning their responsibility to the community for decades of pollution, passing
summary:
• In May 2024, the state-owned Central Energy Fund (CEF) agreed to acquire the SAPREF refinery assets in South Durban from BP and Shell for R1 (symbolic sum), subject to approvals, after it had been flooded in 2022. • A whistle-blower dumped 1000 + pages of documents at OUTA including complicated Due Diligence documents, suggesting that government was taking this decision without proper advice or advice designed to avoid the questions of environmental liability. • Open Secrets then published whistle-blower-backed investigations (July 2025) detailing the R1 sale and the “clean-break/voetstoots” nature of the deal and due-diligence red flags. • One of the red flags is concern about the role of a consulting company Centurion Law Group which has a known poor track record in advising Government on oil and gas, founded by a controversial Cameroonian businessman, Njock Ayuk Eyong , although he claims to have handed over the firm to younger staff members. • Anxiety about the sale feeds into a general concern in the South Durban basin amongst environmental activists and academics that Shell and BP will shrug off their role in polluting the communities in which SAPREF has operated since the early 1960s. • Longstanding community exposure to refinery emissions in South Durban has been found by academics; for example Ecoserv found 124 exceedances of WHO SO₂ guidelines in Merebank (Nov 2000–Oct 2002). Another document logs pollution incidents from 16 Jan 1998 of SAPREF pollution from 16 Jan 1998 – 26 July 2011 (Document DD5 Page 11 – 21 flares, spills, bad smells, toxic chemicals etc) • Its’ quite hard to show tangible evidence showing a direct link between SAPREF and illness, and easier for academics and activists to talk about studies that have been done. • Meanwhile a former SAPREF worker, MK Murugan, not 70 years old, who developed toxic hepatitis from working in SAPREF, has spent half his life fighting the company for compensation. His legal battle to get the company to recognise his illness and then pay him compensation highlights the difficulties that impacted communities might have in trying to get compensation and most importantly acknowledgement from SAPREF that they need to improve their safety record going forward. Improving their safety to lessen pollution will make the newly envisaged refinery even more expensive.

We have access to whistleblower documents which show how consultants shifted their perspective from one year to the next on why selling the SAPREF refinery in Durban was a good idea for government. Those whistleblower documents suggest that behind the wall of silence on the sale in which the state paid a single rand there may have been manipulation to tie South Africa back in to a fossil fuel agenda.
