experts: Rajen Naidooo Bobby Peek Michael Marchant

title: SAMSAM THUBANE - SPINNING RIGHT ROUND
oneLiner: Sam Sam Thubane is taking South Africa’s rawest street culture global - but before the world knew his name… it started in Mbombela.
summary:
From Mbombela Streets to Global Stages. Sam Sam Thubane’s journey represents the modern face of spinning in 2025. From the streets of Mbombela to performing at the Red Bull Hangar-7 reopening in Salzburg, Austria in June, his rise exemplifies how spinning has transcended its local origins to become a globally recognized spectacle. His story perfectly captures what Vic describes as spinning's unique accessibility - it remains the only motorsport that welcomes participants from all backgrounds and communities, making it truly democratic in a way no other motorsport can claim Samkeliso “Sam Sam” Thubane is a spinner from Nelspruit, in Mpumalanga.

- South African Guy that's now an international stunt super star. - GREAT footage - fascinating SA street culture experienced globally - a story of growth, camaraderie and success
caseStudies: SAM SAM THUBANE PHIKO X LAUDRICK GROUND Nicholas Moosa Colani Thela

title: K9 Bond
oneLiner: They call him Bond... K9 Bond - we meet the talented SAPS Search and Rescue dog named Bond, and explore the extraordinary relationship between hound and handler.
summary:
We had to go the full written approval route with the SAPS, and we've been approved for full access to Mak and Bond for two days. We've also got access to the whole Eastern Cape K9 unit, we can see training and demonstrations and do ride alongs etc if they are called out during our filming. We'll also get to speak to the head of the Easter Cape K9 unit. But the focus on the story will be getting to know both Mak and Bond - Sgt Makhosone is well spoken and passionate and I'm keen to find out what makes him tick.

Bond is attached to the SAPS K9 search and rescue unit in the Eastern Cape, and by all accounts, this Belgian Malinois is one of the best in the business.In their relatively short career together, Bond and his handler Seargent Buyisile Makhosone – affectionately known as Mak – have made quite a name for themselves. Bond has even made an appearance in the Western Cape Provincial Parliament, where he was recognised for the significant role he played in the search for survivors during the devastating George Building collapse. But it is beautiful 'bond' between MAk and Bond that make this story worth telling - they're both young, dynamic and ready to take on whatever the job throws at them.
caseStudies: Nompiliso Mchosini Seargent Buyisile Makhosone
experts: Senior EC K9 Unit Official To Be Confirmed

title: Fraudulent Vet
oneLiner: Fake Vet treats animals and orders schedule 6 drugs and gets caught on camera faking his qualifications
summary:
There are 6 cases against him. He posed as a Vet and ordered schedule 6 drugs after falsifying his qualifications. Used the Panarama vetinary services email and Vat number He will come to the NSPCA for the job interview which we will film under cover. After the interview outside the building the police will arrest him. he has treated animals posing as a VET administering medicines. he has offered sterilizations. Tried to sell fake medicines to Pet shops. Lied about being a Vet at the SPCA and created a logo with that. Got onto the Veterinary Councils website and inserted his name there as a registered Vet. Posed as a State Vet using their email address, stole the Veterinary Council Registration certificate. Faked his qualifications from UNISA. Stole several email address and altered them slightly to appear legit. Stole a registered Vets details and attempted to order drugs using their details

Mr. Eric Victor Du Preez submitted job applications to the SPCA in June and again in August 2025. In his second application, he falsely claimed to be a qualified NSPCA Inspector and produced what appeared to be an official Inspector’s Certificate. On verification with the National Council of SPCAs (NSPCA), it was confirmed that: - Mr. Du Preez has never attended or completed Inspector training with the NSPCA. - The certificate he produced was fraudulent. - The signatures of senior NSPCA officials appearing on the certificate were forged. Mr. Du Preez also lied in his CVs, providing contradictory employment histories and false qualifications, including a claim of being registered with the South African Veterinary Council (SAVC) as an Animal Welfare Assistant. The SAVC has since confirmed that multiple fraud-related cases are already pending against him under other dockets. There are 6 confirmed cases pending with SAPS. We are going to have an interview for the position with him next week. Waiting for him to confirm which date. Then we will have him arrested here at the SPCA by SAPS after the interview, where he will once again lie. We will then also open charges. This case raises serious concerns about fraudulent misrepresentation in the animal welfare sector and the risks posed when unqualified individuals attempt to pass themselves off as Inspectors entrusted with powers of law enforcement.
caseStudies: Anita Gerber Sheena Cox Cecilia Vermeulen Kaylee Prinsloo

title: Alabuga Start
oneLiner: Alabuga Start markets itself as a program where female youth between the ages18-22 are given on the job training. The catch, the youth have to relocate to Russia.
summary:
What shot Alabuga into the spotlight in South Africa is a series of posts by South African influencers who claim they were approached by an agency on behalf the program, to recruit young girls. When they were probed on what exactly the girls would be doing in Russia, they admitted that they did not know. After the public outrage where the influencers were accused of participating in Human Trafficking, they deleted the posts and have since issued public apologies. Further enraging South Africans was that Cyan Boujie, a controversial influencer who is also known as a high-end “sex worker”, was flown to Russia to give a virtual tour of Alabuga. She shared the video on all of her social media pages. This further fuelled the suspicions of human trafficking for potential sex work in Russia.

We speak to two key players who are responsible for the program having a footprint in South Africa.
caseStudies: Mzweleni Mthethwa Siyabonga Mhlungu

title: FAILURE TO PROSECUTE Zuko Nonxuba
summary: It’s an investigation that started in 2022 and went on for over a year. Finally, after Carte Blanche pushed and pushed, Zuko Nonxuba was struck from the roll in December 2024. It was a damning judgment with enough evidence to get a warrant issued for his arrest on 22 counts of fraud and theft. Months later, he remains at large. For nearly four years, fraud cases against him have dragged through the courts in East London and Mthatha. With one magistrate recusing herself after watching Carte Blanche’s exposé, while in Mthatha, another magistrate died in a car crash before handing down a verdict, and the retrial was dismissed under Section 147. Meanwhile, the children he defrauded are still without justice, and the millions in court-awarded payouts that were paid over to Nonxuba have vanished. While the children are now dying.

title: UNDER THE COUNTER
oneLiner: From border smugglers to spaza shop counters, we go undercover to trace South Africa’s illicit cigarette trade and lift the lid on the hidden supply chain that keeps it alive.
summary:
South Africa’s illicit cigarette trade is now so big it outperforms the legal market. Run by powerful criminal networks and fuelled by weak enforcement, it robs the state of over R24 billion a year in lost taxes. In this investigative piece, we go undercover to township spaza shops and informal markets, capturing the sale of brands priced far below the legal tax minimum – a sure giveaway of the products illicit roots. These hidden-camera buys, are our foot in to trace the origins. But, we push deeper, posing as would-be sellers looking for a supplier. This sting aims to connect with a middle-man in the supply chain, exposing how illicit stock moves from the border into township shelves. The next step is the origin in SA. I have exclusive border footage from Musina, showing smugglers moving contraband cigarettes from Zimbabwe into South Africa day in and day out. It’s unbelievable. Experts and local Musina voices will unpack how outdated regulation, corruption, and porous borders keep the trade thriving, despite government promises to crack down. It’s a dangerous business, the smugglers have lookouts to secure the path along with armed watchmen ensuring the job gets done at any cost. Locals are fearful and nervous to challenge the smugglers. This is a high-stakes story with gritty visuals: from whispered street-corner deals to brazen cross-border hauls. It’s about more than cheap smokes - it’s a multi-billion-rand criminal economy bleeding the nation dry and undermining public health. Our investigation will expose it, from the shop counter to the border fence.

** A way to tell the Story of Illegal Cigarettes with unique access - UNDERCOVER BUYS - EXCLUSIVE FOOTAGE OF BORDER SMUGGLING - Drone footage of receiving / distribution points - Footage of past recoveries
caseStudies: Hermanus Schoeman SECURITY COMPANY OWNER MUSINA

title: Bribe for a Pillow
oneLiner: An alleged conman is accused of swindling property owners of millions of Rands
summary:
Eugene Swanepoel stands accused of defrauding property owners in the west coast of over R 1 million and stealing luxury sheets. His con: using his contract to supply Eskom with accommodation as a guarantee of future payment but that’s not all, Swanepoel allegedly bribes Eskom contractors to choose his accommodation over other Eskom suppliers.

A purported businessman with links to an Eskom contract is allegedly conning property owners to secure free accomodation for Eskom contractors. That's not all, he's also allegedly bribing Eskom contractors to choose his accommodations over other suppliers.
caseStudies: Cornel Wilsch Chad Simoes Linda Mavuso

title: SKY HUSTLERS
summary:
It’s the most unlikely battlefield for race, class, and legacy in South Africa. Not Parliament. Not a protest. A pigeon coop. South Africa’s newest turf war is happening in the sky. In battered backyards and township rooftops, a new generation of Black pigeon fanciers is taking flight - and taking on an old guard that never saw them coming. Pigeon racing was once the playground of white suburban men: pedigree birds, pristine coops, and prize pots big enough to make a banker blush. Now? The game’s changing. They’re breeding champions in shacks. Clocking birds in car boots. Raising syndicates on social grants and second chances. And they’re not just racing pigeons - they’re upending a bloodline sport built on exclusion… one wingbeat at a time. Young, Black, and from the townships, they’re training world-class racers from the scrap heaps of apartheid’s leftovers. They don’t come from money. But they’ve got the hustle, the feathers, and the fire. And they’re not just racing pigeons - they’re rewriting the pecking order.

Pigeon racing isn’t a quirky side hustle - it’s a multimillion-rand obsession. • A single bird can sell for R5 million. • President Cyril Ramaphosa hosts the AfrikaPro Million Dollar Race on his Phala Phala estate. • Foreign syndicates bet millions. • And now? Township kids are clocking in faster birds than the elite - with none of the pedigree. But here’s the rub: Only a handful of South Africa’s 4,000 licensed fanciers are Black. Most clubs remain white-owned, white-run, and white-sanctioned. This isn’t a story about pigeons. It’s a story about power, access, and how legacy gets built - or stolen. While the elite race for prestige and profit, Black fanciers in the townships are often locked out - despite breeding birds that can fly just as far, just as fast. But a shift is in the air. And it smells like feathers and revolution.
caseStudies: Lodumo Nkala Glenn Lofts

title: The Ismail Family Shooting: Mistaken Identity
oneLiner: This is about what happens when those we trust to protect us may have instead caused irreparable harm.
summary:
TREATMENT: Story Arc: Opening Sequence – 1:30 We open with two parallel narratives: • The Ismail family: Omar, Asma, and toddler Yusraa heading home after visiting Asma’s mother. • The police: National Intervention Unit officers preparing to intercept hijackers in a silver Toyota Etios. Both stories collide in the shootout. We frame the piece as a mystery — not revealing immediately that the shooters are police, nor casting doubt on the Etios’s existence yet. Instead, we simply say that everyone’s lives change in an instant. We hint at the bigger theme: justice delayed, perhaps denied — and that our search for answers leads to revelations more disturbing than the shooting itself. ACT 1: ACT 1 – The Ismail Family’s Story We go into Omar and Asma’s account in detail, building tension toward two major twists: 1. After the shooting, Asma’s mother discovers the gunmen are police. 2. The police haven’t called emergency services. We do scene setting: Give a sense of where this happened a map introduce the re-enactments and graphic representations of the shootout. We also show how the accident has affected the family to continue the storytelling. ACT 2: ACT 2 – The Police Officers’ Story We introduce the officers and their version, reconstructed from documents and affidavits. Their right of reply (their legal defences and reasoning) is woven in here, not tacked on at the end. This will allow the journalism to show without ruining the story. The tension here lies with the blame the police lay on Omar, citing volenti non fit injuria — essentially claiming he knowingly drove into a gunfight. At this point, we haven’t yet revealed that there’s no evidence of an Etios, so the audience is still piecing it together. We then start dismantling the police’s account: • Was there an Etios? • What did witnesses see? • What do the ballistics and scene reports say? We link this to Asma’s shocking account of how Omar was shot, leading to the question: if the family had died, would this version have gone unchallenged? ACT 3 – Law, Delays, and a Twist We break down what the law says about use of force — officers can only fire in self-defence or in defence of others. If there were no hijackers, this defence collapses. We look at the stalled investigations — by the Hawks, IPID, and the NPA — despite compelling evidence. Then comes the final twist: could the delays be due to inefficiency and bureaucracy… or the fact that some of these officers are celebrated heroes? We reveal their role in the high-profile N2 shootout, using passionate media coverage from the time. Finally, we seek direct responses: • From each officer. • From SAPS, NPA, and IPID. We close with a small moment of hope: Baby Essa, in Asma’s womb that night, survived. He turns five next week.

OPENING SCENE Two juxtapositioned Visuals: A white VW Polo glides down a suburban road. Inside, the mother reaches over to hold her child’s hand. The father, driving, glances back with a smile. Passing the graveyard. VO: Moments before their lives would change forever, a husband, his pregnant wife, and their toddler were quietly talking about death. Just a week earlier, a relative had been laid to rest in the cemetery they were now passing. None of them knew that, seconds later, they too would be knocking on death’s door. CUT TO: NIU police officers gearing up — hands loading magazines, a rifle’s bolt clacking into place. Police radio: “We’re looking for a silver Etios.” The screech of brakes. A deafening volley of gunshots. Screams pierce the chaos. Photos from scene after shooting… emergency lights and noises… (Presenter VO):— The years that followed that moment have been riddled with questions… SOUNDUPS: QUESTIONS Two versions of that night emerged — one from the shooters, one from the family in the line of fire. Who is telling the truth? (Presenter LINK): This is about what happens when those we trust to protect us may have instead caused irreparable harm. But it’s more than that — it’s about justice delayed, and perhaps denied. Five years on from the shooting that tore the Ismail family’s lives apart, no one has been held to account. And the reasons may be as disturbing as the shooting itself. FADE TO BLACK… ACT 1: The basic story (Presenter VO): A cold winter Thursday evening — around 7 p.m., July 16, 2020 — settles over Berea, Durban. Omar Ismail drives home with his wife, Asma, and their toddler, Yusraa, after visiting Asma’s mother. Ten weeks pregnant with their second child — a little boy they plan to name Essa — Asma sits in the back seat beside Yusraa, strapped into her car seat. (Asma): (Omar): (Presenter VO): A few hundred metres from their home on Sheringham Road, a white unmarked BMW suddenly swerves into the road. A man jumps out, gun in hand. (Asma): (Omar): (Presenter VO): Omar ducks beneath the steering wheel to avoid the bullets, unable to see clearly — their silver Polo hits the BMW and they drift into a streetlamp. (Asma): (Omar): (Presenter VO): Then… silence. Yusraa is screaming. While trying to make sense of what just happened. Omar lifts his head — another shot rings out from behind. The bullet tears through the headrest, hitting him in the back of the head. He slumps forward. Asma, her right leg hanging by a thread clings to consciousness. She calls her mother, Rehana. Visual: Mother answering the phone, horrified. Rehana: It was close to their house — maybe five minutes away. I drove straight there. (Presenter VO): What she finds is an unexpected twist. Rehana: “When I arrived, the men told me they were police officers. (Presenter VO): But that's not the only strange information she learns. Rehana: But there was something wrong — no ambulance, no flashing lights. They hadn’t called emergency services. It had been nearly ten minutes, and I was the first to phone for an ambulance.” Visual: Photos of vehicles and bullet damage at the scene. (Presenter VO): Asma’s heart stops at St Augustine’s Hospital, but she’s resuscitated. Yusraa - shot in her arm - was luckily saved by her car seat. Omar was shot four times, including his head, and was left temporarily blind. Visual: Timelapse sky, fading to black. (Presenter LINK) with family: “Months later, Omar was left with shrapnel in his brain, and risks paralysis if surgeons attempt removal. Asma lost her right leg and she still has shrapnel in her left. (Presenter VO): Asma works as a lab technician, and standing for hours is painful. Omar, a bookkeeper, has struggled to find employment since the shooting, his current job is made more difficult by his partial blindness and severe headaches. (Presenter LINK) at Intersection: But what really happened at this T-junction of Hill and Sheringham Roads? The story the police would later tell would make the family question everything. This is their story according to their pleas and affidavits. Fade to black… ACT 2: The Two Versions Military-style, authoritative tone; overlay of visuals and VO ON SCREEN: 16 July 2020… Presenter VO (dramatic tone): “Six police officers are on the hunt for a group of hijackers. On-Screen Visuals: Fade into uniformed officers preparing for deployment. (Presenter VO): They’re members of the National Intervention Unit (NIU)—an elite, intelligence-driven tactical unit in the South African Police Service trained for high-risk operations such as armed crime, and violent syndicate activity. They report directly to the National Commissioner of Police. (Presenter VO): Crime Intelligence’s information is that the syndicate’s suspects are in the Berea area—travelling in a silver or grey Toyota Etios sedan with cloned plates. Visual overlay: Show a schematic of two unmarked vehicles in convoy. (Presenter LINK): The Warrant officers wore uniforms but their two vehicles were unmarked. In the BMW (white 1 series) was Talent Mseleku the driver, Yogandran Munsami and Donovan Naidoo. Following them in a VW Kombi (silver) was driver Menzi Michael Shabalala and Mathew Nathoo. ON SCREEN graphic: Display 18:45 over a map. (Presenter VO): As the convoy drove South along Hill Street toward Sheringham Road, the officers in the BMW noticed a silver VW Polo - that’s the Ismail family - but ALSO the silver Toyota Etios they’ve been looking for behind it. It’s implied the Polo and Etios were stationary when the police came across them. They say —”the hijackers alighted their vehicle and were about to hijack the VW Polo when NIU members intervened.” [page 2, iii]. Presenter LINK (raising questions): “The police’s descriptions of the hijackers is scant. They’re male, although the number remains unknown. All that’s reported is that they were wearing balaclavas and were moving in a crouched-over manner toward the VW Polo’s rear. [no where does it say they were stationary] (Presenter VO): Munsami leapt from the front passenger seat of the BMW, shouting ‘POLICE!’ They say the hijackers then opened fire — and that’s when the gunfight began. The police say their shots were aimed at the hijackers in the Toyota Etios, and that the Ismail family’s Polo was caught in the crossfire. They say it wasn’t their bullets that struck Omar, Asma, and Yusraa — but the hijackers. And even if their own rounds did cause the injuries, their defense is that it was a lawful shooting, undertaken to protect the family from a ‘dangerous situation.’ (Presenter LINK): The officers frame their actions as those of ‘peace officers’ defending themselves and the public. Their legal defence even leans on an obscure doctrine — volenti non fit injuria — which means Omar knowingly drove into the line of fire. (Presenter VO): The hijackers fled down Sheringham Road. Shabalala, in the VW Kombi, returned fire while Naidoo shot the Etios’s rear tyre. Mseleku attempted to give chase, but due to the collision with the Polo the BMW was too damaged. After they say they checked on the Polo’s occupants and called for medical assistance. Presenter LINK to next section: Who’s really telling the truth? Carte Blanche has sifted through witness statements, ballistics tests, expert analyses, and hours of CCTV footage — uncovering evidence that punches glaring holes in the police’s account. And it starts with the shocking revelation: Was there a silver Etios? TEXT ON SCREEN: Was there an Etios? (Omar): No car was following us. (Presenter VO):There are nine CCTV camera angles covering different points along this route. They reveal the police’s timeline is out by 15 minutes, but when you track the Ismail family’s Polo across multiple points… even a few hundred metres before the shooting…the evidence is in what you don’t see. No Etios... In fact, there’s no footage of an Etios in any footage. EXPERT INTRO (EXPERT): CCTV footage doesn’t lie — timestamps are locked, and the sequence can be independently verified. This raises serious questions about the police version. (Presenter VO): But it does show something the police left out — the VW Kombi missed the turn into Hill Street, and therefore, was about a minute behind the BMW. That likely means they weren’t there when the first shots were fired — at least not as the police’s version infers. VISUAL: TEXT ON SCREEN: What did witnesses see? (Presenter VO): There were many witnesses like blah blah who we met at the scene. It's what two witnesses for the Ismail family saw, or didn't see, is critical. LINK: Witness One, watching from his balcony, says he saw the whole incident unfold. He describes only three vehicles: the Ismail family’s Polo, and the two police vehicles. No other cars. He also says the police were firing directly at the Polo. Could this have been a case of mistaken identity? (Expert): This points to a likely case of mistaken identity. From the front, a silver VW Polo and a silver Toyota Etios can look similar — but if there was no Etios at all, it suggests the police account of suspects and their behaviour was fabricated. Presenter LINK: Witness Two only heard the gunfire. When he dared to look outside, he also saw no Etios. But he noticed something else — something darker. The officers were collecting their spent cartridges. Was there a coverup? (Expert): That’s scene tampering. Removing shell casings prevents ballistic experts from matching a bullet to a specific gun — and to the officer who fired it. TEXT ON SCREEN: What do the bullets and scene say? Another graphic - we also have photos from SAPS scene recreation report. (Presenter VO): “There are two ballistic reports: the state’s and the family’s. Both agree there were no shell casings, but the eight R4/R5 rifle rounds they did find, were likely from police weapons. But the family’s expert found something more — a ninth bullet from a 9mm pistol. Remember that extra bullet for later. LINK: Both experts also agree on this: there was no crossfire. All the shots came from the direction of the police. The family’s expert says the Polo was deliberately targeted; the state’s expert stops short of saying that outright — but the implication is clear. (Presenter VO): A SAPS scene reconstruction aligns with the Ismail family’s version confirming the Polo was moving and not stationary as the police’s version implies. And that the direction of fire was at the Polo, this resulted in Omar likely panicking and losing control of the vehicle. (Expert): That’s a critical point — it places the Ismail family directly in the line of police fire from the outset. It was because they shot at him that he ducked. LINK: If this was a case of mistaken identity, when did the officers realise they had the wrong car — at the moment Omar’s Polo slammed into their BMW, or when they heard the baby screaming? The missing shell casings and a specific moment during the shooting cast a dark shadow over the officers’ actions. Asma: That must have been when the officers realised something was wrong — what hijacker would have a baby in the car? My husband then popped up his head. VO: Omar had been crouched low behind the steering wheel, then raised his head. Omar: I just wanted to check on them. Presenter: Can you remember that? Omar: Yes. Asma: I was already calling my mother, panicking, trying to get help. And then I saw one of the men with a gun coming closer to the window — and he fired into the driver’s headrest. Omar slumped forward. Rehana (Asma’s mother): I thought my son-in-law was dead. VO: Could this have been from the missing 9mm round? Rehana kept having this question running through her mind. Rehana: Why hadn’t the police called an ambulance? Link: Was there a coverup? Missing shell casings, no ambulances called, the extra bullet round, when and how Omar was shot… It begs the logical question: If the Ismail family didn’t survive, would these events have died with them? ACT 3: TEXT ON SCREEN: What does the Law say? (Expert): It’s also important to consider who fired first. If there were no hijackers, the first shots could only have come from the police. That’s a serious problem — it opens the door to attempted murder charges. Our law is clear: force can only be used in self-defence or to protect others. That clearly doesn’t apply here. Presenter LINK: And yet, years later, the case has stalled. Omar: The NPA says it is still waiting for the Hawks to act. IPID — the Independent Police Investigative Directorate — has also investigated, but that too has gone nowhere. (Expert): When IPID arrives on a scene, their job is to secure the shooting site, investigate whether evidence — like shell casings — was tampered with, and confiscate the firearms used. If those steps weren’t followed immediately, it undermines the entire investigation. Presenter VO: But what about the civil case? That case names the Police Ministry itself, that seeks to awards money to the family for the damage this has caused. Omar: It was supposed to go ahead in September last year, then again this September. But they keep delaying it — getting new lawyers. Instead of settling with us, it’s costing the state hundreds of thousands. I don’t know if they’re hoping we’ll die or something before that from our injuries. (Expert): In law, there’s a provision against wasteful and fruitless expenditure. The police should recognise they have no realistic chance of winning and settle with the family. Continuing to fight is already costing taxpayers hundreds of thousands. (Presenter VO): We asked the police how much they’ve spent defending the civil case. [N2](Presenter LINK): And we wanted to know why there have been such long delays in investigating these officers. Is it simply inefficiency, indifference, or bureaucracy? Or… could it be because two of the officers involved in the shooting are celebrated police heroes? That’s why I’m standing here — on this stretch of Durban’s N2 highway near Nandi Drive. TEXT ON SCREEN: August 4, 2017. TEXT ON SCREEN: August 4, 2017 (Presenter VO): In August 2017, two of the officers now implicated in the Ismail family shooting — Donovan Naidoo and Yogandran Munsamy — were involved in a high-profile shootout. In that daylight battle, five armed suspects were intercepted; three “died at the scene,” while two survived and were arrested. Civilians and officers were injured in the chaos. Naidoo and Munsamy were at the heart of it all. (Presenter LINK): reading article: Naidoo was hailed a hero. He “jumped from the moving vehicle” to shield his disoriented colleagues and continued fighting [on foot]. Though he was badly injured — bleeding from his head — he refused to leave the scene, staying until the SAPS dog unit arrived, and then helped track the fleeing suspects. (Presenter VO): For his courage, he received a bravery award from the SAPS. (Presenter VO): Munsami, was also seriously injured — his face was shattered in the crash and he required facial reconstructive surgery, including the insertion of a metal plate. (LINK): Munsamy was left with poor eyesight and Naidoo has since been plagued by persistent migraine headaches. We don't have full medical records, but these injuries raise an important question: How fit were these officers for active duty at the time of the Ismail shooting? Expert Commentary: A lot of the time there’s pressure from within SAPS for officers to remain on active duty, even when carrying significant injuries. Sometimes it’s the officers themselves who want to continue, especially if they see themselves as still capable or feel a sense of duty. VO: We reached out to the officers involved for their responses. ON SCREEN: Officers’ Response: They said they couldn’t speak because of their upcoming cases. SAPS Response: [Insert official SAPS comment or refusal to comment.] NPA Response: [Insert National Prosecuting Authority’s official stance on the case and the delays.] IPID Response: [Insert Independent Police Investigative Directorate’s comment on the stalled investigation and scene-handling concerns.] (Presenter VO/LINK): Was there ever an Etios? Who fired first? Why was no ambulance called? These are questions that can only be answered in court. But are they questions these officers want the public to know? I guess we’ll wait and see, but for now the Ismail family are waiting for justice. There is some good news. Incredibly, baby Essa survived — he turns five this month.
caseStudies: Omar Ismail Asma Mohamed Rehana Mohamed

title: Chapters- The Johannesburg Library
oneLiner: After half a decade the Johannesburg Library has opened its doors once more bringing hope to a crumbling inner city.
summary:
The Johannesburg Public Library (JCL), located in the citycentre, has a rich history dating back to the early days of Johannesburg. It began as a subscription library in 1890, evolving through various locations and ultimately becoming a vital public institution. A key moment in its history was the opening of its current Italianate building in 1935, and its later desegregation in 1974, making it the first public library in South Africa to open its doors to all races.

A new chapter has opened for the Johannesburg City Library after being closed to the public for half almost decade. For five long years, 1.5 million books, including rare and valuable Africana archives, sat locked away, gathering dust. This year, the library turns 90 years old, a true continental landmark and one of the largest public libraries in Africa. This reopening belongs to the caring citizens of Joburg, heritage groups, civil society, and activists who refused to accept closed doors fighting shoulder to shoulder with Johannesburg Heritage Foundation, Joburg Crisis Alliance, Johannesburg In Your Pocket City Guide, Bridge Books, and many others. In an age of disinformation, inequality in digital access, and shrinking public spaces, libraries are more relevant than ever. They are lifelines for learning, safe spaces for community, and guardians of our shared heritage. Hopefully this is the beginning of the re-awakening of a crumbling inner city.
experts: Flo Bird Nombuntu Mpendulo Elton May

caseStudies: Mandla Ndlovu Lisa Sheard Oupa Pilane Justus Mohlala Sandile Mokoena

title: Ikenna’s Big Kick
oneLiner: At just 9 years old, South Africa’s Ikenna Tladi makes history by signing a 7-year deal with AS Roma Academy, becoming one of the country's youngest football exports to Europe.
summary:
From the dusty grassroots fields of Tshiama Soccer Academy to the floodlights of Old Eds FC, Ikenna’s journey started as soon as he could walk. With a ball never far from his tiny feet and a father — Valentine — who lived and breathed football, the boy’s destiny seemed inevitable. "I didn’t want to raise just a soccer player," says Valentine. "I wanted to raise someone who could command respect through talent and discipline." That discipline often turned heads. Valentine’s strict training regimens were misunderstood by many as too harsh. But Ikenna’s rise has silenced every doubter. His viral footwork clips spread like wildfire across YouTube and Instagram, eventually landing on the radar of Roma scouts. By eight years old, he was named Player of the Tournament at an elite European youth showcase while representing AS Roma's U10s. At nine, he wears the Giallorossi badge.

Move over, Messi. Make room, Mbappé. South Africa has a new name lighting up the world stage — and he’s only 9. Ikenna Tladi, a born-and-bred talent from North West, South Africa, has signed a jaw-dropping seven-year deal with Italian giants AS Roma Academy, becoming one of the youngest international recruits in recent history. Now, fresh from a whirlwind signing trip to Rome, he’s back on home soil — and he’s giving us his first-ever TV exclusive.
caseStudies: Valentine Williams Ikenna Tladi Veronica Tladi

title: Fake Alcohol
oneLiner: We take a look at the trade of counterfeit alcohol, how it's made, sold and how it affects you at home.
summary:
Over the last two years, South Africa has seen a spike in counterfeit alcohol making its way to communities across the country. At first it seemed like small scale “backdoor” brewers who were creating cheaper versions of spirits but that’s not the case. We have uncovered a legitimate brewery in Boksburg that supplies ingredients to alcohol manufacturers, who then brew and sell counterfeit alcohol on the black market. They recycle packaging of Remy Martin, Hennesy, Jack Daniels and different variations of gin. The long and short of it is that the boom of fake alcohol is a national crisis that is affected all South Africans, regardless of race or class.

We have an insider sharing how the fake alcohol is made. Secondly, we confront a brewer where manufacturers of illicit alcohol are purchasing the ingredients. Lastly, we will approach the story from the perspective of the middle class but also explore how it is affecting those of a lower income class, essentially emphasising the point that fake alcohol is a national crisis.
caseStudies: Bongani Makhura Tshepo Rameetse Mr X Anonymous

title: Hout Bay Harbour - what now?
summary:
DFFE Min George stated that the sunken wrecks must be lifted by the 16th June by the owners ,or the Department would do it and charge them. Sunken wrecks hamper the 3 main commercial fishing business - Tuna, Hake and Lobster. That date came and went and on 25th June another site visit – SAMSA are tasked with the job. The dry dock is working again, and Min. George of DFFE has established a working committee with local business and fishing business. Signage and painting within the harbour is underway and security contracts being negotiated. So there is definitely more transparency. BUT the people who work and make Hout Bay harbour what it is - are working under extremely tenuous circumstances. DPW won’t issue leases for more than a year and all maintenance and security is the tenants problem.

Whats the story: Two new Ministers – both DA- both with extremely difficult portfolios of the Department of Public Works and Department of Forestry Fisheries and Environment jointly responsible for the running of the harbours. They have been making bold statements and fresh promises to revitalise the Hout Bay harbour. This is an update on our 2022 story when Derek stood inside stripped buildings and then Minister of Public Works Patricia De Lille made promises - which are still on our website. Hout Bay like Kalk Bay is one of the most visited tourists’ spots in Cape Town. Every weekend people cue to get a spot at Fish on the Rocks. The red tour bus stops outside the Hout Bay market and the place is pumping. Tourism is the big business in the Western Cape - so what's holding up this master development plan for Hout Bay harbour that's been on the cards for the last 15 years?

title: Saving Sandfish
oneLiner: A rescue mission is underway to save sandfish from extinction in the Cederberg.
summary:
This story will follow the urgent efforts to rescue the species from collapse. Led by the Freshwater Research Centre, a diverse team of scientists and local residents is undertaking Africa’s largest freshwater fish rescue. Their goal is to relocate thousands of vulnerable juvenile sandfish from drying river pools – where they are vulnerable to invasive species – into cleared, alien-free farm dams where they have a fighting chance at survival. Now, rescued sandfish that have been reared to a safe size will be released back into the wild. This will happen in the first week of September. Each is tagged with a microchip to track whether these fish return to their birthplace to spawn –the first real test of whether the intervention is working. This is a story about the extraordinary efforts of ordinary people to restore what’s about to be lost. It’s about how we choose to respond in the face of vanishing biodiversity. The sandfish are a vital part of the Olifants-Doring River system’s ecosystem. Characters: Sarah Fransman / Has lived in area her whole life and remembers watching the sandfish migration as a child. Jeremy Shelton / Scientist from the Freshwater Research Centre Cecilia Cerilla / PHD student writing her thesis on this

In the remote Cederberg Mountains of South Africa, a remarkable yet little known natural spectacle takes place each year: the spawning migration of the sandfish, South Africa’s most threatened migratory freshwater fish. Every year in September, sandfish begin their ancient upstream journey in the Biedouw River – a ritual now teetering on the brink of extinction. Once so numerous they formed waves across the river. Six years ago, fewer than 200 migratory sandfish were left in the Biedouw river. And so, Jeremy Shelton, a conservation biologist, started the Saving Sandfish project in a bid to rescue them from extinction. This is a story that goes beyond science – it’s also about cultural memory and meaning. Sarah Fransman, who grew up in a cottage on the banks of the Biedouw river, remembers how the sandfish would make a wave, “the whole school would stretch from one side to the other”. There are also paintings on cave walls in the area showing sandfish migrations on a mythic scale.
caseStudies: Sarah Fransman Gerhard Thom

title: Randburg Jacuzzi
oneLiner: We dive into Randburg's deepest pothole and fish for answers from the City of Joburg
summary:
Last week we filmed it - a huge clear pool with fresh water bubbling out, covering an entire lane. The water flows freely downhill, ironically straight past the COJ Customer Service Centre in Harley Street. I tweeted about it last Monday - asking Joburg Water to please attend to the lap pool on the corner. Somebody tagged MMC Kenny Kunene - unfortunately he was otherwise occupied that afternoon. At the home of murder suspect Katise Molefe. Nevertheless, Joburg Water responded and said they would sort it out. A week later and it has grown - the jacuzzi/pool now cover 1.5 lanes, the water is deep and is clearly a hazard to pedestrians and motorists. Joburg Water has just announced that they will bill customer separately to COJ. Why? Let’s take a look at what it would take to get this one burst pipe fixed. Who tried, who failed, what went wrong? Who is up to the task?

Cape Town has early morning polar plunging into the sea, but here in Joburg we have our own natural spring. On the corner of Pretoria Avenue & Harley Street is a massive open-air jacuzzi. It’s free, easily accessible to everyone, with clean filtered, chlorinated water gushing out 24 hours a day. It started life as a pothole about a few years ago and has been through various incarnations. I’ve seen waste pickers stuffing cardboard and bags of paper in there. Eventually the water leak surfaced and on Google maps you can track the development, from a steady trickle to a serious burst pipe. Last Monday I actually filmed it - a huge clear pool with fresh water bubbling out, covering an entire lane. The water flows freely downhill, ironically straight past the COJ Customer Service Centre. I tweeted about it last Monday - asking Joburg Water to please attend to the lap pool on the corner. Somebody tagged MMC Kenny Kunene - unfortunately he was otherwise occupied that afternoon. At the home of Katise Molefe. Nevertheless, Joburg Water responded and said they would sort it out. This morning it has grown - the jacuzzi pool now cover 1.5 lanes, the water is deep and is clearly a hazard to pedestrians and motorists. Joburg Water has just announced that they will bill customer separately to COJ. Why? Let’s take a look at what it would take to get this one burst pipe fixed. Who tried, who failed, what went wrong? Who is up to the task? Put presenter in a costume and take a dip. Humorous, but serious topic, guaranteed to enrage and amuse.
caseStudies: Lucinda Harman Kenny Kunene

title: Paramotoring 2 - Breaking records
summary:
Paramotoring 2 This insert follows two paramotor pilots — Lawrence Marais and Gary Bowls — as they attempt to fly from the northernmost point of South Africa to the southernmost tip at Cape Agulhas. This journey has never been completed by paramotor, and we will document it as it happens. Filming will take place over 1 to 8 days, depending on flight conditions. This is a true documentary approach: we will follow their progress every day, capturing the real story as it unfolds. A single camera will track the pilots and their road crew from the ground. Erin Bates, our presenter, will join them midway through the journey and again at the end, to reflect on their progress and wrap up the story. Along the route, we will film short sit-down interviews with both pilots as daily debriefs. Their wives — Vicky Bown and Lawrence’s wife — are the support crew, and we will also speak to them about the pressure, logistics, and emotional toll of managing the journey from the ground. In addition, Gary and Lawrence will supply onboard paramotor footage. This material will be used to help illustrate key flight moments and challenges — including landings, weather shifts, and major transitions in the terrain. The goal is to show what it takes to attempt something this ambitious — the preparation, the risks, the flying, and the teamwork needed to pull it off.

Tonight on Carte Blanche: Two paramotor pilots take on a first-of-its-kind journey — flying from Limpopo to Cape Agulhas with only a motor, a wing, and their wives on the ground.

title: Tsitsikama: The Mountain that Made us One
oneLiner: We travel to the Eastern Cape to meet two friends, who were united by sharing their stories in the beautiful landscape of Tsitsikama
summary:
Popina and Andrea met while they were both visiting Tsitsikama. Popina was a varsity student on a break and had taken a solo trip to a place that reminded her of her childhood. She was writing a book about surviving and escaping war torn DRC. While there she walked into a room of travelers from Cape Town, that's where she would meet Andrea and over a three day period their paths would cross on the hiking trails. That's when they would share food, stories and forge a bond through sharing challenges each have faced. They exchanged contact details, later Andera would contact Popina, offered her a laptop for her book writing and financial support for her studies. Andrea also paid for a professional editor to assist Popina on her book which is now out in stores. 'The Small Ones': Popina's journey from war torn DRC to finding a home in the Eatstern Cape. Through this friendship, Popina's dream of documenting her story in a book is realized and a lifetime bond forged.

This is a story of friendship, in a world full of chaos there are still good people. Two strangers meet and their bond makes the dream of another a reality. The meeting of two worlds.

title: Borderline Claims: South Africans and asylum in Europe
oneLiner: Are South Africans fleeing danger — or gaming Europe’s asylum system to escape inequality at home?
summary:
In the last decade, thousands of South Africans have quietly sought asylum in Europe. Their claims span political persecution, targeted gang violence, and sexual orientation-based discrimination. Yet South Africa remains a constitutional democracy — and is officially listed as a safe country of origin by many European states, including Ireland. So what’s driving the surge in asylum applications? Are genuine victims falling through the cracks of a rigid system — or are some South Africans exploiting legal grey areas in an increasingly overstretched asylum regime? Essentially: Are these South Africans claiming asylum or taking advantage? Carte Blanche travels to Ireland, a country now central to this unfolding dilemma, to meet those navigating — and questioning — the boundaries of protection, policy and personal truth. From here, we dig into the core question: Are South Africans genuinely at risk — or manipulating asylum frameworks for the opportunity to escape the world’s most unequal society? Moreover, this reports presents a chance to illustrate how differently systems treat the same nationality, depending on postcode and political pressure. And how South Africans can also be seen as the “other” in a growlingly toxic debate on who belongs where in the world of migration.

Carte Blanche speaks exclusively to two South African asylum seekers in Ireland, bringing the contorversial subject of immigration into sharp focus with a unique South African lense.
caseStudies: Brian Mogotsi Yolinda Pinard Lucky Khambule

title: MASSED MARIMBA - breaking the world record for marimba players en masse
oneLiner: We go behind the scenes of a record-breaking mass marimba concert to find out whose making the music….
summary:
On August the 2nd , 1300 marimba players, most of them school-going age, will descend on Grand West, an entertainment complex near Cape Town, in an attempt to break the record for the largest group of marimba players making music together. The Guiness Book of records for such an event was set most recently by a musical ensemble in Guatamala. https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/largest-ensemble-marimba. What makes this 2025 effort different is that most of the players will be women or girls. https://www.facebook.com/MarimbaJam/ This attempt to set a musical record is facilitated by an organisation called Marimba Jam – a female-driven social enterprise that teaches and performs marimbas in the Mother City. The Guinness book of records attempt creates a visual and audible focus for the Marimba movement which brings so much joy to young musicians across schools and communities in South Africa, and the world. And Marimba Jam provides the logistics to do this. And given the demand for marimbas, we will also meet and interview the young marimba players turned manufacturers who are building instruments for the Record-breaking attempt in a new small factory in Ottery. Here's some historical detail: the origin of Marimbas are lost in time, but they are thought to either have evolved in South East Asia in the 14th century or in Africa, and then carried with slaves from Africa to South and North America in the 16th century, globalising the instrument which has continued to develop over the centuries. https://southafrica.co.za/origins-structure-marimba.html The instrument revival in Southern Africa came in the last centuries when it was often used for worship, with churches using them as orchestras in rural settings. https://www.ru.ac.za/ilam/products/cds/davedargiecollection/ The Marimba Jam organisation was started in 2017 by a woman, Kiara Ramklass, who started playing marimba at school, not stopping through university where she used her music to make ends meet. Her organisation was an attempt to find a musical way to bridge the divide between privileged and disadvantaged schools, and to bring young people together - literally in harmony, movement and melody. Through her growing movement, she has managed to create an accredited African Marimba school curriculum, and teaches about 500 school kids weekly. They particularly focus on women – 90 per cent of their students and a hundred per cent of the teachers are females. And they have prevailed for over ten years. The climax of the feature would be the mass Marimba jam at Grand West with a degree of suspense – will they be able to break the record? And whether they do or not, what would hundreds of marimba players together in song and movement look and sound like? But leading up to that we would profile Kiara Ramklass and two school-girls coming to the jam – one from a privileged school and one from a disadvantaged one. We might also add to this an interview with Dizu Plaatjies, the musician who brought Marimbas from the Eastern Cape to Cape Town in 1979, having been mentored by Ethnomusicologist Dave Dargie who did a great deal to record indigenous instruments in religious settings. Plaatjies started out performing marimbas on Adderley Street as a busker, and from there, created the famous Amampondo percussion band which toured the world, including playing at the iconic Free Nelson Mandela concert in Wembley. When he introduced marimbas to Cape Town in the 1980’s, the instrument was little played, and now it’s a musical force, and part of many schools’ repertoire. If we could bring the now Professor Plaatjies to witness the jam at Grand West, the feature would be all the sweeter.

We have access to film the attempt to break the world record for massed marimba playing, and interview the people organising it. By telling the story of that 10-minute musical moment, we will loop back to tell the story of a successful social business, Marimba Jam, founded by Kiara Ramklass, who brings people - mostly women - together to learn and play the marimbas. The story will show how universally loved this instrument has become in South Africa, and how useful it is as a tool to create harmony and unity between different groups of people, from different backgrounds. The piece features two school girls from different ends of the socio-economic divide who experience marimbas in a way that makes them forge a common bond with others.
caseStudies: Kiara Ramklass Jordan Coetzee Alice Bekker Akhanya Smooi

title: PARK CAPTURE
summary:
[OPENING ACT – VISUAL INTRO] Visual: Sweeping drone shot over Marks Park—lush fields, joggers, kids on swings, dogs chasing frisbees. Cut to the City of Joburg skyline creeping into frame. (Presenter VO): “Lease rationalisation.” “Non-core assets.” And the word that says it all—“alienation.” They sound like routine municipal processes. But in Johannesburg, they’re being used to describe something far more contentious: a proposal that could see iconic green spaces—our city’s lungs—under threat. Visuals: We need to have a montage here are visuals from the story of coming up – maybe from confront/juxtapose with protest/angry residents (Jonker): “These aren’t just empty plots — they’re vital public spaces the City now wants to dispose of, rezone, and sell off. It’s a land grab.” Visual: Map graphic – highlighting RE/33 Braamfontein 53 IR with overlays of areas like Marks Park, Emmarentia Dam, Botanical Gardens, Froggy Pond, Westdene Dam. (Presenter VO): What’s at stake? This—173 hectares of public land that includes some of Joburg’s most treasured parks and recreation zones. It’s not “just the sports clubs” as the City claims—it’s an entire green corridor that could change forever. [STORY FRAME – SETTING THE STAKES] (Presenter Link): The City insists it’s just policy. But to residents, it feels like a land grab. And behind the bureaucratic jargon lies a simple question: if this was really just about updating leases — why not just renew them? Why launch an entirely new process that opens the door to rezoning, reclassification, and even permanent disposal? That’s what we set out to uncover. Visual: Insert of JPC’s Sizeka Tshabalala from Facebook, then overlay headlines: "SIU finds Helen Botes guilty", "JPC in HAWKS crosshairs", "Joburg residents in uproar over parks". (Presenter VO): PREVIOUS STORY RECAP The Johannesburg Property Company—tasked with leading this controversial land review—says it’s working to rebuild public trust. But its credibility is in tatters. Last year Carte Blanche reported on how its former CEO, Helen Botes, was found guilty of financial misconduct in a Special Investigating Unit probe into COVID-era cleaning tenders—yet she was kept on. Now, formal charges have been filed, and the HAWKS are investigating a lease deal involving Proton House—an inner-city property allegedly handed to politically connected interests under questionable terms. (Presenter Link): The JPC says it’s cleaning house, but keeping Helen Botes in the fold has raised eyebrows—and so has their strategy to earn back the public’s trust. By targeting parks and sports grounds in a bid to boost revenue, are they not alienating the very communities they’re meant to serve? (Presenter VO): Johannesburg Property Company General Manager, Sizakela Tshabalala, has been everywhere—on radio, in print, online—reassuring residents this isn’t a land grab, but a cleanup. Upsound – Facebook video: “Some people are still paying R2 or R49 a year on leases that were signed more than 30 years ago. It’s not sustainable.” “We’re not taking anything away. We’re just trying to modernise, to make it fair.” (Presenter VO): She insists it’s just about bringing outdated leases in line with today’s market. But residents aren’t convinced. Is this really about revenue—or is there a deeper, politically driven agenda at play? Visual: Park/sports visuals throughout entire piece to illustrate what they’re used for. [ACT 1 – THE ALARM IS RAISED] Visual: Cut to Cllr Nicolene Jonker at her desk, flipping through the Council agenda. (Presenter VO): It was buried in the paperwork. A dry-sounding council item about lease reviews. But when DA councillor Nicolene Jonker looked closer, one phrase jumped off the page: Municipal Asset Transfer Regulations. (Jonker): “This isn’t about updating leases. This is a formal alienation process—the first legal step toward disposal.” Visual: Council document highlighting ATR references. Zoom in on phrases like “alienation,” “surplus land,” and “public participation.” (Presenter VO): And that matters. Because the Asset Transfer References are only triggered when a municipality intends to sell or transfer public land. Not when it's simply renewing a lease. Visual: Community protests. Residents holding placards: “HANDS OFF OUR PARKS!” “MARKS PARK IS OURS!” Visual: Cut to the comedic AI-generated protest song. (Presenter VO): Just bringing up this issue sparks outrage in the community. It’s struck such a nerve, even the protests have gone musical. A viral AI-generated anthem did what formal petitions couldn’t—put Joburg on notice. So let’s take a look at the land in question. Visuals: MAP again (Presenter VO): The area flagged in JPC’s own documents spans up to 173 hectares—a sweeping green belt that includes Pirates Club, Marks Park, Emmarentia Dam, Melville Koppies, and parts of the Botanical Gardens. Land is a sensitive subject, but also a political bargaining chip. Now, political parties are jumping on the bandwagon—framing green spaces as a luxury. Some argue these areas could be better used for low-cost housing, rather than recreation. In a city like Johannesburg, green spaces aren’t luxuries—they’re lifelines. Parks and sports grounds are protected public assets, meant to serve communities, not be quietly sold off. (Jonker): The leases could be undervalued, but currently its normal for them to be only R500 a month, not millions. And the current lease holders take care of the properties paying the water/elec/lights, mowing the lawns, so they have value. (Presenter VO): In interviews Tshabalala has said these properties like Marks Park could be worth R10 million. 00:04:00–00:04:22 “So if you look at Marks Park and the fact that when we enter into a lease … considering the value of that property … the lease, if we are looking at its market value today, we anticipate that the rental that we need to get as the city is in excess of R10 million.” (Presenter VO): But could they know that if there’s been no feasibility study done? (Jonker): They’re doing this backwards, you first do the feasibility study, then you do the public participation process, and you give more information about the land. Currently we know nothing. (Presenter VO): And what Sizeka doesn’t say—is that the lease for Marks Park is a notarial one, registered in 1994, valid until 2043. Legally binding. And already limited to sport and recreation. [Examples of where JPC has failed] (Presenter VO): And why should residents trust the Johannesburg Property Company? Its track record is riddled with poor management. Just look at James and Ethel Gray Park—where paddle courts appeared overnight. Jonker (upsound): “Why would you allow these to pop up—and then have no benefit to the City?” (Presenter VO): Was it simple oversight that none of that revenue goes back to the City? And what about Bryanston Sports Club—did residents somehow miss the public participation signs? Jonker (upsound): “They were stuck at the back of the room, facing the wall. No one saw them. Public participation feels like a box-ticking exercise.” (Presenter VO): Now, that sports club is under review. Its future? Completely up to the City. And that’s exactly what’s raising concern. CASE STUDY: PIRATES RUGBY CLUB Cut to: Pirates Rugby Club, where the local manager describes years of community investment, public use, and rising anxiety. Pirates owner: “We run this space for the people. We pay for water, electricity, maintenance—and we’re the ones being targeted?” Visuals: Maybe some humour with presenter – take a breather park visuals. (Presenter VO): On 702 radio, Sizeka Tshabalala says the review isn’t about selling parks, but about unlocking more sports and community opportunities. (approx. 8:52–10:49): “We’re simply looking at how to diversify usage — can we introduce additional sports codes, make these facilities more active and community-focused?” ... We are saying that if there are football grounds, what other sports can we bring into that facility to make it more active?” (Presenter VO): But is that really the job of a property management company? Shouldn’t they be managing assets—not deciding what sports should be played? And if this is really about revenue, why aren’t they looking for money elsewhere? Pause visuals… [ACT 2 – THE MONEY AND WHO DO YOU TRUST?] Visual: Split-screen — on one side, JPC statements. On the other, maps showing affected areas—up to 173 hectares. Cut to aerials of Melville Koppies and Emmarentia Dam. (Presenter VO): And yet, nowhere in the JPC’s own business plan is “disposal of public green space” mentioned. (show business plan visuals) Graphic: City-owned derelict buildings. Hijacked inner-city properties. Overlay: “Why not start here?” (Presenter VO): If the City really wanted to boost revenue, why not start with hijacked buildings? Why not recover millions in unpaid advertising fees or charge city departments for building maintenance? (Jonker:) “If the City was serious about revenue, it wouldn’t be coming after parks. It would be going after hijacked buildings, collecting what’s owed in advertising revenue, its collected none of that this year! You know they maintain the Joburg city department buildings, they could be billing its own departments for maintenance.” Presenter VO: So come back to the question: why? Presenter Link (on camera, walking through park): We’ve asked a lot of people, some say the City’s budget is under pressure—and instead of fixing its own broken revenue systems, it’s going after the low-hanging fruit: functional parks and sports clubs that already work. With the 2026 local elections approaching, could green spaces be eyed for future low-cost housing? (Presenter VO): On radio, Tshabalala insists that the idea of building housing hasn’t even crossed their minds. Tshabalala Tshabalala on radio interview. “We have not even considered — it has not come to our mind — that there can be potential for a block of flats or residential for that matter. For now, we are looking at the facility in terms of its right, which is looking purely at sports.” (Presenter LINK) [Walking Into Frame – Confront Setup]: Tshabalala says it’s all above board—just about updating old leases. But with the scale of land involved, the laws used, and little transparency, residents are asking: is that really the full story? (Presenter VO): We sat down with Tshabalala to find out. [THE CITY RESPONDS in act 2] LEGALITY & PROCESS You’ve said there’s a notarial lease in place until 2044 for Marks Park—so on what legal basis are you trying to override it now? Isn’t that lease binding? If this is really just a lease review, then why not simply renew the leases? Why invoke the Asset Transfer Regulations—meant for disposing of public land? Why is public participation only happening after Council approval? The law says it must come first—aren’t you in breach of that? TRANSPARENCY & TRUST Why hasn’t the public been told that up to 173 hectares of green space could be affected? At James and Ethel Gray, padel courts popped up with no participation process—and none of that revenue comes back to the City. Why? What participation process was there at Bryanston Sports Club? Posters were hidden. You see, this is why people don’t trust JPC. FINANCIAL LOGIC You’ve claimed Marks Park could generate R10 million in rent. Based on what? Has a feasibility study been done? These clubs already pay for water, electricity, security, and rates—what exactly is the City contributing in return? Wouldn’t it make more financial sense to recover the millions owed by other City departments to JPC for building maintenance—rather than threaten functional green spaces? Why target well-used parks and clubs when hijacked buildings and rundown city properties lie neglected? Why not start there? JPC’S ROLE & OVERREACH Why is the Johannesburg Property Company deciding which sports are “relevant” enough to keep? Isn’t that the mandate of the Sports Department? Where in the City’s business or asset management plan does it say that parks, sports fields, and cemeteries are up for disposal? [FINAL 3 – WHAT’S AT STAKE] (Presenter Link): In principle, most of us agree—land and housing for the poor are essential. But is it any wonder that when proposals like this come from the City, they’re met with deep scepticism? This is the same administration that once promised a “Mega City”… and was later exposed for looting COVID relief funds. Now suddenly, it’s about building homes for the poor? The public’s cynicism isn’t unfounded. Visual: Families in the park. Tai chi in the grass. Soccer games. Laughter. (Presenter VO): If Marks Park falls, what’s next? Melville Koppies? The Botanical Gardens? Jonker: “These spaces aren’t luxuries. They’re constitutional rights. And once they’re gone—we never get them back. You need them to actually put up high rise flats, its part of the city cy-laws to have green spaces” (Presenter link): The City says this is about financial value. But green spaces offer something far more valuable: breathing room, community, connection. (Presenter VO): And before we give that up—we need to ask: who benefits from this? And what will be left for the rest of us? OUTRO – Fade to black. Park aerial fades into city skyline. END.

We are going to take the story forward and not just recap, we are trying to get to the bottom of why by questioning everything. We have an interview secured with Sizakela from JPC.
