title: THE MOUNTAIN SYNDICATE
oneLiner: rchestrated by a mysterious and elusive figure known only as Charley, this illegal syndicate targets vulnerable youth, manipulates desperate parents, and weaponizes sacred tradition in a high-stakes e
summary: Charley and his syndicate identify or lure teenage boys and surprisingly, girls—often those in distress or from troubled homes—and transport them to a remote area under the pretense of a traditional initiation. Parents only learn their child is missing after a frantic search. Then comes the call: “Your child is with us. He’s seen sacred rituals. If you don’t want him initiated, pay a fine—R4000 or more.” The parents are told their child cannot leave because they are on a "waiting list," and having witnessed rituals, they must now be "cleansed" or "compensated for." Parents report that their sons begin idolizing Charley and the "brotherhood," often running away again to rejoin it.

title: Fake Injectors
oneLiner: Exposing South Africa’s underground injector economy
summary:
The aesthetics boom isn’t just for the rich - it’s become a cultural movement. But beneath the filters, something darker brews. Picture this. You’re scrolling through social media and come across an advert for injectables - fillers and Botox - offered by an ‘aesthetic doctor’ in Cape Town for a fraction of the usual costs. According to her profile - which boasts thousands of followers and pictures of dozens of ‘before’ and ‘after’ pictures of clients, ‘Dr’ Vanessa Sobol is a Russian cosmetologist with over 10 years of experience helping clients achieve their beauty goals. She also works as a stripper at Mavericks nightclub in downtown Cape Town - while moonlighting as a medical professional who offers training in lip fillers and other dermal filler treatments - with certification - for R20 000. In South Africa, only a doctor or dentist registered with the Health Professions Council of South Africa (HPCSA) can legally inject dermal fillers and Botox, and its illegal for anyone else to perform these treatments - given the potential risks. But Sobol is just one of a number of untrained injectors that have been flooding social media platforms like Instagram of late, offering aesthetic procedures at often too-good-to-be-true or exorbitant prices. ‘Bare Aesthetics’ is run by a flight attendant for FlySafair, Karolinah Nunes, and offers mobile filler and Botox treatments, as well as ‘Botox parties’. She also sells black market Ozempic at a third of the actual price. Ozempic can only be prescribed by a medical doctor in South Africa. While these illegal injectors continue to perform these procedures without authorisation, another concern is of the safety and efficacy of the products being used - many of which are cheap, counterfeit, non-medical grade and dangerous products purchased from China, Korea and the black market. The dealing in unregulated scheduled medical substances is both illegal and an extreme safety risk to patients. Experts say that these counterfeits most commonly lead to bizarre infections and abcessess and bacteremias, also due to unsterile manufacturing techniques. Necrosis of tissue is also a common cause, and these illegal products can also lead to severe allergic reactions, anaphylaxis, and even death. Long term effects can include nodule formations, disfigurement, and severe deformities. Registered aesthetic and cosmetic doctors who are members of the Aesthetic and Anti-Aging Medicine Society of South Africa (AAAMSSA) say the situation is becoming worse on a daily basis, and even though they’re constantly reporting unlicensed injectors and fake doctors to the HPCSA and SAHPRA, nothing is seemingly being done to hold these charlatans to account. Fraudsters impersonating healthcare professionals training the lay person is also hugely concerning, given that anyone can now be able to inject filler into another person’s face. They say that counterfeit doses and unlicensed providers are harming patients, and that procedures are being performed in makeshift medical offices - including Airbnb’s, and that these criminals’ are contributing to the burgeoning black market with unlicensed and counterfeit botox and fillers from South Korea and China. It’s estimated that in South Africa, unlicensed injections outnumber legitimate licensed practitioners three to one - with one-quarter of procedures being done in someone’s home/makeshift medical setting, rather than at an accredited clinic. * This story will investigate and expose serious flaws in the South African beauty and aesthetics industry - that are endangering lives, and leaving people at risk of being scarred for life. * It will also examine the true cost of beauty in South Africa, and what needs to be done to ensure that the safety of patients is maintained in aesthetic medicine - when the market is being flooded by counterfeit medical professionals and counterfeit goods?

Exploring South Africa’s underground world of unlicensed Botox and filler injectors, where air hostesses and strippers perform medical procedures - illegally and with unauthorised products.

title: MURDER IN PRISON - the death of Quintin Fortuin
oneLiner: Tonight we unravel what really happened to a 39-year old awaiting trial prisoner at Goodwood Prison in the Cape
summary:
On the 16th of February, an awaiting trial prisoner at Goodwood Prison failed to emerge immediately out of his cell when called for roll call. According to insiders, he had been doing drugs all night and was slow to react when the other prisoners were called to come outside to kneel down to be counted. He was chivvied by the two warders on duty, who got him to join the tail end of the group. But then an altercation ensued. According to Correctional Services, this prisoner, allegedly a senior general in the 26 gang, produced a home-made sharp object and stabbed a warder. In the scuffle the two warders were injured, one broke his arm, and both are home still recuperating over six weeks later. As for the prisoner, Quinton Fortuin, he ended up naked and fatally injured, and was declared dead in Karl Bremer Hospital four and a half hours later. What happened between about 08h00 in the morning and 11h30 that day when he was declared dead is now contested. It is alleged that Inmate Fortuin was beaten up by wardens who set dogs on him, and then by the EST, the Emergency Security Team that enforces law and order inside the prison walls. It is also alleged that he was dead on the scene and the Department of Correctional Services is desperately trying to cover it up, pretending he died in hospital. They unnatural death - now a criminal investigation into murder - shows how the prison system fails itself, its inmates and the community at large. It raises the problems of understaffing at prisons, the over population of prisons, the lack of humane control, the lack of any type of rehabilitation or leadership and the lack of technological resources. It's been revealed that none of this was captured on camera because the contract to keep the cameras had not been paid in three years, so while the camera could provide images in real time, it could not record.

We are able to tell the story of the murder of Quinton Fortuin in Goodwood Prison on the 16th of February 2025, because we have been leaked so much information about it: photographs of the dead body, phone calls, the post mortem, an initial inquiry by the Judicial Inspectorate and the answers to Parliamentary questions on the matter. None of this information squares up to the official version disseminated by the Department of Correctional Services of the death of this notorious inmate who grew up in gang-ridden Delft, and who has been in the crosshairs of the judicial system for his entire adult life.

title: Oyster Bay
oneLiner: A battle is brewing in a small coastal town in the Eastern Cape where a pristine beach meets a controversial mining plan.
summary:
According to the draft basic assessment report on the project compiled by Algoa Consulting Mining Engineers (Acme) on behalf of Schoenmakers Mining, the mine will operate for up to five years. There will also be an estimated 20 to 40 truckloads of sand being moved from the beach on a daily basis which will impact the only dirt road into and out of the town. The mining company believes the project will help the town overcome its sand migration problem, but residents don't buy this, and believe coastal sand mining will have a detrimental environmental impact. There are however some residents in favour of the mining company. These residents live in Brander street which is on the beachfront and sand encroachment has caused their homes to be "swallowed" by the dunes. They argue that the current so-called “mining” issue is a misnomer. What is proposed is not industrial-scale extraction, but rather controlled sand removal combined with ecological restoration. It’s a basic environmental management task, not resource exploitation. They say the intensity and irrationality of those in favour of the project resemble the behaviour of a cult.

Oyster Bay is a town of just 140 permanent residents. It's pristine beach and hiking trails are a drawcard for tourists. But, an application to mine a portion of the beach, has those living there, in an uproar. Many believe it will destroy the character of the coastal hamlet. Schoenmakers Mining, a holding company of Gqeberha-based Glendore Sand and Stone, plans to mine sand on a 5ha site on the primary dune - it will affect about half of the beach. The company applied for a permit in December last year, but residents say they have been left in the dark, and the public participation process has been non-existent. Residents claim they have been trying to register as interested and affected parties but that the mining company doesn't acknowledge their emails.

title: Foreign Special: Rags to Ruin - The Cost of Fast Fashion in Ghana
oneLiner: Where do clothes donations end up?
summary:
Charity bin donations from Europe arrive in Accra by the ton, only for the large quantity of unsellable garments to be dumped in landfills, or burned, polluting the air and waterways of Accra's Old Fadama slum. The neighborhood is located by a lagoon, which has been transformed into a huge open sewer, completely clogged with textile waste. Respected community leader Mohamed Salifu is concerned: “This comes from Europe. How much longer will it have to stay here and pollute our land?” Salifu is also responsible for health issues in this deprived neighbourhood, and beyond the water, what worries Mohamed is the air quality: “You see the smoke? They have no choice but to burn the clothes if they don’t want to be overwhelmed.” Residents are slowly poisoning themselves on toxic fumes, a situation made worse by the threadbare healthcare in Old Fadama. Non-profit Plastic Punch tries to clean the area, but it is an uphill battle, and Director Richmond Kennedy Quarcoo warns, “if we don’t act quickly, future generations won’t be able to enjoy the ocean at all.”

Ghana has become a global dumpster for fast fashion's cast-offs. The turnstile for Africa's secondhand clothing trade, the port of Accra ingests a staggering 11 million pounds of discarded garments from around the world every single week.

title: LifePod Launch
oneLiner: University of Stellenbosch Medical students are turning the tide on South Africa's organ donation crisis.
summary:
Jonty Wright is a fifth year Stellenbosch University medical student who met Lynette Stuurman at the Stellenbosch University canteen. She’s been waiting for a kidney transplant for years, and has dialysis several times a week. Her story moved Jonty, and sparked his interest in this field. Together with fellow students, they created “Lifepod” – South Africa’s first official dedicated transplant ICU at Tygerberg Hospital. After brain death, and consent from family members, potential donors can be moved to this new ICU instead of occupying trauma unit beds. Last year, these students competed in Ironman 70.3 to raise awareness and funds, and raised R400,000 through crowdfunding campaigns. They conceptualized “LifePod” with Tygerberg doctors and lecturers. And designed and wrote all operational policies. LifePod could save up 100 lives annually, and turn the tide on South Africa’s organ donation crisis.

Over 5000 people across South Africa are waiting for lifesaving organ transplants. It can take years to reach the top of the waiting list. But, a group of university medical students is determined to improve the rate of transplantations in South Africa.
caseStudies: Lynette Stuurman Jonty Wright Naazim Nagdee

title: Respecting the dead
oneLiner: Meet two rather unusual people: Christopher Fitchet from the Southern Cape and Eugene Liebenberg from Gauteng, both paying homage to the dead by visiting their graves.
summary:
Christopher Fitchet’s mission began 8 years ago when he searched for his ancestors. Even though the surname is uncommon, few documents were available on the family tree. He turned to the cemeteries across the country in the hope of finding family graves: his search took him from the Eastern Cape to the Free State and all the way down to the Western Cape, photographing every single Fitchet gravestone and documenting the family tree. It turned out there were 1500 South African family members with that surname (Pretorius is about 200 000 in comparison). He traced his founding mother, Mary-Anne Collison, born in England and his Founding father from Calcutta who ended up in South Africa when their ship landed in the Cape in 1817. During this mission to document the graves of the ancestors he noticed the state of neglect of the graves in cemeteries across the country and that is ‘when the penny dropped’ said Christopher. I had to photograph every single grave in the cemetery as a method of preserving the dead as tomorrow it might not be there any more. In some instances the burial register is gone which means if the graves are destroyed the dead will forever disappear in living history. From the caretakers he heard stories of people removing the headstones to sell, others were digging for jewelry in the boxes as they believe it is buried with the deceased, and the worst is stealing the ashes of the dead to mix with street drugs like Nyaope. In Bloemfontein he spent 4 days picking up ashes and putting the memorial plaques back again - including those of his family buried there. Christopher’s passion to preserve the history of the dead has resulted in over 350 000 photos taken of the graves in many towns, cities and even on farms. The photos are then donated to the Genealogical Society of South Africa’s Gravestone Photos Project and available on their website for anyone searching for a family member. There are a number of organisations focusing on documenting graves, but none were focusing on the rural areas and the farms so this became his focus over the last 3 years. For Christopher this is a way of giving back because life is not just about taking, he says. Over the years he has met very interesting people and places like Uniondale known for its ghost of a lonely young woman who hitches a ride and then when people offer her a lift, she gets into the car and then simply vanishes. The ghost, known as Maria Roux, was a young woman who tragically died in the early hours of 12 April 1968 when her fiance lost control of the car in which they were travelling. He visited the farm nearby the exact place where the accident happened and it was a strange eerie feeling, he remembered. Christopher’s next photographic grave project is Swellendam in the Western Cape, a historic town established in 1745 named after Governor Hendrik Swellengrebel and his wife Helena ten DammeIt. There are over 50 provincial heritage sites, 4 cemeteries, and a large number of farm graves in the district. Eugene Liebenberg’s story is rather different: Having fought in the border war he pays homage to the fallen soldiers in Operation Askari and Operation Sceptic, also known as Operation Smokeshell. He finds the grave sites from the records on the South African War Graves project, whose aim is to archive photographs from South African and Rhodesian wars. He then locates the graves to pay homage. He found most of the soldiers’ graves neglected, overgrown and unsafe to visit. “Some graves, like the ones in Boksburg cemetery, are so overgrown that I spend hours clearing my way through the weeds in search of the graves”, says Eugene. “It takes hours sometimes and I can’t believe that no-one cuts the lawn and keeps the place clean”, says Eugene. After clearing the site around the grave, Eugene cleans the dust from the headstone and places a small bunch of flowers on the grave as an act of respect and remembrance. He then takes a moment of silence to remember the fallen soldier. In a symbolic act of honouring the soldier and their journey in the afterlife he drinks a toast to angels as a way of acknowledging their presence in the world of spirits and offering respect to their guardian angel. Eugene has struggled to come to terms with the war he had a part in - not of his own choice - and this he feels is a way of finding peace and remembering the brothers who did not make it alive, says Eugene. For Eugene it is a matter of finding closure on a war he did not choose, paying his last respect. For Christopher every roadtrip to a forgotten cemetery on a farm or a town or a hamlet is a journey back into the past where he painstakingly captures frame by frame a tombstone of a family member creating a “window to the past”, etched in memory. And for those who cannot get to the graves, being able to see their loved ones' burial site online is a special feeling, says Christopher. Riana Le Roux manages the Photographic Grave Project on the Genealogical Society of South Africa’s website. She spent a decade cataloguing and posting hundreds of thousands of photographs from graves in South Africa and neighbouring countries on the website for viewers to find at the click of a button. The search engine is easy to navigate. All graves that have been photographed and sent to Riana will be available online. By simply entering the name and surname of a loved one and the province where the person was buried, the photo of the grave and exact location will be displayed on the screen. “We are constantly updating our site and are thankful for people like Christopher who dedicate their spare time on taking photos for those who cannot get to the grave, and some people who live far away and are not able to go to the cemetery to pay respect”, says Riana. We will conduct a zoom interview with Riana who lives in Baberton; spend a day with Eugene in Boksburg at the local cemetery and a day with Chrisotopher at cemeteries in Swellendam. In addition we have graves from cemeteries in the Northern Cape and Ceres, taken by our cameraman when he travelled through that area. ADDITIONAL VISUALS: Photos from Eugene in his army days; photos from an ex soldier who served on the border and kindly made his own photos available; plus 50 seconds of licensed film footage, purchased from Peter Lamberti, a professional filmmaker, to ‘set the mood’ of the Border War. On the Fitchet family, we have photographs of the graves Christopher managed to find plus a family tree graphic to illustrate the genealogy and family line dating back to the ‘Stam moeder” / matriarch. All photos on the Photographic War Project is available for us to download. ________________________________________________________________________________________________

Christopher had a burning desire to trace the origin of his rather unusual family name and Eugene, still haunted by the ghosts of the border war, to pay homage to the fallen brothers in arms.
caseStudies: Eugene Liebenberg Christopher Fitchet Riana Le Roux

title: Police Scam
oneLiner: It's a scam with a dramatic sense of theatre - victims are convinced they face imminent arrest by supposed police who've contacted them on video calls - only to be left traumatised and out of pocket
summary:
Once the "policeman" has done his part, the victims are handed over to a so-called "prosecutor", often a female scammer. The prosecutor tells victims they can be let off the hook, if they help the police to catch the money launderers. In order to do so, victims have to pay over large amounts of money into a "special investigation" account. The so called police tell the victims they will use the money transfer to monitor the "money launderers" after which the victims will receive their funds back. Once the scammers have your money, R250 000 in one case, they of course disappear into the shadows.

Our research shows that the "video call scam" has seen a huge increase over the past few months. The scammers M.O. is simple but elaborately planned and executed. Victims receive a phone call from a so called "customs" officer. He tells them a package with their name on has been intercepted at one of our airports. The package contains drugs and fake passports. The victim has to send their details to a WhatsApp nr to clear their name. Once they've done that, they receive a video call from another scammer, dressed in a police uniform. For the next two hours they are threatened with arrest, sent fake asset forfeiture documents and warrants, told they're part of a human trafficking and money laundering operation, and convinced the police are going to arrest them for a crime they did not commit...
caseStudies: Burt Jooste Mike Combrink

title: Safe Haven or Tax Haven? The Rise of South Africans on the Isle of Man
oneLiner: A a new migration trend is quietly taking root — and SARS is struggling to keep up. The Isle of Man, a rainy, wind-battered Crown Dependency in the Irish Sea, is fast becoming a preferred destinatio
summary:
The Isle of Man is fast becoming one of the world’s most rapidly growing enclaves of South African expatriates — a scenic outpost with zero capital gains tax, no inheritance tax, and low corporate rates. While most South Africans here speak of quality of life and safety as primary reasons for leaving, experts warn that the exodus — especially of high earners — is a clear signal of eroding confidence in South Africa’s fiscal future. But it’s not just fear — it’s strategy. More and more South Africans are looking to keep their options open and safeguard their wealth by parking assets offshore, setting up trusts, or restructuring businesses via jurisdictions like the Isle of Man. What began as financial emigration has now evolved into a well-oiled playbook for tax-efficient living abroad.

This story unpacks the rise of this unique offshore community, explores the implications for SARS and the national tax base, and investigates whether the South African government has the will or the resources to prevent mass base erosion and profit shifting.
caseStudies: Chanelle Sukhoo Rich Mulholland Roelf Odendaal Vanessa Naude

title: UPDATE: ImPossible Tour
oneLiner: From the brink of death, Grant Lottering has found new purpose in pushing himself to the limit.
summary:
Grant completed 36 repeats of Chapman's Peak, then took on The 13 Peaks, a 110km trail run that circumnavigates the Table Mountain reserve and links some of its highest summits. He cycled 350km in 20 hours then ran 91km and completed the whole challenge in 61 hours 17 minutes. It was all to raise awareness of mental health challenges faced by South African youth, and Grant plans to use his own example to encourage young people to seek help and face their challenges with determination.

He's no stranger to the impossible. Twelve years ago, Grant Lottering nearly died on an Italian roadside. Doctors told him he would never cycle again – he decided to prove them wrong. Since then, he’s tested his endurance on over a dozen crazy challenges. We catch up with him after his latest, unprecedented, challenge: 24 hours of cycling followed by 110km of trail running, all in under three days.
caseStudies: Grant Lottering ImPossible Tour

title: MAYDAY - AIR TRAFFIC NAVIGATION SERVICES IN CRISIS
oneLiner: We expose the growing risk in air safety in South Africa as a result of a crisis at the heart of the Air Traffic Navigation Service
summary:
It appears that South Africa’s safety guardians of the sky have been in trouble for some years – at least critically from 2017 when as the industry insiders say the “cracks began to show”. However, those cracks became a chasm in July 2023 when vital safety instruments were suspended by the regulatory body the, the South African Civil Aviation Authority, SACAA. https://www.caa.co.za. These procedures create the legal route for aircraft to land and take-off from South Africa's airports, and if they are not properly sanctioned and administered, the safety risk increases dramatically, and in some instances, scheduled flights can not take off or land, causing delay and huge financial penalties to airlines and passengers, and the economy as a whole.

We are able to pull together the complex picture of air safety in South Africa, narrated by industry players outside of the organisation charged with ensuring that safety, the ATNS, as well as from inside the agency which has been failing to meet its deadlines and is compromised by allegations of disfunction.
caseStudies: Miles van der Molen Barbara Creecy Aaron Munetsi Zola Majavu Boyd Fichardt

title: Global Chaos after Liberation Day Tariffs
summary:
SA is the 2nd largest exporter of citrus in the world, after Spain, and the largest in the Southern Hemisphere. It brings R33 Billion into our economy. Its labour intensive in an environment of 40% unemployment this is critical. Busy picking right now, for the next few weeks fruit that would be destined for USA will go to Europe and the Middle East, but pretty quickly there will be an oversupply, markets flooded. Ecape and Limpopo export to those markets and so if WCApe diverts there they will be impacted. In CT the shipping options are limited- Europe, middle East and the States - the Far East don’t even stop here because the port delays are so extreme SA does not compete with USA Cirus farmers as we have the opposite/complementary seasons, and mandarins and oranges has been a growing market. Also USA is wealthiest markets, so its critical to keep our markets there Gerrit has been exporting to USA for the last 25 years, they have an exporting importing company in Maine Massive uncertainty currently – we need a clear policy decision- but with the GNU in its rocky state they extremely concerned Biggest impact in rural areas - Already 40% unemployment- Cirtrusdal survived 2 floods, and two bad seasons, this year was a good season, fruit looking good and they hoped to begin to recover. Cirus is labour intensive and can create employment. They planted trees to expand the market which have just started bearing and by 2030 they were going to generate 100 000 jobs.

The world economy and geopolitical order will never be the same, the last two weeks have seen chaos across global markets and trade relations after Trumps "Liberation Day" tariffs. Stock markets plummeted and are recovering with Musk adding 36 billion dollars to his fortune - was this all engineered by Trump and Musk? How do we make sense of this? We speak to Economist Dawie Roodt to give us the global economic perspective and impact locally. Roodt has weather many economic storms but says he has never lived through anything like this - even with the 90 day moratorium and 10% tariffs - the world will never be the same again. He as also never witnessed our own Budget go through this kind of turmoil and instability in the last 30 years. Stock markets once bitten twice shy, they will not invest as they have in the past. Roodt asks how long will the US dollar remain as the reserve currency? He predicts slower global economic growth, and inevitable growing unemployment in South Africa and the social instability and crime that goes with it. What does all this mean for citrus farmer Gerrit Van Der Merwe in Citrusdal, who produce must hit the markets on time, or be lost to competitors. In the last two weeks they have been packing and picking oranges for export.
caseStudies: Dawie Roodt Gerrit Van Der Merwe

title: Richmond – Refuel; Refresh and Re-Invent
summary: Richmond, for years simply a place to stretch your legs, refuel and grab a snack before you continue your journey through the Karoo. Richmond lies just off the N1, between Johannesburg and Cape Town. It’s the signs to the dorp, that litter the NI, that are more obvious then the town- that is until you turn off the tar and enter Richmond wonderland. Loop Street with its picture perfect converted houses and B and B’s. There is a rich saddle horse history in the Richmond area. The earliest settlers, called Trekboers, had spent a lifetime in their saddles, and were among the best horsemen in the world. When diamonds were discovered, opportunities abounded for breeding carriage and draught horses, and for carting goods around the area. -The Horse Museum, in Loop Streett one of only two of its kind dedicated to the riding horse. . Johan Tolkien is the curator. Richmond was occupied by the English in the Anglo Boer war and under attack from Boer troops in Bloemfontein. Fort Vegkop , known to British as Flaghill to the Boers as Flagkop, Is the fort British soldiers would defend their occupation of Richmond. John Donaldson owner of Richmond Books and Prints – specialises in the history of the Anglo Boer War.
caseStudies: Johan Tolkien John Donaldson Abrie Fourie Lientjie Wessels

title: Bitcoin - Witsand
oneLiner: From Witsand to Mossel Bay, we hit the road to find out why Bitcoin is catching on — and why some still say no.
summary:
Small towns along South Africa’s Garden Route, led by Witsand, are quietly adopting Bitcoin for everyday use — from buying groceries to paying for boat repairs. While the rand remains the official currency, locals are turning to Bitcoin as a faster, bank-free way to transact. But not everyone’s convinced. Carte Blanche goes on the road to find out if this is the future of money, or just a digital detour.

It sounds crazy: a small South African town where you can buy groceries, fuel, even tip your waiter — all in Bitcoin. But it’s happening. We go see for ourselves.
caseStudies: Eldrie Hill Edwin Jones Jones Gerald Boezak

title: Foreign Special | A Majestic Menace
oneLiner: Who’s paying the price for Botswana's elephant conservation success story?
summary: Botswana has more elephants than any other country on the planet. But what’s been hailed as a great conservation success story has become a deadly problem. While they have turbo charged photo tourism, in some parts of the country there are two elephants for every human and stories of elephants causing havoc, destroying crops and even killing people is fuelling anger towards these majestic animals. On Foreign Correspondent reporter Stephanie March travels across the stunning Botswana landscape to see who is benefiting and who is paying the price for this conservation triumph.

title: PRIVATE SECURITY UNDER THREAT
oneLiner: Is private security at risk? Proposed regulations could cripple an industry vital to public safety.
summary:
Proposed changes to South Africa’s private security regulations could place new restrictions on armed response, tighten operational controls, and increase compliance costs. With police resources already stretched thin, what could this mean for public safety? We unpack the concerns and their potential impact on everyday South Africans.

- Relevant to South African’s safety - Ride-along element - Crime visuals - Call to action
experts: Mr. Johan Booysen Morne Du Toit Mr. Martin Hood Attorney Dr. Johan Burger

title: CMR NORTH
summary:
CMR North Why is CMR North in Brits and Haarties removing children without proper documentation, placing them in unsafe homes, and fabricating stories against family members to keep children in the system? Our investigation reveals a deeply troubling pattern: vulnerable, low-income households—often unaware of their rights—are being targeted and systematically stripped of their children under the guise of protection. What emerges is a shadow system of unchecked authority, legal shortcuts, and a devastating disregard for the Children’s Act. Background CMR North operates in the Northwest province, in communities where access to legal aid is minimal and families often cannot afford to fight back. We've received multiple reports of misconduct by CMR social workers, particularly Annamaria Scheepers and Nadia van der Merwe, and disturbing allegations surrounding Magistrate Moteane—accused of rubber-stamping removals without due process. Case Study 1: Samantha Lee Mays Samantha, a single mother and survivor of systemic abuse, had previously been in the child welfare system herself. When she became pregnant, she was offered accommodation by Mr. and Mrs. Welthagen—a couple who housed other mothers and children on their plot. Izak Welthagen reportedly made inappropriate advances on Sam. After giving birth, Samantha briefly returned to an abusive ex before moving in with a trusted friend of 15 years, Alma. Later, Samantha voluntarily checked into rehab for PTSD, leaving her daughter Jenna temporarily in Alma’s care. While Samantha was in rehab, the Welthagens complained to CMR, claiming child abandonment. Without a Form 22 (a legal requirement for placing a child in alternative care), social worker Annamaria Scheepers removed Jenna and put her in the Welthagens care. Legal Breaches: • No Form 22 submitted • Detention order signed for a child under 12 (illegal under the Children’s Act) • No interview or affidavit from Samantha before the court ruling • Magistrate Moteane presided over the case Allegations of Abuse: Jenna said to her mom on the phone “Mumma, can Jesus see what Oom Izak does under the blankets?”—prompting Samantha to reach out to civil rights groups. Outcome: Anari from the Purple Foundation intervened and filed a kidnapping case against Scheepers. In a voice note to Anari, Scheepers implied the child would be returned if the case was dropped. Jenna was returned the following day. Fearing retaliation, Samantha has since relocated to Mossel Bay. Case Study 2: Wilmien & Arizaan Background: Arizaan was placed in her grandmother Wilmien’s care after her father was accused of sexual assault. Months later, social worker Nadia van der Merwe removed Arizaan without paperwork or a court date and placed her with Mr. and Mrs. Horn, who were unregistered with DSD but operated under an NGO license. Under the Horns care: • Children (including Arizaan) were removed from school and homeschooled by the Horns without legal authority • Monitored video calls; no in-person visits allowed • All girls bathed by Mrs. Horn, including children as old as 7 • Children given "night vitamins"; Arizaan showed unexplained bruises • No court-approved guardianship, no oversight Exposed: A tutor recorded Mr. Horn in a room with Arizaan. Horn was later arrested for sexual abuse and alleged child pornography. Only then was Arizaan returned to her grandmother without paperwork or explanation. Despite the charges, Wilmien has not been asked for testimony. This trial started on the 28th March and has been postponed to June. But the prosecutor says there was evidence of pornography on his laptop or phone. Access – to this family, the tutor is still thinking, but I think she will speak. I need to get the video. Case Study 3: Benita & Colin Background: One of four cases taken on by AfriForum. A child was removed after allegations of sexual assault against her mother, stepfather, and grandfather. Leon Nel, a private investigator, later provided proof that all three were innocent. The case was dropped, but I'm not sure what the latest is from Afriforum. Legal Misconduct: • CMR used a private physician (on CMR payroll) for J88 medical reports—twice, four weeks apart—violating the Children’s Act, which mandates state hospitals for such assessments. • The child was placed in a foster home without the father being notified. Outcome: Colin, the father, and Benita, his new wife, had the financial means to challenge CMR legally. They won custody and have documented extensive evidence of illegal conduct throughout the case. Case Study 4: The Bleckmann & Rheeder Families (Cornerstone Safe House) Allegations: Cornerstone, an unregistered safe house, has reportedly been used by CMR to warehouse children. Multiple children claim: • Physical abuse • Surveillance cameras in bedrooms • Forced separations from families despite lack of legal grounds Bleckmann Case: Children were removed without proper documentation and accused their father of abuse. Charges were dismissed, but the children were never returned. The magistrate was again Moteane. The family has since had another child not removed by CMR, raising questions about the legitimacy of the original removal. Rheeder Case: All four children were removed. The father, accused of sexual assault, died after being jailed without access to medication. The mother completed rehab, but CMR refused reunification. One daughter, at 16, became pregnant while in the care of Cornerstone. CMR tried to remove the baby as well. After legal action, the family was reunited. Systemic Concerns • Unlawful Removals: Children taken without Form 22 or proper court orders • Unregistered Foster Homes: Children placed in homes without DSD approval • No Due Process: Parents are often not interviewed or given legal representation • Pattern of Abuse: Reports of physical, emotional, and sexual abuse ignored or minimized • Judicial Complicity: Magistrate Moteane repeatedly signs off on removals without scrutiny • Fabricated Reports: Allegations of tampered medical records and false claims used in court What Now? When the Department of Social Development (DSD) attempted to hold CMR accountable, the organization fought back in court and won—on a technicality. The South African Human Rights Commission is compiling evidence for a comprehensive report on CMR North’s conduct. At the heart of this issue is a critical question: Are the very institutions tasked with protecting children the ones doing them the most harm by not following state laws?

Story Synopsis A quiet power has taken hold in a region where the state should protect its most vulnerable. Once a public child protection body, CMR North captured the system. Guided by a strict Christian ideology, it removes children not based on law, but on belief, filtering families through a moral lens instead of legal standards. They believe they're doing good. But behind closed doors, children are being separated from their homes without due cause. And the state, fully aware, has been forced by CMR's powerful legal teams to look the other way. This is not a story about failure. It’s about a takeover. It's about what happens when ideology replaces law—children are left to suffer in its shadow.
caseStudies: Charmaine Botha Benita Prinsloo
camera: Thomas Pretorius Ruan Visser Kobus Zietsman

title: Sacred Traces
oneLiner: A forensic artist is using foraged materials to recreate the paints and brushes used by San people thousands of years ago.
summary:
Stephen uses technology to help reproduce paintings that have faded over time. He does not use ordinary paints, but instead has experimented for years using bones, eggshells and the faeces of raptors to create pigments. He also makes his brushes, even using the hair of a ground squirrel once. He tries to get into the headspace of the artists whose work he recreates. He was inspired by his uncle’s interest in rock art and remembers seeing his first San painting at the age of 14. His uncle Ginger Townley Johnson also documented hundreds of rock art sites across South Africa. Stephen believes these paintings were a portal to another dimension, a spirt world that existed on the other side of the rock.

Stephen Townley Bassett has dedicated his life to the study and recreation of rock art. He is a forensic artist living in the town Komani in the Eastern Cape and has spent decades experimenting with pigments, using foraged materials to recreate the paints and brushes used by San rock artists. As a young man, studying archaeology at the University of Stellenbosch, he spent almost two years documenting San rock art sites in the Cederberg.
caseStudies: Stephen Townley Bassett

title: Wanted: Dead
oneLiner: Was it a shootout or did police go too far?
summary:
Extortion incidents in the Eastern Cape have been catching on like wildfire, prompting the Eastern Cape SAPS to open an extortion hotline for locals to report these crimes. Premier Mabuyane has called for military intervention in order to limit the disruptions to state infrastructure, schools and local businesses. The National Police Commissioner called for its National Intervention Unit to investigate. It’s against this backdrop that two accused extortionists have been killed by the police’s National Intervention Unit (NIU) within the past 6 months. Both reportedly, in shootouts. Given their reputation it's unsurprising it's said, they will not be missed by many.

We use social media video to reveal how the police's specialized unit may have gone too far.
caseStudies: Thandeka Ndaba Clara Mbatha

title: The Last Cast
oneLiner: We look at how skipper John Matambu vanished at sea and why his alleged murder continues to evade justice.
summary:
A respected fisherman. A fugitive on the run. A boat that vanished—only to resurface, torched and abandoned on a remote Mozambican beach. This is not just a story about a man who disappeared at sea. It’s a story about a system that failed—again and again. In this investigation, Carte Blanche exposes the glaring gaps in the justice system that allowed convicted fraudster Ferdi Visser to manipulate the law, evade parole, and escape custody—not once, but twice. How did a known fugitive manage to slip through the cracks so easily? And with Visser still on the run, will authorities finally be held accountable?

With exclusive interviews, tons of B-roll, and other exclusive footage, viewers will feel as if they are tracking Ferdi Visser and piecing together John's disappearance themselves.
caseStudies: Cherie Eilertsen Janine Shaw Marcus Joubert Frank Ayanda Nomandla

title: UPDATE: Art Awakening
oneLiner: A programme teaching art to children with little else has attracted a generous donation.
summary:
Art Canvas Factory has donated 100 canvases to Luc's art group, which Luc is using in workshops and plans to donate to the City of Cape Town.

Luc van der Walt spends his days bringing art to the children of Masiphumelele, one of the Cape's most poverty-stricken and dangerous townships. Now his passion has inspired Graham Sanderson, the owner of Art Canvas Factory, to provide a generous donation. And Luc's children are paying it forward.
caseStudies: Graham Sanderson Luc Van der Walt

title: Refugee Roulette
oneLiner: Uncovering widespread corruption in South Africa's refugee system, where asylum seekers are forced to pay bribes to secure their status.
summary:
The Refugee Appeals Authority of South Africa (RAASA) is facing a staggering backlog of 133,582 appeals, leaving many genuine asylum seekers in limbo. How it works is, an individual arrives into the country and goes straight to the home affairs office and claims to need asylum. Home Affairs is compelled to give you three months, with hardly any investigation done about whether or not you deserve one. Then from there you have to apply every three moths and if HA says no, you are allowed to appeal. So that’s the baglog that I am referring to I’m referring to. Meanwhile, those with the means to pay are able to buy their way to asylum status, regardless of their eligibility. My research is focused on the Home Affairs Marabastad office in Pretoria, where agents are working in cahoots with officials to sell asylum statuses for R1500. I have sent spy cam footage of these agents and officials negotiating bribes and making demands for payment. But it's not just the corruption that's alarming - it's the human cost. We spoke to the Moyo family, who were told they would be deported despite having lived in South Africa for years and contributing to the economy. The wife, a critical care nurse with a master's degree, was refused refugee status indefinitely, leaving her family's future uncertain. Immigration lawyer Claryn Ferreira is fighting for justice, representing families like the Moyos and demanding answers from Home Affairs officials. Our footage captures her confrontation with a supervisor, who fails to provide valid explanations for the corruption.

Undercover footage reveals a web of corruption involving Home Affairs officials and external agents, who are exploiting vulnerable individuals fleeing conflict and persecution.
caseStudies: Claryn Ferreira Ruth Moyo Dr. Leon Amos Schreiber

oneLiner: Fast. Full Contact. Brutal & Unexpected. Roller Derby - a sport not for the faint hearted.
summary:
Women in roller-skates, faces in war paint, fishnets and tutu wearing helmets and knee pads. It’s a sport that gained international popularity with the 2009 movie Whip It!

- not widely known sport - quirky characters - fast paced
caseStudies: SUMIA KUBEYA KATHERINE REYES LUAMI CALITZ AIMÉE PLANK

title: HEADACHE CLINIC DOCTOR
oneLiner: Fall from grace of 'medical pioneer'
summary:
World-renowned headache doctor Dr Elliot Shevel is a maxillo-facial and oral surgeon who started The Headache Clinic in 1992, and has served as its medical director ever since. But over the past year, the reputation of the man and his internationally-acclaimed clinic has been in tatters. Dr Shevel appeared in the Randburg Magistrate's Court in November 2024 following his arrest - charged with the murder of one of his patients - who died hours after receiving treatment at his clinic. Another patient suffered irreversible brain damage that's left him in a permanently vegetative state. The 81-year-old headache specialist was arrested at his Illovo home, accused of the murder of 38-year-old Marinella Avvakoumides, whom he treated on 15 July 2021. Shevel is alleged to have performed his eponymous Shevel Desensitisation Procedure on her, which involves injecting the patient with a thick needle at the back of the skull to "permanently numb" pain signals from tendons connecting the neck muscles to the skull. Shevel is also accused of the death of another patient in 2024, who died under similar circumstances to Avvakoumides. In September, Shevel was suspended from practicing by the Health Professions Council of South Africa (HPCSA) amid an investigation into the deaths of his two patients. Only nine doctors have been suspended, pending the institution of a formal inquiry since 2020, according to the Health Professions Council of SA. The case continues on 11 March.

Renowned maxillo-facial surgeon, Dr Elliot Shevel, is facing murder charges in the deaths of two patients who underwent his eponymous 'Shevel Desensitization Procedure'. The allegations are that his age - he's currently 82 - could've been a contributing factor to his ability to perform the complicated and invasive procedure.
caseStudies: Roedolf Matthee Andrew Avvakoumides Tristan Clarke Rachelle Roberts

title: Gold for Life
summary:
Following on our previous story which showed how the Scoin shops "collectible" Mandela coins are not a worthwhile investment, we will show how Gold for Life (a subsidiary of Scoin and the SA Gold Exchange - all owned by Alan Demby & son Rael Demby) targets low income South Africans with the promise of a safe investment. However, their products are over-priced, and once the sale is concluded customers have to wait months of not years to receive their coins. What's more they are paying for safe storage of their coins, when in fact there is no vault or storage facility. This amounts to fraud.

A whistle blower has come forward to give details of how customers are scammed by Gold for Life. According to him "They are selling coins they don't have." They might have coins in their Scoin shops in various malls throughout the country, but these are purely for display purposes. Even if you pay cash for a coin, or set of coins, they will not hand it over straightaway. They have a mandatory 45 working days collection policy. After the 45 days has passed, that's when the real wait begins. They will come up with a multitude of excuses and hoops to jump through before you can collect your coins. Another scam is the safe custody option, SafeGold, where they offer to store your gold coins for a fee: 1 year - R1500; 3 year - R3500; 5 year - R5500; 10 years - R10 000. This includes insurance in the event that your coins are stolen. If you want to collect your coins you have to provide a POP to show you are paid up for this service. You also sign a contract with clear terms and conditions. However, our whistleblower claims there is NO safe custody. They simply sell your coins and when you notify them of your intention to collect, they will make you wait months, if not years before you get your coins.
caseStudies: Nelson Hantise Mary Tsogang-Hantise Kabelo Sebati Johannes Mavuso
camera: Justin Barlow Kobus Zietsman Aristo Mukeba

title: NHI: Irish Medical Exodus: South African Doctors seek greener pastures in Ireland
oneLiner: South Africa’s NHI dream risks collapse as South African doctors leave for better opportunities abroad, fuelling a critical healthcare brain drain
summary:
The government's National Health Insurance (NHI) plan that envisions South Africa as a healthcare hub characterised by modern medical infrastructure supporting universal access. Bu that will remain a pipe dream if the country fails to retain its highly skilled and experienced medical Doctors which are seeking opportunities abroad. Dr. Lindsay Kaberry and Dr Ememabasi Edem, South African doctors now practicing in Mayo and Tipperary in Ireland represent just two of thousands of medical professionals who have left South Africans. This personal story anchors an exploration of the healthcare brain drain from South Africa, examining the causes and consequences of this exodus. As well as how a national health insurance system works elsewhere and its challenges.

An exclusive viewpoint of South African doctors abroad that have left South Africa due to a lack of opportunities and ability to specialise in a field of their choice. Exposing the pitfalls of implementing a universal healthcare system without the requisite medical personnel which are choosing to leave the country.
caseStudies: Lindsay Kaberry Ememabasi Edem

title: Sharks
oneLiner: This is a story about both a great conservation success, and a massive conservation failure off the coast of South Africa.
summary:
Our main character is internationally acclaimed ichthyologist and wildlife photographer and conservationist Chris Fallows - he is extremely articulate and engaging on camera. Chris became famous in 1991 with his iconic images of “flying” sharks, and for the next 22 years he and Monique led shark cage diving trips to Seal Island (they are spectacular images to which we have full access). Shark cage diving became a booming tourist industry, South Africa was the international mecca for film crews and tourists flocking to witness these athletic creatures throwing seals into the air. It was a billion rand industry. In 2018 he took his last picture of a Great White in False Bay. The Shark Cage diving industry has all but collapsed.

We start on a high with Masa on a boat off Yserfontein with Chris and Monquie Fallows watching a superhighway of Humpback Whales. It’s a spectacular site, and one of the world’s greatest conservation success stories. ( Hopefully the boat will be surrounded by whales, but Chris has footage he is willing to share to add to whatever we capture. ) Since the international ban on whaling in 1986, whale populations have steadily increased. Chris estimates there once over 300 000 Humpback whales off our coastline, whaling reduced their numbers to 5000. Our West Coast is on a super highway of whales and the numbers keep growing. In 2019 they spotted 70, using the unique patterns on a whale’s tail fluke to distinguish them, there are now over 12,000 sightings.
caseStudies: Chris Fallows Karyn Cooper

title: Bulungula Update
oneLiner: In September last year, we investigated a crime wave sweeping the picturesque Wild Coast in the Eastern Cape. In the months since our story aired, the crime has continued unabated.
summary:
Tony and Jean Robertson were attacked last year and were featured in our first story. In this update, we interview them again. They were attacked for the second time in just eight months in February. Tony was shot in the leg and foot, his wife pistol whipped. Both are severely traumatised. They had increased their security, but their alarms did not frighten off the intruders who escaped with their cellphones and iPads. They had also hired a night watchman who ran away when two gunmen pointed a firearm at him.

We investigated a terrifying crime wave sweeping the picturesque and remote Wild Coast in the Eastern Cape. Since our story aired in September, crime has continued unabated. Despite promises of increased police visibility in the area, there has been no assistance for communities living in fear.
caseStudies: Andiswa Tshayiso Tony Robertson

title: Water Ambassadors
oneLiner: They're called Water Ambassadors, volunteers working with the Municipality to improve water supply in their area.
summary:
In 2020 as Covid hit, people in the area faced a water supply crisis. The water scheme, built in 2015 for R150 million, had become completely unreliable due to poor maintenance. For months, people had no water. Children were missing school as they couldn’t wash their uniforms. There were more cases of diarrhoea, as people were collecting untreated water. The water scheme supplies water to over 30,000 people. But, instead of litigating against the Municipality the Equality Collective decided to work with them, using volunteers called “water ambassadors” from the community to collect data across six reservoirs. By 2022, they were collecting data from all 33 reservoirs. There are 32 volunteers who visit the reservoirs every day to check if they are receiving water. Water is pumped from a dam to the reservoirs and then distributed to communal taps.

Equality Collective, an activist organization based in the Eastern Cape, has been working with the Amathole District Municipality to fix water issues that have plagued the community for years. Volunteers called "water ambassadors" head out every day to collect data from reservoirs and feed the information back to the Municipality.

title: Foreign Special | Venice Tourist Overload
oneLiner: The city under threat from overseas visitors
summary: Venice's Tourist Overload Venice is one of Europe's top tourist destinations, but this iconic city is under threat. Kumi Taguchi from SBS Dateline, meets the locals who say over-tourism is destroying the city they love.

title: Skybound - The Take off
oneLiner: Tonight on Carte Blanche: Strapped to a motor, lifted by a wing—meet the daring pilots pushing paramotoring to new limits, soaring where no one thought possible.
summary:
**Summary:** Paramotoring—pure flight with nothing but a motor on your back and a wing above. It’s thrilling, it’s dangerous, and for a handful of South Africans, it’s an obsession. Meet Jean-Pierre Seger and Lawrence Marais, two pilots pushing the limits of what’s possible. From flying the first-ever paramotor journey from Joburg to Cape Town to planning an even greater challenge—crossing South Africa from north to south. With the sky as their only road and the wind as their greatest ally—or worst enemy—this is a test of endurance, skill, and survival. Our presenter takes to the skies to experience it firsthand, uncovering the risks, the freedom, and the sheer adrenaline of powered flight.

A first-hand look at the thrill and danger of cross-country paramotoring, as daring pilots defy the impossible—soaring across South Africa with nothing but a wing, a motor, and sheer determination.

title: Predatory Lenders
oneLiner: Exposing Exploitation: Investigating allegations of a corrupt social worker in the Eastern Cape who is abusing her position to exploit vulnerable grant recipients through predatory lending practices.
summary: Meet Thebelihle Vara, a pensioner whose life was turned upside down by a social worker turned loan shark. Noludwe's illicit lending scheme has left a trail of financial ruin and emotional scars throughout the community. But Thebelihle's story is just the tip of the iceberg. A shocking report by the Black Sash reveals that unregistered loan sharks like Noludwe are preying on vulnerable pensioners and grant recipients nationwide, using coercive tactics to exploit and manipulate them. Through Thebelihle's heart-wrenching journey, this narrative exposes the dark underbelly of South Africa's illegal lending crisis, highlighting the urgent need for stricter regulation and protection for vulnerable communities.
caseStudies: Nkosinphile Nodumo

title: The Independent Development Trust, the suicide and fake news -
oneLiner: Journalist Pieter-Louis Myburgh explains how he was framed by politicians and colleagues in a bizarre bid to diver attention away from corruption allegations at the IDT
summary:
Last year, news broke of a corrupt tender handled by the Independent Development Trust on behalf of the Department of Health to supply medical oxygen facilities to 55 hospitals across the country. The journalist in question wrote an article about it and attempted to meet the director of the so-called ghost company which had got the tender. They met - but three days later he was dead, and the cause of death was suicide. It was clear to Pieter-Louis that there was more to this story, and possibly a bigger tale of corruption at the IDT. As a result of digging, he found himself hot on the tail of other tenders. But suddenly in early January, he also found himself flagged as a corrupt player in allegations aired in the media by fellow media practitioners and politicians, who accused him of receiving cash to plant bad stories on behalf of the Minister of Public Works. The stories were eventually retracted but the battle lines have been drawn.

We have background information provided by a whistleblower as well as access to the journalist who can explain to us how he attempted to investigate corruption in a series of stories which appear to have triggered a push-back in the form of fake news, publicised by politicians and fellow journalists.

title: Shelly's Legacy
oneLiner: A Cape Town woman has been transforming lives for decades by providing wheelchair related services to families across South Africa.
summary:
She embarked on finding therapists and accessing information from abroad (it was before the internet) to try and understand what was possible and what was being done overseas. She researched how she could assist her daughter to sit up straight so she could see her mother, and she looked into ways her daughter could communicate more effectively. With the help of UCT, her child’s wheelchair for outdoors with full body support, that could go up and down, and in which she could move around herself, was built. Shelly was able to drive herself around by the age of eighteen months. Shona started an organization called Interface, that focused on helping non-verbal people communicate. She built different types of chairs for different children from her garage and did fundraising for those who couldn’t afford it. She realized the need was much greater than she had imagined. By 1992, she had outgrown her garage and realized she needed to turn it into a business. That was when she launched "Shonaquip Social Enterprise" which provides wheelchair related services to families across South Africa. Now, she has 85 people in her team and they work across seven countries. They make equipment for people living in rural areas, where wheelchairs are used off road. Furthermore, Shona's wheelchairs are designed to help children improve their function. Assistive devices are just a tool, but Shona’s work also looks at early child development, play for all, assistive technology and a parent network. She launched a parent network during Covid. She wanted to give parents knowledge and trains parents online three times a month. Nine hundred parents are trained every two weeks. They are upskilled and can run advocacy and anti bias workshops in their communities. Results of the training provide Shona with data that she reports to government to show where systems are failing. Shona has a fully inclusive team, with disabled people working in the factory as well. Her factory is in Ottery. She lives in Noordhoek with her three daughters. They all live on one property.

Shona McDonald has been changing lives since her own daughter, Shelly, was born with severe disabilities more than forty years ago. Her daughter was born with cerebral palsy because of medical negligence. At the time, doctors advised Shona to put her child in a home. She refused. She also did not take legal action against the hospital as she wanted to turn it into something positive. Instead, she approached the biomedical engineering department at UCT and asked them to help her build the first paediatric electric wheelchair in Africa.

title: From SWAK to Strength - the story of how Crestway High turned its fortunes around
oneLiner: We show how Crestway High, the school with the worst matric marks in 2024 in the Western Cape was able to turn itself around to get a dramatically improved pass rate the following year
summary:
This is a story about how an inspirational academic, teachers and community members took the school with the worst performing matric class in the Western Cape in 2023, and worked on it to become arguably one of the most improved schools in 2024, despite challenges of poverty, substance abuse, teenage pregnancies and a gang culture which impact on the learners. Academic Prof Jansen has mentored the staff to assist with improving the discipline and the culture of the school, while the teachers have knuckled down to do the extra work required to get the students over the line, meaning that their matric result improved in a year from just under forty per cent to mid-sixties. One of their strategies was to bring the accounting students over to tourism, in order to get them the matric they need to go on to further studies or work. We profile the change specialist, Prof Jansen, the headmistress and teachers and a learner who as a result of her hard work has just passed well in matric, got a place at a university which will be funded. She has now a dream of a future, despite the difficult circumstances in which she has grown up, fostered by an aunty in a rough suburb in Steenberg, near the school. Help came from all sides, through donations of time, money and food, and in one special case, dental care, discounted by a dentist near the school.

We have unique access to a struggling school in Retreat, on the Cape Peninsula, which is on the edge of Cape Ganglands, and provides an academic home for about a thousand children from severely disadvantaged backgrounds, children who don't always have enough to eat, often live with family members as their parents do not take responsibility for them, and who have to manage a rough world of gangs and violence outside the school gates. Academic Prof Jonathan Jansen, having read about the plight of the school when they scored the worst in the province for their class of 2023 in January of 2024, decided to intervene and built on efforts already being made by the teachers, community and alumni to drag this school up, out of the doldrums and give the children the chance to dream about a better future by getting a better matric. And as a result of strategy and effort, the school is showing progress, by doing considerably better in matric this year and providing a foundation for young people to tackle the next phase of their education.

title: (Un)Traceable Grain: Dirty Logistics
oneLiner: Carte Blanche hunts down a logistics syndicate threatening the country's food security by the grain load.
summary:
The clock is ticking for the agricultural industry - criminals are engaged in a dirty game forcing farmers and transporters to play but there are no rules. For years, the logistics industry had been under siege, no commodity is off limits for these greedy syndicates determined to profit off legitimate businesses sweat. Ben Wepener is a transporter and a former cop based in Delmas. In the dead of a night in June 2023, he received a call - his truck stood stationary kilometers from the silo where a client's grain was supposed to be loaded AND, his Zimbabwean driver was nowhere to be found. This set the wheels in motion for a one man investigation conducted by Ben. The goal: to track down his client's missing load. Through his determined sleuthing, he tracked the grain to AFGRI's silos. AFGRI is one of the leaders in the grain and production cycle. How did his client's legitimate load, "hijacked" by a criminal syndicate end up in AFGRI's legitimate silos?

Carte Blanche hunts down a logistics syndicate threatening the country's food security by the grain load. - Intercepting a compromised grain load before it's handed over to a criminal syndicate - Selling a sacrifical load to a legitimate grain leader: no questions asked - Confronting criminals as they alter horses and trailers at shady yards - Following the trail of a syndicate's grain hit

title: Ricollin Moodley: Lipstick Artist
oneLiner: Some may use paint and brushes… but Ricollin Moodley uses nothing more than lipstick. Now the self-taught artist is gaining a large following from his unique art.
summary:
Recognition and Growth Ricollin’s work gained attention on social media, with celebrities like Tyla sharing his art, and even the Springboks following and commenting on his posts. In November 2023, he was invited by Siya Kolisi, captain of the Springboks, to attend a rugby match, where he had the chance to paint live at the event—an unforgettable experience for him and his family. Though he hasn’t yet exhibited in galleries due to high fees, some galleries have bought his art at a low price and resold it for much more. Ricollin dreams of seeing his work displayed worldwide, believing that art can open doors and change lives. A Life Transformed by Art At 24, Ricollin Moodley’s story is one of resilience and passion. His journey proves that art is not only about skill but also about survival, hope, and vision. Despite facing significant challenges, Ricollin continues to build a future where his art connects with people globally, proving that creativity can truly transform lives. Interviews: We can visit Ricollin, as he lives in the South Coast near Margate. His parents are happy for us to interview them as well. You may have seen him on the Supersport commercials about him drawing the team, after Siya and the guys made such a fuss of him on social media. He now has 129k followers! I’m sure Mnet/ Superport would love for us to celebrate him as well and highlight their ad with him. Right now his family’s rent and income is solely based on his artwork, and we can go to his house and he’ll show us all his artworks, and we can watch him work – he’ll do a lipstick drawing of one of our presenters or of anyone of our choosing. He’s a really inspiring young man who is changing his life and that of his family’s by following his passion.

Ricollin Moodley: The Lipstick Artist Ricollin Moodley, a self-taught artist from the South Coast of South Africa, has gained recognition for his unique art created using lipstick. His journey, filled with challenges, perseverance, and creativity, highlights his passion for art that helped him overcome adversity. Early Life and Struggles Born in Ladysmith, Ricollin grew up in a mixed-race family, with an Indian mother and a Xhosa father. Their marriage faced significant racial prejudice from both sides. For the first ten years, his parents lived apart due to these challenges. Financial hardship was a constant struggle, and his father’s income was barely enough to cover rent. During his teens, food was scarce, and Ricollin often took on the responsibility of finding meals for his family. In 2017, Ricollin moved to Port Edward. As a Grade 11 student, he began exploring his passion for art, using discarded materials like library colouring pages to sketch. This creative outlet provided him a way to express his frustrations with his difficult circumstances. The First Breakthrough Ricollin’s first paying customer appeared while he was sketching on the beach, hungry after several days without food. A man approached and asked him to draw a portrait of his grandchild. In return, Ricollin asked for groceries. The man returned with not only groceries but also money and a phone (so he could start his journey as an artist). This act of kindness marked the beginning of Ricollin's career, showing him the potential of art as a means of survival. The Rise of the Lipstick Artist With the phone, Ricollin created a social media page to promote his work. Despite slow sales at first, he continued to take commissions and use art as a lifeline. In 2020, the COVID-19 pandemic hit, and Ricollin’s father lost his job. The family became homeless for a while, but Ricollin began creating portraits in shopping malls, raising money for rent. The pressure of creating portraits quickly improved his skills. Using Unconventional Mediums Facing financial difficulties, Ricollin adapted by using whatever materials he could find. He used coffee grounds, food colouring, sand, and even discarded Woolworths shopping bags. His breakthrough came when he discovered a box of unused lipstick, which he began using as a medium. His "lipstick art" became a distinctive style, symbolising his journey of survival and transformation.

title: Trapped In the Deep
oneLiner: Desperate and dying - a group of illegal miners trapped underground in an abandoned mine shaft might finally be saved after a standoff with authorities that lasted months. But is this a rescue or reco
summary:
Mine Rescue Services, who specialises in these kinds of operations, have arrived at the site and are starting recovery and rescue operations today. A cage will be dropped more than a kilometre below surface, to where the miners currently are. MRS will start with the removal of bodies before the live miners are rescued. SAPS is on site to arrest survivors. If the body count is above 100, it puts this disaster amongst one of the biggest death tolls in mining history in SA. Meanwhile, desperate families arrive at the site every day, unsure of whether their loved ones will emerge from the disaster alive. This is news story with a some deep human interest elements,

The group of miners are some of the thousands of illegal artisanal miners who have been working below ground in and around existing mines in the Klerksdorp, Stilfontein and Orkney areas. The current tragedy was set in motion when police, under their Operation Vala Umgodi that has targeted illicit mining across the country. According to sources, there are at least 400 men stuck underground, and they have sent letters to the surface stating 109 of them have died underground. Two videos have been released to the media by a group representing the miners, that seem to show at least three dozen dead bodies and emaciated miners. They claim the miners stuck underground are dying from starvation, because the police aren't allowing food supplies down.

title: Breaking Barriers: Aimee Barrett-Theron Whistles Her Way to Rugby History
summary: Breaking Boundaries – Aimee Barrett-Theron’s Trailblazing Journey in Rugby A CB viewer sparked the idea. Story Summary: I grew up in a sport loving and participating family , as did my wife. I recently gave my view on a Facebook Rugby group after the Springboks played Portugal. I stated that the referee handled the match quite well , but that I am struggling to get to terms that it was a lady (Holly Davidson). My comment was "crucified" by half of the memebers and I received a thums up from more or less the other half... Would you be willing to produce something about the topic ? Maybe get a public rugby figure for and against my view. I just think that men and women are absolutely equal , but that they must stick to their roles and participate equally with their own gender groups. March 2024 https://www.facebook.com/watch/?v=385678904095068 I think what first caught my attention was Aimee Barrett- Theron’s interaction with and Sharks captain Bongi Mbonambi during the URC game between the Sharks and the Lions. Mbonambi was unhappy about a TMO call and, as a result, the situation could have escalated, but Barrett-Theron did brilliantly to calm the situation down, while also demanding respect from the 33-year-old in an incident that went viral online. She started by asking the Sharks skipper: "Bongi, can you walk with me please, this way?" before going on to say, "Bongi may I speak please? Listen, I fully respect you and who you are, and I am well aware that all of your players have probably played more games than I have refereed in the URC. "But we are on the same field so if you could show me the same respect that I show you, that would be very much appreciated." ……… Rugby has long been seen as a sport “by men, for men” steeped in traditions of masculinity, physicality, and male camaraderie. For decades, the game excluded women, not only on the field but also in coaching, management, and officiating roles. Despite modern shifts towards inclusivity, entrenched biases remain, particularly in South Africa, where some men still question whether a woman belongs in the referee’s whistle-blowing role. Enter Aimee Barrett-Theron—a former Springbok rugby player, trailblazing referee, and outspoken advocate for gender equality and neurodiversity. Aimee has shattered stereotypes at every turn, from representing her country as a player to becoming the first woman appointed to officiate in the European Challenge Cup. Her success is even more remarkable when seen through the lens of her autistic identity, which she credits for her unique focus and resilience under pressure. Approach Follow her in pre paring and refereeing a match. 1. Early Years: - Born in South Africa Aimee Barrett-Theron was born on June 27, 1987, in Cape Town, South Africa. She spent her formative years in Durban, attending Northlands Girls' High School. She later returned to Cape Town, where she currently resides and continues her groundbreaking work in rugby. - From a young age, she defied expectations by excelling in a sport traditionally reserved for men and boys. 2. Playing Career (2007-2014): - Represented South Africa as a Springbok Women’s Rugby player, earning respect for her talent and tenacity. - Played in the Women’s Rugby World Cup, showcasing her skill on the global stage. - Unfortunately, her playing career was cut short due to recurring injuries, forcing her to retire in 2014. While devastating, this setback opened the door to a new chapter in her rugby journey. 3. Transition to Refereeing (2014): - Retired from professional play and took up refereeing, driven by a desire to challenge gender norms and stay connected to the game she loved. - Worked her way up through school and club matches, proving her mettle in high-pressure environments. 4. Breaking Barriers (2016-2023): - Became one of the few women to referee at the highest levels, including men’s matches in the Currie Cup. - Officiated the 2021 Women’s Rugby World Cup final, cementing her place among the world’s best referees. - South Africa's only female referee at the Rio2016 Olympic Games. 5. Historic Appointment (2024) - Made history as the first female referee in the European Challenge Cup, breaking new ground in international rugby. Issues 1. Rugby: A Man’s Game? - Unpacking the traditional view of rugby as a sport rooted in masculinity, with insights into its history and the challenges women face breaking into the field. - Interviews with South African players and fans who feel women shouldn’t referee, juxtaposed with Aimee’s determination to prove them wrong. https://www.facebook.com/watch/?ref=search&v=1503361947014869&external_log_id=6d3aab41-f2b4-48b5-ac25-439fa71ba019&q=aimee%20barrett%20theron Lots of negative comments on woman referee. https://www.facebook.com/watch/?ref=search&v=198427022416427&external_log_id=6d3aab41-f2b4-48b5-ac25-439fa71ba019&q=aimee%20barrett%20theron Smile FM https://www.facebook.com/watch?ref=search&v=1349141225799708&external_log_id=654169b9-2b51-4b0c-a229-a1369d0d8cd8&q=Aimee%20Barrett-Theron Interesting debate on females in rugby. https://www.facebook.com/watch?ref=search&v=883880178887344&external_log_id=654169b9-2b51-4b0c-a229-a1369d0d8cd8&q=Aimee%20Barrett-Theron 2. Aimee’s Journey - Aimee’s reflections on her playing career, transition to refereeing, and the sacrifices involved. - How her **autistic identity** enhances her ability to focus, manage high-pressure decisions, and thrive in a demanding environment. 3. Breaking Barriers: - Insights into the challenges of refereeing men’s games in South Africa, where some players and spectators openly question her authority. - Footage of her commanding respect on the field, with testimonials from players and coaches who admire her professionalism. The Future of Rugby - How Aimee’s success is inspiring a new generation of female players, referees, and administrators. - Her advocacy for gender equality and neurodiversity as essential steps toward making rugby a truly inclusive sport. Visual & Emotional Appeal - Archival footage of Aimee as a Springbok player and early refereeing days. - Emotional interviews with her family, highlighting the personal sacrifices behind her achievements. - Powerful game footage showcasing her authority on the field, contrasted with interviews revealing the criticism she’s faced. - Scenes of her mentoring young referees, reinforcing her role as a trailblazer.
