title: Out in the cold: The Fight for South African Citizenship
oneLiner: An exclusive that dives into the personal stories and political tensions surrounding a controversial law that has left thousands of South Africans abroad disconnected from their homeland.
summary:
This unique feature unpacks the deeply personal and legal consequences of South Africa’s controversial citizenship laws through the lens of South Africans abroad who unexpectedly lose their citizenship or face an uphill battle to maintain their rights to a passport or exercise their right to vote. By weaving together emotional narratives, expert perspectives, and political context, the story explores Section 6(1)(a) of the Citizenship Act, which has left millions of South Africans abroad in limbo. It highlights the diaspora's struggles to maintain their connection to home, with voices like Hayley Reichert driving advocacy and legal challenges. With an impending Constitutional Court ruling, the story delves into themes of identity, belonging, and state accountability, raising critical questions about the balance between sovereignty and diaspora rights. Combining on-the-ground reporting in London, Budapest, and Pretoria, this feature provides an intimate and nuanced perspective on an issue that could reshape the lives of South Africans around the world.

This exclusive story uniquely highlights the personal and emotional toll of losing South African citizenship through Jadene Tager’s as well as several other South Africans' experience while unpacking the broader legal and political implications. title: Lesotho -South Africa porous borders
summary:
Summary: South Africa’s border with Lesotho is at the center of a troubling crime wave. Every week, stolen vehicles are smuggled across the Caledon River, livestock vanish in the night, and communities face violence from armed gangs. A recent incident in the Eastern Cape saw unclaimed corpses of illegal crossers underscore the deadly risks of these journeys. Despite efforts by SANDF and police, resource constraints leave the border largely open to exploitation.

This story investigates the growing crisis of illegal border crossings between Lesotho and South Africa. Through compelling accounts from affected farmers, victims of vehicle theft, and overwhelmed law enforcement, it highlights the human and economic cost of unchecked crime and border insecurity. We will also have access to transporters who help illegal crossers into South Africa. We will be able to show how lax border control is at the Tele and Qacha Nek crossing in the Eastern Cape. We will also have access to chiefs who have been struggling to clamp down on illegal immigrants crossing into their villages and have set up camp and assumed citizenship.

title: Human decomposition
oneLiner: On the slopes of Table Mountain a team of scientists are experimenting with ground breaking ‘decomposition’ research that could help the police in real life cases.
summary:
For the last seven years forensic science research at the University of Cape Town have focused on the estimation of the time-since-death and the reconstruction of the events leading up to the discovery of human remains. The purpose of the study was to provide accurate decomposition information which will contribute to the work of the Forensic Pathology Service and the South African Police. For the purpose of the experiment, pig bodies were used as they share many similarities with humans including organs and anatomy. (In South Africa it is illegal to use donated human bodies for decomposition research). And to replicate the forensically realistic information, clothing the pig carcasses were central to the study. The pigs were dressed in clothes to obtain forensically realistic information as clothing degrades too.The pigs and their specially tailored outfits were central to research conducted by a group of forensic scientists known as taphonomists. They study the environmental forces that drive changes to a body after death. A key aspect is estimating time-since-death, the length of time between death and a body being recovered. Ascertaining this detail can help to identify the person and reconstruct the circumstances around their death. The pig carcasses were left to decompose in two forensically significant Cape Town habitats, Delft on the Cape Flats, and the slopes of Table Mountain - two known hot spots for murders. In the Table Mountain experiment, pig bodies were also traumatised to match the forensic similarity of stab wounds. The study was conducted over several seasons to compare the decomposition rate. Summer-season clothing accelerated the proceeds and the carcass weight loss was directly affected by the scavenging of the Cape grey mongoose which accelerated the decomposition rate. These findings helped deepen the understanding of how soft tissue desiccates (dries out or mummifiies), which is central to improving the accuracy of time-since-death estimations and can assist in criminal investigations. In the heat of summer, the body rapidly desiccated, with tissues losing moisture, reaching a state of mummification in under 30 days. In the coolness of winter, the process took much longer. The bodies reached a stage of advanced decomposition and lost about 20 kg of their initial weight but never lost more weight and never reached the skeleton stage. The Cape grey mongoose was one of the key scavengers captured on the infrared camera traps placed at the decomposition site. The study revealed that the mongooses’ daily scavenging activity had a significant effect. The experiment also revealed that the mongoose target smaller, more manageable body parts from the carcass and move them undercover to eat. It was also the first time that the scavenging habits of the Cape grey mongoose provided the answers to a live police case - rather than looking at the traditional method of measuring the temperature and decomposition rate of the human corpse - the scavenging and scattering patterns of the mongoose was key to piecing together the puzzle. A real live example was in 2017 when a corpse without a face and fingerprints were found on the slopes of Table Mountain. The mongoose scat was analysed and fibres matching the deceased clothing was found at the scene. A ring and a watch - found in a burrow nearby where the mongoose fed on the hand and finger - provided further identification to the deceased. This research is the first of its kind in South Africa to implement a transdisciplinary approach to understanding the role of scavengers on the rate of decomposition of clothed and traumatised bodies. It is one of the world’s first synergistic investigations of decomposition, and the first to utilse an automated data collection approach. The story: We will capture the deployment of the next experiment scheduled for the 13th of January. The pig bodies will be dressed, traumatised and positioned in a secured site on the slopes of Table Mountain. This study will run until the end of March when the findings will be shared with us and the programme can be broadcasted. In addition to our own visuals we have been given access to visuals of the previous experiments on the Cape Flats dune strandveld. The story will be told through the various disciplines and their findings. We will give an example of a real live police case to demonstrate how the accumulated insights of the study could be crucial to the identification rate of the victims of unnatural deaths by accidental or criminal means.

When the police recover skeletonised or heavily decomposed bodies, they need forensic experts to make sense of what they’ve found. One important question in such cases is: when did the person die? The answer could be found by reconstructing the circumstances from time-since-death. In the Western Cape - the province with the highest rise in murders in 2024 - sharp force trauma, e.g. stabbing, slashing, has been identified as one of the leading causes of death. Now, in a first-of-its kind study in South Africa, a team of scientists from the University of Cape Town have provided new insights on the role scavengers like mongoose play, and the effect of sharp force trauma on the human corpse during decomposition.
caseStudies: Varushka Bachan Victoria Gibbon Devin Finaughty Calvin Mole

title: The NPA: Tell no lies, claim no easy victories
oneLiner: The NPA says they are not in a crisis, but to date despite promises they have not won a single case. In a challenging interview we ask the leadership what they are doing wrong
summary:
In 2019 Shamila Batohi returned from the Hague to lead the National Prosecuting Authority. During the Zuma presidency, the once proud NPA had been hollowed out by state capture. Batohi was a welcome appointment. She promised to restore the NPA and ensure speedy convictions of the state capture perpetrators. That same year, Hermione Cronje was appointed to head up the Investigating Directorate, the sharp end of the NPA that would investigate, arrest and prosecute those responsible. Batohi and Cronje -two powerful women, with the same aim- to hold those accountable for bringing the South African state almost to its knees. But within two years, Cronje left the NPA for a second time. Cronje is a straight shooter. She believed that there was a crisis in the NPA and that Batohi wasn’t leading effectively enough to turn it around. She believes the crisis in the NPA is ongoing. In an interview she says: My personality is such that I don't have great finesse so if I see a problem I will call it out. And you're free to disagree with me. You can tell me that I have the wrong understanding of the problem, but I want the space to be able to say that this is the problem I'm experiencing, and I think we need to address it. Cronje says there were powerful and corrupt people still inside the organisation attempting to sabotage her work, one of these was Knorx Mollele. The NPA eventually charged him but it came too late -by then, Cronje had already left. He should have faced criminal charges, but instead the leadership made a deal with him and eventually he left, only to reinvent himself as head of Lesotho’s anti-corruption unit. The bad apples in the NPA were just one of Cronje’ s concerns. Another was the serious lack of skills to prosecute complex corruption and money laundering crimes and the spin they were putting out instead, of doing the real hard yards. Now as Batohi tells the public that impunity is no longer a given, and the NPA is fit for purpose, those comments are undermined by the facts. The NPA has not to date won a single state capture case. “There's far too much emphasis on we've got to look like we're winning this battle. It is important to look like we're winning the battle, but it has to be based on interventions that actually is going to ensure that we win the battle !” Glynnis Breytenbach who supported Batohi’s appointment is scathing. “Just give us one win!” she told her recently, “and we will all go away.” But alas there are no high profile perpetrators in orange overalls. And as for the Gupta’s they are long gone, any cases they had to answer to, are currently dead, so if you see them at Heathrow, wave them by. There are no Interpol red notices out for their arrests, and no charges against the state capture mastermind.

Spicy interview with the head of the NPA Shamila Batohi, and her deputy, the former head of the Independent directorate and several other high profile interviews, internal meeting recordings of the NPA
camera: Ruan Visser Kobus Zietsman Greg Nelson

title: Komani in the Dark
oneLiner: 30 days without electricity is a nightmare for matric exam students, but it's also a matter of life and death for those dependent on life-saving equipment in hospitals and refrigerated medications at
summary:
MAIN CHARACTERS RESEARCH: Daniel Lombard “Doc” – hidden identity interview. He is specializing at Frontier hospital, located in Top Town. Doc is in the surgical department. The children died in the paediatric ward. 1. Two babies were on ventilators when the generators failed, and both died – he has spoken to the 2 doctors and 2 nurses who were there. Obviously, everyone is scared and none of them will speak.Doc says the hospital head has told everyone to be quiet. But essentially they had no oxygen, because the ventilators were switched off 2. He says the lack of electricity has been difficult in a situation where they already have nothing a. They have no working toilets in the entire hospital b. No catheters c. No sutra material d. No linen – meaning the operating theatres can only do one surgery a day 3. I suggested I do a walk through of the hospital and film all of this – he will make me a map and take photos today of all the issues for me 4. He wants to speak because he says he has patients he has to send home because he simply can’t do his job. The pharmacy isn’t able to operate without electricity – so over the weekends there’s literally no medication available for patients – patients have to wait until Monday. He’s beyond frustrated and makes him want to leave, cos he’s afraid of more patients dying Nangamso Ncobo, Matric student at Queens College, lives in Blue Rise. 1. November began the "hard" exams, but electricity outages started – she’s looking to get into University because her marks are good enough, but at home she’s had to study via candles, and she has to buy almost everyday cos they burn out fast. She also can’t charge her phone for past exam papers, so it’s become extremely challenging. 2. Only place to charge phone was at school, adding extra pressure. 3. Some mornings, no time to iron clothes due to electricity outages. 4. After writing 3-hour exams, would return home, nap, and wake up to darkness, reducing motivation to study. 5. Studying with candles, torches, or paraffin lights feels insufficient. 6. Difficult to adjust to daily life without electricity during final exams. 7. She also can’t wash herself properly because there’s no hot water, and some people don’t have water because the water pumps require electricity. Alasdair Mcdonald, community leader. 1. He’ll talk about the current electricity issues - Komani's infrastructure is rapidly deteriorating, with some areas now enduring power outages for as long as 30 days now. This ongoing crisis is the result of years of neglect and mismanagement by Enoch Mgijima local municipality, compounded by the misallocation of equitable share grants, which have been primarily used to pay Eskom. Since 2020, the municipality's Eskom debt has skyrocketed from R350 million to an eye-watering R1.4 billion. As a result, a large portion of the municipality's funds is now consumed by debt repayment and staff salaries, leaving little for critical service delivery. 2. The heart of the problem lies in the failure of three key electrical cables that supply power to Top Town, where the Water Works are located. Without power, the pumps cannot deliver water to the town, exacerbating the crisis. One of these cables also supplies power to Frontier Hospital, which has been without electricity and is now relying on backup generators to stay operational. The nearby Madeira Old Age Home is also struggling without power. Just a few days ago, there was a dramatic explosion, and we have footage of this incident, which has been shared with Chwayitisa. 3. The situation has worsened over the last 3.5 weeks, with a series of electrical explosions caused by overloaded cables. In an attempt to address the issue, the municipality has been adding new sections of cable to the existing infrastructure. However, this patchwork approach has only led to more frequent failures. A key issue is the lack of protection systems in the substations—when a fault occurs, it doesn’t just affect one area; it trips the entire town's power grid. This not only disrupts daily life but also inflicts serious and lasting damage to an already fragile infrastructure, further jeopardizing the town's ability to function. 4. What is the current plan? The municipality's current plan involves bringing in new cable sections to extend the old infrastructure, but this is essentially just delaying inevitable failures further down the line. Lucy Lyons, chairperson of the Madeira Old Age Home Board. It’s located Top Town 1. Located next to the hospital, they are having the issues – they’ve had no electricity for 30 days now. They can only afford to run the generator because of high diesel costs (6-8 AM, 6-8:30 PM). It costs around 16,000 rands for two weeks. Generator can't power washing machines, causing hygiene issues for elderly residents. 2. There’s been cold weather and lack of reheating facilities for the 65 residents who are between 65-95 years old; spoiled food adds to costs, and some residents have gotten sick because they can’t afford to go buy new food. Power outages jeopardize refrigerated medications like insulin and other health-related equipment. There are also hygiene challenges – soiled linen can’t be washed and it's taking a big strain on the staff. 3. The Mayor has been away in China during the crisis, avoiding questions and created confusion. The municipality has had a slow response to power outages in general, unresolved infrastructure problems for over 5 years. Local business owners - Cooks, bakers, and laundromat owners affected by outages. 4. Komani is in a state of decay, and is “literally collapsing”, with Potholes, burnt-down public buildings from protests, and then there’s no power or water- this has created an "apocalyptic" atmosphere.

We have an insider at the hospital willing to confirm the death of the children. As per my treatment we will be focussing on a specific area of Queenstown- toptown and we will tell the story from there where the hospital and old age home is. Blue rise is nextdoor where our student lives, so its geographically where our story will be told from. The frontier hospital will have an undercover where I'll walk in and film the areas the doctor points me to. And we'll also visit the old age home nextdoor. Komani's infrastructure is rapidly deteriorating, with some areas now enduring power outages for as long as 24 days. This ongoing crisis is the result of years of neglect and mismanagement, compounded by the misallocation of equitable share grants, which have been primarily used to pay Eskom. Since 2020, the municipality's Eskom debt has skyrocketed from R350 million to an eye-watering R1.4 billion. As a result, a large portion of the municipality's funds is now consumed by debt repayment and staff salaries, leaving little for critical service delivery. I spoke with several key local figures to better understand the situation, including community leader Alasdair McDonald, journalist Bongie Solundwa, and Jacques van Zyl, head of the local business forum. They all pointed to a deeply troubling reality. The heart of the problem lies in the failure of three key electrical cables that supply power to Top Town, where the Water Works are located. Without power, the pumps cannot deliver water to the town, exacerbating the crisis. One of these cables also supplies power to Frontier Hospital, which has been without electricity and is now relying on backup generators to stay operational. The nearby Madeira Old Age Home is also struggling without power. Just a few days ago, there was a dramatic explosion, and we have footage of this incident, which has been shared with Chwayitisa. The situation has worsened over the last 3.5 weeks, with a series of electrical explosions caused by overloaded cables. In an attempt to address the issue, the municipality has been adding new sections of cable to the existing infrastructure. However, this patchwork approach has only led to more frequent failures. A key issue is the lack of protection systems in the substations—when a fault occurs, it doesn’t just affect one area; it trips the entire town's power grid. This not only disrupts daily life but also inflicts serious and lasting damage to an already fragile infrastructure, further jeopardizing the town's ability to function. What is the current plan? The municipality's current plan involves bringing in new cable sections to extend the old infrastructure, but this is essentially just delaying inevitable failures further down the line. The frequency of electrical explosions has been overwhelming—it's a clear indication of the grid’s collapse.

title: Val: The Tiny Town with a Big Heart
oneLiner: Nestled in the open fields of Mpumalanga lies Val, South Africa’s smallest town. With its population barely reaching double digits, Val is a place where time seems to stand still. But behind its qua
summary:
This story explores Val’s journey from a forgotten railway town to a living time capsule. We meet Rita Brits, the spirited woman at the heart of Val’s preservation, whose passion has transformed it into a historical gem and a haven for artists and wanderers. From meticulously restored buildings to tales of bygone eras, Val embodies the power of preservation and community spirit.

Val isn’t just a town—it’s a glimpse into South Africa’s rural heritage, made vibrant by a one-woman mission to keep its stories alive. This narrative weaves the charm of small-town life with the universal appeal of resilience, history, and nostalgia.

title: Books Galore
oneLiner: Books, books, books... Joburg's Literary District is brimming with books from across the world, from R15,000 first editions to religious pocket guides...
summary:
Once in a while you downsize, you clear your bookshelves, drop some books at your local SPCA or bookshop… But where do those end up? This is not a story about waste or recycling… it’s a story about the overwhelming demand for books in the JHB CBD. It’s called Johannesburg’s Literary District — with over 70 booksellers within an approximate 1km radius. These were mapped by Griffin Shea, a former AFP journalist who settled in South Africa. He opened Bridge Books in Helen Joseph street, Jhb and focusses mainly on local, African authors. He sources his books from many of the local dealers. Present is a bookhunter, for the lack of a better word… he takes you into a building, down a passage into the dark basement. Opens a door to a room full of books, just some of his stash. He used to store them under Park Station, but the rats and fires caused serious damage. The cheap books are sold on the street, mid-cost ones go to the more formal sellers and the very rare books are sold to exclusive book collectors, like James Findlay Collectables run from the basement of the Rand Club.

It’s 2024, the era of fast information, knowledge at our fingertips. An age when someone spots a headline on the internet and suddenly they’re an expert… So how relevant are books? They’re a luxury for many in terms of money and time… There is a belief that no-one is reading anymore, books are obsolete… But you're wrong!

title: The Historian
oneLiner: Is it an Egyptian? Is it a Roman? Is it Napoleon? Get ready to suspend your disbelief and step back in time with a man on a mission.
summary:
Gareth took History as a subject in high school, but has not studied the subject at tertiary level as he believes the syllabus is skewed. Instead he immerses himself in books, podcasts, videos, and online articles, and speaking to people about their experiences. He calls it "engaging with history". He threw out his television, and turned his TV room into his History Room. This is where he does his research and sews all the outfits that he wears. He now has almost 80 outfits, including shoes, head dress, weapons and other historical items. On weekends he likes to spend an entire day in the park, immersing himself in a particular period. He sets up camp, eats period food, etc.

Gareth Sephton (24) is a unique character with a passion for history who believes he is fulfilling “my dutiful mission to bring the wisdom of the past back to the present.” He has decided to literally put himself in the shoes of people who lived before us, to experience what life was like for them. On any random afternoon one may spot him in the Botanical Gardens: an Inca warrior, an Ottoman trader, a German WWI officer, a knighted Crusader patrolling the forests. Some dog walkers look confused and hurry by; others stop to find out what it's all about and learn some facts; some dogs take exception and go in for the kill. Gareth believes history is more than just memorising a string of facts - for him learning is a sensory experience: one must immerse yourself in the textures, and tastes of a period to truly understand what it was like for our predecessors.
caseStudies: Gareth Sephton

title: Jerry’s Rangers

Witness Jerry's unwavering dedication as he: 1. Confronts heartbreaking cases of animal abuse. 2. Navigates limited resources and funding. 3. The impact of community-driven change. 3. He's cultivating a new generation of animal advocates through: 1. "Jerry's Rangers" - empowering youth to become animal guardians. 2. Community outreach and education. 3. Collaborations with local authorities.

title: The Epic African Electrical Motorcycle Road Trip
oneLiner: Tonight we let the sun power us across Africa on a rugged motorbike with a team of scientists...proving it can be done
summary:
The story will be told through interviews with the four people below, a bit of B-Roll filmed in their interviews, and through a daily video diary the team kept as they travelled 17 days from Nairobi and Stellenbosch, arriving here on the 16th of October. It was the brainchild of PROF THINUS BOOYSEN, founder of the University of Stellenbosch’s Electric Mobility Lab, who is pushing research in affordable electric vehicles that are rugged enough for the African continent, for working people, and made on the continent. The motorbikes were mostly driven by Stellenbosch Doctoral Student STEPHAN LACOCK and Kenyan engineer MASALULE KITUYI of ROAM, the Swedish-Kenyan company that makes these tough, rugged Electrical motorbikes. In Kenya, they are used a lot as delivery bikes. Tther members of the team, which included Stephan’s father and brother, and THINUS BOOYSEN, also drove the bike as part of the team experience. We also interview DR JASON SAMUELS who works in a private company GREENX across the road from the Department of Electrical Engineering, and was in charge of the solar panel element of the trip. His company puts up solar panels on schools across the country, sponsored by the University of Stellenbosch. His dream is to use this research to build a model where schools can power their electric buses with the solar power on the roofs to provide transport locally for school kids. When we do the interview, he will take us to a school and show us what he does. It will provide us with a different but clear application of renewable energy visually. The three South African interviews are confirmed, but I am still waiting to hear if we can interview MASA KITUYI by zoom as he is back in Nairobi. MASA KITUYI is the lead engineer on the ROAM motorbike product, and a motorbike stunt driver. The team of four people drove up from Stellenbosch to Nairobi in mid-September with a custom built bakkie, holding solar panels and a large battery. Once they got to Nairobi, they had to haggle ROAM for enough smaller motorbike batteries to make the trip possible. They managed to persuade them to increase an initial offer of four to ten. ROAM lent them two bikes, one of which was in the back of the bakkie as a back-up should the first fail. The riders swapped out but mostly Stephan Lacock and Masa Kituyi rode the bikes. They then set out and drove 6000km through Kenya, Tanzania, Malawi, Zambia and Botswana to South Africa, experiencing sun, clouds, rain and hail, traffic and empty landscapes. They camped most nights where they stopped, on the side of the road. They travelled as two teams over 17 days. Every morning the solar panel team would set off at about 4:00 am, drive 200km to find a good sunny spot to put down the solar panels – a soccer field, or a river bed, or just by the side of the road. This team would charge the huge battery they had bought from South Africa while waiting for the motor-biker to arrive. At first light, the motorbike would set out with a support car, swapping out the small electric battery every 50 to 100kms, depending on weather and traffic conditions. Once the biker had caught up with the solar panel team, they would do another set of battery swaps and swap the bike-rider out. All this time, the solar panels would be recharging the big mother battery which would also be used to power the bike batteries at night. Then the biker would set out again and do another 200 kms about to find the place where they could camp for the night. And at about four, once the sun started losing its power and angles, the solar panel team would pack up and follow them, getting there at about 08h00 pm to set up camp for the night, and prepare for a 4 am start the next morning. This above information would be best presented or supported by a graphic with a map to show their route. The video diary is fairly shakily shot with moments captured here and there, rather than a cinematographic spread. But there are some splendid drone shots which are very useful and it is more cinema verité than National Geographic. They have 1.2 TBs which is usefully organised and labelled. The students were collecting data on battery consumption and vehicle efficiency, which is to show how many units of energy they used per km to show that EV’s are viable over long-distance, even without charging stations. They discovered that there were a number of factors which impacted on their progress: They weight of the driver The contour and steepness of the road The weather, in particular the wind while driving The weather, in particular when there was not sun enough to power the batteries through the solar panels The traffic – driving behind big trucks protected them from the wind and saved energy The temperature – the higher the better The efficiency of the driving – the more acceleration, the harder on the battery The speed they drove While the quest was a scientific experiment, it also became a personal and emotional journey for the participants. They found that they could break down barriers between people and themselves by explaining the electric bike and interacting with people along the way. There are some good moments that are caught on camera of these interactions, but not beautifully shot. Tension moments on the road were: • When it rained in Malawi and their progress was slowed down due to lack of sun and camping space • When it hailed – more of a surprise than anything else • When they set up the solar panel field next to the Lusaka airport and police tried to chase them away (no visuals of police but visuals of their solar camp) • When they moved away from the equator and the tilt of the earth required a greater tilt of the solar panels to capture the sun’s rays, and they battled to find the right things to prop them up on • A decision to do a 1000km final day finish to show that the motorbike could do that distance in a single day – and then made it.

We will tell a story of a group of students and academics who proved that the African sun can power a locally-made motorbike across four countries from Nairobi to Stellenbosch in two and a half weeks, despite there being no charging stations on the route. While being a scientific experiment, it was also a stunt to raise awareness about the potential for Electric Vehicles in Africa, while championing local skills, both the expertise of the students from the US and in the ROAM motorbike factory in Kenya.
caseStudies: Stephan Lacock Jason Samuels Masulule Kituyi

title: Breaking the ice: The Ice Hotel
oneLiner: South African designer Corban Warrington recreates a steam train out of snow at the mythical Ice Hotel in Sweden
summary:
Corban Warrington, a South African designer, is only the second African in 35 years to design a room for the world-renowned Ice Hotel. His design, Yesterday’s Tomorrow, brings South African heritage to life in the heart of the Arctic, transforming blocks of ice into a visual paradox of culture and art - prestigious milestone in any designer's career. Key Themes: Visual Paradoxes: - The Ice Hotel’s construction site of chaos, turned into a palace of ice and snow. - Corban’s design of a steam train, sculpted from ice, inspired by the Elgin railway market brings to life steam - the antithesis of the freezing cold – in an ice sculpture - How culture and artistic expression bloom in the frozen Arctic winter where so much struggles to survive The Mythical Torne River: - The Ice Hotel is built with ice blocks cut from this river, which melt back into it each year - "From which the ice hotel comes, it will eventually return." Artistic and Environmental Impact: - Focus on the hotel’s artistic energy, environmental consciousness, and impact on local communities. - Sustainability of the project in the face of changing climatic conditions and the snow arriving late each year.

Corban Warrington is only the second African in 35 years to be showcased at the mythical Ice Hotel - a boutique hotel that pops up out of nothing once a year in the Swedish lapland.
caseStudies: Corban Warrington Luca Roncoroni Yngve Bergqvis Charlotte Karlsson Jaeyul and Daeho Lee Annasofia Mååg

title: Art Awakening
oneLiner: A Cape Town man is introducing art into the lives of children as a way of helping them build confidence and tap into their creativity.
summary:
An art workshop in Masiphumelele, a township on the Cape Peninsula, is introducing art into the lives of some of the children living there. Luc van der Walt says he does not teach the children how to paint, and many of them are new to this world, yet many of them take to art so naturally. He says the old Masters describe children's art as playful, inspiring and brimming with imagination. The results of the children's artwork is beautiful, and Luc is now looking to partner with galleries to exhibit the art, sell the art and channel that money back into the community. Luc has experience using art as a tool for healing, in refugee camps in the Middle East and the Democratic Republic of Congo. He has brought those skills back to South Africa, and is using them in his workshops with children aged between six and twelve years old.

Luc van der Walt believes art should be accessible to everyone. He's taking his art workshops into townships to show children that art materials are all around them. Using recycled materials to paint on, he turns discarded boxes into canvases. He shows them how to make paint and charcoal, and even paintbrushes. The creativity is extraordinary, yet many of the children he works with, have never been exposed to art.
caseStudies: Philiswa Mlahlo Luc Van der Walt

title: Eden to Addo
summary: Title: Eden to Addo: Corridors of Preservation This program follows a 400-kilometer trail from the ancient Knysna Forest to Addo Elephant Park, delving into the urgent need for wildlife corridors to preserve South Africa’s biodiversity. With the presenter as our guide on a condensed version of the trail, viewers encounter conservationists, farmers, and experts who reveal the complex challenges of modern conservation. Through this narrative, the programme will “walk the talk,” experiencing firsthand the five distinct biomes along this remarkable trail. Narrative Structure: Introduction The program opens as the presenter steps into the silent beauty of the dense Knysna Forest. Themes of balance and fragmentation in nature—and the need to protect our biodiversity—are introduced. Oupoort – the last free roaming elephant in South Africa. Walking along the trail, the presenter soon meets SANPARKS’ Lizette Moolman and tracker Karel Maswati in their search for Oupoort, the last free-roaming elephant in South Africa. Their discussions reveal Oupoort's isolation and vulnerability, symbolizing lost wilderness. Through their efforts to track her movements, viewers understand the critical need for wildlife corridors, which would allow species like Oupoort to roam freely once again. The history of the Knysna forests and its elephants is also explored here. We sleep in the forest in the evening and speak to Karel Maswati or perhaps Justin Barnado of the Inqua people. Early in the morning Katot Meyer joins us on the hike. Although he works primarily in the Keurboom River he talks about his work in the valley. Conservation on the Ground - The Keurbooms Corridor Continuing the journey, the presenter meets Katot Meyer, who works tirelessly to remove invasive species from the Keurbooms Corridor. Working without pay, he singlehandedly clears the invasive plants, restoring water flow to Plettenberg Bay. His work illustrates the delicate balance required to sustain ecosystems and the threats invasive species pose to water systems and native plant life. Through Katot’s perspective, viewers gain insight into how critical corridor ecosystems are, not only for wildlife but for human survival. The presenter will also highlight the various biomes encountered along the way and their unique contributions to biodiversity. Springbok Vlakte – Rhian Berning , the CEO of Eden to Addo walks with us and shows us how the fences have prevented tportoises from migrating. She will explain the plans and the need for conservation and the benefits of the initiative. That night we stay over at the farm of Hannes Horn. The Conservationist Corridor Farmer - Hannes Horn The presenter then meets Hannes Horn, a farmer whose land forms part of a corridor connecting two major parks. This segment explores the intersection of agriculture and conservation, showing how Hannes balances farming with environmental stewardship. By maintaining a conservation-minded approach, Hannes demonstrates how farmers play a vital role in creating functional, sustainable corridors for both wildlife and livestock. Addo Elephant Park - A Contained Wilderness At the journey's end, the presenter arrives at Addo Elephant Park, a sanctuary for elephants once free to roam as far as Knysna. Through the corridors they will be able to traverse these areas again. Here, Dr. Sarah Hendricks discusses the benefits and constraints of confined parks, explaining how the loss of corridors affects elephants' migratory paths, social dynamics, and natural instincts. This segment raises an essential question: what does it mean to protect wildlife if their natural behaviors are curtailed? The Call to Action - Restoring Connections The documentary concludes by revisiting Oupoort’s isolation, underscoring the need for conservation corridors to safeguard genetic diversity, ecosystem health, and cultural heritage. Reflecting on the journey, the presenter leaves viewers with a clear message: when conservation efforts unite, they create a much more significant impact. Filming Approach This documentary will capture stunning visuals of forest landscapes, rugged trails, vibrant native flora, and intimate wildlife moments. The tone will be contemplative and reverent, honouring the region’s majesty and fragility. The programme will have a loose, exploratory style, immersing the audience in the presenter’s walk along the scenic trail. Issues of conservation arise organically as the journey progresses, enhancing the beauty of the landscape and inviting viewers to see conservation from a fresh perspective. The walk itself underscores the pressing need for new approaches to preserving our natural heritage. Interviews 1. Lizette Moolman 2. Karel Maswati 3. Justin Barnado 4. Katot Meyer 5. Joan Berning 6. title: Saldanha Red Dust
oneLiner: Red dust isn’t just a nuisance in Saldanha Bay—it’s a crisis.
summary:
This story isn’t just local; it’s a reflection of corporate responsibility, environmental impact, and the power of a community united in action. It’s time for the world to see the red-stained truth behind Saldanha Bay. We speak to the West Coast District Municipality (WCDM) local business, and Kumba / Transnet group, to get the facts! We discover there is a much larger crisis looming in the near future…

This isn’t about a few dirty walls. It’s about lives disrupted, businesses stifled, and communities fighting to breathe clean air. Iron ore dust from the port has painted the entire landscape red—houses, cars, even pets. Despite efforts by Transnet to suppress the dust, it continues to seep into every corner of the town, damaging property and peace of mind. Imagine living in a place where opening your door means inviting a red storm into your kitchen. Where your home, no matter how many times you clean or repaint, is never truly clean. The Red Dust Action Group is trying to help, determined to hold powerful corporations accountable for polluting their community. They’re not just pushing for cleaner air—they’re pushing for justice.

title: The Surgeon 2
oneLiner: For six years specialist surgeon Dr Soraya Patel has been on the Health Professionals Council of South Africa's radar. We ask why is she still allowed to practice and how is it possible that Arwyp Me
summary:
On the 30th of April 2019 a group of concerned doctors practicing at Netcare Sunward Park Hospital sent a detailed letter of complaint about Dr. Soraya Patel after witnessing what they considered serious cases of malpractice, long theatre times and unnecessary procedures and lengthy stays in hospital. The doctors were supported by the Association of Surgeons who encouraged them to lodge the complaint. The doctors provided the names and information of deceased patients. An investigator from the HPCSA started an investigation but left the before completing the investigation. The complaint dragged on and by the 25th of September 2019 there was still no ruling. On the 15th of November 2019 Advocate Khumalo from the HPCSA recommended an investifation by an ad hoc comittee to see if she needed to be suspended.8 Months after the complaint was lodged Patel was summoned to appear in front of the preliminary committee. However when she appeared Dr Mothabeng from Sunward park had added 8 new cases. Patel claimed this was unfair as she had no time to study the complaints and patient reports. Again the case was postponed to the 1-8 February 2020. Patel brought a court order as the HPCSA had not made any strides in the case. A hearing was held in November 2020 and the committee decided that Patel should not be suspended as she did not pose any imminent danger to the public and claimed that there was not enough evidence to suspend her. It took two years for this ruling. Dr Patel also claimed that the doctors obtained the patient files illegally and brought the complaint without the permission of the patients or their families. The doctors admitted to this however in the case of Mr Gopaul Ramsunder one of the Sunward doctors was asked by Patel to have a look at her patient. He informed her early in the morning that the patient was critical and needed to go back to theatre. Patel arrived in the early hours of the morning and took him to theatre at 02:00 . The anaesthetist's report said that he was in critical condition due to sepsis. The procedure took 4hours and 30 minutes. Two hours later Mr Ramsunder died. Patel claimed Ramsunder had Crohn's disease and was not informed about it.His family claims that he did not have the disease and that Patel did not inform them about the procedure and that they did not sign consent. With all of this information at hand the HPCSA did not ask for medical reports from Sunward Park nor did they speak to any of the family members. A proper investigation was not done . From an inside source we were informed that inspectorate and investigation units do not have any doctors in their teams.The public is left to rehabilitation professionals and PhD holders to investigate complaints. They cannot read the clinical records with discernment and they cannon therefor make informed decisions on progressing the complaints. The investigator allocated has a Phd in Philosophy . Patel stated in her charge against the HPCSA that she was unable to work after being suspended from Netcare and suffered serious financial loss. We know that this is not true . She started to practice at Arwyp Medical Centre on 1 December 2019. The hospital claims that she was vetted and had no issues to give her admission rights. For six years she practiced at Arwyp with many botched operations and mortalities reported. The hospital claims that they were not aware of any complaint but we are in possession of emails sent to management and case studies who will testify to the fact that numerous complaints were lodged. Medical Aids have blocked Dr Patel and is being investigated for fraud.

Dr Soraya Patel is a general surgeon specialising in laparoscopic and weight loss procedures. For the past six years there have been numerous complaint lodged at the HPCSA about long, unnecessary and botched surgeries. It is also alleged that the mortality rate is above average. But why is it that after so many years Dr Patel is still practicing and why did Arwyp Medical Centre allow her to practice there claiming that they did now know about any complaints against Dr Patel?

title: Stellenbosch Police Failures
oneLiner: Stellenbosch - a seemingly quiet and peaceful university town - has been rocked by a number of abductions and violent crime. In October last year, we brought you the story of a terrifying crime trend.
summary:
In October last year, we broadcast the story of a terrifying new trend in Stellenbosch - the abductions of university students. Since our story aired, we have been investigating why police were not thoroughly looking into these cases. And we uncovered that the spate of abductions started as far back as February. Just days before our story went to air, a Stellenbosch University student, 19 year old Jesse Mitchell was murdered. He was cycling home after working on a project with fellow students, and was attacked, robbed of his backpack and cellphone, and stabbed in the neck. Could his murder have been avoided?

In the weeks since our story aired, we have uncovered failures to investigate violent muggings by the Stellenbosch police station. Not only that, the spate of abductions that we thought started in June, in fact started as far back as February last year. Tonight, we bring you the story of a town in crisis, as police fail to properly investigate cases from muggings to abductions.
caseStudies: Eleanor Cornelius Debbie Lee Jodi Aigner Aaron Mitchell Michèle Mitchell

title: THROW-FORWARD: Lowveld Hijacked
oneLiner: Illegal mining like you've never seen it before.
summary:
Illegal mining has become an all-too-familiar story around South Africa, with zama zamas moving into residential areas and even digging underneath the Johannesburg CBD. But when our team travelled to Pilgrim's Rest to investigate reports of zama zamas threatening tourism in the heritage town, we had no idea of the scale of what we would find. The entire Lowveld, from Pilgrim's Rest to Barberton, has been hijacked by illegal mining operations. And on this scale, that means organised crime, as syndicates move in with firearms and explosives. And the impact on local communities is dire: from violent crime, to the destruction of the forestry industry, local agriculture, and the tourism on which this region depends.

Visiting the lowveld to follow up on reports of zama zamas operating in and around Pilgrim's Rest, we uncover illegal mining on a scale that has to be seen to be believed.

title: UPDATE: Sebokeng handover (CBMADT) 2024
oneLiner: We close the circle on our most ambitious project yet, as the Trust hands over a unique paediatric emergency centre at Sebokeng Hospital.
summary:
In the last decade, the Carte Blanche Making a Difference Trust has built two paediatric high-care wards at Sebokeng. But they’re operating beyond capacity. So the Trust stepped in again. In 2023, construction began on a brand new centre dedicated to triaging and treating paediatric emergencies. Thanks to this centre - first of its kind in a South African state hospital - children will no longer need to share the adult casualty, where they are often retraumatised, and don't have access to the specialised treatment and equipment that can make a difference to their health. This week, the Trust proudly unveils the completed, state-of-the-art facility, and hands it over to the hospital and its community.

The Carte Blanche Making a Difference Trust has a longstanding relationship with Sebokeng Hospital. Now, we've completed a first-of-its-kind trauma facility that is being handed over to save the lives of Sedibeng's children.

title: Poisoned
summary:
Poisoning of children after exposure to pesticides is a major public health concern, particularly in countries with poorer urban populations, such as South Africa. This may stem from the illegal distribution and domestic use of street pesticides, which are highly hazardous agricultural pesticides - Child and adolescent mortality associated with pesticide toxicity in Cape Town, South Africa, 2010–2019: a retrospective case review Pesticide poisoning is a global health concern with approximately three million cases being reported on an annual basis. The latter includes both intentional and unintentional poisonings. Organophosphorus and carbamate insecticides are frequently found to be ‘responsible’ for pesticide poisoning in developing countries. In South Africa, aldicarb is the most potent carbamate pesticide and is sold in the informal markets as Temik. This publicly available list of Highly Hazardous Pesticides, hitherto shrouded in secrecy and closely guarded by the pesticide industry, and using the categorisation and criteria developed by the FAO/WHO Joint Meeting on Pesticide Management, shows that there are 192 highly hazardous pesticides (HHPs) registered and in use in SA. Of this, only 16 have partial bans or restrictions.

A surge in food poisonings amongst children assumed to be as a result of fake foods but could it be something else?
caseStudies: Nokuphila Mayeye Bonga Ngendu

title: Boys to Men
oneLiner: A non-profit company is changing lives... one boy at a time.
summary:
In South Africa, 60% of children grow up in single parent households. Four out of five boys grow up without positive male role models, according to estimates. Child psychologists believe a boy's entire sense of self can be negatively impacted, without the influence of positive male role models. Depression and aggression are just some of the side effects. Boys can turn to gangsters to provide them with guidance, ending in a cycle of violence. But, The Character Company, is changing this ...one boy at a time. We visit a group of children in Delft, one of the most violent suburbs on the Cape Flats, to meet some of the children being mentored. And we see firsthand, the difference its making in their lives.

It's called The Character Company and it focuses on creating positive male mentorship for boys with absent fathers. The programme is offered across the country and provides consistent mentoring and safe spaces for boys to develop emotional intelligence. It's an opportunity for South African men to volunteer and become part of the solution of fatherlessness that is so prevalent in South Africa. The non-profit believes much of our country's trauma stems from boys growing up without positive male role models.
caseStudies: Raymond Weaver

title: Forged Promises, Broken Laws
oneLiner: A trusted lawyer weaves a web of deceit, forging legal documents and stealing millions from unsuspecting clients—leaving lives and fortunes in ruin.
summary:
Zietta Janse van Rensburg, a once-trusted attorney in Malelane, used her legal expertise and position to orchestrate a series of elaborate frauds, targeting unsuspecting individuals and businesses with high-value property transactions and investment opportunities. Over the course of several years, she misappropriated millions of rands from her clients by fabricating legal documents, forging communications, and creating false identities. In each case, Zietta leveraged her clients' trust by convincing them to invest large sums of money into property deals or investment projects, assuring them that she was handling the legal and financial aspects. Victims such as the Findlays, the Joneses, and Mr Patel were all duped into believing they were on the verge of securing valuable property or substantial financial returns. Zietta repeatedly used delaying tactics, making excuses about processing times, while providing fake proof of payments and title deeds to buy time and avoid suspicion. Her schemes often involved the use of deceased individuals or non-existent legal entities, making the deals impossible to complete from the outset. In the end, none of the promised transactions materialised, and her victims were left financially and emotionally devastated, with over R14 million collectively missing and no property or investments to show for it. Zietta’s fraudulent activities came to light after years of deception, as multiple investigations revealed the depth of her crimes, leading to legal actions against her.

The shocking abuse of trust by a lawyer who used her legal expertise to craft an intricate web of deception, defrauding her clients through sophisticated forgeries, fake legal documents, and false assurances. What sets this apart is the combination of high-level financial manipulation with the emotional impact on victims, who believed they were securing their futures, only to be devastated by someone they trusted implicitly.
caseStudies: William and Bronwyn Findlay Allan and Joy Jones Irma Green

title: Exorcism Deaths
oneLiner: In the shadows of South Africa's spiritual landscape, a sinister practice claims lives: exorcisms gone wrong. Investigating the alarming rise of exorcism-related deaths, this exposé uncovers the toxi
summary:
A KZN family demands justice after the death of their 17-year-old daughter in 2022. Prior to her death, Thozama Sonjica's family suspected that her uncharacteristic disobedience and bad behaviour was beyond teenage misbehaviour. They suspected that she, along with her group of friends, may be possessed by demonic forces. The families of the friend group decided to consult a local pastor who confirmed their worst fears – the devil was at work. The pastor ordered that an exorcism be performed on the children and vowed to do his best to help. He got some church members to be part of the rituals and over the next few days, even families participated in prayer sessions. Little did the families know that the exorcism would escalate from songs and prayers to assault and torture of the young girls. Five days later, Thozama was dead and her four friends who survived the gruesome experience were rescued by police. The pastor and church members were arrested, and the families expected to be notified of the progress in the case and to be called upon to witness the subsequent trial. Thozama's family shocked when, about 2 weeks ago, they bumped into the suspect pastor, walking free. The family had received no communication from police investigators nor the prosecuting authority about the status of the case and the reason for the pastor's release. They demand answers about what they believe is the pastor's early release and justice for their daughter.

Behind closed doors, South African exorcisms turn deadly. This investigation exposes the dark underbelly of traditional healing and charismatic churches, where desperation meets brutality, claiming innocent lives
caseStudies: Mxolisi Jula Thandazile Sonjica-Jula Bishop Ndovela Ndovela

title: Food for the Future
oneLiner: Tonight on Carte Blanche, witness how billionaire visionary Arturo Elizondo is revolutionizing the way we eat—by creating the world’s first egg without a chicken, and potentially changing the futu
summary:
Arturo Elizondo is revolutionizing the global food system with his groundbreaking innovation, the chickenless egg. Raised in a small Mexican-American community in Texas, Arturo's journey from humble beginnings to becoming the founder and CEO of The EVERY Company is a testament to his unrelenting passion for sustainability and food security. With degrees in government and diplomacy from Harvard and experience working alongside U.S. Congressman Henry Cuellar, the USDA, and even interning for President Barack Obama at the White House, Arturo left the political arena to tackle a new frontier: protein production. Armed with little more than ambition, Arturo moved to San Francisco to reimagine the future of food. Through The EVERY Company, he developed the world’s first animal-free egg, crafted using precision fermentation, which has already made its debut in Michelin-starred kitchens. This profile piece explores his relentless drive, the science behind his innovations, and how he’s reshaping how we think about food sustainability. Arturo's mission is clear: to democratize access to sustainable protein while preserving our planet for future generations. His story is one of disruption, determination, and hope for a greener, more sustainable future.

The exclusive access Carte Blanche has secured to US-based visionary billionaire Arturo Elizondo, offering an unprecedented glimpse into his groundbreaking innovations and mission to transform the global food system.
caseStudies: Aturo Elizondo

title: BUDGET CUTS Canary in the Coalmine
oneLiner: We show how national budget cuts will cripple delivery in the public service
summary:
The National Government concluded a wage agreement with Public Servants last year which was greater than the government could afford. As a result the treasury has passed that shortfall down to the provincial governments, so increased the wages of the civil servants but not provided the provincial paymasters with the cash to fund that increase. As a result the provinces are scrambling to cut budgets and are doing that by slashing personnel numbers, plunging service delivery into crisis. We talk to a doctor and his patients on the one hand that has been affected by this and a teacher who has lost her job and is now lost to the education system and then test their views against the political heads in the Western Cape of how they are handling it. This unreported story has been present in news pages, but because the Western Cape is the only one complaining and possibly threatening an InterGovernmental Dispute they are the canary in the coalmine in terms of what will happen in other provinces.

This is an unreported story but will have devastating consequences on the ground where people will not get services in health, education and social services as a result of the freezing of posts and the cutting of budgets which were unfunded.
