title: Isabella's dream
oneLiner: we bring you a story about how a moment of pure joy can make everything right with the world. It’s about the power of the South African spirit to hold each other up when life wants to take you down.
summary: On Saturday the 28th of September South Africans locally and abroad sat down to support the springboks, but it wasn’t just the national team that took centre stage. With her hero's by her side, a 10-year-old girl fighting cancer walked onto the field and captured our nation's hearts. Isabel is 10 years old and was diagnosed with a rare cancer in April this year. In the absence of any real treatment plan, her medical team, at Frere hospital's paediatric oncology unit, is taking the most aggressive approach in the hopes of beating the cancer growing in her liver, ribs and lungs. She has returned to East London, her hometown, after six weeks of radiation in Cape Town. During the next five days, she will be given five rounds of chemotherapy every day for five days. This is a brutal treatment that will wipe out Isabella's immune system, but it's only one of many. She will need 21 rounds of chemotherapy in order to be able to beat this cancer. In the end, there is no real prognosis, just a treatment plan and hope. Although Bella is facing a monster of a disease, for the most part she is a happy kid who isn't letting the daily grind of cancer get her down. Before April she was playing rugby with a local club, she’s obsessed with the sport and supports the Boks during every game. So when her paediatrician asked her what her dream was it was a no brainer. She wanted to meet the springboks, her hero’s. Reach for a dream came to the party and not only did she get to meet them, but she got to run onto the field with them during the past weeks rugby finals. South Africans locally and abroad were brought to tears by Bellas story. Her story stole the hearts of all South Africans.
caseStudies: tara esterhuyse

title: Waterberg on fire
oneLiner: What do you do when a fire approaches you at 60 kilometres an hour? you leave everything behind and run... but what happens when you return to the ashes of what was once your entire life?
summary:
In the Free state, an 80 year old woman burnt to death in her farm house amidst raging fires destroying thousands of hectares in the province. Scores of houses burnt down in Pretoria and surroundings and even as Far East as Mpumalanga. But in Limpopo, farmers say, they have never seen fires this big. Some fire walls stretched over 300 meters and raged for five consecutive days, leaving everything in its wake, in ashes. When a couples house caught fire and they got stuck inside, they frantically called family to say their last goodbyes. But somehow they escaped to safety and live to tell the tale.

Some say it's the worst fires to hit the Limpopo province in over 80 years. Scores of farms, houses and businesses burnt to the ground while we get a first hand account of a couple who escaped their house with the clothes on their backs.

title: Lowveld Hijacked?
oneLiner: A fact finding mission to Pilgrim's Rest to investigate zama zama activity leads to an alarming expose' - has the Lowveld been hijacked by illegal miners?
summary:
We have access to never before seen areas where large scale zama zama activities are taking place in the Lowveld. We have been given a lot of exclusive footage of zama operations as well. We have access to sources working on intelligence gathering on zama operations - who can open this hidden world. We will show the scale of the problems in areas such as Nelspruit, Sabie, Pilgrim's Rest, Waterval Onder and Barberton. In e each town we have insiders who can give us exclusive access into the hidden world of the zamas.

We spent a day in the sleepy tourist town of Pilgrim's rest, where our producer went undercover as a tourist taking in the sights. We'd heard reports of zama activity in the area, and that the situation had become dangerous for tourists. Although Pilgrim's is by no means overrun by zama zamas, they can be found in the town, processing gold bearing material at the river just 500 meters away from the main tourist attractions. But our producer dug a little a deeper, and has uncovered that the illegal mining problem in the Lowveld is possibly even bigger than what residents in places like Guateng's West and East Rand are dealing with. With the surge in zama activity, major tourist hotspots in the Lowveld are on the brink of disaster - as the illegal mining in the area has caused a sharp increase in violent crimes, and just as concerning, a major ecological threat to our natural heritage in the area. Illegal miners are constructing so called "Cyanide Baths" next to important waterways such as the Sabie and Crocodile river, using deadly poisons such as cyanide in the process of processing the gold ore.
caseStudies: Mongezi Mlambo

title: LET IT BURN
oneLiner: Ineffective and under resourced municipalities are literally unable put out fires around some of the country’s major cities – but rather than welcome private fire fighting services – there’s
summary:
Let it Burn! That’s the attitude of Gauteng Municipalities when it comes to fire fighting. These departments have been crippled for almost a decade – under resourced and in effective. Now with the emergence of an actual private firefighting service that can do the job – these JHB, Ekurhuleni & Tshwane municipalities are kicking back. In this piece we explore the shortcomings of municipalities, the challenges on the ground and explore the solutions while confronting the seemingly senseless push back to a private security service.

* ACTION - an exclusive ride-along with a firefighting team * UNDERCOVER – visits to key fire stations around major centres in GP * INSIDER – first hand perspective of the status quo * FOOTAGE – dramatic footage of fires

title: Birdman
oneLiner: He flys through the air at 400km an hour, just using gravity and the air under his wingsuit- he's the second fastest person in the world- for now
summary:
The WWL is a huge event, sponsored by the Chinese Government launching off the majestic Tianmen Mountain. The 10th World Wingsuit League Competition has just taken place in the Hunan Province, China. Its, the world’s most daring air sports competition. The pilot’s flying performance is truly incredible when you consider they only have gravity as their engine. Free fall flight has many different disciplines, and the Grand Prix includes two- speed flying and target accuracy competition. Each of the pilots strikes a paper target in flight, much like human archery. The pilots wear a pole on their helmets to pierce the target and a high-speed camera is used to judge the score. The target is a 1m square, piece of paper and they launch at 1 kilometre away and the pilots are travelling at over 180km/h! All 3 winners scored a bullseye- just 10 cm wide - in the final round and so they had to look back at the practice rounds to see who won. JJ grew up skydiving and by the time he was 12 he had done his 1st tandem dive. By Grade 8 he completed his accelerated freefall course, and by 18 he had completed over 1000 jumps. At 35 he has done 14 000 jumps and many 1000 base jumps and miraculously has never been injured. He describes it as like being in a giant swimming pool and moving through it like a fish and the more he fly’s the more he unlocks a matrix of moves. He is way past being an adrenalin junkie- he is perfecting his ability to fly. The sport of wingsuit flying takes skydiving and BASE (Building, Antenna, Span, and Earth) jumping to a new level. Skydivers and BASE jumpers jump out of planes or off tall objects, free fall, and pull a parachute before they get too close to the ground. Wingsuit flyers, on the other hand, wear suits that allow them to glide through the air before they eventually lose altitude and pull their parachutes. The flying squirrel-like suits are made of highly durable fabric and have two wings, one below the arms and one between the legs, creating a flat surface to make gliding possible. As the flyer shoots forward, small adjustments to their body position drastically affect their trajectory. This makes steering intuitive, at the WWL they did a circuit where they were not allowed 7meter from various obstacles flying at speeds of over 200km. The art of wingsuit flying is 120 years old, 96% of the flyers have died testing these suits but the more scientists apply their minds to this desperate craving to fly, the safer the suits are getting. JJ most regular jump is off Table Mountain, he spends about R30 000 a year on the cable car. When he started there were just 3 jumps- now he has developed over 50. 80 seconds of freefall and 30 seconds in the parachute- crazy fast.

As children we have all dreamt of being able to fly like a bird, and I still have dreams where I am flying, wingsuit flying is truly the embodiment of the dream of human flight, and South African Jean Jacques Wallis has just proved he is the 2nd fastest person in the world, the fastest person was just 6 hundredths of a second faster. On the 16th September competing against the top 16 fastest pilots in the world at the 10th Wingsuit Grand Prix in China JJ flew at speeds of over 230 km per hour, completing the 4000 meter course in 24,766 seconds, just +0,063 slower than the fastest – Australian Tahi Munroe 24,703 – less than a blink of an eye. The type of gaps you see in F1 racing.
caseStudies: Jean Jacques Wallis Katie Wallis Alexis McNaughton

title: THROW-FORWARD: Living on the Dead
oneLiner: In the Eastern Cape, a longstanding housing crisis has led to a tussle for land between the living and the dead.
summary: In an upcoming episode of Carte Blanche, we travel to Duncan Village, outside East London, to witness for ourselves a bizarre phenomenon: desperate for somewhere to live, and with government housing contracts failing or stalling, people are taking to the neglected cemeteries, building their houses right on top of the final resting places of the dead.

title: Lucky's Chess Garden
summary: Hlulabantu Chess Garden This is a gorgeous gentle story of the start of a small chess club on the side of the road in rural KZN. At the end of 2023 Basil Stathoulis, an orthopaedic surgeon and photographer in Durban was driving up to Tembe Elephant Park in northern KwaZulu Natal with a few friends. The R22 winds along the flats from Hluhluwe north to Tongaland. Just before the town of Mbazwana you cross cattle grids into and out of a corridor of Isimangaliso World Heritage Park that connects the northern shores of Lake Saint Lucia with Mkhuze Game Reserve. There are raw concrete bus shelters on each side of the road before and after the cattle grates with speed bumps to slow the tourists and locals down. As they crossed the northern cattle grate, they saw a road side stall that looked different. There were some iron braai stands and other implements, but he noticed old sheets of silver metal with black and which chequered patterns, and then he noticed the chess pieces. He stopped to investigate and met Lucky, a well-spoken, kind hearted gentle soul. He asked about the chess sets. From Basil’s blog. “Are you selling them?” “No, I invite the children to play.” He has a 1980’s yellow Toyota Corolla parked alongside his wares for sale. The chess board was tilted on an old tyre, but not enough for the pieces to fall off. “Would you like to play a game?” Mike, Basil’s friend asked Lucky beamed. He motioned to Mike with respect to sit and they started. Mike plays chess, and used a standard beginners opening move to test Lucky. The game was over soon with an invitation to play again. I bought a braai tripod from Lucky for Mike to use at his bush home, Twalambiza, to remember the day of chess. A couple of weeks later Basil was driving in the area and stopped at Makro in Amanzimtoti and bought ten chess sets, all made in China. Lucky was speechless when I drove up again with Mike and opened the boot of the car, saying “I have something for you” “For me?” Like all we usually do is stop and haggle for a better price on his metal braai stands. Lucky had a crowd of men he was busy with and we were on our way to Mkuze Game Reserve and could not stay. Later that evening I received a grateful message from Lucky inviting me back. I drove up alone. The rural R22 is in excellent condition and the landscape is dotted with homesteads and general dealers. Cows roam freely, proudly herded. It looked like rain and as I left Isimangaliso I saw a herd of zebra grazing with some illegally positioned cows. Lucky’s car was there, on the other side of the cattle grate. There was a group of young girls huddled at a table next to the car playing chess. The on the other side was a long table and another, with eight pairs of young boys playing chess with the new boards, and at least as many watching. As I got out of my car Lucky approached me. He was barefoot in jeans with a white shirt and pin stripe waistcoat on. “This is your gift” he motioned to the players. He had hired chairs for the children to sit on and play. The winner of each set was given R10 as a prize. All the children received a small packet of potato crisps to sustain them. At the end of the games he challenged the winner to a game, wrapping his King in a shroud of the pink of a R50 note with a thread of green grass. Basil’s article above was published in a weekly called The Kakibush. After the publicity, some friends passed by and left money with Lucky. Lucky asked the children what they wanted to do with it. Unanimously, they all said they should play for the money as a prize. The winners then went to the local store and bought chips for everyone. Ubuntu in action. Another friend donated another fourteen chess sets. I delivered these and two electronic chess timers on the Easter Weekend. Lucky and his students have now built a chess garden on the other side of the R22. The chess garden is set under the shade of trees and is bounded neatly by a rim of buried upturned glass bottles. The entrance is flanked by two neatly painted tires with white writing announcing the chess garden. There is a table that seats six with bench seats. Then there are smaller tournament tables for two players with benches. All the woodwork was done by Lucky and his students. They buy used wooden pallets and new nails from the local store. While taking this all in, I gave Lucky a cardboard roll. He unfurled the contents, a banner showing chess pieces and the South African flag and proclaiming the “Hlulabantu Chess Club.” He beamed and the students crowded around, taking in something that was theirs. Proudly they scouted a site and then hoisted the banner and posed beneath it for the victory photograph. Lucky and I have been talking about contextualising and translating chess for his students. Lucky went to the Hlulabantu Primary School near where he teaches chess to the children of his village. This is my edit of our conversations and his texts explaining to me why he teaches chess and how he contextualises the game for Zulu children living away from cities: “Chess, to me, is not merely a game but a symbolic representation of strategic conflicts akin to the battles waged between nations or clans. The intricacies lie in the roles of the pieces, with a king symbolizing leadership and a queen embodying the power and grace of a matriarch. However, when attempting to impart this understanding to my fellow Zulu-speaking community members, I encountered a significant barrier—language. The challenge extended beyond mere language differences; it pertained to a lack of relatability and context. The conventional way of teaching chess often assumes a universal understanding, but the intricacies of the game can get lost in translation. To bridge this gap, I found it essential to contextualize the game, making it more relevant to the daily experiences of those I aim to teach. The metaphorical association of chess with a war between nations might not resonate deeply within our community, where such matters are typically entrusted to soldiers or warriors. Instead, my goal is to anchor the game in the fabric of our daily struggles, demonstrating its potential as a tool for personal growth and problem-solving. I explain the game as a clash between two families competing for fields. The king and queen are Mkhulu and uGogo, respectively elder or grandfather and grandmother. The back line of the board are their supporting friends, including the bishops who are good and bad witch doctors (the good move diagonally on the white squares and the evil move diagonally on the black squares). Other friends include the horse that is easily understandable and the rook or castle. The Zulus still have rooms in their homes called “indumba” reserved for the ancestors, and I have called the rook after this. The pawns of the children of the family who need to obey the elders by moving only forward except diagonally when they can attack. In this way the children can understand chess in their own language and culture.” At this visit Lucky asked me if I knew what terms his students used for “check?” The students gathered around and pointed at an imaginary king with their fingers: “Pasopa Mkhulu,” from the Afrikaans “pasop” for beware and the Zulu “Mkhulu” for a respected elder. “And do you know what we say for “checkmate?” Their little fingers motion the fall of the king and they answered: “Lala phansi Mkhulu.” This blew me away. “Sleep peacefully, respected elder.” Lucky had single handedly removed the war imagery and lordship from chess. “Now” Lucky said, “we are ready for a tournament!” Below the last article in the blog. Umhlabuyalingana, known for its mystic roots and powerful magic, welcomes visitors seeking guidance in money matters, love, and ancestral affairs. Just across from the Hlulabantu Chess Club, a prominent road sign marks the entrance to this enchanting place, often capturing the attention of passersby who stop for a quick photo to share on social media. Two weeks ago on a Saturday morning before the national elections in South Africa, the air buzzed with excitement as children prepared for a chess tournament. A young man, adorned with bravado and scarification marks from a recent visit to the sangoma, arrived proclaiming his invincibility. Mxolisi, the eleven-year-old Hlulabantu Chess Club champion, took on the challenge. Despite being off his game recently, Mxolisi faced the challenger but ultimately lost. Lucky, the club’s founder, acknowledged the victor’s strength with humility, “Indeed, your magic was stronger than the power of the minds that learn chess with me.” Arriving the day before, I sat down with Lucky at one of the little tables to catch up. The growth of the chess club is a community effort. Maria Kouvarellis and her father Nick donated woodwork tools, pink paint for outdoor furniture, and some of the chess sets. The plasticized boards are nailed to tables, and pieces from twenty-five sets harmoniously mix in a large woven Zulu basket. The children respectfully pick up the pieces and place them on the boards, each understanding its role in the chess village. Elizabeth Billis donated paving and a giant chess set with a dedication hand-painted in memory of Andrew , my father’s godson, marking the thirty-year anniversary of his passing. Lucky reverently transports the giant chess pieces from his homestead to the chess garden for tournaments in his 1980’s Toyota Corolla. Maré Worthmann, a dietician at Netcare Kingsway Hospital, contributed foodstuffs and treats as prizes for the tournament. The tournament began slowly. In rural areas, high school students attend compulsory extra lessons on Saturday mornings, leaving them exhausted by the time they arrived for the final competition in the afternoon. Lucky organized the tournament meticulously, with students diligently recording names in school exercise books that doubled as prizes. The display of prizes, especially a kilogram of brown sugar, elicited audible gasps of excitement. The final eight players competed with intense concentration, timed on new chess clocks for five-minute games. Winners were decided based on remaining pieces if the game didn’t end in checkmate. The final match between Mxolisi and Kholeka took place on the new giant chess set. Mxolisi, regaining his chess mojo, won on points. A sizeable crowd, some seated on newly constructed spectator benches, watched the thrilling game. Proudly, Lucky presented the prizes to the winners on the giant chess board. Mxolisi beamed as he unpacked his prize, with the kilogram of sugar being the most impressive component. As I chatted with Lucky about the tournament, Mxolisi and Kholeka excitedly ran home to show their families the prizes. Every participant received something, fostering a sense of community. I left meat and charcoal for a shisa nyama (barbeque) celebration, knowing they would have a good time. The tournament taught us valuable lessons. The best time for competitions is Sunday afternoons, avoiding conflicts with Saturday school and Sunday church. Prizes entice participation, and a small monetary prize could further motivate the children. In the spirit of Ubuntu, winners often share their prizes with others, making prize money a palatable incentive. Moving forward, we need support for Lucky to manage the club’s social media accounts effectively, amplifying the club’s reach and impact. The Hlulabantu Chess Club’s tournament wasn’t just a competition—it was a celebration of community, learning, and the timeless magic of chess.
caseStudies: Lucky Nxumalo Basil Stathoulis Philani Gwala Muzikayise Gumede Mxolisi Mthethwa

title: Bela Education
oneLiner: A bill that sparked big debate with some saying it will cause the end of the government of national unity... but the emotions aside, does Government have the money to implement the controversial Bela
summary:
Its gonna cost resources... and lot of it... does government have the financial and administrative capacity to implement the controversial Bela Bill? Grade R is now compulsory. In the most ironic turn of events, government earmarks R16 billion necessary to establish infrastructure and appoint teachers to fill the gap. But at the same time, teacher retrenchments are underway. The Western Cape just announced the retrenchment of 2400 teacher due to budget cuts.

What's all the hype about the Bela bill if government doesn't even have the money to implement it?

title: ANOTHER KETTLE OF FISH
oneLiner: When even our fish are getting hooked on drugs, we have real problems in South Africa
summary:
Now that the majority of Rhino have been either poached, saved or dehorned, South Africa’s natural world is facing another major challenge that few may have seen coming; Fish poaching. Our freshwater dams are being stripped down of its fish species, seemingly by highly organized syndicates controlled by immigrants. And what the consumers are unaware of, is that the fish may cause devastating illness and even death. This while South Africans either work for the syndicates or unknowingly create a lucrative market, keeping the criminals in business.

When dangerously high levels of toxins revolt fish eagles and Cormorants from eating fish, why is fish caught in the Klipvoor dam fed to humans?
caseStudies: Gift Romoaktedi Andre Hoffman Christof Truter

title: Stellenbosch Student Attacks
oneLiner: The university town of Stellenbosch is known for it's beauty and relative safety, but an alarming crime trend has struck fear into the hearts of students living there.
summary:
Crime in the once relatively safe university town of Stellenbosch has spiked in recent months. Students reporting incidents of violent muggings has become a daily occurrence. On September 18th, a first year student was walking to the engineering faculty just 500 meters from his home when he was held up at gunpoint in the morning. His backpack was stolen and the two attackers fled on foot. Most concerning are the abductions. Parents of students are so concerned they have created safety WhatsApp groups and are urging students to sign up to private security companies.

In the past four months, there have been five incidents of abductions involving students from the University of Stellenbosch. In June, a girl was abducted outside a nightclub in the early hours of the morning, and released unharmed after being driven around. In the same month, a student couple who had stopped to star gaze on the Franschoek Pass, was abducted and taken to an abandoned house where their parents were phoned and a ransom demanded. Both parents paid, and the couple was released unharmed. In August, a student was abducted and released 9kms outside of Stellenbosch, after being robbed of his cellphone and money. In a recent incident on the 8th of September, a university student was abducted outside a nightclub and driven around for several hours. He was robbed of his valuables and eventually released unharmed in Cloetesville, in the early hours of the morning. In the most recent case, on the 3rd of October, a 20 year old Stellenbosch University student was walking home in the early hours of the morning when she was abducted and held for ransom. Once her family paid, she was released the following day. The alleged kidnappers, two Zimbabwean nationals, were arrested, and face charges of kidnapping, extortion, rape and contravening the Immigration Act. They will apply for bail on the 23rd of October in the Stellenbosch Magistrate's Court.
caseStudies: Andrew Setzkorn Keryn Askew Jodi Aigner Zion Sewraj Jolene Mather

title: Living on the Dead
summary:
Living on the Dead is the story of gross mismanagement of the Buffalo City Metro told through the decades long abandonment of several cemeteries by the municipality. In 2023, BCM was the leading contributor to irregular expenditure in the Eastern Cape at R 6.5 billion of R 10.6 billion total. Are the dead safe from corruption/mismanagement? With cemeteries becoming the site of muggings, stabbings, druggies and now shacks - it appears not.

People building houses on graves

title: Bayanda Walaza - The World's Fastest Teenager
oneLiner: Meet the world's fastest teenager: South African sprint sensation Bayanda Walaza
summary:
He has an amazing back story: He comes from Katlehong at 8 years old, he wrote a letter to his heroine: Caster Semenya, saying he wanted to emulate her feats of winning Olympic gold His mother Tholiwe was also a sprinter in her youth and he’s inherited her sprinting genes She’s raised him as a single mother, after his dad was murdered when Bayanda was just 10 Since he burst onto the scene, he’s had offers from colleges in the USA to go attend on an athletics scholarship but he’s decided to stay in SA and continue to work with his current coach Thabo Matebedi “I’m not going to change coaches because that can cause a lot of difficulties. It’s better to chill with the coach that’s working for me. He made me get two gold medals, and silver at the Olympics, so why must I leave him?

An intimate portrait of one of South Africa's rising superstars: 18-year-old Bayanda Walaza. With the world at his feet, we provide a compelling journey that takes in his past, present and potential future From his compelling backstory of a young boy who at just 8 years old, dreamt of emulating his heroine Caster Semenya in winning Olympic Gold to his current status as Olympic Silver medalist and 100m, 200m winner at the world junior champs, could he become the next Usain Bolt?
caseStudies: Bayanda Walaza Tholiwe Walaza

title: UPDATE: Hope and Healing
oneLiner: A doctor changing lives by changing faces - and now extending her philanthropic reach.
summary: Dr Ansua Steyn is an aesthetic surgeon who, last year, realized that there is a great need for a foundation to help those in dire need of facial reconstructive surgery. She collaborated with a team of experts to start offering surgery pro bono to those who cannot afford it. Now her reach is extending through partnerships with state and private institutions, and this month she will collaborate on a project to provide a corneal replacement and restore a man's sight.
caseStudies: Gerhard Botha
experts: Ansua Steyn Juandre Kruger Johan Kruger

title: UPDATE: Ibogaine Killer
oneLiner: After seven years, Dr Anwar Jeewa is brought to justice.
summary: In 2019, we told the story of Dr Anwar Jeewa, a dentist running a rehab clinic in Durban. Jeewa dosed his patients with ibogaine, a controversial psychedelic substance that treats the symptoms of opiate withdrawal and reportedly treats addiction. But in 2017, a young Canadian man who came to Dr Jeewa for help with his prescription addiction died just hours after arriving at the clinic. Since then, Milos Martinovic's family has been desperately hoping for justice. Now, seven years later, Jeewa has been convicted of culpable homicide and five other charges.

title: Botmaskop Fynbos Estate and the Gated Estates of the Winelands
oneLiner: We show how the wealthy and well connected in Stellenbosch are bagging valuable land for mansions for the super rich
summary:
An half an hour walk up the mountain above Unie Park in Stellenbosch takes you to the top of the Botmaskop Fynbos Estate, which is under construction. Roads have been laid on the steep slope, and reinforced to prevent erosion, and an expensive clearvu fence erected, which I was told had been paid for by the municipality, to keep the public out. A reservoir has been erected at the top as well, which the environmentalists claim was done so illegally. On their website the developers claim that this is the highest residential estate ever approved above sea level – almost 400 metres. But the question is this: Was it ever properly approved? Or has the rezoning of this development, and a subsequent landswap with the municipality to change its boundaries, been a sleight of hand? There are no boards on the gate which indicate which, if any Environmental Company has done the assessment in anticipation of approval. The property was bought and zoned in 2006 for a small mountain retreat which would be 15 chalets not exceeding 400m² each, so 6000m² of development as well as a hotel with 10 rooms not exceeding 2800m² . The rest of the 30 hectare property was zoned for agriculture. The Botmaskop Fynbos Estate development currently underway exceeds the 2006 footprint 9.4 times, with each one of the 73 stands between 701 square metres to 2735 square metres. They range in price too with the most extensive plot retailing at over R31-million. The mystery is how the developer did it under the noses of Stellenbosch residents who are fighting the onset of gated estates on all sides of their town. In fact, there are multiple gated estates popping up or planned across the Winelands, aimed to accommodate wealthy and middle class semigres flocking into the Cape, as well as foreigners with cash to burn. A signboard at Pniel shouts to passing motorists: Book your Place in the Winelands Now (maybe not exactly like that, but words to that effect) In this instance, the developers say their earthmoving is all above board, and they have a piece of paper to prove it, dated 2021. It’s authored by an official in the provincial department of planning and says that the change in the 2006 zoning for a hotel carries through to the environmental impact on the property today, although the project has dramatically changed. This is hard for anybody outside of the development process to believe, watching the bulldozers tear up the mountainside. There is also a great deal of information that has been hidden from the public in an extensive paper trail of lawyers letters and objections and municipal and provincial assurances. Key amongst the missing documents are: 1) A legal settlement between an earlier developer and the Stellenbosch Municipality over the rezoning for 73 erven in about 2014 which appears to have automatically legalised the rezoning – this has been deemed secret and the municipality has refused to show it to the SIG 2) Any Environmental Assessment for the current development 3) Any Heritage Assessment for the current development 4) Reasons why appeals against the development have been turned down 5) Reasons why appeals against the objections to the land swap been turned down There is big money at stake at Botmaskop and in the industry of gated estates in the Winelands. This project shows how rezoning agricultural land for a luxury gated estate has dramatically increased the value of the land. In 2003 the 31 hectares land was bought for just over 3 million Rands, ostensibly to develop a hotel for which it engaged in a prolonged public and state approval process. Twenty years later, the current developer, Staytus, buys the same piece of land for R200 million, now with zoning rights. It is bonded for R320 million. It was sold to Staytus by a company called Reset Properties who had bought it in 2017 for R14 million. Reset Properties falls under Foundation Capital which is an office owned by one of South Africa’s wealthiest families, and they were the ones who managed to get the non-substantive amendment passed in the provincial department of the Environmental Department. At the heart of this dispute are two conflicting visions over the future of Stellenbosch and the Winelands. One group – the wealthy property developers and their friends – want to create a safe space for the very rich, in the beautiful setting of the Winelands, through the ongoing building of gated estates, and the complimentary sponsorship of the town’s projects and aesthetic needs. The other would like to see Stellenbosch develop more slowly, where there is greater integration of the different economic groups, and the town develops sustainably on its own commercial success, respecting the beautiful spaces and agricultural land in which it is set. This is my interpretation after many discussions with people in the area and the town.

We can show through both a paper trail and interviews how developers have cooked the system to get the approvals to carve up a mountainside for a luxury gated estate just outside Stellenbosch, extending the urban sprawl and angering many townsfolk.
caseStudies: Brian Du Preez Pieter Schaarfsma Marius Van Stade Allison Smith

title: Nuclear Miracles
oneLiner: We are using nuclear technology to save lives, add a billion rand in exports and make groundbreaking steps forward in several industries in South Africa.
summary:
In medicine, we use different elements to create these isotopes—none of which involve uranium. At this point, the presenter will step in to explain how radioactive isotopes work. “I am here at our nuclear reactor….” They’ll explain that we received special permission to show you exactly where these isotopes are made—at the SAFARI reactor in Pelindaba. And we’ll meet our main character Dr Zeevaart with a little about his background. And the creation of I-131 radioisotopes which we make here locally. This project earns around 1.3 billion rand per year by selling our locally produced radioisotopes. And he will show us the lab where the Cyclotron particle accelerator is – this is where the nuclear miracles are born (protons are accelerated in a circular ring to speed close to light, which interacts with material making it radioactive), producing medical radioisotopes. You had some questions after my pitch I’ve asked Zeevaart to answer: Jan Zeevaart: Do we produce the isotopes ourselves? Yes, we do. They are made at the SAFARI reactor in Pelindaba, and we’ll get to see the process in action. Regarding the term “cure” for cancer—there isn’t one single cure. Each type of cancer is unique. However, we can say that we’ve developed groundbreaking treatments for prostate cancer, and the focus is shifting to breast cancer next. How do cancer cells die? When radioactive material decays, the isotope releases energy, causing breaks in the DNA double strands. This triggers apoptosis, or programmed cell death, which is essentially what kills the cancer cells. How are the correct cancer cells targeted? The radioactive pharmaceutical or drug is directed by a targeting compound, like a GPS, which guides the isotope to specific areas, allowing it to treat multiple sites as needed. When it comes to nuclear processes, radioactive decay—fission, or the splitting of an atom—occurs in a nuclear power reactor. In power generation, the focus is on the heat produced during fission, not the byproducts. In contrast, in nuclear medicine, we focus on isolating specific isotopes from that process. For power, uranium is split to generate heat, but in medicine, we extract various isotopes from the same nuclear process and apply them for targeted treatments.

Nuclear Radioisotope Technology When you think of nuclear, you might picture dangerous materials, but South Africa is actually at the forefront of using radioisotopes—materials produced during a nuclear reaction—in some truly groundbreaking ways. Our guide on this scientific journey is Dr Jan Rijn Zeevaart from Necsa. With over 20 years of experience promoting the safe use of this technology, Dr Zeevaart has been involved in numerous groundbreaking projects. Dr Zeevaart received his PhD in the Netherlands, and since 2002 has been head of the Radiochemistry group at Necsa. He’s co-authored over 100 international publications, has 6 patents and was awarded the South African Chemical Institute’s Raikes Medal (2007) and was part of the international team awarded the Marie Curie award (2018). He'll lead us through a series of incredible discoveries: from a stage 4 cancer patient being healed, to the eradication of malaria-carrying mosquitoes, and even the use of this technology in ‘save the rhinos’ fight. We have secured permission to film nuclear reactor at pelindaba.
caseStudies: Jan Rijn Zeevaart Mike Sathekga Govemore Munhenga

title: Taxi Associations vs Motorists
oneLiner: From violence to intimidation, taxi associations will stop at nothing to maintain their grip on the transportation market. They say carpooling and lift-clubs are affecting their business.
summary:
Taxi associations, determined to protect their profits, have launched a campaign of intimidation and harassment against motorists who dare to share rides. Some commuters said they have encountered situations where mini-bus taxi operators have tried to prevent them from carpooling, being in lift clubs and even, in some instances, ordinary motorists giving lifts to friends and colleagues. The victims are not just carpoolers, but anyone who happens to have more than two people in their vehicle. Pedestrians who accept lifts from acquaintances are also being targeted. The taxi associations' tactics range from verbal threats and physical assaults to vandalism and even violent attacks.

In a country plagued by traffic congestion and rising fuel costs, carpooling and lift clubs seem like a logical solution. However, taxi associations are waging a fierce battle to prevent motorists and commuters from sharing rides, even going so far as to intimidate and harass those who dare to defy them.
caseStudies: Danisile Shabangu Godole Mdletshe Renecca Phala Zola Radebe

title: Cape Town’s Illegal Street Racing
oneLiner: Join us as we dive into Cape Town’s underground world of illegal street racing and the elite Ghost Squad’s relentless pursuit to bring these speedsters to justice.
summary:
Cape Town has become a hotspot for illegal street racing, a dangerous pastime that has led to countless accidents, fatalities, and a growing public safety concern. The Ghost Squad, an elite division of the Cape Town Metro Police, was formed to combat this threat. Operating with unmarked vehicles and covert tactics, the squad has become the frontline in a battle against street racers who show little regard for the law or human life. This episode will explore the origins of illegal street racing in Cape Town, delving into the thrill-seeking culture that drives it. We'll follow the Ghost Squad on their night patrols, capturing their high-adrenaline confrontations with racers and offering viewers an inside look at the challenges they face in maintaining order on the city’s roads.

This story highlights the daring operations of the Ghost Squad, a covert unit within Cape Town’s Metro Police, dedicated to curbing the rampant street racing epidemic that endangers lives. The squad's efforts showcase a crucial fight for public safety against a deeply embedded culture of speed.

title: Winston Fani Africas First Blind Tour Guide
summary: Meet Nqabohlanga Winston Fani – Africa’s first Blind Tour Guide His tours have been described as unique, evocative, fascinating and expect the unexpected. Winston Fani is blind and in his words: For people who are blind they don’t see with the naked eye they see with the eyes of the heart but in order for the eyes of the heart to kick in you have to give people a picture. A two hour walking tour through the heart of Salt River, Cape Town, is Winstons flagship project. A unique expedition for sighted and the visually impaired, taking in giant artwork and intimate local art studios where sculptured and diverse artistic endeavours come to life. A lot of the artworks now have QR codes, which lead you to audio clips with Winston’s voice giving the detail. Despite having never seen the artwork, he describes the murals and unpacks the work with those on tours with him.
caseStudies: Nqabohlanga Winston Fani Enver Dominny Tanya Robertze

title: Child Trafficking Ring
oneLiner: A dodgy compound in a Johannesburg suburb is the site of an unimaginably evil crime - the sexual exploitation of children. We join the police on an early morning raid to catch the perpetrators and sav
summary:
I accompanied Brave to Love and the police when they obtained statements from the sources, and the information was deemed very credible. The sources also took a crime intelligence officer to the location of the compound and they observed the young girls at the location. Brave to Love have asked the NAT JOC to mobilise on the case, and a search warrant for the premises is being obtained, based on the witness statements and the crime intelligence officer's report. We can join the raid as the media, BUT I have to obtain clearance from a Brig Mathe who is the head of SAPS Communications National. I have reached out to her but have not received a go ahead yet. The SAPS will provide a media liaison, possibly Brig Mathe herself, since this is going to be a big case for them, on the day and we'll be able to interview police as well as members from the Brave to Love team. We'll also try and get interviews from the international law enforcement present. If the raid is successful and the girls are rescued, this should make for a compelling story.

We have been offered exclusive access to a police operation through counter trafficking NGO Brave to Love. According to sources we've met two Nigerian men, one known only as Emeka, and another who is a pastor going under the name Apostle Dr Roland online, but is known to the sources as Ronald, are pimping out a group of young girls between the ages of 12 and 17 as sex workers. The same children are also apparently being used to film live online strip/sex shows on several lap top computers kept on the premises. Because the children are underage, if the allegations prove to be true, this will automatically be classified as human trafficking, among many other criminal charges. The police are obtaining a search warrant, and several agencies, including international law enforcement, will execute a search warrant on the premises very soon, possibly this coming Sunday.

title: Baboons run amok
summary:
For the last 3 years, the once internationally recognised urban wildlife baboon management programme has broken down after a massive social media campaign waged by baboon activists after the Kataza saga. The situation came to a head in Kommetjie last Sunday when residents held a peaceful protest outside a burned-out building in the main street of Kommetjie. The baboons come down from the mountain every night and are escorted into town by a self-appointed baboon monitor, Briton Pauline Sudders. Her concern is that they don’t get run over - but she doesn’t stop there. She shouts at children skateboarding that they must keep quiet because the baboons want to sleep and confronts people carrying any kind of defence against being attacked. Matters have been brewing since the Kataza saga 3 years ago where residents protested the relocation of a male baboon from Kommetjie to Constantia, which the baboon activists saw as him being removed from his family. Activist Jenni Trethowan escorted him back over the mountain, but on hisd return, Kataza rejected his so-called “family” and headed out again. He was relocated to Limpopo amid a media storm, and later released into an area where farmers boast of having shot over 200 baboons – there is a good chance Kataza has also been shot. Kataza was a turning point for the City of Cape Town because the social media backlash was so extreme. This activist media campaign called on international tourists to boycott Cape Town because “we kill baboons”. The city could ill afford to lose any more tourism after the Covid-19 pandemic. Internationally recognised wildlife academic and baboon specialist, Dr Justin O Riain, was labelled “Dr Death” and a deep fake video circulated of him “doing vivisections”. Complaints were lodged on a daily basis to his employers, UCT. He was investigated numerous times and eventually asked to stop his research because the media campaign was so vicious. It nearly ended his career. He received repeat death threats to both himself and his family. The City stopped implementing the scientific protocols on how to deal with wildlife on the urban edge - a world-recognised programme that had worked for over 10 years. Fake science and the emotive media campaign were too much for the authorities. Now when residents are being attacked in their own homes, the baboon activists stand outside and say “I am filming you - don’t hurt the baboons”, and offer no help. This is a voice note from a mother whose entire week’s food was destroyed, her 10-year-old trapped under the stairs. For three days running, the same baboon attacked her home. One evening her 6 foot tall, 19-year-old champion windsurfer son tried to hold the door closed in the face of an aggressive male baboon - he lost the tussle and the baboon got in, trapping them in the bedroom. People fear defending themselves because their activist neighbours threaten to burn their homes down The three responsible authorities - SANparks, CapeNature and the City of Cape Town - have for decades tossed this hot potato back and forth, all claiming they either don’t have jurisdiction or funding. Finally, in 2023 then Environment Minister Barbara Creecey interceded and appointed a Joint task Team. SANParks agreed to put R8-million into strategic electrified baboon fences. CapeNature put in R2-million but don’t have budget for operational costs; and the COCT are cancelling the rangers’ contract at the end of September. The fences are useless without rangers.

There baboons have literally moved into town, taking over, and nobody is taking responsibility and the level of trauma of residents is falling on deaf ears, never mind the level of damage to property. A few statistics from Kommetjie - 55% of residents have DAILY encounters with baboons; 70% have had damage to their property; 85% have had baboons in their homes; 35% keep their windows permanently closed; and 11 % have had to have pets euthanased. Baboons are holding residents hostage in their own homes in Kommetjie and Simon’s Town. They are no longer afraid of people. They used to be frightened of men but they have become so habituated that if confronted they just bare their teeth and rise up in attack stance. Children are so traumatised that they won’t play in their own gardens. They are not safe at home or school. The baboons recently walked into a preschool and grabbed the food from the hands of a terrified 3-year-old, a carefree confident child now clings to her mother’s legs. A large male baboon slipped into a home and entered the bedroom where a dog was asleep. The startled dog awoke and was ripped apart. Its eye torn out, ear ripped off and scalped. The vet had no alternative but to euthanase it. A dog let out to relieve itself in the rain after its owner had checked the baboon alert group was attacked so badly, it also had to be euthanased. A child with severe autism’s companion labrador came between a child and a baboon when it entered their home; both child and dog are now severely traumatised

title: Yandisa, the penguin and seabird ranger
oneLiner: We get a unique glimpse into the life of a female ranger who lives with hundreds of penguins and seabirds on an island whom most of us only remember as a maximum security prison.
summary:
Robben island is situated 11 km from Cape Town harbour. It was declared a marine protected area in 2019 and is managed by Table Mountain National Park. It is a UNESCO World Heritage site best known for its iconic landmark: the maximum security prison where Nelson Mandela and other political prisoners were incarcerated during apartheid. Other iconic landmarks include the Robben Island lighthouse (built in 1864) and relics from WWII when the island was an important military base. But few people know about the penguin colony and for good reason: it is strictly out of bounds for visitors and only a select few are invited to spend a day with these endearing birds in the company of their full time ranger, Yandisa. Yandisa grew up in Lusikisiki in the Eastern Cape, 45 km from the sea. Her interest in marine life and its creatures was sparked during a life-changing visit to a marine protected area along the Eastern Cape Wild Coast. After completing her degree in Zoology she specialised in marine biology. After graduating she worked under the National Research Foundation as a research assistant intern for two years in a Marine Conservation Genomics laboratory at Stellenbosch University before taking up a post at the Southern African Foundation for the Conservation of Coastal Birds (SANCCOB). “My passion and love for the African penguins really began here at SANCCOB where I first worked as a researcher. When the position of ranger became available I immediately applied. I wanted to be on the ground, close to the penguins and other seabirds and to see where they are being rescued. I also wanted to contribute towards the efforts of conserving marine life, especially the endangered African penguin”, says Yandisa. Yandisa’s passion and dedication for her work is evident. Monitoring over a thousand breeding pairs of penguins is no mean feat. Crawling on all fours to check in on the conditions of the newborn chicks or rescuing sick or injured birds, it is all part of a day’s job. “We are always monitoring the chicks on the island especially for being underweight. Penguin food sources have diminished so much due to the overfishing of sardines and anchovies that penguin parents must travel far distances to find food, often leaving their chicks alone for very long periods of time, sometimes not making it back at all. This makes the chicks and eggs vulnerable to predators, bad weather and starvation”, says Yandisa. On average, 500 - 600 African penguin chicks and 300 to 400 African penguin eggs are brought to SANCCOB chick rearing facility at Table Bay each year by rangers from across the 6 penguin colonies with numbers increasing by 256% in the last seven years. The numbers speak for themselves. Abandoned chicks are on the increase and efforts of rangers like Yandisa are critical to the survival of the African penguin. Robben Island is a hotspot for seabird biodiversity, including endangered cape cormorants, bank cormorants and African penguins. It lies in the middle of major shipping lanes, and the risk of oil spills to local seabirds has been well documented. Dr Katta Ludynia, renowned marine biologist, with a Phd spearheads the research department at SANCCOB. She was Yandisa’s mentor whilst being an intern at SANCCOB before she was appointed penguin ranger on Robben Island. She saw Yandisa’s potential if given a chance to prove herself as a ranger and she wasn't disappointed. Katta frequently visits the island to see how the penguins are doing and to see how they can improve the monitoring systems and tools they have in their disposal. The research conducted on the island is critical as it examines the consequences of fishing activities on African penguins and other seabirds’ population dynamics. The research contributes valuable data on the condition of South African seabirds admitted for rehabilitation. Sick or injured birds and abandoned chicks get sent to the mainland Chick Rearing facility where they are then rehabilitated. Shared with research institutions like Earthwatch - an international charity environmental group, these findings play a crucial role in shaping conservation efforts. As part of the national transponder project led by SANCCOB, all released birds are equipped with transponders. For Yandisa, this has been a great two weeks, having enthusiastic people to share her passion with. “The most important thing for me is that I want to contribute towards the efforts of saving endangered marine life especially the african penguins so that is what keeps me going and my passion and love for nature”, says Yandisa. The story: The story is about Yandisa, the penguin ranger and her dedication to help save the penguins. Dr Katta Ludynia, marine biologist working closely with Yandisa will also be on the island to share her concerns for the dwindling penguin population and how they are pulling out all the stops to help preserve this seabird from extinction. We will check the monitoring tools which read the transponders implanted in the penguins, weigh and measure a chicks, check the nests and look for any abandoned chicks or eggs. Katta will also talk about the longstanding penguin project on Robben Island and how the research has given insight into the penguins’ behavioural patterns. We will stay overnight on the island to get early morning and later afternoon shots of the penguins as they go out to sea to forage and return to land to feed their chicks. It is a personal narrative of the penguin ranger and how she spends her life on the island. The science then is a layer on top of that. It becomes more impactful to talk about the impact of climate change, man-made, and the current state of affairs with the penguin population if we have the personal narrative that the viewers can attach themselves to. From thousands of penguins to less than 900 breeding pairs is the reality we face on Robben Island, once the largest breeding colony. Food scarcity, oil pollution and climate change (rise in temperatures, storms, nests flooded) have all contributed. Interviews: Yandisa Cwecwe - Penguin and seabird ranger Dr Katta Ludynia - Marine biologist

Meet Yandisa Cwecwe, Robben Island’s very own penguin and seabird ranger. She has a full time job looking after more than 900 African penguins nesting on the island. Yandisa is the only penguin and seabird ranger stationed on Robben island but from time to time environmentalists and scientists visit the penguin colony to conduct fieldwork and check if the equipment to monitor the penguins’ moves are fully functional.

title: Listeriosis Class Action
oneLiner: Six years after South Africa's listeriosis outbreak ended the ill effects are still being felt - and a thousand victims still wait for compensation.
summary:
Between Nov 2016 and 2018 Tiger Brands produced, distributed and supplied ready-to-eat meat products (particularly colony) contaminated with listeriosis. The food poisoning resulted in the deaths of 216 people. However, many more people suffered harm (about 1000) and the effects are still being felt today. An article published in the New England Journal of Medicine shows that because of the high prevalence of HIV in South Africa, listeriosis caused disproportionate cases of illness in pregnant girls and women (465) and HIV infected persons. Of the 465 pregnancy cases, 405 were neonates/newborn babies, as listeriosis can be transmitted from mother to foetus. In 2018 the Gauteng High Court certified Richard Spoor Inc and LHL Attorneys Inc as class attorneys in a class action against Tiger Brands. The claim is based on the findings of the National Institute for Communicable Diseases (NICD). The NICD conducted an investigation into the listeriosis outbreak, which included a microbiological investigation.

Interviews with the scientists who have proved through extensive genetic sequencing that the listeriosis outbreak originated from the Enterprise Factory in Polokwane. Interviews with some of the claimants who suffered damage as a result of contracting listeriosis. (Cerebral palsy in children, loss of a breadwinner etc) Interviews with the specialist lawyers who are representing the claimants in their class action against Enterprise Foods and holding company Tiger Brands.

However, the hospital lacked a dedicated facility for pediatric emergencies, which is where the Carte Blanche Making a Difference Trust steps in. We'll follow the story from the cramped, temporary unit where children had treated to the new facility, now near completion , thanks to the Trust and its partners. title: Bragin
oneLiner: we confront a bully of the worst kind, a grown man verbally abusing woman and children.
summary:
Llewelyn Bragin is a seasoned bully, ruling through power and dominance. Hiding behind a ‘strong leadership style’, he belittles and abuses both staff and students. He is the principle of a top all boys preparatory school in Pietermaritzburg. A school that prides itself on being a leading specialist institution for boys. Yet, he stands accused of sexual harassment, bullying staff and verbally abusing boys as young as 7. Gift, the head of sports was so destroyed by Bragin constantly berating him that he started working longer hours to try and be perfect, he stopped eating properly, stopped sleeping and lost all confidence in himself. Eventually, after trying to commit suicide, he checked into a clinic and was diagnosed with depression. Melissa was Bragins PA, he harassed her from day one making wildly sexually inappropriate comments like – "If I wasn’t married I would F-k you sideways." She tried to ignore him and just wanted to hold onto her job, but when he took two weeks mental health leave, she immediately confided in the deputy principle. More staff came forward, and eventually the deputy had 52 complaints against Bragin. 52 grown adults who for nearly 2 years had been suffering in silence, too afraid to lose their jobs or stand up to the bully. But it wasn’t just the adults he was bullying and abusing. Rourke, aged 9, was a boarder at Merchiston suffering from separation anxiety which the school was aware of. One day Rourke had a full-blown panic attack, and no-one could get near him. Bragin heard the commotion and ran towards Rourke screaming “if you don’t calm down, I will call the police, and have you sent to a juvenile center and you will never see your mother again” Rourke was removed from the school by his parents and has not been back to any school in two years. He is now home schooled and is seeing a play therapist regularly to get over the PTSD of that day. But BRAGINs reign of terror didn’t start at Merchiston. Previously He was the senior deputy principle at another upstanding private boy’s preparatory school, Kind Edward VII in Johannesburg. Where one woman, Sam Thorne, tried to stand up to him and was retrenched. She built a dossier on Bragins abusive behaviour and tried to get anyone to listen, but neither the GDE nor SACE would hear her. When things started to get hot at KEPS he moved to Merchiston, but this time there were enough people to stand up against Bragin. The SGB took the KZNDOE to court to have Bragin removed. DOE held a hearing and he was charged on 11 counts including misappropriation of funds He was found not guilty on every count except the funds, as there was a paper trail. Main comments from DOE – must we dismiss someone now for complementing someone Rourke – his mom took too long to complain, so it couldn’t have been that serious Bragin was reinstated and reported for duty at the end of July, but the parents locked him out the school and refused to budge. The fight to stop Bragin coming back to Merchiston continues in court for now, but the bigger picture is why is the DOE fighting to keep this obvious toxic human in the schooling system?

This story will speak to adults too, its about the bully in the office as much as the bully in the schooling system.

title: Kinematically Aligned Knee Arthroplasty
oneLiner: A groundbreaking new technique for knee replacement has been performed in an African-first surgery right here in Johannesburg, led by renowned surgeon Dr. Hannes Jonker.
summary:
The amazing results are already being shown with our first case study: Mr Schalk Burger (not the rugby one). [The three patients who have already undergone surgery will be at Lenmed MooiMed Private Hospital in Potchefstroom for checkups on Aug 7th.] One of the patients, Mr Schalk Burger, is a 58-year-old electrician (who goes up and down ladders all the time) from nearby Klerksdorp, Ottosdal, who has spent his life working on his knees. Before the surgery, he could barely walk due to severe pain in both knees, particularly his right knee, which was described as being bone-on-bone in his X-rays. He had to lean against objects for support and had a very low quality of life. Once an active individual who served in the army and played rugby, and was in agricultural college – all of which contributed to his knee problems. Burger found himself limited in movement, gained weight, and became depressed. Now, just a week post-surgery, he is already walking pain-free and feels as though he’s 23 again! He can hardly believe the transformation. Although he will need surgery on his left knee in a few weeks, this procedure has given him a second chance at life. Our other patient, Mr Andre Van Pletzen, is 56 years old and is a cinema, automation architect they make cinemas, and have a showroom in Kramerville, JHB... This job requires mobility, but Andre has struggled due to issues with his left knee. He can’t climb stairs, get on all fours, or perform daily tasks without difficulty. Van Pletzen is scheduled for surgery on August 7th, and we will be following his journey both before and after the procedure.

You might assume that when replacing body parts with implants, they should be aligned in a straight line—specifically in alignment with the hip, knee, and ankle (HKA alignment, both from the front and the side). This approach, known as mechanical alignment, has been the traditional method for implanting knee replacement prostheses. The idea was that this alignment would reduce stress on the knee, promoting the long-term durability of the implant. However, our bodies aren’t perfectly designed; individuals often have anatomical variations in their knees and surrounding ligaments due to normal wear and tear. Since 2019, the perspective on prosthesis implantation has shifted to a new philosophy called kinematic alignment, which has shown significantly better outcomes. This approach aligns the prosthetic with your body’s natural or native alignment—essentially reflecting how your body functioned when you were in your 20s and pre-arthritic. Kinematic alignment is a fresh perspective on implants and has been applied to other types of prosthetics, such as hip replacements. What is different in this ‘Africa first’ surgery is that it’s the first time an actual implant has been specifically designed and implemented (the SpheriKA prosthesis) around this innovative philosophy. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BGuGJSxpLoE “Kinematic Alignment (KA) is a technique designed to restore the knee to its pre-arthritic anatomical alignment. It focuses on customising replacement components to a patient’s unique anatomy, biomechanics and motion patterns, aiming to achieve more natural knee movement, better functional outcomes, improved range of motion and greater implant durability.” The first surgery in Africa using this prosthesis was performed by Dr Hannes Jonker last week. Dr Jonker faced considerable pushback from fellow orthopaedic surgeons when he began questioning the traditional method, with many dismissing him as misguided. However, as scientific evidence emerged, it became clear that the key lies in achieving better balance. Studies indicate that kinematic alignment can provide significantly more balance—sometimes doubling that of mechanical alignment—resulting in less pain and improved long-term outcomes for patients. He explains in the video how the prosthesis is curved allowing the patella to move more freely around the knee joint.
caseStudies: Hannes Jonker Schalk Burger Andre Van Pletzen

title: The Aboriginal Nation - a Khoi-san Scam
oneLiner: Tonight we show how people are being scammed into giving money to a so-called Khoisan Empress and her henchmen and women
summary:
In following up the story of the Khoisan ID allegedly provided to MK for padding their lists of signatures to get on to the ballot, I have stumbled upon a number of Khoisan Identity Scams where people claiming to lead the Khoisan target and exploit working class coloured people. It’s a hornet nest of competing interests. In particular, a Khoisan Grouping who have organised themselves around Queen Valerie Sabina Letsie 111, who they claim is an Empress of all Indigenous/Khoisan people, and her Ambassador, one Edgar Adams. They target people who they describe as so-called coloureds and help them believe that they are Khoisan/Aboriginals/First People and have the right to own all the wealth of South Africa. They have collected devotees through word of mouth and persuaded them through a whatsapp group to first pay for their Khoisan ID (which has not materialised) and also pool funds to start an Aboriginal Bank which will create wealth for all those with IDs. Through crude propaganda and a mixture of evangelical religion, they groom their followers and encourage them to donate. The admins of the whatsapp group delete all negative comments. They publish the amounts saved on the whatsapp group. In a few weeks they raised about R80k for their devotees, many of whom claim to be poor and battling to afford the R100. They have written a song that refutes their coloured status and reclaims them as an Aboriginal nation Queen Valerie Sabina Letsie 111 and her followers including her three handmaidens are marching on Parliament on the 30th of July which is Tuesday. She is actually from Durban and is in a wheelchair. They are in fact a splinter group off another Khoisan grouping led by so-called Dr Gregg Fick, who had been holding workshops around the country getting people to sign up for a Khoisan IDs, on the premises that they might get a part of a mult-million rand pay out in the Equality Court. He called his Group First Indigenous Nation of Southern Africa (FINSA). Fick is at war with an MK MP who calls himself is Kai Bi’a Glen Taaibosch, King of the Kei! who worked with him originally, but then apparently stole his Aboriginal ID database and gave it to Zuma to get on to the ballot paper. Taaibosch was working with Fick before he split and sided with Zuma. He calls his organisation F If this is sounding a bit crazy, it is. I have been sitting in the whatsapp group of the Empress Letsie the 111 since the elections. I have spent two hours with Gregg Fick, but he is not that keen to go on camera. However, he is eloquently on Facebook, and took time to rebut our Carte Blanche piece on Facebook. The crux of the story is that conmen and women are exploiting a sense of identity insecurity to persuade people to first hand over their personal details and secondly hand over cash, promising them future wealth which will not materialise. It’s a hoax.

This is an exclusive dive into a movement aimed at reviving the heritage of the Khoi and San which appears to have been hijacked by people interested in making money off poor coloured people. We join the dots to explain how the Khoisan ID came to South Africa and how people are manipulating a sense of identity to give people false hope of great wealth

title: There's a Kudu on My Stoep
oneLiner: Marloth Park - the bush veld holiday town shared by thousands of humans and wild animals. But there's nothing left to eat, and culling is illegal.
summary:
Marloth Park holds 4500 residential stands each measuring 1500 m2. In between the stands are parklands which are meant for grazing. But overpopulation and mismanagement of the wildlife means there is hardly anything for the animals to eat. In 2001 the Nkomazi Local Municipality took over Marloth Park. Since then there has been no Environmental Management Plan adopted or implemented by the NKLM. Unlike other wildlife estates, there is no special levy. Residents only pay normal and fairly low municipal rates. In 2015, NKLM (who employ a Conservation manager and 12 game rangers) began a culling programme, taking off hundreds of animals to relieve the situation. But the carcasses were taken to the Mauricedale Abattoir for processing, which is across the N4, the red line which denotes a foot & mouth area. The meat was then sold with the proceeds going to the Municipality. But meat cannot be traded across the red line. In 2016 the culling programme continued, with rangers hunting animals at night, between the houses, using spotlights. However, there were reports of bullets flying through windows and into walls, thereby endangering the residents. In 2017 the Marloth Park Ratepayers Association brought an urgent interdict to stop the culling between the houses as it is illegal to shoot in a residential area without good cause, it was dangerous and put lives and properties at risk. Since then there has been a population explosion, both in animals and humans, and the Municipality seems unable to enforce basic by-laws, never mind an EMP. Neighbouring reserves like Mjejane and Sabie Sands has offered to take impala etc off their hands but the Municipality regards the animals as their assets and they want to cash in on the meat. Currently the rangers are allowed to shoot sick or injured animals, and are also picking up animals that have died from starvation. The count is between 60 and 70 animals per month. Within Marloth Park is another game reserve called Lionspruit. A solution put forward has been to capture game in temporary bomas and transport them to Lionspruit for culling.

It's unique in the country: an enclosed suburb, a sunset to sunrise curfew, wild animals dependent on humans for feeding, and the local municipality the only managing authority. It seemed like a good idea at the time. In 1977 Marloth Park was established as a holiday town bordering the Kruger National Park. The animals could come and go as they pleased by simply crossing the Crocodile river. But years later, when foot & mouth disease and TB became a concern, veterinary services installed a fence, effectively capturing the game inside Marloth Park. Now, 47 years and 3800 home owners later, it's over-crowded, over-grazed and the animals are dying of starvation.

title: Cash For Days

summary:
It happens in two ways: ● those travelling via bus give touts or conductors a total of R400 (R300 is to bribe dodgy border officials and the R100 for the touts). ● Those travelling by foot put R300 in their passports and the immigration officers take it and give them a maximum of 90 days. It is so bad that conductors could have about 20 people in a bus whose have overstayed in the country or who simply need the full 90 days. All of them give the conductor money

title: THROW-FORWARD: Water tenders
oneLiner: Hailed as ground-breaking projects to supply long-needed water to Eastern Cape villages, one bulk water tender after another has fallen prey to delays, irregularities and allegations of corruption.
summary:
The R200 million Ntsonyani Dam project in Port St John was intended to supply water to 40 rural villages, but 3 years after its due date, it remains incomplete, with no end in sight. Yet the company that won the tender was paid more than 60% of the budget after completing only 30% of the work. And the same company continues to receive tenders for similar construction projects around the province, raking in substantial payments while leaving a trail of unfinished infrastructure and desperate communities behind it.

We uncover widespread corruption and irregularities in the awarding and construction of bulk water projects in the Eastern Cape, with exclusive access to tender documents and an investigation into the supplier's history of dubious dealings.

title: Global attack on Health care systems
summary:
The NHLS is an independent service which hospitals pay for, and the backbone of the health services. By shutting out the NHLS from its online system the hackers have denied 80% of the population access to their own medical records. South Africa has become an easy target for hackers with a series of major hacks in the last few years. Spending and updating security is money the Health Department has been reluctant to spend. Now although the labs are running, the tests have to be printed out and distributed on paper. Lab reports are normally automatically generated and sent to the doctors or made available on web view. But the hack has disabled this function. Doctors are spending hours on the phone trying to get urgent results – people simply cannot get through to the few phone lines that are being operated. If the laboratory is in the hospital, student doctors have to physically collect them – they say they are clocking up to 34km a day walking the corridors of a large hospital like Baragwanath. NHLS was a prime target for hackers because the stakes are so high, and spending money on security systems has not been a priority within State services. And state institutions have a policy of not responding to hijack threats and made no contact with the hacker, “Black Suit”. A week after the hack on Saturday 22 June, the hackers’ middleman contacted medical journalist Chris Bateman trying to get the NHLS to pay the ransom. “Over one terabyte of data can be released – or deleted,” was the threat made.

South Africa’s National Health Laboratory Service (NHLS) was hacked in a ransomware attack in late June, and doctors say it has thrown medical care back two decades to an era when computerised systems were still rudimentary by today’s standards. Global attacks on health care systems is on the rise, with 1163 facilities attack in Africa in the last year, and NHS and Irish health care systems have also been taken down taking months to rebuild and causing back logs in blood results of up to 6 months. Thousands of operations have had to be cancelled in South Africa. Doctors cannot access their patients’ histories, or get results from tests or biopsies performed in the last few weeks - 6.3 million blood tests would have been conducted since the attack. The knock-on effect is that hospitals which are already over-burdened are slowing down, unable to release patients because treatment is taking much longer. Outpatients have to keep returning to clinics because results are delayed. The fear is that critical illness will simply go untreated. As happened with Covid-19, the full extent will only be understood in six months’ time.
caseStudies: Jenni Nash Chris Bateman

title: Kgothatso Montjane : Wheelchair Wimbledon Champion
summary: Overview: This feature story will delve into the inspiring journey of three time Grand Slam Champion ,Kgothatso Montjane , a Limpopo-born wheelchair tennis player who has risen to the top ranks of the sport despite numerous challenges. Currently ranked number eight in the world in the women’s division, Montjane’s story is one of resilience, determination, and triumph. Story Angle: The narrative will highlight Montjane's early life struggles, her remarkable achievements in both dance and tennis, her contributions to her community, and her recent victory at Wimbledon. It will also touch upon her aspirations and the message she wishes to convey to the world about overcoming disabilities. Structure: 1. Introduction: The story will open with a powerful scene-setting introduction that captures the essence of Montjane's origins in Limpopo and her current status as a world-class athlete. 2. Early Life and Challenges: This section will provide a background on Montjane’s congenital deformity, the amputation of her foot at age 12, and her initial foray into competitive ballroom and Latin-American dance. 3. Discovering Tennis: The narrative will explore how Montjane was introduced to wheelchair tennis at Helen Franz Special School and how her teachers recognized her talent, leading to her representing the school in Johannesburg. 4. Rising Through the Ranks: The story will chronicle Montjane’s rise in the international wheelchair tennis circuit, including her participation in major tournaments like the Australian Open, Japan Open, NEC Singles Masters, and the Paralympics. 5. Unbeaten at Home and Giving Back: This section will focus on Montjane’s unbeaten streak on domestic courts for nine years and her philanthropic efforts through the Kgothatso Montjane Foundation, which provides sports facilities and equipment to disadvantaged communities. 6. Recent Victory and Future Aspirations: The feature will cover Montjane’s recent Wimbledon women’s doubles victory with Yui Kamiji, her preparation for the upcoming Paralympics, and her broader aspirations, including community projects and business ventures. 7. Conclusion: The story will conclude with Montjane’s reflections on her journey, the importance of hard work and dedication, and her message to people living with disabilities. Visuals and Interviews: Archival footage and photographs of Montjane’s early life, dance competitions, and tennis matches. Interviews with Montjane, her coaches, family members, and teachers from Helen Franz Special School. Coverage of her recent Wimbledon victory and homecoming celebration.

title: Counterfeit Joint OP
summary:
We're in the age of immediacy fuelled by an addicition to social media. People know what everyone is wearing, what they sleep on and in, what and where they are eating and what they are driving to get there. The pressure is on and fueled by a desperation to keep up with the jonses in these tough economic times - some consumers are willing to pay the least for cheap knock-offs. The counterfeit goods market has been labelled as the world’s fastest growing and most profitable industry and it’s reaching epidemic proportions. It's estimated to be between 7% and 10% of the world’s total trade. Due to it shipping routes, South Africa is one of the biggest markets on the continent as landlocked countries abuse it to move their counterfeit consignments. Research on the value of losses runs into the billions but is difficult to quantify because one cannot conclude that a counterfeit goods buyer would necessarily purchase the original.

A joint operation between the CIPC, SAPS, SARS and other brand protectors to combat the sale of counterfeit goods.
